## INTRODUCCIÓN — INTRODUCTION

[p. 5] The widely divergent orientation given by philosophers, artists, art critics, and scientists to the investigation of aesthetic value has engendered a great diversity of conceptions concerning the nature and limits of the discipline called Aesthetics—a term first employed by Baumgarten as the name of a special science devoted to the study of sensible phenomena, with the aim of ascertaining their norms and the application of these to the fine arts.

By Aesthetics, however, is generally understood the philosophical science whose end is the study of beauty, in its various forms, under its twofold aspect, subjective and objective. This study comprises the analysis and explanation of the nature and development of the emotion produced by the beautiful and the ugly, in their various degrees and shades; it examines the forms of our activity in artistic production and seeks to determine the constant characters of the beautiful and the ugly, subjectively and objectively, in Nature and in Art, so as to formulate precise conceptions of those characters and to fix the bases of aesthetic judgment.

«To signify, with precision, the nature of the beautiful; to circumscribe the confines of Art; to develop the phenomena of artistic representation; to observe the aesthetic phenomenon in the impression, in the feeling, and in the thought; to reveal the law or the idea that dominates and [p. 6] governs it; to follow it through the course of history and to give an exact account of its differences»: such, in Gallo's view, must be the task of aesthetic science in our time.

Without accepting the scientific criterion by which Gallo studies the philosophy of the beautiful, excluding the lofty problems it contains, the objects he attributes to Aesthetics are numerous enough to demonstrate its vast extension—embracing the whole of Nature, Art, and the life of man—and to make us grasp the complexity of its questions and the high interest they arouse at present, in view of the new artistic orientation imparted to Philosophy.

II. Philosophers do not agree as to the place this science occupies in the classification of human knowledge. Neither Plato nor Aristotle assigned a determinate place to the problem of the beautiful, which was posed with a metaphysical character and independently of the theory of art.

Aristotle, however, fixed the position of artistic activity in his classification of the sciences. For this philosopher, the sciences are classified according to the three manifestations of the intelligent being, namely: speculation, action, and creation. Hence the division of the sciences into theoretical sciences (mathematics, physics, metaphysics), practical sciences (ethics, economics, politics), and poetic sciences (poetics, rhetoric, dialectic). The first treat of the necessary, that is, of what does not depend on the will; the others, of the contingent, or, in other words, of what does depend on the will; but the poetic sciences have for their object works external to the will, whereas the practical sciences concern, on the contrary, the will itself.

Moreover, Aristotle established a precise hierarchy among these different sciences. [p. 7] Logically, the poetic sciences are subordinate to the practical sciences, because creation implies action. In their turn, the practical sciences are subordinate to the theoretical sciences: action demands, in effect, the conception of the intelligence. There is more: within the theoretical sciences there also exists a determinate hierarchy. Mathematics, which treats only of the measure of being, and physics, which sees only its motion, are subordinate to a higher science whose object is no longer being from a particular point of view, but being as being in itself, absolute being; this science is first philosophy, metaphysics. In this way the sciences constitute, as it were, an edifice whose parts are held in a precise order and of which metaphysics is the keystone.

After Aristotle, some have placed Aesthetics among the theoretical branches of knowledge and others among the practical, nor has there been wanting one who placed it within propaedeutics, the science that served as an introduction to Philosophy. Thus Baumgarten included it in Logic, a part of Propaedeutics, which Wolff, his master, called the key of science, or first science.

Bacon, Bentham, and Ampère assigned it different places in their systems for the classification of knowledge. Kant hesitated much over the position it should occupy, deciding to situate it in the critique of aesthetic judgment, midway between theoretical and practical philosophy. His disciples placed it among the theoretical sciences. For Schelling, Nature and Spirit—manifestations and fundamental forms of the absolute—constitute the content of two sciences: the Philosophy of Nature and Transcendental Philosophy, or the Philosophy of Spirit, a dualism that is only apparent, so that his system has a general aesthetic character. But, apart from that character, Schelling, in his system of transcendental Idealism, which contains only the philosophy of the [p. 8] human spirit, devoted an entire section to the fundamental propositions of the doctrine of Art. Holding that the product of Art depends on the opposition between conscious and unconscious activity, this philosopher placed Aesthetics among the practical branches of knowledge, as did his disciples, for whom the end of Art was to study objects of human activity.

Hegel, like Schelling, placed Aesthetics among the sciences that treat of the manifestation of the absolute or infinite of the human spirit. According to the idealists, man rises to the knowledge of God through Religion, through Art, and through Philosophy, though they disagree as to which of these manifestations is the first. Hegel divides this manifestation into three moments: 1st, Art; 2nd, Religion; 3rd, Philosophy; and he develops the aesthetic problem within his Philosophy of Spirit. The positivists, Comte and Spencer, in their systems of classification, have left aside literature and the arts, and even Philosophy. Comte, in his encyclopedic series, treated the aesthetic problem under Sociology. Spencer included it under Biology and Psychology. The positivists, his disciples, follow his example.

Even in contemporary times this uncertainty persists. Wundt subordinates to philosophical psychology the various domains that deal with the particular forms of the life of the spirit and with its general development in the history of humanity. These domains are chiefly those of Morality, of Art, and of Religion. Ethics and the Philosophy of law together, and Aesthetics and the Philosophy of Religion, form the three special parts of his Philosophy of spirit. Each of them relates the phenomena of the separate sciences to the general principles of Psychology, Logic, and Metaphysics.

Grasserie, Goblot, Trivero, and Croce, in their [p. 9] respective theories on the classification of knowledge, assign Aesthetics different places, this variety of criteria depending on the variety of philosophical systems and, above all, on that of the methods of investigation. Having psychology as its fundamental basis, Aesthetics, in the study of aesthetic pleasure, tends, like psychology, to enter into scientific organization; but, being at the same time under the necessity of finding a supreme principle that may serve as a criterion for taste, that may orient criticism toward a single objective and link the aesthetic problem with the other philosophical problems bearing on Nature and man, it penetrates also into the domains of pure philosophy. For this reason its position in the system of human knowledge is similar to that of Morality; because in Aesthetics, as in Morality, the dominant problem is that of freedom.

III. Aesthetics, it has been said, bears two characters that distinguish it and are peculiar to it: it is absolutely positive and completely disinterested; it is, moreover, the science that departs least from the real sphere and never withdraws from the spirit as it lives in society, and the one that bears most upon life. From this—from this complexity—derives its special position in the category of philosophical studies. It has need of them all for the solution of its problems; it is, as it were, their crowning; in it are reflected all the divergences the philosophical movement contains, and it profits from all the advances that science, like philosophy, achieves in the study of man and of Nature.

Aesthetics may therefore be regarded as an independent science, in course of formation, having Psychology and Sociology for its bases and whose principles link up with the problems of Metaphysics. In this sense the place Wundt assigns it in his classification of human knowledge is exact.

IV. [p. 10] The differing criteria by which Aesthetics has been placed in the general system of the sciences explain not only the complexity of the aesthetic problem and the vast compass of its terms, but also the relation this science bears to the others, especially to Biology, Psychology, and Sociology.

Since the subjective aesthetic phenomenon affects, at once, feeling, intelligence, and will, Aesthetics, in studying that phenomenon in its whole breadth, penetrates the domain of Psychology and is bound up with Logic and Morality. Its affinities with Psychology are of such a kind that Aesthetics has been regarded as a chapter of that science by all those who deny the existence of the beautiful as independent of the subjective phenomenon. Aesthetics has, in effect, Psychology for its principal foundation; but it is not pure psychology, as is believed, but a separate science, with its own ends and principles, which have moreover their root in the aesthetic observation of Nature and of Art.

Hence results the relation of Aesthetics to Biology and Sociology—the first the base, the second the crowning of psychological science—of which, again, it forms no part. For this reason Goblot has characterized the aesthetic phenomenon as a biological-psychological-sociological phenomenon in its total evolution, from the moment objective beauty impresses man until the work of art is produced and this exerts its social influence as a human product, destined to serve as a bond within humanity; a characterization that does not, however, explain aesthetic value, which is independent of Biology, Psychology, and Sociology.

In the philosophical order, Aesthetics also maintains relations with Logic and Morality. With Logic, through the common principle of order, and by comprising the pro[p. 11]blem of method and studying the aesthetic characters of science; and with Morality, chiefly through the common principle of freedom and, in practice, through its influence on the education of the will.

But Aesthetics is not related only to the various branches of subjective Philosophy; it is related also to the objective, or Metaphysics, in examining the fundamental critical problem of the value of our aesthetic knowledge and in rising to general, simple, and transcendental principles of the concept of the beautiful. The biological and psychological study of the beautiful is connected with the anthropological metaphysical problem; the study of the beautiful in Nature raises the spirit to the cosmological problem; the study of the beautiful in Art, to the problem of social solidarity. The very study of the beautiful in itself constitutes the metaphysical aesthetic problem, which is considered a problem of synthetic philosophy, or the philosophy of objective spirit, as Trivero designates it in his classification of the sciences.

Aesthetics, moreover, in examining the laws and conditions of the particular arts—in Architecture, Sculpture, Painting, Music, and Poetry—is related to Mechanics and Mathematics, Anatomy and Physiology, Optics and Acoustics, Metrics and Philology, which offer art their teachings.

As sources of inspiration, the kingdoms of Nature enter into Aesthetic Physics, which for that reason, and because of the study Aesthetics makes of their laws in the inorganic and organic kingdoms, has direct relations with the Natural Sciences—though the naturalist and the aesthetician study created beings from different points of view and with distinct, if harmonious, ends.

As the foundation of Art and as charged with interpreting the ideals of humanity in the analysis of its [p. 12] works of art, Aesthetics maintains close relations with the social and historical Sciences, which set out to find the laws of the social order and to establish those of human progress through time. The History of art is a necessary complement of all history, and the Philosophy of the history of Art—that is, the determination of the laws that have presided over the production of works of art—is an essential part of the philosophy of history, or of general sociology; only that Aesthetics and History study and appraise the development of Art in time in different ways, the former with respect to the principles of the beautiful, the latter in relation to individual and social progress, to its civilizing influence. No history, says Ménard, reveals better than that of Art how great is the action that peoples, like individuals, can exert upon their destiny. Another lesson to be drawn from this study, in relation to the philosophy of history, is that it helps us to understand the relations that exist between the morality of peoples and their civilization, of which their art is the highest expression.

V. All that has been set forth already demonstrates the importance of the study of Aesthetics and the difficulties proper to its problems. Aesthetics has the importance and excellence of all philosophical studies. To these belongs, says Soriano Sánchez, the study of the psychic world, of its laws and of the manifestations of its affective, intellectual, and volitional activity, in its individual and collective development; and, in general, to philosophy pertains the reflective and synthetic conception of all things.

Hence, even though some believe that philosophical studies are remote from reality, they are, nonetheless, the ones that embrace it most through their character of generality and that penetrate it most deeply; for there is nothing more intimate in reality, or of greater [p. 13] importance, than human consciousness, thought, and activity, governing the moral world and the physical world as well. Of the same character, importance, and moment partakes Aesthetics, too, in the field in which it unfolds. «An order of ideas and feelings that awakens in the spirit the most intense, varied, noble, expansive, and fellow-feeling emotions; that peoples the intelligence with images, with forms, with harmony and irresistible expression; that, in deep and suggestive associations, provokes in the soul lofty, generous, disinterested, most pure ideas and feelings; that draws back for us, in one of its most secret and ample parts, the veil of reality, directly kindling inspiration and taking hold of genius, so as to penetrate, together with it, the regions of the sublime; and that studies, in short, man as creator, producing a whole world of beauty, full of life and variety—a science that thus profoundly enters into the spirit and dignifies human nature is, assuredly, of the greatest importance.»

As a study of practical application, Aesthetics has equal value. It elevates the feelings, develops the ideas, ennobles the conscience, and invigorates and impels to activity along paths of higher perfection. «The man who loves and understands beauty and its laws of harmony—adds the same Soriano Sánchez—hates instinctively and irresistibly disorder and moral disturbance. Aesthetic education is a great force of moralization. Thinkers who believe they foresee the ruin of the religions strive anxiously to establish a nucleus of moral power in the education and the cult of beauty. Eminent psychologists, sociologists, and philosophers who, alarmed by the sad spectacle of division and even of hatred presented by the clashing [p. 14] interests of men, wish to create bonds of sympathy and solidarity among them, seek in aesthetic education, in art, the ties of union and support for that strange humanity shaken by grave contradictions. Historians and sociologists who desire to understand the spirit of the ancient and modern civilizations, who endeavor to point out in them what is characteristic, spontaneous, intuitive, intimate, need also to investigate in human art the first key of the problem.»

Aesthetics, as a philosophical science, has, then, the importance of widening the horizon of our ideas and of offering new data for the solution of the complex problems of psychology, morality, and metaphysics. As a science of application, it is a teaching not only of solidarity but, still more, of freedom; and it has, besides, the special importance of serving as the foundation of the study of the fine arts, fixing the principles to which they must submit and satisfying the needs of the imagination and of feeling in the appreciation and criticism of works of art.

VI. The task of this science is not easy, however. The complexity of the aesthetic problem; the lofty social import of its principles; the rudimentary state of the sciences that form its experimental basis; the discredit into which have fallen the metaphysical doctrines that gave it laws in the old philosophy; the fragmentary character of the scientific studies of contemporary positivist aesthetics; the profound division of the philosophical doctrines from which Aesthetics may draw the elements for its theories and criticisms; the superior importance of artistic studies over the purely philosophical ones in this science—all these make the aesthetic problem present serious difficulties: not only by reason of quality, but also by reason of the insufficiency of data for the formation of [p. 15] great syntheses to serve as a basis for aesthetic science. This same difficulty is presented by all the philosophical sciences that find themselves in a period of crisis and of reorganization.

For this reason, too, the disagreement among aestheticians begins as soon as it is a matter of fixing the method to be followed in the investigations of this science. This problem of method is capital, not only in Aesthetics but in the sciences that serve as its basis, such as psychology and sociology. Confining ourselves to the first, which is the more essential, Rauh, in his analysis of the psychological method for the study of the feelings—after analyzing the physical method, which regards feeling as an organic phenomenon; the physico-mechanical method, which regards it as a phenomenon of consciousness; the physico-chemical, which regards it as an intellectual phenomenon; and the voluntarist theory, or the principle of the tendency toward being—concludes by asserting «that scientific psychological theories are simply means of interpretation or explanation, usable according to the case, and that the task of the psychologist must be to observe the facts, to join to the observations some empirical laws, ceaselessly corrected, and then to join to those laws opinions rather than theories; because science has the phenomenon for its limit and seeks not unity but foresight and action; and to foresee and to act it is often necessary to use extraneous means». But not even science itself is content today with the empiricism Rauh attributes to it; rather it tends to seek unity. Philosophy seeks it too, and, to attain it, is content sometimes with probable or possible experience, and at other times rises to a higher, metaphysical or moral, certitude—but always passing beyond the phenomenon. Lalo is right, therefore, in condemning induction, to which science claims to restrict itself, as the exclusive method of aesthetic investigation.

[p. 16] If the purely empirical method, regarded as scientific or positive, cannot directly furnish us principles with the generality and unity of philosophical principles, the purely rational or ontological method is, likewise, insufficient to explain the nature of the aesthetic phenomenon. The first fixing its attention rather on the form of beauty, and the second attending especially to its essence—the former inducing the principles and rules for the study of aesthetic works, and the latter rising immediately to the idea of the beautiful in order to formulate universal principles of aesthetic judgment—, neither is the one able to grasp art in its generality, nor does the other, keeping to the sphere of the ideal, know how to make itself concrete to the various particular arts so as to appreciate, in each of their productions, those principles.

Aesthetics, a science at once real and ideal, speculative and practical, demands, consequently, the employment of induction and of deduction, of analysis and of synthesis, of the empirical-rational procedure. The end of Aesthetics is not the knowledge of the psychological phenomenon exclusively, but the determination of the principles that are to norm aesthetic judgment; hence the necessity of completing the experience of aesthetic phenomena—acquired through the study of their present state and of their evolutionary genesis—with the establishment of principles that only philosophy can form, by means of generalizations effected by reason in the field of that experience.

The aesthetician Lalo, who regards Aesthetics as a Philosophy of art criticism—a synthesis of art criticism, of the history of Art, and of philosophical aesthetics—has occupied himself extensively with this question of method, giving it such importance that its problems are for him the most fundamental.

[p. 17] The method of Aesthetics, says Lalo, must be deductive and inductive at the same time. «The deductive method, in isolation, aspires to give aesthetic laws the function not of ascertaining what is, but of proposing what ought to be; not of studying the real, but of formulating an ideal. But an a priori explanation of those laws runs the risk of being completely abstract and, in the end, verbal; such an ideal being highly arbitrary, because, not having been drawn from the phenomena, it refers to them only in the measure in which the theorist has contrived to be unfaithful to his own principles.»

«This explains—adds Lalo—the reaction brought about by the experimental aesthetics of Fechner, which is founded on three inductive methods: the aesthetic association of ideas, statistics, and the general spirit of his system itself, which inaugurated the so-called aesthetics from below. Only that Fechner himself acknowledged a certain usefulness in the deductive aesthetics of the “above,” as a control upon the experimental one, even while he regarded it as a mere complement, very premature and dangerous if made exclusive.»

Positive investigation presupposes, according to Lalo, three factors at once: prior observations, a guiding idea—whether generalization or hypothesis—and a verification of this in experience; factors that in turn depend on the personal temperament of the scholar, on the degree of advancement of the science, and on the more or less concrete nature of the object: variable conditions that necessarily produce a certain degree of uncertainty in the science, as happens in contemporary Aesthetics. The guiding idea, placed between the phenomena that suggest it and those that verify it, is the deductive aspect of the method according to this conception; it is obtained by induction and then serves as the basis for deduction.

[p. 18] Lalo regards as closely bound up with the foregoing methodological problem the question whether the method of Aesthetics ought to be metaphysical or positive. The metaphysical method is the deductive one in isolation, and the positive the inductive, which cannot be applied separately. The true relations of Metaphysics to Aesthetics ought to be none other than those of Metaphysics to every other possible kind of knowledge. Science is the domain of verified hypotheses; Philosophy, in the broad sense of the word, that of hypotheses logically verifiable but not yet scientifically verified; Metaphysics, that of unverifiable hypotheses.

Metaphysical reflection ought not, then, to precede aesthetic facts any more than it precedes those of another order; rather it ought to follow them. It is absurd to wish that sensible beauties should derive from a supposed «beauty in itself,» which would be a principle independent of every thinking subject; for all beauty is a value, and there is no value outside a valuing consciousness. If there are no facts in themselves, still less is there «value in itself,» adds Lalo—who does not thereby claim to reject all metaphysical speculation in Aesthetics, but rather to place it after experience and upon it.

Lalo next examines the problem of the integral or fragmentary method in aesthetic science; that is, whether specialization is at present required in it. He recognizes the drawbacks of every excessive specialization, which breaks the unity of criterion; but he admits also the great importance of a clear knowledge of a group of special phenomena. Aesthetics can and should be monographic; but it must always be regarded as such—as incomplete and provisional. It cannot, however, methodically propose to be fragmentary. It must accept every occasion of suggestion or of verification; it must admit every hypothesis [p. 19] that leads to an investigation; but these various methods must complete one another reciprocally and collaborate in common; each is a necessary moment of integral aesthetics, which is evidently no more than an ideal—but an ideal that it is good to keep present in our mind so as to make its course clear.

Lalo rejects the exclusivism of the various methods, which interpenetrate and assist one another reciprocally as partial points of view, integrated in the measure in which synthesis is accessible at each moment of the evolution.

For the rest, these false problems of method transfer the question onto points common to all the moral sciences and in no way special to Aesthetics. The method a given aesthetician or art critic follows depends essentially on the conception he forms of a fundamental notion: that of aesthetic value. The three great problems of method, for Lalo, are those bearing on the existence and formation of this value, on its capacity to be generalized or not, and on its autonomous or heteronomous character. It matters little how they are treated—whether by induction or deduction, in detail or as a whole, by metaphysical hypotheses or by facts—; all these procedures of general method always reduce to three moments common to all experimental reasoning, which it is useless to keep in question under their abstract form.

For Lalo the true methods are a part of the investigation itself; they are not given before it, but are realized along with it, since they are no more separable from it than is the direction of the movement from that movement itself. The method of a science is nothing but the direction of its movement, if the living science is that very movement. Now, if we set aside the sterile negations, the artificial or ill-[p. 20]posed questions, and the general considerations that are common to all kinds of possible study, the true problem of aesthetic method is, for Lalo, the problem of aesthetic value, which he subdivides into three others.

The first inquires whether there really exist for the aesthetician values, or only facts; in other terms, whether his study limits itself to ascertaining and explaining what is, or whether it goes so far as to judge and appraise it according to some conception of what ought to be—whether it goes so far as to measure reality against an ideal. In a word, it seeks to know whether this study ought to be theoretical, speculative, and descriptive, or else normative and regulative, or imperative. Such is the problem of value properly so called.

In the second place, once it is admitted that values of art do indeed exist, one asks whether those values are individual and subjective, or else impersonal and objective; whether Aesthetics is the science of art, or merely a work of art about art. Such is the problem of impressionism and of dogmatism.

Lastly, it is a matter of knowing whether, values existing that are not arbitrary, they are specific to Art, or whether they can be fixed only in relation to other, non-aesthetic values; that is, whether Art is autonomous, or dependent on and subordinate to other human phenomena; whether, just as one ordinarily judges the true and the good in themselves and without reference to the beautiful, one may judge the beautiful without submitting it to the criteria of Science or of Morality; whether aesthetic values, being relative like all possible values, are above all relative to one another, or else relative to other, more external data; whether they are of an intrinsic or an extrinsic relativity; whether Art has its principal end, its measure, and its criterion within itself or outside itself. Such is the question of Art for Art's sake.

[p. 21] For Lalo these three problems are essential, and essential only, in aesthetic method; because they correspond, within its domain, to the three great elements of all experimental reasoning: the facts that suggest the law, the hypothesis suggested, and the new facts that verify it. To what facts should the aesthetician turn by preference, so that they may suggest to him the most fruitful hypotheses? To theoretical ascertainments and explanations, or to normative judgments? And then, will they be phenomena of beauty or of ugliness, natural or artistic? Such is the first problem. Will these hypotheses be general and objective laws, or only individual, arbitrary, and subjective imaginings? Such is the second problem. Lastly, which will be the phenomena best suited to these hypotheses of values in order to verify them? Must this confirmation be sought outside art itself, or within it—in the other arts, in Science, in Morality, or in Metaphysics? Such is the third essential problem.

These three problems mark, for Lalo, the three necessary moments of aesthetic method, which impose themselves upon one another reciprocally and whose specific characters realize, within that domain, the three necessary moments of every method. On the solution of these three problems depends the whole conception of modern Aesthetics and of modern Art Criticism; for, if Aesthetics is not reduced in its entirety to a Philosophy of art criticism, at least all that is essential and positive in it must be reduced to that philosophy, and all the rest is nothing but the application of those principles or the generalization of those facts.

There is no doubt that the three problems posed by Lalo are essential to Aesthetics; but it is doubtful whether they have the character of methodological problems, in the sense attributed to method in Logic. They are prior problems, which mark the direction that [p. 22] is to be given to aesthetic investigations; but the solution of those very problems imposes a method upon thought. Moreover, the question of aesthetic value entails that of knowing whether there exists an aesthetic experience distinct from the other social experiences, whether there is an autonomous aesthetic phenomenon that explains itself; and this question may be resolved either by a metaphysical method, characterizing the phenomenon by an a priori principle, or by appealing to internal and external observation alone—and that already requires a method. Furthermore, it matters to know whether a hypothesis suggested by the facts must be formulated, or whether that guiding idea is inseparable from all scientific observation. The knowledge of the nature of the aesthetic phenomenon—in order to affirm whether it is a pure fact, or a value, or both; whether it is purely subjective, or objective, or subjective-objective; autonomous or heteronomous—may be obtained by the positive way or the metaphysical, or by both united; that is, by induction or deduction, or by both means simultaneously. The Aesthetics prior to Fechner followed the speculative way, proceeding by deduction, after intuitively acquiring the essential principle. With Fechner a reaction is effected throughout psychology and, consequently, in Aesthetics. Positivism aspires to reduce this science to the same function as the empirical sciences of Nature, giving to induction the principal, if not the sole, role in the method of scientific investigation—without succeeding in explaining aesthetic value. Aesthetics and the other sciences of its kind having been converted into philosophical sciences, speculation was joined to pure experience, and the inductive method fulfilled the aim of preparing the application of the deductive or philosophical one. Such is the direction adopted by the aestheticians—psychologists and philosophers—of contemporary times.

[p. 23] Following that method, Aesthetics must begin its study by determining the nature of the aesthetic phenomenon in consciousness, which offers an immediate experience and one of the greatest certitude.

## LA CONCIENCIA ESTÉTICA — THE AESTHETIC CONSCIOUSNESS

### I. LA TEORÍA DE LA ARMONÍA — I. THE THEORY OF HARMONY

[p. 24] Psychological, or subjective, aesthetics has for its object the study of the aesthetic phenomenon in consciousness—as feeling or emotion, as idea, and as the product of volitional activity. The affective phase is the one that presents itself most prominently in psychological investigation, even though it lacks the clarity offered by the perceptive aspect and the importance that the function of the will has in the genesis of the aesthetic consciousness. For this reason it is fitting to begin this study with the analysis of aesthetic feeling, or emotion.

The subjective aesthetic phenomenon has been studied with a view either to its modality or to its finality. Those who have considered it from the first point of view have made harmony the essential thing in aesthetic feeling, leaving aside its end. This definition of aesthetic pleasure by harmony is the most ancient and the one that serves as the foundation of classical aesthetics. The role played by the idea of harmony, or order, in Hellenic philosophy is well known.<sup>1</sup> That idea dominates affective psychology. For Plato, true and durable pleasure is the pleasure of reason in possession of truth and the good. Pure or unmixed pleasures—those relating to knowledge and to the beauty of figures, of colors, and of sounds—always have, in themselves, a certain measure and a limit, which depend on reason. Pleasure itself is a harmony, and pain a dissolution; the state of [p. 25] equilibrium produces a kind of existence nearer to the divine life, superior to the variations of the sensibility. What constitutes true pleasure is not intensity, but quality. That same character is found in Platonic love. Reason and love are, for Plato, one and the same power, at once divine and human, intermediary between the sensible and the intelligible, bond of Earth and of Heaven. Love is the ordering dialectic.

<sup>1</sup> See my exposition on the ideas of order and freedom in the history of human thought.

This principle of harmony prevails also in Aristotelian philosophy. Grandeur and order constitute beauty, as they do all perfection. The intelligence is that ordering power which, in giving matter a form, produces the works of art we call beautiful. Aristotle exalts the ordering function of human reason. His dominant idea is that of order, of fitness, of harmony, of beauty. Right reason, regulative, without being properly speaking imperative, is man himself knowing himself, such as he is, in the truth of his nature.

Form is the expression of order in Nature, as in Art; it is order in itself, which Aristotle regarded as eternal. The free thought of the artist creates the aesthetic order, as the divine thought creates the universal order, penetrating all reality. The finality of form for form's sake enters into both. The end, as the principle of movement in art, is so too in artistic Nature, because that end is the beautiful, desired by reality. God is the absolute and eternally desirable, because he is the absolute and eternally beautiful. Universal finality thus becomes aesthetic finality. The contemplative life of the sage is the germ of that divinity, to which Aristotle rises by induction. In that life, which expresses artistic contemplation in the classical world, [p. 26] logical feeling constitutes the essence and the ground of aesthetic feeling. Sage and artist are merged in the same pleasure, and the aesthetic order and the logical order are the same thing.

That static ideal of harmony or of equilibrium, proper to classical civilization, in being realized in Nature or in Art, produces aesthetic pleasure, which is thus defined by harmony, even without consideration of the end that the one or the other pursues. Considered in respect of their respective finality, aesthetic pleasure is always harmony between the activity and the end; it is fitness of ends and means, which likewise expresses a harmony.

The definition of aesthetic feeling by harmony has persisted down to our own days, notwithstanding the transformations undergone by the philosophical systems and the advanced investigations in the psychological domain. The affective factor has been subordinated to the cognitive or rational one, from which the ordering power is derived. The persistence of intellectualism has perpetuated that definition.

Thus Paulhan recognizes in aesthetic emotion, as its character, its being a system, a harmony. According to this philosopher, what is common to all works of art is to offer a system of linked parts; what there is in common in all aesthetic emotions is, precisely, the particular feeling that certain particular conditions make us experience: the representation, the acquisition, or the penetration into us of a system of linked parts or, more simply, of a system.

Aesthetic feeling is, properly speaking—says Paulhan—that which makes us experience a subjective systematization, which may have absolutely no scientific value, but which presents itself to us with enough vividness or force that our [p. 27] spirit takes pleasure in receiving and contemplating it. Aesthetic emotion, consequently, besides being disinterested, is inspired by a system; it is itself a harmony of sensible and intellectual elements. To feel in an aesthetic manner is, then, to comprehend a whole and to be moved by this comprehension.

Moreover—Paulhan adds—aesthetic emotion has this particular feature, that it is due to a complex excitation, highly systematized, arrested, by its weakness, at the point where the tendency created by the excitation gives birth to phenomena of sensation and of intelligence. In this Paulhan confirms Spencer. For him, the particular character of aesthetic emotion is that the object of admiration is considered in itself and for itself, and not in relation to other objects. The tendency toward the positive act does not exist.

But aesthetic emotion is, above all, intellectual, and is accompanied by the highest operations of the spirit. It is produced—says Paulhan—by the comprehension and the intellectual contemplation of a system, of a harmonious whole of elements of any kind.

This character of intellectuality separates this theory from the biological one, adopted by Spencer and the physiologists, who give greater importance to the biological element.

Fouillée likewise recognizes in aesthetic emotion that intellectual character. For him, aesthetic emotions are bound to the very nature of our sensibility and to its relations with our other faculties. In aesthetic feelings we feel in order to feel, rather than in order to comprehend or to act; but a pleasure that is in no way intellectualized and that does not take on the character of intellectual enjoyment is not an aesthetic pleasure. Aesthetic emotion is the most immaterial and the most intellectual of human emotions, says Guyau as well.

According to Ribot, all forms of pleasure are joined to organic modifications. In its origin, pleasure is physical, bound to a sensation; but afterward it becomes an anticipation, a presentative-representative state, as Spencer says, and later still it appears joined to pure representations and to pure concepts, like the pleasures of artistic creation.

Fechner distinguishes, in his analysis of the elements of the beautiful, the direct factor, sensation, and the indirect or associated factor, the idea evoked and associated: factors that only logical analysis separates.

The intelligence perceives a harmony, which imprints on feeling the aesthetic form: such is the basis of the theories that give predominance to the intellectual factor in the composition of the aesthetic phenomenon.

Guyau believes that aesthetic emotion realizes, besides, a sociological harmony through its tendency toward association. Aesthetic emotion, he says, is a prolongation, a kind of resonance of sensation in our whole consciousness, above all in our intelligence and in our will. Artistic emotion is, in the last analysis, social emotion, which makes us experience a life analogous to our own and united to our own by the artist. To the direct pleasure of agreeable sensations is added all the pleasure we draw from the sympathetic stimulus of our life in society with the imaginary beings evoked by the artist. According to this theory, all the arts, at bottom, are no more than manifold ways of condensing individual emotion in order to make it social, in a certain manner. Fiction is joined, finally, to expression, to multiply to infinity the contagious power of emotions and of ideas. Aesthetic emotion is, then, essentially social, according to Guyau. In its form of artistic activi[p. 29]ty, it has, for Guyau, the property of enlarging individual life, merging it with a more extensive and universal life, thus making of individual harmony a social harmony.

This harmony, regarded as essential in aesthetic emotion—thus active and communicative—is not, however, directed toward a useful end, even if only that of putting all spirits in harmony, associating them in a common ideal. For intellectualist philosophy, aesthetic emotion is contemplative only, and such is its proper modality.

Thus, for Brunschvicg, who vividly describes the harmony of the aesthetic consciousness, the aesthetic life is the work of ideas, the result of the rational contemplation of harmony. The tendencies, in this description, are ideas that are prolonged in us; freedom consists in finding, within ourselves, the reason of our decision, and reason is the faculty of unity. It engenders harmony, in which the aesthetic life rejoices in immanent freedom, in that negative freedom of equilibrium, which produces the serenity of the spirit and engenders the classical ideal.

The aesthetic theories that make disinterestedness the essential character of the subjective aesthetic phenomenon consider it from the point of view of its finality, as an activity that is realized completely in the aesthetic consciousness or that is externalized in artistic forms. Kant's aesthetics defines the pleasure of the beautiful in the first sense. According to the Critique of Judgment, a representation is aesthetic when it is not bound to a determinate concept of the object, but there dominates in it the pleasure «that springs from the free play of our cognitive faculties, without any special purpose». Then the finality, or harmony, that we suppose in Nature lacks any positive en[p. 30]d; it is a finality without an end. Only the representation of finality can be aesthetic, insofar as it is formal and subjective, insofar as it is harmonious with our faculties, leaving aside the material element of the representation. The aesthetic judgment thus turns out to be a judgment of pleasure or of pain, but always a manner of knowing.

This definition of aesthetic feeling, notwithstanding its finalist foundation, is a definition by the harmony between the cognitive faculties, which in Kantian psychology represent variety and unity respectively, and it may be referred back to the traditional definition.

When finality is appraised in relation to artistic forms, the examination of aesthetic emotion is reduced almost solely to the one produced by Art, the feeling of the beautiful being confounded with artistic taste—from which some contemporary psychologists separate it, such as Piazzi, for whom aesthetic feeling penetrates only in part into artistic enjoyment, as an impression of common life, with the character of utility and by association.

But if the intellectualist doctrine of harmony explains the aesthetic phenomenon in that moment of wholly joyous contemplation, in which the intellectual factor predominates, it does not explain the one that follows it in its evolution and is the precursor of artistic creation: a moment of upheaval and of struggle, often painful, that ends with the bringing forth of the work of art and in which the will characterizes the aesthetic phenomenon. It is not, then, freedom in its immanent form that constitutes the essence of the subjectively beautiful, but freedom in its most active and fruitful form. A contemporary aesthetician has developed this intellectualist doctrine of the aesthetic consciousness: Lalo.

### II. LA TEORÍA DE LA EINFÜHLUNG — II. THE THEORY OF EINFÜHLUNG

[p. 31] Harmony explains, in part, aesthetic value, but it does not explain it completely, and it includes values that are not aesthetic. All romantic art, which expresses the disharmonies of an inner struggle, remains outside that explanation; and, on the other hand, the moral harmonies contained in the common or ordinary acts of life do not enter the aesthetic domain.

Moreover, it is not known whether it is the knowledge of harmony, its mere representation, that constitutes aesthetic value, arousing a feeling of pleasure; or whether, on the contrary, it is the feeling of interior harmony that gives aesthetic value to the representation. In the first case it is a matter of an objective value, and in the second, of a subjective one. How is the operation of those two harmonies to be verified, if neither of them explains aesthetic value?

That fusion, that identification, is effected by EINFÜHLUNG, according to the partisans of contemporary sentimentalism. This notion signifies a kind of sympathy, of projection of our self into objects, of objectification of our affective life, of identification of subject and object by means of feeling. When the objectified state of the soul is more profound, when it is, in sum, the feeling of our self, of our whole personality, that we lend to the represented object, then our thought becomes aesthetic: such is Einfühlung, according to Lalo.<sup>1</sup>

<sup>1</sup> See Contemporary Psychological Aesthetics in the first course of Aesthetics.

Thus, for the new sentimentalism, all aesthetic principles and all aesthetic phenomena can be reduced, more or less directly, to the identification of our [p. 32] Self with objects; they are but diverse forms of this fundamental function of the spirit, or, at least, they presuppose it.

The ultimate content of this fundamental operation is, at bottom, nothing other than expression; it is more still, it is the ensemble of the inner state, or the manner of being of the inner attitude, from which emanates each of the acts of the will and of the attitude of the self; or, more briefly, it consists in the personality that the self sees in the perceived object, with which it identifies its affective states.

The feeling of beauty is, in a general way, a feeling of life; it is the feeling of pleasure we derive from force, from plenitude, from inner harmony, or from the freedom of vital possibilities or realities; it is also the feeling of pleasure that arises from spreading, without obstacles, our own vitality outside ourselves. What is in question here is the life and the vital expansion of the personality, or of the psychic—not the organic—individual. The feeling of bodily well-being is not aesthetic except as a variety of the current of psychological life. This free expansion of life is the realization of the ends of every individuality: it is an enjoyment of self.

All value is born of man or is made by man; it resides, then, in life or in the conditions of life. We have an immediate consciousness of aesthetic value; it is the intuition of a reality that passes beyond the sounds or the forms. The characteristic of aesthetic feeling is its depth: depth in the object thought, depth in the thinking subject. For this reason it is in no way assimilable to any sensible pleasure whatever, such as taste or sound. The agreeable, always superficial, is in no way a criterion of beauty. All beauty is the symbol of a personal life and of an expansion of our life. Affective sta[p. 33]tes, in a general way, are manners of being of the feeling of the self, and the fundamental feeling par excellence is the feeling of psychic life: it is Einfühlung, the common foundation of all feeling of beauty.

It is, then, inexact to attribute to any one part of the affective life a marked predominance over the others; what comes into play in Einfühlung is our whole personality. It is an anthropomorphism, an aesthetic personification. Einfühlung, says Volkelt, is a special and irreducible faculty.

When from the affective life one removes all that is organic sensation, memory, indeterminate and free representation, processes of thought, pleasure and displeasure, there remain—says Volkelt—two original and fundamental faculties or functions. First, the will, the tendency to produce, to realize—an immediate datum of consciousness, which does not allow itself to be reduced to any simpler form. Next, the affective function, original and specific to consciousness, which does not coincide in any way with the function of pleasure or displeasure—a particular sensation of special nerves—but is the immediate consciousness of ourselves. All affective movements are, in the last analysis, manners of being of the personal feeling. Even the feelings of participation in the life of others, or of self-renunciation, are but varieties of the feeling of self. What is understood by affective function is not the thought or the obsession of oneself, the vision of what is within one, the order and the finalist combination of our capacities and states; those are forms of self-consciousness, characterized rather by the dominion of the intelligence and of the will. What Volkelt calls the affec[p. 34]tive function is much more elemental, more obscure, more conformed to nature; it is the vital feeling of the Self, it is the Self, in its unity of consciousness, enclosed, so to speak, in an obscure matrix. That feeling of the self, that immediate intuition of living one's own vitality, cannot be understood as a mere sum of certain things, such as sensations of our organs and sensible feelings of pleasure or displeasure.

It is true that there exist principles, general forms of aesthetics; but all the formal laws of our sensations remain abstract. In the aesthetic object, the sensible is always the symbol of a spiritual content, is animated or spiritualized. Only thus does it become an aesthetic object and acquire a value.

### III. CRÍTICA DE LA TEORÍA DE LA EINFÜHLUNG — III. CRITIQUE OF THE THEORY OF EINFÜHLUNG

[p. 35] Lalo, combating this theory of Einfühlung, sees in it the predilection for losing oneself in a vague pantheism, which is found in innumerable manifestations of German aesthetics; he denies that the aesthetic character of the thought of the critic or amateur is in proportion to the intensity with which he experiences the same emotions as the being represented; he affirms that the colder the critic or amateur, the more master of himself he is; that it accords ill with the facts to take the intensity of the projection of the self, or of the feelings, as the measure of aesthetic value, just as it does to take the intensity of any pleasure whatever as the rule of beauty; and that, consequently, the incontestable psychological phenomenon that is invoked is, on the contrary, as an aesthetic phenomenon, highly objectionable.

According to Lalo, the specific character of the aesthetic phenomenon does not lie in the feelings it evokes—for these are found everywhere—but in the existence of a technique to which this thought is applied; that is what would determine artistic criticism, to which Lalo confines himself, because art is, incontestably, the highest manifestation of aesthetic thought, the notion of natural beauty being more confused.

Lalo attributes to the hypothesis of Einfühlung no other importance than that of permitting a more acute analysis of the aesthetic phenomenon; but one that has the disadvantage of giving an obscure explanation and that is worth only as much [p. 36] as the aesthetician who makes the analysis is worth. That inner imitation, which supposes no model; that symbol which represents no one but the one who thinks it; that externalization of our sensibility, which creates in us a new sensibility of which we would not be capable without it; that exaltation and that depth of the affective life, which exclude the most exalted and most profound impulsions of the sensible life, such as those of the sexual instinct, and which is produced even when it is physiologically impossible, as when men are reproached with experiencing feminine feelings and women wholly masculine impulses; that identity, in short, in which the two terms are at once distinguished and opposed, and which is so reciprocal that in the result there ought to remain nothing of its own in either of the two beings, although it be the supreme exaltation of their individuality—all that, says Lalo, is the eternal «I know not what,» charged with explaining all the facts for want of a better explanation; but for the psychologist it is no more than the sign of an insufficiency of analysis, and for the logician an insufficiency of explanation.

If the notion of Einfühlung, from the two points of view of aesthetic and psychological value, is indeterminate and little specific, it has no more value for its philosophical consequences. So it would result from the examination of these three problems, which offer here a dogmatic interest: the relations of feeling with representation, the existence of a «feeling of possibility,» and, lastly, the irreducibility of the feeling of the self.

Aesthetic representations, according to Volkelt, are impregnated with feelings, are akin to affective states to the point of being confounded with them. Only thus is the predominance of feeling that distinguishes the aesthetic attitude possible. But, seen close up, this resem[p. 37]blance of representative and affective states reduces, in Lalo's view, to a higher degree of confusion or of obscurity in the aesthetic representations. With this approximation of feeling to the intellectual states, the problem becomes insoluble, since one does not understand why aesthetic feeling is a psychological entity irreducible to every effort of the intelligence.

The certitude of the possibility of exercising each of our faculties, supposed in Einfühlung according to Volkelt, is not for Lalo a better-defined datum; rather, it remains voluntarily indefinable. This certitude of power, which constitutes the ground of the problem of psychological freedom and which the mystical spiritualism of Bergson has introduced in our days, Lalo rejects as a datum inaccessible to scientific analysis. The philosopher cannot see in Einfühlung, therefore, anything but a first step toward mysticism, opposed to all rational and scientific explanation.

But, considering only the aesthetic consequences of that doctrine, which reduces criticism to an operation so personal and so rebellious to analysis, Lalo condemns it as ineffective. An aesthetics that did not manage to establish precepts or norms is a contradiction in terms, says Volkelt himself; consequently, Einfühlung is one, because, reducing the aesthetic phenomenon to an interior contemplation, it does not lead to a normative knowledge.

The hypothesis of Einfühlung, which does not stimulate positive analysis, leads logically to mysticism, which is of a nature opposed to the subjective aesthetic phenomenon; a phenomenon which, even though it is constituted by an exterior perception that is an illusion, we have practical reasons for maintaining and aesthetic reasons for attributing to it feelings that exist only in us. Those practical rea[p. 38]sons constitute, above all, the presence of one of the multiple needs of our activity, and those aesthetic reasons constitute, above all, the presence of a «technique».

In the two cases, the mechanism of objectification or of illusion is, if not identical, analogous. In the two cases, its necessary—if not sufficient—condition is the presence of a powerful motive of suggestion. We believe real the states of consciousness destined normally to remain ideal, or vice versa, whenever a lively impulsion leads us to that result.

Now, that motive, when it is a matter of common life, is any tendency whatever, and the feeling that corresponds to it is, then, one of the banal forms of signification or of sympathy, in the etymological sense of the word: instinctive sympathy. But when it is a matter of the aesthetic life, the impulse that leads us to that illusion is, above all, the pressure exerted upon our consciousness by that ensemble of collective conventions and habits, which vary in the course of the evolution and which Lalo calls the technique. By this we understand, he says, the exigencies of our individual, physiological, and psychological nature—oriented, directed, disciplined, and rendered obligatory, in a certain way, by our taste, in virtue of the supreme authority of the social milieu.

Where this technique exists, Einfühlung can be produced with an aesthetic character; but where our consciousness does not feel itself obliged by the technique, this interpretation is not produced at all, or has no aesthetic value, in Lalo's view.

For the vulgar, the contagion of the feelings whose manifestations are represented constitutes very [p. 39] often, no doubt, the principal criterion of beauty, entering into the very vast genus of interpretations of a practical and utilitarian order, which form almost all our perceptions, according to the analysis made by pragmatism; but that contagion cannot serve as an artistic criterion.

Consequently, for Lalo, the essential problem of aesthetics is not resolved by Einfühlung—which is an unaesthetic and banal fact, of interpretation or of perception—but by the individual and, above all, collective conditions that make certain explanations aesthetic and others unaesthetic. Modern aesthetics can be nothing but a philosophical reflection upon the principles and results acquired by the criticism of art, just as philosophy, in its entirety, is nothing but a reflection upon the most definitive data of our science.

The new aesthetic sentimentalism, like the Scottish solution of the problem of external perception, invokes a special and irreducible faculty, setting aside the essential point of the question—namely, the knowing under what conditions we tend to objectify our states of consciousness and under what conditions we are loath to do so. Those conditions are of a utilitarian order when it is a matter of perception, and of a technical order when it is a matter of aesthetic interpretation. If one accepts this positing of the terms of the problem, aesthetic Einfühlung is an effect and not a cause, is the accompaniment, not the essence, of the true facts it studies. Now, the essential phenomenon in aesthetic activity is this cause—namely, aesthetic thought, the technique special to art—and not this operation, banal and unaesthetic in itself, which is made to consist in the externalization of an emotion. To make it aesthetic, it will be surrounded with a multitude of diverse shades, destined to differen[p. 40]tiate it from all the other forms of the affective life; but the first of those shades is the presence of a technique historically constituted, collectively accepted, or even «obligatory,» since it is sanctioned by opinion, by admiration or failure, of which the consciousness of the artist or of the amateur always preserves the intimate feeling.

For this reason the multiplicity of the functions of this aesthetic thought has forged multiple interpretations of those «technical» states of mind, making them real-ideal, as when the musician forgets the true sounds of an orchestra so as to hear them only as an interior and spontaneous music; or else making them symbolic, almost real, as happens in the works of the plastic arts and in the literary arts, in which the triumph seems to consist in carrying the illusion as far as hallucination.

Einfühlung acts upon us as every intense suggestion can act upon every state of consciousness. The suggestion of feelings does not, then, exercise at all a monopoly in the aesthetic consciousness. To Lalo, this double-effect interpretation seems secondary and in no way proper to aesthetics; on the contrary, the collective influence of the technique seems to him capital.

Now, the study of this influence is, in great part, objective, like the study of every collective form of thought. For this reason Lalo believes that the exclusively subjectivist tendency of the new sentimentalism is the opposite of the true aesthetic science.

Lalo includes in the critique of aesthetic subjectivism what he calls its mystical form, to which aesthetic vitalism leads. Aesthetic vitalism is the form, confused par excellence, of sentimentalism; it is the aesthetics of [p. 41] intuition. The first consequence of aesthetic mysticism is that everything is beautiful; the second is that, inversely, every man who possesses this state of profound thought can, by right, equally relish all beauties: consequences absolutely opposed to the facts; the last consequence is the arbitrary.

For Lalo, a mystical theory is a work of art and not a work of science; because mysticism, which is not repelled by internal contradiction—that triumph of irrationality—escapes all rational criticism; it places itself deliberately beyond the true and the false; so that one can say that to adopt it or to reject it is not so much a question of truth or of error, or even of probability, as a question of taste. Now, one may relish mysticism greatly as a personal attitude, as a motive for reverie, as a provisional anticipation of truths that surpass all our science; but consider it very little as an explanation in the domains where it is already possible to do work of science.

Thus, setting out from the idea of sympathy or of objectification of the feelings, one arrives necessarily, according to Lalo, at the theory of life, and from there one slides imperceptibly into mysticism. These three tendencies are bound together. They are the three normal phases of sentimentalism in its internal development. The aesthetics of feeling, when it is logical with itself, comes to disguise and even to deny the facts it ought to explain.

Mysticism, for Lalo, is the tendency that consists in distrusting reason and in substituting for its methodical analyses a belief without proof. Whether it be called psychological and reflective intuition, the free activity of a will capable of determining itself without motives, or supernatural revelation, it is some act of faith or other, once it is proved to be irrational—that is, confused and rebellious to analysis.

### IV. LA TEORÍA CIENTÍFICA DE LALO — IV. LALO'S SCIENTIFIC THEORY

[p. 42] The point of view chosen by Lalo for analyzing the subjective aesthetic phenomenon is that of thought. According to him, neither sentimentalism nor mysticism has perceived the exact and manifold role of feeling in the aesthetic life, because they are more concerned to lead it to the absolute, at all costs, than to observe impartially its various forms. On the other hand, intellectualism—which claims to explain the concrete facts of psychological life by eliminating, as far as possible, the affective forms they take on, so as to consider only their intellectual aspect—is no less insufficient.

In order to define the legitimate and very considerable part that affective phenomena play in every activity, without falling into exaggerations or superstitious depreciations, Lalo analyzes them by distributing them into diverse groups, which correspond to well-defined functions.

He thus distinguishes three great species of feelings at play in the aesthetic consciousness—that is, three principal «moments» in aesthetic thought. Among the affective states, some are the causes, others the accessory accompaniments, and others, finally, the effects of the aesthetic attitude.

The affective states that are effects of the contemplation of the beautiful can be gathered into a single word: aesthetic pleasure. These agreeable feelings are al[p. 43]ways found in each of our judgments upon beauty, and for this reason some theorists have claimed to define beauty by pleasure—taking the part for the whole, or the effect for the cause, and betraying a deficient analysis of the idea of the beautiful and that of the agreeable.

Those effects of the state of the aesthetic consciousness, or those feelings of aesthetic pleasure, reduce to three principal ones, which Lalo designates by these three words: admiration, sympathy, and vitality.

Admiration is the feeling of a superiority, founded upon a judgment of value; it is a synthesis of comprehension and of subordination, of possession and of desire, in which neither of the two terms ever prevails completely over the other; for which reason the agreeable predominates in it, even when it reveals our impotence to equal or to comprehend fully the masterpieces, and even in the moments when it truly transports us, in spite of ourselves. Admiration is the beginning of love, or at least of a certain species of love. Carried to great extremes, it is the intellectual intoxication of superior spirits; it is the enthusiasm that puts the exceptional phenomena of inspiration within reach of everyone and makes us share for an instant the transport of genius.

This feeling, as soon as it analyzes itself, is formulated by a judgment of value. For that it suffices that it become a little more distinct and that it be associated, in some degree, in conscious reflection, with reasons that justify it. This judgment of value is a positive affirmation of beauty or a negative qualification of ugliness, according as the impression—without being neutral, that is, unaesthetic—succeeds or not. Beauty recognized is success or glory. Ugliness arouses a disdain or a censure that, in the aesthetic order, is frequently tinged with the ridiculous.

Under its positive form, this feeling of admiration is the universal seal of all satisfaction of aesthetic tendencies. It is more or less intuitive and spontaneous, or more or less reflective. It is always the effect and not the cause of the aesthetic impression.

In the state of aesthetic contemplation, alongside admiration we commonly experience another affective state, very different in its nature, though it develops parallel with it, being also a result and not a cause. Such is sympathy, by which we relate ourselves to the author or to the public in whose feelings we participate.

We sympathize with the author if the work seems to us beautiful. His thought seems to us, then, a kind of ideal toward which we rise and in which we commune with him, not without complacency toward ourselves. We remain mocking, on the contrary, or even hostile, if the work seems to us mediocre or bad and the thought that created it inspires in us, above all, a pity that the very secret complacency at the superiority of our judgment or of our taste does not fail to accompany. So that, positive or negative, the aesthetic judgment is, in a certain measure, an agreeable triumph of our personality.

We sympathize with the public when our feelings are in unison with theirs, be it a praise or a censure. For this contagion to be produced, it suffices that there be identity between the judgments of value we hold and those we see pronounced, or that we divine, in an imaginary milieu. This common judgment may also be positive or negative.

There is, finally, a third order of effects of aesthetic activity. It is the feeling of a growth of our vital energy, which is but the continuation of [p. 45] that feeling of an easy and spontaneous activity that fills our spirit—an exaltation that seems to us, rather than provoked, to have arisen freely from our own nature, as if our natural spontaneity had been amplified beyond measure, all at once, under the magic action of art.

Many synonyms can express this indefinite irradiation of a source of intense energy throughout our whole being; and the theorists have multiplied them at pleasure, calling it spontaneity of life, harmonious play of faculties, expansion of our personality, free development of the creative imagination; but none of those formulas exhausts it; all only approximate it. We are in the presence of one of those cases of general diffusion of activity, such as is produced in every powerful excitation when it acts upon an organism prepared to receive it by the accumulation of reserves of energy, which ask only to be spent along the lines of least resistance. Now, such is the case for every man in a state of true aesthetic contemplation, because this state of higher concentration is not realized, nor is it realizable, at every instant of our life, since it supposes an enthusiasm, a favorable attitude, a somewhat exceptional predisposition of our consciousness, a privileged orientation of our mental synthesis.

Lalo believes that these incontestable phenomena contain the greater part of the truth, and that they express, in their way, the mystical aesthetics of life or the sensualist aesthetics of pleasure—these theories having taken, as the essence of the beautiful, an effect of concrete aesthetic activity, and even one of the least characteristic effects, because it belongs indistinctly to a multitude of its manifestations. Thus, for example, a purely [p. 46] moral, or purely religious, or patriotic emotion irradiates as much and takes hold of us as powerfully and profoundly as any impression whatever of beauty.

Moreover, admiration, sympathy, and vitality are three names that sum up numerous very complex phenomena and a thousand different shades. Admiration—the first of the passions and the mother of the others, according to Descartes—expresses the personal reaction of the thinking subject upon the object thought, which is here translated by a judgment of value. Sympathy is but the affective reaction of thinking subjects, the one upon the others. The increase of vitality, finally, represents the reaction of the whole of our being upon each partial impression; that is, the irradiation of the two preceding phenomena and of all aesthetic activity throughout our organism and our consciousness.

From this analysis Lalo deduces two conclusions.

First of all, the three feelings described are not special to art. With multiple and changing shades, they are found also outside it. They could not, then, characterize its proper nature. In effect, admiration, like pleasure, does not define the aesthetic state either. Like beauty, and sometimes more than it, one admires strength and even health, luck and skill, merit, purity, grandeur, or, as one says by metaphor, moral beauty. Not everything that is admired is aesthetic. Not everything that seems to us superior and exerts upon us an attraction or a pressure is always directed to our aesthetic consciousness.

As for sympathy, with all its derivatives, it is much more evident still that it offers nothing particular to the beautiful. Many symbols have only a moral, social, or religious value.

Lastly, the excess of energy that the aesthetic attitude procures for us is but a particular case of the general excitation caused in us by every pleasure and even by every strong impression whatever.

In other terms, those three effects of aesthetic activity may be also effects of our non-aesthetic activities; other, more characteristic elements, which condition them, permit us to qualify them aesthetically.

In the second place, these feelings are not produced, when we contemplate a beautiful work, without the development of an aesthetic activity properly so called; or, what is the same thing, those affective states do not arise from the category of the beautiful except when there is supposed in them a pre-existing aesthetic thought, which alone permits us to qualify them from that point of view when it conditions them, but whose nature and origin are independent of them.

Lalo concludes this analysis by characterizing as aesthetic sensualism this explanation of the aesthetic phenomenon by the feelings indicated, as an explanation founded solely upon the idea of pleasure. In his view, it is incomplete and, above all, superficial.

Lalo next studies a second category of feelings aroused by aesthetic activity, no longer as effects but as accessories, as accompaniments of aesthetic thought. He calls these states of the soul unaesthetic, because they are neither beautiful nor ugly. These common, or in themselves unaesthetic, feelings become aesthetic only by their accidental combination with a multitude of other conditions foreign to their physiological and psychological nature. But, in virtue of a characteristic illusion, it seems as if they were, many times, the essential thing in art; and it is, above all, to experience them that the great, little-[p. 48]educated public seeks aesthetic impressions—because these are, very frequently for it, no more than stimulants, suggestions of unaesthetic emotions, mere occasions apt to favor other impressions more intense for it and which, at bottom, are the only ones capable of interesting it.

Lalo finds here too the three great characteristic reactions of the affective life, which he sums up in these three terms: the personal attitude, the affective contagion, and the general conception of life.

One may call feeling of personal attitude—says Lalo—the reaction that we oppose accessorily to aesthetic impressions and that, in fact, always accompanies them, in virtue of the complex constitution of our character or of our personality. A multitude of unaesthetic elements intervene, then, here: temperament, habits, associations of ideas and the actual content of the memory, moral ideal or religious convictions, scientific knowledge, and so many others besides. Their reflection comes, inevitably, to color, in its own way, our contemplation and to impose on it a dominant tint.

This personal reaction is the one that all the unaesthetic elements oppose to aesthetic spectacles—elements that tend to give to the objects of our thought values: personal values of the agreeable or of interest, religious, moral, political values.

It is very difficult for the aesthetician, the amateur, or the professional critic to abstract from those elements of partiality, by means of which art is so often confounded with morality or politics, and from which unjust conflicts frequently arise.

These parasitic feelings are a small matter in true and pure aesthetic activity; but alongside these wholly personal and essentially subjective feelings there come to be placed very different states—so different that Volkelt himself has proposed to call them, as if by antiphrasis, objective feelings. Such are the states of soul that we attribute to the beings, or even to the things, represented in works of art, when these express their outward signs; we acquire them by contagion and they become ours. Our Self is merged, for an instant, with that of another; it substitutes itself for him or for the one we symbolically attribute to him. One recognizes almost the Einfühlung of the modern Germans.

Nothing more real and more important in life than this operation of the spirit, which Lalo calls more simply suggestion, expression, or better, contagion of emotions—which is the contrary of a personal attitude, because it is, so to speak, a foreign attitude, a state taken from our fellows, many times in spite of ourselves, and which arouses frequent conflicts.

This unison of multiple states, which we take from others, is very different from the contempt or the pity that we personally feel for them. This sympathy, in the etymological sense of the word—this symbolic identification, this psychological vibration by influence—we experience stronger and surer with our fellows, and it acts in two opposite directions, like every strong suggestion, because it makes the beautiful images that represent objects seem real, and the products of art that represent nothing seem unreal. This contagion is not produced only between the one who loves art and the beautiful objects, but also between the artist and the public. Nothing more contagious and imperative than collective emotion.

Just as this other, unaesthetic sympathy is associated with aesthetic sympathy, so to the feeling of vitality that results from the emotion of the beautiful there corresponds a general conception [p. 50] of life and of the world, which frequently accompanies it, but which never constitutes its essence and which is but the echo, an indefinite irradiation, of the two feelings analyzed above.

Nevertheless, Lalo remarks that one of the pretensions of metaphysical aesthetics and, in particular, of the principal German aestheticians of the nineteenth century, is to refer all beauty and, chiefly, all sublimity to an impression of the infinite, to a judgment upon life and the world, to an identification of our being and of things with an absolute Spirit.

Under more or less vague forms—says Lalo—it is an axiom of all German metaphysical aesthetics that in the least emotion of beauty we find a total intuition of the world and of the true essence of all things, as if in every artist or every amateur there were a pantheist unaware of himself.

Reducing these excessive pretensions to true phenomena, Lalo finds that we rarely come away from the contemplation of a great work of art or of a great beauty of nature without obtaining from it an impression so profound that it irradiates beyond measure and that we very normally extend to the whole of our knowledge: a diffuse irradiation, which lacks all precision and which the author of the work of art directs and desires. But this individual and optional interpretation remains foreign to the work of art.

From this second analysis Lalo deduces: that those accessory feelings are not proportioned to the aesthe[p. 51]tic character of the thought they accompany; that they do not exist, or are plainly arbitrary, in certain cases in which that aesthetic character of our thought is, nevertheless, certain—for example, in the purest forms of absolute music, such as the orchestral symphony—; that they are, then, unaesthetic accessories, however natural and however important they may be in the whole of our activity, and that they are disproportionate to the beauty of the impressions they escort.
