The intensity of our personal reaction, of the contagion, or of the irradiation of our feelings, if it is very great, disturbs the contemplation of our consciousness and diverts it from the true aesthetic point of view; so that it is, many times, inversely proportional to the intensity of our impression of beauty properly so called.

The depth of feeling that one believes to find in many works is simply sincerity—that is, the conviction and the aesthetic probity of the artist. Pure contagion, the Einfühlung that we imagine ourselves to experience, is evidently but an arbitrary imagining, an ad libitum play of our spirit, which amuses itself in divining what it does not know, what it cannot penetrate, and which is always content with little expenditure when its curiosity is at play. Lastly, since there are never two identical beings in the world; since the consciousness of the individualities foreign to us, and even of those most like us, remains, in reality, impenetrable to us, every contagion of this kind is, at bottom, an illusion.

This illusion is much more apparent still in aesthetic contagion than in any other. It is said, in effect, that aesthetic sympathy differs from physical or moral sympathy in that it is symbolic, feigned, imaginary—that is, that it rests upon states that we lend so[p. 52]lely to beings or objects, whereas the others rest upon real states. But a sympathy that is symbolic—that is, whose contagious character we ourselves create—is no longer a sympathy; to sympathize one must be two, and here we sympathize only with ourselves. There is there, if you will, an activity of our creative imagination, stimulated by a suggestion, that is, by a strong impression; but Lalo believes that the phenomenon of sympathy is improper for expressing the essence of the aesthetic phenomenon; which does not mean that it is absent—far from it, for it is everywhere—but that it is improper because it contains something more and something less than the aesthetic phenomenon, because it is always something else. This marks, in his view, the true importance of Einfühlung in aesthetics: that it is very real, but very restricted.

As much should be said of all the other accompaniments of our thought; their supposed necessity is but an illusion. It may be useful, surely, but not necessary, to have a personal attitude or a religious opinion in order to appreciate the beauty of a work; but that adds nothing to aesthetic emotion—on the contrary. Nor is it necessary to form a positive conception of life, of the world, and of the infinite apropos of every sensation of beauty.

All the feelings examined above, in order to have the right to be qualified aesthetically, presuppose, then, according to Lalo, an aesthetic thought, of a wholly special nature, which grounds them and which gives them a value of art by its presence.

### V. LA TEORÍA CIENTÍFICA DE LALO (CONTINUACIÓN) — V. LALO'S SCIENTIFIC THEORY (CONTINUED)

[p. 53] For Lalo, the states of soul truly characteristic of the beautiful are those he calls technical feelings, because they all suppose the immediate intuition of that ensemble of means of action, accepted by a collectivity that evolves in time and in space, less through individuals and by chance than in groups and according to laws; in a word, that organized form which imposes itself on the aesthetic consciousness of each one as a social imperative, and which one may call, extending the usual sense of the word, the technique.

Lalo calls them feelings only because they are confused thoughts, sensations, habits, or impulses; but their content, under its intuitive form, is, for the most part, of an intellectual and experimental order.

Aesthetic feelings properly so called are, then, for this writer, hardly feelings; or, in other terms, what characterizes, in the last analysis, aesthetic activity—notwithstanding sentimentalism and mysticism—are not feelings, in the usual sense of the word, such as love, pity, anger, but rather manners of thinking in which sensible experience and intellectual elements predominate, but which have taken on in the long run an almost entirely intuitive appearance; which have incorporated themselves closely into our personality, in virtue of all the [p. 54] habitual processes that normally produce the inseparable association and the fusion of our representations; which impose themselves, at last, upon our individual consciousness as an imperative ideal, as a discipline superior to us, in virtue of their social origin. All that they have of the sentimental, in the proper sense of the word, is their intuitive and confused character, which is acquired; which is not absolutely irreducible and mysterious; which is but a complex by its origins and its composition.

Taking as the type of the aesthetic attitude the contemplation of the work of art, as its most finished form, Lalo sums up the affective relations that are established between the work and us under the names of feelings of aesthetic play; he calls feelings of technical superiority those by which the work unites the author with his public; and, finally, he names feelings of harmony the diffuse states of soul that the internal and external relations we perceive in the work, and in the aesthetic milieu in which it is presented to us, awaken in us.

Occupying himself with the feelings of aesthetic play, born of the relations between the work and the spirit that contemplates it, Lalo believes it necessary to make precise this notion of play, introduced by Kant, Schiller, and Spencer into the aesthetic domain.

Many metaphysicians and romantics have claimed to designate by that notion an absolute freedom, a creation of our imagination, in the rigorous sense of the word to create: an almost divine, irreducible faculty, participating in the absolute, rendered all-powerful by art and forging for itself a world of its own, through creative fiction, outside and above the laws of this world.

Lalo rejects this concept, because beauty does not exist in nature as an empire within an empire; because, however elevated it be supposed, it is, on the [p. 55] contrary, very human, and if it does indeed surpass our mediocre individuality, it is, above all, by what it adds of the social—which is a very different thing.

On the other hand, empiricist observations have seen in play nothing but the expenditure of an excess of force or, in the inverse sense, an acquisition of force—two processes opposed in appearance, which are perhaps not incompatible—; or, finally, a very necessary and very interested apprenticeship, in the child, of the future instincts of the adult, and, in the latter, a useful repetition, an idling of his serious activities. All these theories have their part of truth, and each applies very exactly to certain games, if not to all; but all neglect, to excess, one of the essential parts of human play: the convention of a rule, of a discipline.

For Lalo, there are in aesthetic play—and one finds in certain games properly so called—three essential elements: a luxury, a discipline, and an illusion. Hence three fundamental feelings that, under certain conditions, become aesthetic; their triple combination appears only in the contemplation of the beautiful, so that it is its characteristic.

Experience shows that play is, at once, free and disinterested and, on the other hand, disciplined and regulated and subject to a sanction. Play is also an illusion, which involves the ordinary mechanism of all mental suggestions—one that goes on reinforcing itself, systematically, as it extends in the spirit, unless other, stronger impressions come to arrest it in its spontaneous progress.

Play resembles, then, art, or certain forms of art; it merges imperceptibly into them, and we find in it, with diverse characteristics, the same constitutive elements.

Thus, art supposes a positive feeling of illusion; it supposes in us a contradiction, repugnant to pure logical thought—a voluntary illusion, a self-conscious deception. There is a logic of the feelings, a logic of the will, perhaps also a social logic, which are not the logic of the intelligence and in which there dominate the idea of value and of finality, not those of causality or of contradiction or of identity. There is also, if the word be permitted, an aesthetic logic, which is not the logic of Aristotle and of Stuart Mill. It is not the logic of truth; it is a logic of illusion, which has its methods and its laws like the other—less strict, no doubt, but no less imperative or less normative.

Now, an illusion tends to be produced whenever a very strong representation comes to oppose the impression of sensible reality, without finding in it a sufficient counterweight. These two species of force, successively, balance or supplant one another reciprocally.

In art, the force that thus comes to counterbalance sensible reality is the feeling of a technique, which is produced only where an aesthetic illusion exists. It is, then, the influence of the technique—according to Lalo—that replaces the influence of reality and imposes the aesthetic illusion.

The technique is like a language, which becomes in the aesthetic consciousness of the artist what the mother tongue is for common thought. And just as we always think with words, even when we remain mute, and with that inner language that never abandons us, so likewise every impression of beauty enters into those acquired forms of our aesthetic thought, which have become, in fact, its inseparable conditions.

If every impression of art implies a conscious and voluntary illusion about the nature of its object, it supposes also a feeling of luxury. By luxury is understood an expenditure of excess, in view of our own enjoyment: an expenditure of money, of physical force, of mental activity—it matters little—provided that it be a surplus held in reserve and not an indispensable consumption. Moreover, an enjoyment egoistic in principle, like every enjoyment, but which may be natural or moral.

In this ensemble of excesses, Lalo distinguishes three principal shades: luxury properly so called, as the inferior form; play; and art.

Play is a luxury emancipated from the slavery of the inferior pleasures—that is, illusion is essential to it, and it proposes to itself as immediate ends, in place of those pleasures, a certain number of higher functions, and, moreover, ones difficult to reduce to unity.

Art is a superior luxury, nearer to moral than to physical activity, and characterized, above all, by a much more complex organization and one less arbitrary in its conventions, more penetrated, at once, with individuality and with tradition, and for that very reason more amply human. The aesthetic attitude—says Groos—is the state of mind of a holiday; it implies a feeling of exception, of happy freedom, a relief on emerging from serious and obligatory activity. The aesthetic attitude is contemplative; it demands self-possession, which is a repose, and the consciousness of a superfluity of forces to be spent.

This is better proved by the manifestations of art than by those of natural beauty. It is true that there are professionals of art, as of play; but the professional himself has the feeling of art or of play only in the more or less spaced-out moments in [p. 58] which he can procure for himself the feeling of an activity of luxury in the midst of his obligatory work.

Aesthetic activity remains, as a whole, useless for the utilitarian struggle for life, apart from the original and passing one of an apprenticeship of great social activities. For the rest, though useless, it is precisely, in that case too, an excess, which belongs only to the undifferentiated and much-mixed forms of primitive art.

For this reason there is not, according to Lalo, a religious art, nor a moral art, nor an industrial art, but an art that associates itself with religion, with morality, with mechanical labor, and that lives under their custody until the day when it is art that will have custody of them: a precarious protection or collaboration, for the rest, and dangerous for both.

The contemplation of the beautiful, at the same time that it is a luxury, is a discipline. It is indeed the synthesis of those two notions that, in Lalo's view, characterizes its principal social function. From that superior point of view, art is, above all, the discipline of luxury.

This word may surprise those who are accustomed to regard art as the domain, par excellence, of freedom—the only one even, as has been said, in which we are truly free. Lalo finds no opposition between these ideas of freedom and discipline, since all freedom reduces to obeying a consented discipline, in which the inner parts of our nature are submitted to higher laws.

All beauty is an ideal, and to conceive an ideal is, by definition, to feel obliged to attain it, to realize it insofar as it is in us, because such is the state of soul of one who lives under its law. In reality, a feeling of discipline is observed wherever a scale of values establishes the consciousness of a human superiori[p. 59]ty and, consequently, of an imperative, of a practical rule for action, of a normal law whose application or violation is accompanied by more or less determinate sanctions, as in the moral conscience. Now, it is easy to see that, in fact, so long as we are not under the influence of our aesthetic consciousness, we feel a true obligation to seek beauty and a true repulsion at producing or enduring the ugly. This does not mean confounding aesthetic obligation with moral obligation. Morality aspires to dominate the whole of life and to present its laws as absolute, whereas aesthetics is, on the contrary, wholly relative—so that one may say that art is the morality of luxury, because it is the only thing that saves it from egoism and makes it excusable, by giving it a social function.

Art has, then, its obligations and its discipline too, as the artist has his aesthetic virtues. The artist has not only his probity or his impurity, his more or less lofty consciousness of a mission that goes beyond his mere craft, but his work involves sanctions, morally and materially very important, and in which the confused feeling enters as an integral part into the state of mind of every man who has an aesthetic thought. The outward manifestations of that permanent content of the collective consciousness are success or failure, admiration, censure, or ridicule.

The three shades of the feeling of aesthetic play—illusion, play, and discipline—being thus analyzed, Lalo examines what he calls feelings of technical superiority, which are born of the moral relations existing between the author and his public—sympathy or antipathy, as results of aesthetic thought—and, as accessories of this same thought, contagion and a substitution, as stimulants of the consciousness.

When one analyzes any work of fine art whatever—says Lalo—one finds, as an irreducible residue, the feeling that one could not have done anything better with the same technical procedures. Hence that feeling of the absolute, of the finished, of the perfect, of the definitive, that takes hold of us when we are possessed by the contemplation of a masterpiece. This feeling of superiority in the technical order implies, above all, change—that is, evolution, personality, life. Stagnation, pure and simple repetition, or the mechanical copying of models, with which luxury may, at most, content itself, are sleep or even death.

But by technical superiority one must not understand a purely material richness, exactitude, or skill. True technique comprises, besides the material means, their intelligent employment, their adaptation to the circumstances. Into it one must put life—that is, flexibility together with adaptation. The supposed «personality,» of which the essence of art has been made, is but a superior manner of understanding the technique, of incarnating it in oneself, of identifying with it one's activity and one's thought. For this reason we call more personal than another the work of a superior technique, and for this reason too it is inimi[p. 61]table and unique; it will perhaps be surpassed, but not repeated, because the technique of art is like a living being whose evolution is never entirely identical with itself; its law is movement; from the moment it stops, it ceases to exist. Herein lies why, in the artist, it is, so to speak, the «technical personality» that alone interests us; his feelings interest art only in the measure in which they influence the technique. In sum: if the conception of technical superiority is ordinarily confused, it is not, according to Lalo, because it involves the special and specially inviolable mysteries of genius and of personality, but only because a more detailed analysis must be reserved for the art critic, charged with establishing, apropos of each particular work, the exact shades.

The work of art, or the beautiful object, presents itself, moreover, necessarily, to our thought as an ensemble of relations, interior and exterior, whose complexity goes on to infinity. Thus, the confused thought of those relations implies the most complex feeling of all those that compose the aesthetic consciousness. It is, in a general way, a feeling of harmony, which may be considered from two principal points of view, because these relations are simultaneous or successive. Lalo studies it by considering it in its technical character.

The harmony that the parts of a beautiful work maintain among themselves has frequently been presented as the principle of all beauty. Leibniz defined it as the perception of unity in multiplicity. Unfortunately, the disciples of Leibniz add also that it belongs to all our perceptions, and it is by that principle that they define, in general, thought or ideas and, by its degrees, all the degrees and even all the possible forms of consciousness; because each state of consciousness is a diversity of elements gathered in a synthesis, and all our ideas can be subordinated regularly, going from the most obscure and most confused to the clearest, to the most distinct, to the most adequate. In this universal hierarchy, beauty is, then, characterized only by this paradoxical property of being the greatest unity but at the same time the most confused, since it is essentially sensible and of the greatest multiplicity of parts. It is thus that the simple proportion 4 : 5 : 6, clearly conceived by the spirit under its mathematical form, [p. 62] has no beauty; but perceived confusedly by the ear under the form of a sonorous relation, it constitutes the beauty of the perfect chord, the basis of all musical harmony. The beautiful would be, then, the greatest confusion compatible with the greatest unity. The intellectualist conception thus defines beauty like all the other forms of thought, with this sole peculiarity, that the relations of the whole with its parts have there an inexplicable mystery. It is—says Lalo—to resolve an enigma with a contradiction.

One also speaks frequently of a harmony of form with matter; but one never well knows what this form and this matter are. Their definition and their relations are very arbitrary; one does not know where the one begins and the other ends, nor what it is that unites them while they are separate, nor what distinguishes them while they are united. The defect of all these conceptions is that of not setting out from true aesthetic phenomena—that is, from art—when they are willing to consent to set out from phenomena.

If one wishes to define with more precision the specific character of beautiful perceptions, one must say that this harmony is the harmony of elements of a technique, which resides in the rational use of those pre-established elements, which makes them yield the most they can give. Now, it is on this question of harmony that the theorists have permitted themselves to take the principles of science with the greatest partiality. Choosing arbitrarily, in the series of the sciences, the one that seems to them the most instructive or the most representative for the aesthetician, some consider this harmony, like the Pythagoreans and the Leibnizians, under the mathematical form of a simple relation; others, like Helmholtz, under the physiological aspect of a good state of our sensory organs; [p. 63] finally, the greater number conceive it as a complex psychological phenomenon, a harmony of our states of consciousness or, more generally, a mutual accord of all our faculties.

Lalo imputes to the greater part of the theorists the error of keeping to one only of those points of view and of believing that the principle of the beautiful is, necessarily, single and simple, when, in reality, it is diverse and complex, as the functions of art are manifold, each of the elements indicated having its role in the harmony necessary to all. But to these diverse elements, placed in the order of decreasing abstraction, must be added the most concrete of all and, on that account, the most important, since it must come to crown all the others and presupposes or contains them all: such is the sociological factor, by which is explained the collective formation of a technique, which imposes itself upon each of us and in which harmony alone is characteristic of our judgment of the beautiful, such as it presents itself in concrete life.

The harmony that is in question in every impression of beauty has certain abstract conditions—mathematical, physiological, or psychological, for example; but it has, above all, a historical origin and signification, outside of which it is impossible to comprehend it entirely and to assign to it a value of art. This harmony is not abstract, is not harmony in every sense, is not the maximum of possible harmony, because one knows how much remains of tolerated, accepted, or even desired discordances. It is the harmony of elements, imposed by this complex ensemble of collective ideas and conventions—what one may call a technique. The idea of harmony does not suffice; it is added only to that of technique, in order to qualify [p. 64] it as good or bad, according as its execution is more or less rational, according as the idea is more or less happily realized.

Harmony is the abstract law of every work, as the equality of action and reaction is the supreme law of every physical change of forces, without ever permitting one to divine, by itself, the proper nature of those forces. The notion of harmony cannot explain why such a form of art seems harmonious to one generation and little harmonious to another.

According to Lalo, so long as the individualist theories do not put in the first rank this problem, which seems to them secondary, they will not observe the true concrete aesthetic phenomena, which are, in Lalo's view, collective phenomena, because they display, in the last analysis, a social stamp, coming from a superior pressure, which transforms and orients the psychological, physiological, or mathematical elements that are subordinated to it in every human activity.

### VI. LA TEORÍA CIENTÍFICA DE LALO (CONTINUACIÓN) — VI. LALO'S SCIENTIFIC THEORY (CONTINUED)

[p. 65] There is a term—says Lalo—that adequately expresses the affective form normally taken on by the thought of the beautiful; that term is consciousness, more exact than that of feeling.

He calls consciousness the immediate and intuitive knowledge that we have of ourselves or of the states that constitute our self. Consciousness means a knowledge whose object is no more than one of the manners of being of the thinking subject itself and which constitutes but one with it, since to be and to think is for us an identity. Immediate knowledge—that is, no reasoning or experience is necessary to inform us, and none comes to interpose itself as a conscious intermediary between our thought and its object. Intuitive knowledge—that is, one that does not lend itself to being divided into juxtaposed parts that may remain exterior to one another and foreign to us, but whose components, isolated only by abstraction, interpenetrate in an organic and living synthesis; so that it is more exact to distinguish there immanent and virtual parts, successive or simultaneous «moments,» than elements, strictly speaking, of which it would be the sum.

A new notion is associated with that of intuition when it is a matter not merely of passively registering phenomena, but of desiring and of judging—that is, of esta[p. 66]blishing values. A value is still a phenomenon—Lalo observes—but a phenomenon of a special order, a phenomenon raised to the second power, so to speak, since it consists, properly speaking, in a relation established between the objective phenomena and our active nature: a relation of superiority or of inferiority, of possession or of need. Thus, truth, beauty, and the good are the three great species of human values, which the three sciences called «normal» study, because they have for their ultimate object to formulate, not speculative laws, like mathematics or biology, nor even useful applications but exterior to man, like the mechanical or industrial arts, but precepts or ideals—that is, direct applications of a theoretical science to the interior conditions of human life, to the very motives of our actions.

The legitimacy of this ambiguous notion has sometimes been objected to—says Lalo. It is held, in effect, that all science is theoretical and that all application is an art and not a science; between applied art and pure speculation—it has been said—there is no middle term; a combination of the two is alone possible. Nevertheless—Lalo replies—even from this point of view it is necessary, at least, to recognize two species or two notable degrees of applications: one exterior and mechanical, and another human and interior to our consciousness. The applied sciences modify materially exterior phenomena; but the normal sciences regulate the modifications of our consciousness with respect to those phenomena. Such are Logic, Aesthetics, and Morality—synthesis of a science and of an art applied to man himself, and which, for that reason, merit a name that marks well their intermediary situation between pure theory and pure mechanical application.

Thus it is that moral science is the immedia[p. 67]te intuition of a practical value or of a law of action, which makes it obligatory: of a duty. Apart from the psychological theory of self-knowledge, one scarcely speaks of consciousness except apropos of moral values. But it is understood that this notion must be enlarged: there is an aesthetic consciousness and a scientific consciousness, as there is a moral consciousness; the three cases are found, equally, under diverse specific characters: the immediate intuition of a value, of an ideal, of a law applicable, in the last analysis, to our personal activity, destined to modify it directly, so as to act only indirectly, and through it, upon the exterior world.

Naturally, these two characters have nothing of the absolute, as nothing human has. The intuition, wholly spontaneous in appearance, that we ascertain in ourselves is not indivisible and immediate except at the present moment, for the adult man and in the moments when his spirit abandons all critical and reflective attitude. But a long experience of the individual or of the species has formed it, little by little, out of diverse elements, associated, fused, and synthesized in the course of the ages; many relations, more or less conscious, enter necessarily into all our moral or aesthetic appreciations. Likewise, an ideal, whatever it be, is relative to our present condition; it varies with us, is not such except for us and by us, since, by definition, it does not exist outside the concrete thought that establishes it.

If this is so, one can speak, without paradox, of the existence of a true «aesthetic consciousness,» and this term sums up, for Lalo, almost all that is positive in the idea of «aesthetic feelings.»

We—he adds—judge, in effect, normally of an impression, calling it beautiful, without recourse to reasoning or to the memory of innumerable associations of [p. 68] ideas and feelings that experience has, no doubt, accumulated in us; rightly or wrongly, this impression seems to us immediate and indivisible: to judge and to enjoy are here one and the same act, which envelops only all the degrees of intelligent analysis, from the flashing and irresistible revelation of a glimpsed beauty to the long meditation that ripens, little by little, all our impressions and forms, in the long run, the sure taste of the art critic.

Likewise, the ideal character of the beautiful involves the feeling of a wholly special obligation, which diminishes gradually from the artist down to the vulgar. It has frequently been said that beauty is an ideal; but one often thinks one sees a difference of nature between the moral ideal, which is an obligation and, in the proper sense, a discipline, and the aesthetic ideal, which is an attraction. Now, it is very difficult to conceive an obligation that does not attract and an attraction that does not oblige. There is between the two the opposition that the physicist establishes between propulsion and attraction: a difference of points of view only, because, in both cases, the mechanical nature of the forces is identical; the equation of movement is the same.

One understands, then, that, notwithstanding their profound divergences, art and morality, the impressions of the beautiful and of the good—to which must be joined that of the true, which is also a «value,» established as a function of our intellectual activity—present numerous and fruitful analogies and perhaps a true kinship of nature.

The three are, in effect, a discipline: the disciplines of activity, of sensibility, and of intelligence, if one accepts provisionally this division of faculties, a little arbitrary and inexact for Lalo. According to [p. 69] him, these disciplines prescribe to us to subordinate ourselves to an authority, to orient our individual tendencies toward a higher ideal. Each of those faculties has its own, since they are in no way confounded; but it is not indifferent in life to know how to bend oneself to a discipline, whatever it be; each is, up to a certain point, an auxiliary to the others; and it is always good to feel an ideal above oneself, even when it is only partial and itself subordinate to higher ends.

Every ideal is, in effect, under certain aspects, a disinterestedness. To know how to choose among one's tendencies, to eliminate the most egoistic, the basest, and the most material, to make the intelligence penetrate into the sensibility and to direct the one by the other: such is the psychological function common to the aesthetic consciousness and to the moral consciousness. Aesthetic education is an apprenticeship of disciplined freedom, of reflective spontaneity, and even of responsibility before our own taste, or of the solidarity that binds us to the approvals or the reproaches of another: an apprenticeship that is superior to many others and that no other could effectively replace in the sufficiently ample proportion of self-education that our social life has disclosed to it.

But if art, morality, and science can and must collaborate in the culture of our self, those who have supposed an identity or a mutual reduction of those three forms of human life fall into error. There is no lack of scholars who hold that truth is the sole human ideal and that all the others dissipate before it, or are but insufficient and provisional expressions of it. Art and morality would thus be but the infancy of a science unaware of itself. Optimists, they repeat that art or science always lead to ethics and that one has only to follow them in order to reunite them, at least, in the ideal. The beautiful, it has [p. 70] been said, is the splendor of the true, and the good is reason made practical by itself. The reason of being of the world and of life is a moral reason. Dilettantes affirm, on the other hand, that there are no forms of duty that are not beautiful and that it would be necessary to reject them if they were not, because that is the sign of all value.

Lalo rejects all those affirmations, because, when they do not rest upon a mere love of paradox or upon a preconceived religious faith, they express, frequently, naturalist convictions extended at once to aesthetics, to morality, and to science. Now, in aesthetics, naturalism is the theory of natural beauty, but not of artistic beauty. What is sound and normal in nature is perhaps, at the same time, beautiful and good; but what art has made beautiful does not necessarily have an ethical value. Quite the contrary, luxury has, in itself, something exceptional, unjust, whose moral foundation is doubtful. If it is not forbidden, it is not prescribed, and it must even be severely limited by a well-understood justice. It is, then, very natural that art, the discipline of luxury, should have other objects and, so to speak, stand at the margin of true morality, the discipline of serious activity, as of science, the discipline of speculative thought.

In reality, these three ways are not convergent, but parallel. None of those activities could effectively supply the place of the other two, each being endowed with specific and irreducible qualities. All the functions of humanity are relatively bound in solidarity, certainly; but this ideal and always imperfect solidarity does not prevent their natures from being radically diverse and their orientations very different; it is an «organic» and not a «mechanical» solidarity. Thus, moral value can coexist with aesthetic value, as with [p. 71] scientific value, their convergence being able to be an ideal, and being able also to enter into struggle.

The aesthetic consciousness properly so called must, then, be profoundly distinguished from all the other forms that the intuition of a value can take on in individual or social life. A multitude of psychological shades separates it from them; but they may be subordinated to two principal characters.

Aesthetic intuition is, above all, that of a pleasure. The agreeable presents itself to us always as the conscious end of our normal activity, and only an organism in a pathological state could act continually in view of a pain—that is, of a diminishment, of a destruction of self. But pleasure, or even happiness, may be only an accessory end, lost from sight, being altogether a necessary accompaniment. So it is for the moral man or for the sage. Satisfaction, self-enjoyment, remains for them in the second rank, although, by definition, so to speak, neither the one nor the other ever acts save for a satisfaction of his moral or scientific consciousness.

On the contrary, the artist or the amateur treats pleasure, at once, as end and as means. It is through enjoyment that they arrive at the idea of the beautiful, and through the idea of the beautiful that they enjoy; the two terms are for them inseparable, and the priority of one of these two elements seems more logical than chronological, more ideal than real. In truth, painful feelings or impressions frequently accompany aesthetic pleasure and can even be its necessary condition. But, in virtue of the magic power of art, the excitation of the feelings most painful in themselves comes, in the end, always to be translated into joy.

Since in aesthetic intuition pleasure seems to us, at once, end and means, the kind of obligation that results from it is very different from moral obligation, in which the role of pleasure is much more subordinate. It measures, in effect, another kind of value; and that is its second character. Moral obligation is the discipline of all serious life, and none of our essential acts must escape it; it regulates the ideal of all the vital forms of activity. Aesthetic obligation, on the contrary, fixes the ideal of a very special activity: that of play. It suggests to us a discipline, but only the discipline of luxury.

For this reason art is not destined to supplant, in the future, morality or religion, nor even to generalize itself indefinitely among all men. It is true that more than one effect, or more than one accompaniment, of contemplation—such as admiration, sympathy, or the expansion of our cosmic conceptions—have in themselves something at once moral and religious; but they are not all of morality nor all of religion. And a society in which all the members were artists, or even amateurs, would not be viable, because it would perish of inaction, from excess of luxury and lack of the necessary. An aesthetic imperative could not be universalized without restriction, on the same footing as a moral imperative, but only generalized in a limited sphere of our faculties and of their objects, or in a specialized mode of society. That is the gravest consequence implied by the aesthetic relativism of modern art criticism.

Each of the three normative sciences that correspond to the investigation of the true, of the beautiful, and of the good supposes an intuitive consciousness of its object, endowed with specific characters, with that common trait of being the seat of a true obligation. No[p. 73]w, this entails, in its turn, the presence of two species of data: some individual, physiological and psychological, and others collective or sociological.

One can speak also, in the same sense, of an intuition of truth, of an obligation of method, of a scientific consciousness. All scholars, with their professional scruples, their ideal never satisfied and always more exacting, feel the obscure intuition.

As there is a moral consciousness and a scientific consciousness, there is, then, also an aesthetic consciousness. This means that there is an intuitive and normal aspect of the rules of art, as there is one of the moral or logical laws. Like all the others, the aesthetic consciousness has its satisfactions and its remorse, its austerities and its relaxations, its revolts and its capitulations, its exquisite modesties and its play-acting, or its abuse of public exhibitions, and, lastly, its positive and negative sanctions: glory and admiration, or failure and ridicule. As for the moral man and the sage, they are never, for the artist, anything but a distant end, which it is dangerous to fix too directly, but whose existence is no less felt subconsciously, as a necessity and a justice, as a superfluous crowning, moreover, of which each individual desires a demonstration.

Thus, on the one hand, beauty, truth, and morality each have their specific characters; they are not confounded except to the detriment, at once, of all three, because, in the last analysis, a very moral or too truthful art is less aesthetic, and a very aesthetic or too naturalistic morality is less moral. As for science, it is nothing but itself; it suffices to itself. Art is not contrary to morality or to truth, but is something different from them. It is a parallel intuition and, some[p. 74]times, of the same direction, because all obligations, all ideals, can give us an analogous feeling of respect for «value,» and each raises us, in its own way, above ourselves. On the other hand, the different values can also enter into competition or even into conflict, and their diverse attractions draw us in divergent directions. It is by considering, at once, all the conditions that can make normal the full development of the individual and of society that one can reconcile those multiple exigencies and equitably rank all the tendencies, in view of the integral development of humanity.

The freedom of art, like all the others, consists in obeying a consented discipline, and the richest life is the one that knows how to bend itself, at once, to many disciplines, provided that they be reconcilable in one and the same harmony; one must distrust him who has but one; he will be the strongest, but also the poorest; his life will be more upright, because it is simpler, but it will be the least human.

Lalo concludes his study of the aesthetic feelings with the following affirmations.

The feelings that play a principal role in aesthetic thought are multiple and unequally characteristic. What most profoundly characterizes art and beauty is the «technique»; it is a rich and diverse synthesis of material and moral conditions, of sensations, of reflections, of collective habits, of conventions, if you will, but not of artifices—of influences superior to our individuality, of movements in the incessant evolution; it is that powerful and confused ensemble, reduced, in the long run and under the pressure of the social milieu, to a single intuition, in appearance wholly spontaneous, and which acts upon us as a permanent [p. 75] suggestion. The technical feelings are the aesthetic feelings properly so called.

The other affective states—admiration, sympathy, vitality, contagion, personal attitude, conception of life—are effects or accompaniments of the former, which remain the only truly indispensable ground of every thought of beauty. Their associates can only reinforce them powerfully, as also, in certain circumstances, they harm them. These may appear, disappear, vary in nature or in degree; but the former alone guarantee, in the last analysis, the aesthetic qualification of the thought. Their triple character of play, of technical superiority, of harmony, is necessary to every consciousness of the beautiful; its suppression, on the contrary, would take from it all aesthetic value.

Now, those technical feelings are but the confused form, profoundly assimilated to our whole being, that the ideas take on in the long run—ideas that may very well have been clear and that always become so, in some degree, in the criticism of art or in the artist when he knows how to reflect upon himself and upon his works. It is not, then, their confused form—that is, their affective character—that characterizes them or creates their aesthetic signification; and in this sense sentimentalism falls into error in making of it its favorite principle. The multiple principle of the psychology of the beautiful is constituted by the diverse but solidary characters attributed to technical thought by an activity of suggestion or of illusion, of luxury, of discipline, by the respect for a superiority and the perception of a harmony, at once numerical and physical, physiological and psychological; in short, by the sense of a collective consent, endowed with sanctions, and of a historical or sociological evolution.

That these characters usually take on the form of [p. 76] a feeling—that is, the confused aspect of which each of our tendencies is susceptible—that is not doubtful. But there is nothing there that is special to the thought of the artist or of the public and that can legitimately define it. Feeling is by no means the proper organ of beauty. Nor is it, on the other hand, the proper organ of any of our activities, since it can appear in all; it is but a moment of each of them.

One might say, in effect, still more exactly of feeling what Spencer affirms of pleasure: that it is the necessary form of our sensible intuition, as space is of our intellectual intuition. Just as we do not act without being impelled by a tendency, whose obscure face is an affective state, so likewise we are never consciously active save when we propose to ourselves, under whatever title and as indirectly as one likes, a pleasure, which is the positive value of every affect. Feeling alone is practical by itself, whether it be a matter of moral, utilitarian, religious, aesthetic, or even scientific practice.

Feeling intervenes in all our activities; but, precisely because feeling is supposed in all our activities, it characterizes none. Thus, moral, religious, aesthetic sentimentalism perpetually fails of its end, if its end is, not to impel to morality, to religion, to art—to make itself an act of faith, of duty, or of beauty—but to explain their functions, to analyze, not to construct, to constitute a moral science—that is, a whole formed of a theory and of an applied art, a work destined to direct human practice, but not to be itself a bastard model of this practice.

Aesthetic thought presents itself, then, as a [p. 77] very complex combination of heterogeneous elements, whose synthesis has taken on, in the long run, the aspect of an intuition: a character that has, moreover, nothing of the absolute; quite the contrary, because analysis and criticism make of it, implicitly or subconsciously, an integral part. But this ensemble takes on a more fundamental character; it involves in our eyes the form of an obligation—that is, its effects arise from a collective and sanctioned judgment of value; all beauty supposes a public, real or imaginary, past, present, or even future, whose approval alone makes it exist, even in the eyes of its author, since he is not, in the end, satisfied except when he has obtained it.

Consequently, all that the notion of feeling contributes here of the positive is the idea of an aesthetic consciousness—that is, of the intuitive and normal character of aesthetic thought, which is what most exactly expresses it. Feeling enters into the appreciation of the beautiful no more than it enters into morality, and even perhaps than into science, in which it has a suggestive role. If aesthetic thought is more sentimental than the others, it is only in the sense that it is more sensible—that is, more confused. Surely, beauty is not demonstrated like a theorem, and each of us is persuaded, by himself, of the value of his own judgments of taste only by a wholly subjective belief; and, however convinced we may be, we scarcely think of imposing them on others except with a thousand precautions and for the personal satisfaction of our critical spirit, to reinforce them in ourselves by analysis, much more than to persuade others. In this sense one may evidently say that we have the feeling rather than the clear idea, even though this clarity may involve all the possible degrees.

But if by feelings one understands the common affec[p. 78]tive states, ordinarily designated by this word, such as love, hatred, or ambition, for example, their role in aesthetic thought is relatively exterior; they are but the effect or the accompaniment of a more essential activity, and the only specific one. Nevertheless, such is the organic and systematic character of consciousness that, whatever be their exact character in principle, they act in it, in the end, as a motor of its activity, charged with giving it the initial impulse that sets it vibrating. Foreign, in sum, to the essential organs of the machine, they give it movement; or, rather, we attribute movement to them, because they are the subjective form under which our tendencies necessarily appear to us as ours.

In effect, in psychological life, every effect or every accompaniment associated with the ideas of any activity whatever becomes normally the efficient and final cause, at once, from the moment our consciousness considers them, because such is its organizing and finalist nature, such is the mental chemistry that is elaborated in its living retort. In the aesthetic life the same happens as in all normal and even abnormal life: feeling seems to us an end because it is the effect of a tendency. We obey the tendency believing that we seek the feeling, which is but the face of it that most interests our enjoyment. In the end, the nature of the excitation and its mode of action upon creative thought remain almost completely indeterminate.

If, then, three very diverse species of feelings enter into our aesthetic life, in truth the aesthetic consciousness of the amateur, like that of the artist, ordinarily proposes to itself, as its object, as its final cause, these three species of states of soul at once, and it is in order to experience the three together that we most [p. 79] normally seek the impressions of art.

The amateur of art frequently has the consciousness of seeking only a pleasure or the accessory feelings. The essential of the aesthetic phenomenon presents itself only to reflection; and more than one theorist has been able to glimpse its true nature, without clashing with the superficial experience of common sense.

The intellectualist is the one who, limiting himself to analyzing, in the content of consciousness, the elements whose presence he distinctly recognizes, fails to recognize the confused character of aesthetic thought and the sentimental associations that come to reinforce it or to constitute for it an affective timbre: thus, a physiologist might wish to ignore the true repercussions of organic facts in our consciousness and would study only the material elements.

The sensualist is the one who explains aesthetic thought by the investigation of pleasure—that is, by its effects—as one would justify nutrition by the mere agreeableness of digestion.

The sentimentalist is the one who conceives as essential in the consciousness of the beautiful the feelings that Lalo calls accessory. It is natural that we seek them, and we do so at every instant; but the forewarned physiologist does not believe he has found the fundamental and even sole reason of being of nutrition when he ascertains the pleasures of taste, which accompany now a food, now a poison, and appear or disappear without altering the essential of the phenomenon.

The true aesthetic phenomena—Lalo repeats—those that are always present to every thought of beauty, escape our lesser reflection, but in virtue of which a more profound law nevertheless makes us think and act. To these feelings there remains, then, no longer much of their own nature, [p. 80] and their true name must be that of aesthetic thought or of aesthetic consciousness, because they are formed, at once, of sensations, of concepts, of reasonings, of habits, of voluntary conventions—and the feelings properly so called, those of common life, play there in no way a preponderant role. The action of the feelings is very real, but indeterminate, like that of a powerful motor that yet directs and organizes nothing.

Neither intellectualism, nor sensualism, nor mystical sentimentalism: such ought to be the watchword of scientific and positive aesthetics, according to Lalo. To study methodically aesthetic thought, aided successively by the data that each science can bring to it, without disdaining any, from mathematics to sociology, and, from those diverse points of view, to present, finally, if it be possible, a philosophical synthesis: such is, for Lalo, the ideal program of the aesthetics of the future.

### VII. TEORÍA EVOLUCIONISTA DE FANCIULLI — VII. FANCIULLI'S EVOLUTIONIST THEORY

With the same scientific criterion G. Fanciulli has studied the aesthetic consciousness.

According to this psychologist, the human consciousness may, before any reality, be found in three diverse aspects: first it observes the world and thought itself, it knows; in another attitude, it records and organizes the impulses and tendencies, it wills; and in yet another, it represents reality, not in order to know, nor in order to will, but simply in order to represent. This is the aesthetic consciousness, which reveals and affirms itself in relation to the work of art, all the other cases being reducible to this typical and primordial one. Nature herself can be enjoyed aesthetically only on condition of being contemplated as a work of art. Moral beauty too can be reduced to this one; for an action is beautiful when man, who is its cause, is considered as an artist. The aesthetic consciousness must, then, be regarded as a relation that exists between the human soul and all those objects generally gathered under the name of art.

The psychology of the aesthetic consciousness, in relation to the work of art, may be attempted from two diverse points of view, according to Fanciulli. On the one hand, one may inquire, in the evolution of the species or in the individual phenomenon, how the work of art is made manifest: by what path one arrives at the production of aesthetic objects; on the other hand, one may investigate why and how the work of art [p. 82]modifies the consciousness of one who does not contribute to its creation. In other terms, a psychology of the artist is possible, and a psychology of the spectator, which has been neglected.

Common sense has been content to regard contemplation as a self-evident phenomenon; but scientific theory has sought to demonstrate that, in substance, aesthetic production and contemplation have the same psychological basis, so much so that, in studying the one, one comes implicitly to treat of the other.

In the wish to define this relation, it has been affirmed that, in reality, in every contemplation the spectator repeats the psychic process that was necessary for the constitution of the work of art, and that, without this, the work itself remains uncomprehended and ineffectual.

The clearest upholder of this theory is B. Croce, who establishes the following comparison:

The complete process of aesthetic production has four moments or stages; the aesthetic phenomenon has four sides, which are: a) impression; b) expression, or aesthetic spiritual synthesis; c) the psychic reverse of the expression (aesthetic pleasure); d) the physical reverse of the psychic organism (sounds, tones, movements, combinations of colours and lines, etc.). Once objectivation has taken place, the process continues and repeats itself indefinitely, through the soul of other men who are spectators. The phenomena, which may be called psycho-physical, that accompany the spiritual expression can be awakened in the organism by determinate physical stimuli. When these are reproduced, it follows, as a consequence (all the other conditions remaining unaltered), that the already produced expression or aesthetic intuition is reproduced. The process of reproduction will occur in the following order: e) physical stimulus; d) sub-physical phenomenon (soun[p. 83]ds, tones, mimic movements, combinations of lines and colours, etc.); b) aesthetic synthesis; c) psychic reflex.

The spectator passes through all the moments that the artist has traversed, allowing himself only a few modifications in the itinerary. Notwithstanding this process, Fanciulli does not believe that aesthetic production and reproduction are a single phenomenon, that each man is a creator in contemplating, and that those variations of itinerary do not imply a substantial difference. According to Fanciulli, aesthetic production and contemplation, save for their natural relations, remain independent and can, consequently, be studied separately.

Fanciulli begins his study by tracing the genesis of the aesthetic phenomenon from its deepest roots in animal life. He analyzes the sexual aesthetics of animals, their constructive attitude, their play, their sensibility before human art, only to conclude that this does not demonstrate the existence of aesthetic feeling in animals, but rather an obscure and vague potentiality, a tendency still too weak to emerge from the fatal circle of vegetative life and to rise to a higher sphere.

The aesthetic world is a domain exclusively human. Between the animal world and the human world there is interposed, in this respect, an insuperable abyss; if the attitudes of the animal consciousness reappear in man, they assume a new power in him.

Primitively the aesthetic consciousness in man was receptive and creative at the same time; the spectator contemplated his own work, and the aesthetic process was carried out according to the following schematic formula:

[p. 84]A) CREATIVE ACTIVITY. a) Fundamental practical tendencies; b) Accessory aesthetic tendencies. B) RECEPTIVE CONSCIOUSNESS. a) Pleasure from the satisfaction of the practical tendencies. b) Enjoyment from the actuation of the accessory tendencies. c) Complacency in the creative act.

In that element b), however tenuous it may be, lies the germ of the whole later aesthetic evolution, according to Fanciulli, to whom it now appears evident how impossible it is to write the history, to seek the first vibrations of this pleasure, without taking into account the creative activity to which it closely corresponds.

Aesthetic activity, lost at first amid elements of another order, becomes, little by little, isolated and independent. Thus there are extra-aesthetic tendencies alongside the aesthetic ones that serve as their basis, and they may be distinguished into two great groups: a) purely practical tendencies, connected with the satisfaction of the needs of vegetative life; b) spiritual tendencies, among which Fanciulli includes these: 1st, self-love, the desire for power, and the sexual instinct; 2nd, the desire for communication with the divinity; 3rd, the desire for communication with one's own fellows (sympathy).

Fanciulli studies the practical and the spiritual tendencies separately. As regards the former, he observes that the desire to defend oneself from enemies, to procure better and more abundant food, leads man [p. 85]to the choice of suitable means; that is, to the fabrication of weapons, rural implements, dwellings for beasts and for men. Such objects present, from the beginning, qualities wholly foreign to the fundamental end: 1st, a form, which in the greater part of cases is symmetrical, and 2nd, a surface, polished in the objects and coloured, presenting ornamental designs, engraved, sculptured, coloured, etc.

To explain the existence of these aesthetic elements in the first productions, there has been talk of aesthetic creation; but Fanciulli rejects this explanation, which is not scientific; for the creator can be nothing but a part of what is created, a cell of this vast organism of which the ancient philosophers had a brilliant intuition. Man, at most, is a filter or a marvellous crucible; he gathers the raw materials in order to produce the finest essences or precious metals, but he creates nothing absolutely new. Man is capable of producing life; that is, an energy that will shine on, outlasting him in time; but that life he has already taken from infinite beings and even from himself.

The same happens with aesthetic procreation; the phenomenon shows itself most clearly in the first manifestations. The form of objects, for example, is born taking experience as its basis. The primitive men, the savages, do not deliberately invent forms; artistic expression is the result of prior impressions, among which the visual and tactile predominate. Man imitates, but not for the pleasure of imitating, rather because he is constrained to imitate Nature, without being able to «go out» of her; and if, unlike all the other animals, which have a circumscribed and uniform sphere of action, man has been able to constitute a world of his own, the child of his soul, this world has had, necessa[p. 86]rily, to repeat the world already existing, even though it be with infinite variations, transformations, and developments.

This does not mean that the profound originality of human activity in general, and of aesthetic activity in particular, is denied. Theoretically, the impressions or suggestions offered by Nature must have been infinite; but Fanciulli observes that the concept of «suggestion» is a relation, and it is well, therefore, to bear both terms in mind.

Now then, it is evident that, among the many possible impressions, man, by his special conformation, must have felt and received only some. Of the terms of a primitive selection we know but one: that which we call the whole, the Universe; in reality, we do not know what Nature may be in herself, all the life and the death that surrounds her; each animal species must have of her a representation of its own. But beyond this there exists a second selection, much more important for us, obtained on the basis of attention.

In interpreting the sense of this word, Fanciulli begins by rejecting the opinion founded upon the profound astonishment, upon the «curiosity» of the primitive man or savage, to whom a nature very like our own has been attributed, believing him capable of «admiration». The savage is still constrained to see certain spectacles and certain objects; little by little he perceives the forms of nature; and in this «selective attention», for the most part unconscious, lies the root of the whole later aesthetic process. In the multiplicity of impressions, man appropriates only some and makes use of them for successive production. Imitation is sometimes easy and complete, but frequently it is scarcely recognizable, because it does not tend to reproduce a [p. 87]particular object, but rather associates discordant elements.

In the «formation» of the objects of suggestion, which man has most commonly gathered from nature, there has existed that of symmetry: the observation, even summary, of one's own body, of animal forms and of plants, offers the intuition of space divided into proportional parts. This does not preclude that some peoples, the Japanese, for example, have on the contrary gathered up all that in nature is asymmetry and variety.

Fanciulli then examines the facts that refer to decoration, in order to sum up, in a synthetic formula, the analysis of the enjoyment inherent in it. In the first place, he posits a factor common to every process of creation; that is, the joy of producing, of being a cause. In the second, the pleasure caused by the recognition of the accord, more or less desired, between the aesthetic suggestions accumulated in experience, gathered from nature, and those which the new object provokes. This element is the fundamental one; and, wishing to give a content to that accord, we may recall the sense of colour, of symmetry, of unity, of variety, etc. Afterwards, there is a pleasure of the imagination, since, around the perception of the artistic object, there extends a network of associations, a labour, more or less complicated, of the fantasy, which has an eminently agreeable tone. Finally, in the more evolved cases, that is, when there is a more conscious investigation of the effect (imitation of forms), there exists an emotion sui generis, due to the correspondence of the real perception with a preexistent imaginative representation. But this pleasure is felt vaguely and soon forgotten by those primitive craftsmen who do not go beyond pure decoration.

[p. 88]After having determined how, during the course of the practical tendencies, aesthetic tendencies can arise and affirm themselves, Fanciulli examines the second group, that in which the basis of the aesthetic phenomenon is more especially spiritual or sentimental. These fundamental tendencies, joined to a certain degree of intensity, demand an objectivation. Psychic life, in substance, consists precisely in this imprisonment of energies, in this outspreading of forces, which no dynamics can calculate exactly. And the most characteristic fact is that such forces do not develop solely by necessary mechanical laws, links of that great chain of causes and effects that constitute our world, but, on the contrary, in the external becoming they may even have the end of revealing their nature or, better, the nature of the source from which they spring. Only in the superior organisms is the manifestation of life possible with the pure intent of manifesting life.

Such a capacity, naturally, has its maximum power in man. The pleasure, the pain, the desire that stir within him, at a certain moment abandon the impenetrable mystery of the psyche, to become exterior, tangible phenomena. Well then, from this objectivation of energies has arisen true and great art. But the passage from the psychic to the physical is not immediate; rather there is a moment which, being internal, is an essential condition for the further development of the process. In the first place, there is revealed, more or less clearly, the generic end to which the tendency aspires, and before action can effectively be joined to it, there is a whole internal labour for the choice of the most suitable means. Under the impulse of the energy that at the moment predominates, the whole treasure of images, gathered through experience, successively lights up, vanishes, and comes [p. 89]to rise again; it may happen that one of these elements persists amid the animated fluctuation, and that then other numerous elements concur, unite, and merge with the first, until the sought-for means is found and the tendency remains ideally enclosed in a diverse quid that can be clearly expressed and that the artist expresses.

There develops, in substance, a true process of crystallization, with this difference, however: that, whereas the molecules of the mineral are ordered by necessary laws, the molecules of the imagination are received and rejected by that power which mysteriously presides over the psychic phenomena themselves: the self.

In a second moment, there is the actuation or realization of the model; the psychic phenomenon is converted into an external phenomenon, into a concrete object. That execution may seem, at first sight, most simple: we are so habituated to experiencing, in such immediate succession, thinking and doing, that we scarcely become aware of the difference, of the mystery that such a passage implies. But it will suffice to recall the very common cases in which the passage is not easily effected, or is altogether impossible, to reestablish the awareness of the long interval. In the first steps of art, the mystery may come to be less profound, or not to exist at all.

These considerations established, Fanciulli inquires which are the primitive tendencies that have had so peculiar a manifestation, and what aesthetic objects they have as their product.

In the first rank he places self-love; a tendency that appears with man. Setting out from it, the individual desires to be, or to appear, the strongest, the most powerful, the most admired possible; by means of these aspirations, there is not slow to constitute itself a brilliant ideal self; tha[p. 90]t is, a fantastic construction. The materials are those offered by the whole of experience. Man makes himself the centre of all the suggestions of beauty that can be gathered from the surrounding nature and from his embryonic art; he wishes that from him should emanate those impressions which he prizes and which he knows to be prized by others; this imaginative content will vary according to the conditions of life and the psychic level attained. Hence are born tattooing and the portrait, which have their deepest roots in the religious feeling. An indirect, but not negligible, influence upon the development of the representative arts has been exercised by the desire to communicate, at a distance, with one's fellows.

From this analysis Fanciulli infers that the elements that enter into the representative arts are: a) the pleasure of creating, of being a cause; b) the satisfaction at the actuation of the spiritual tendencies that have determined the whole process; c) elementary aesthetic feelings, due to the perception of certain forms, colours, etc. (that which in decoration was the fundamental element); d) a more properly aesthetic element lies in being aware that the imaginative representation and the material execution, the ideal and the objective, coincide more or less; e) the pleasure of the imagination, richer in content than in the preceding case; f) finally, there presents itself the factor that only exceptionally could exist in the presence of primitive decoration, but which imposes itself and comes to be the central fire of all enjoyment once certain limits of psychic progress in general, and of artistic progress in particular, have been reached. The artist may dispense with being the creator, he may not recognize the derivations or the composition of his own work; but that work moves him like an object of nature, for what it is, without more, simply.

[p. 91]Gathering, among all these elements, those that most directly matter, that constitute the receptive aesthetic consciousness, Fanciulli observes how, in sum, the enjoyment of art results, 1st, from seeing gathered together, in more or less organic syntheses, the aesthetically agreeable impressions born in the course of prior experience, and 2nd, from such syntheses being expressions, besides of the perceptions, of feelings, of profoundly human tendencies.

If now it is a question of knowing why, from that synthesis and that expression, aesthetic pleasure develops, that cannot be answered; for, according to Fanciulli, for this problem no solution is to be found; the question fixes an insuperable limit, beyond which lies the intimate nature of the human soul with all its mysteries.

It might be objected against this analysis, says Fanciulli, that one posits as the characteristic element of the enjoyment inherent in the representative arts the consciousness of the more or less adequate expression of a fantastic construction, this being, on the contrary, an element common to all the arts. Fanciulli replies to this objection that, even granting it, one observes that that special consciousness and the pleasure obtained can be said to be common to all the arts only formally; but the content is always diverse. According to the case, there is a different fantastic construction and, consequently, a different execution. The same feeling of self-love, of religious faith, etc., may give rise to a construction of visual or plastic, auditory or motor images; and in those various cases one will have painting, or music, or dance.

In this way Fanciulli finds, for the larger group of the representative arts, the first roots of aesthetic activity in its creative and recept[p. 92]ive aspect, even though these general aesthetic tendencies be a very poor thing, a negligible quantity for one who takes account of quantity alone. An infinity of causes has contributed to the development of those elements; above all the progress of the general conditions of existence. In order that the accessory tendencies should be universally recognized and actuated, it has been necessary that those fundamental conditions could develop fully and freely. Only after this has it been possible to attain and to foster that enjoyment which is in a certain way accidental.

The primitive soul has been enriched with new forces, and the progressive technique has been able to find, for each one, a fitting expression. Parallel to this general progress, the individual differences affirmed themselves ever more. Nature, this old world which originally, for all men, was perceived in the same vague and confused manner, was transformed into a plurality of worlds, according as it entered into relation with various types of souls, of fantasy.

Aesthetic activity is completed in a second group of arts, which Fanciulli calls expressive —Music, the Dance, and Poetry—, and through which he continues the analysis of that activity, in order to conclude by affirming that the aesthetic form does not derive from the practice with which it is primitively associated, and that the modifications in the receptive consciousness do not necessarily correspond to those of the creative consciousness; even though, once the separation between the one and the other has come about in the aesthetic evolution, the psychic process of the simple contemplator is justified by the same reasons that hold for the artist; for the work of art, once produced, can move him who contemplates it, by itself, inasmuch as it is what it is.

[p. 93]Thus is the complete evolution of the aesthetic consciousness understood. In its origin, none was a creative artist; but out of the homogeneous ground that constituted «man» there arose a thousand types to form «men»; life comes to be a phenomenon too complex and profound for each one to be able to gather it whole within his soul; therefore a privileged class had the function of producing beauty; but such a caste did not separate itself from the world; a stranger among its fellows, it celebrated no mysteries; its works were accessible to the many, because the soul of each one gathered in germ even those forces that had prepared its marvellous efflorescence. The finest title of glory for the artist lies precisely in this labouring, more than for himself, for others; in making organic and alive all the scattered, vague fragments, not comprehended by the collective soul.

After having traced the genesis of the beautiful in the species, Fanciulli traces the ontogenesis, that is, the path traversed by the individual, raising the second question: whether the new individual has had to repeat the process that was accomplished in the species, or, more simply, whether hereditary germs have developed in him. Analyzing the aesthetic process in the individual, Fanciulli finds that the three fundamental moments or stages traversed by the aesthetic consciousness of the species are repeated.

a) There will be, that is, above all, the analysis and the selection of the data offered by experience (the perception of certain colours, forms, sounds, movements, etc.). After this, b) there will be a period in which the child is an artist like the primitive man and knows how to enjoy aesthetically only before his own work. It has been seen that to make art was a necessary preparation in order that the art of another might be understood and relished as a mere spectator; the same happens in the individual. Finally, c) [p. 94]through the exercise contained in the previous states and through the direct influence of education, there begins the most elevated and complete period, at the end of which one arrives, when one does arrive, at the enjoyment of great human art; there is fixed the type of aesthetic consciousness that will remain fundamentally for the whole of life.

Developing this programme, Fanciulli studies: 1st, the formation of the first impressions in the child, especially the visual, auditory, and movement sensations; 2nd, the free activity, developed in infantile play and engendering imitation, the games of imagination that reveal the individuality of the child, his creative tendency, which initiates artistic creation, whose unfolding follows the same process as in the species; and he studies, in the 3rd place, aesthetic enjoyment in the child, which cannot be compared with that of the savage, and which passes through successive degrees, from the contemplation of the material aspect of things to the profound emotion of the beautiful, continuing, more or less, the line of development followed by the primitive artist, in order to become capable of pure contemplation, to transform himself into a mere spectator.

Fanciulli declares that the uncertainty grows great when one attempts to fix the concrete content of the hypothetical evolutionary line, because of the individual differences that multiply to infinity; and for this reason he circumscribes his analysis to the fully evolved type, which is the habitual subject of all psychological studies.

True aesthetic enjoyment begins when the mind is capable of gathering into more or less vast syntheses the perceptions localized in space and in time, when it is capable of feeling, as an organic whole, that which before was fragmentary and dispersed. The capacity to perceive the formal relations in the work [p. 95]of art, and indeed the enjoyment that follows upon it, is conquered by degrees. In representative acts it is difficult to separate out the impression that the represented thing directly arouses. Here one has an intermediate stage, through which one may arrive at the true and complete comprehension of the artistic work. In the work of art we see something more than that which it is as a pure material object, and in seeing this «something more» consists, at bottom, the whole of aesthetic contemplation. Finally, after many preparations and long detours, one arrives at the true and complete aesthetic enjoyment, in which sense, intelligence, and emotion cooperate to give a single impression.

Thus, through a long series of experiments and trials, «taste» is formed; that is, the capacity to feel aesthetically the creations of human art. But if it is then a question of adapting to real men the ideal model of aesthetic enjoyment thus conceived, it is necessary to make corrections; for here, as in all else, the ideal is too vast with respect to reality. The conception of the world is diverse in each individual, considered not only as an artist, but also as a spectator. Education, moreover, completes the natural dispositions and selects among them.

Man, elaborating, like the species, the data of the senses, comes slowly to construct the world of beauty, the world of art, under all its various forms; in such wise that the individual who presents himself to life today receives a rich inheritance, a treasure accumulated by the labour of infinite generations; but he finds himself as though under tutelage; he cannot take immediate possession of his goods and must first show himself worthy, repeating, in the first years of life, the labour of the species. After having seen how the treasure is constituted, we behold the new man during the period of [p. 96]preparation, and even in his first impulse of freedom, when at last he comes to possess all beauty. But what this ideal possession may be, that is, by what paths one comes each time to feel the beautiful, and what precisely this very feeling signifies, are problems that still await a definitive solution.

### VIII. TEORÍA EVOLUCIONISTA DE FANCIULLI (CONTINUACIÓN) — VIII. FANCIULLI'S EVOLUTIONIST THEORY (CONTINUED)

Having set out the genesis and the ontogenesis of the aesthetic consciousness, Fanciulli enters upon the analysis of the subjective aesthetic phenomenon, recognizing in it a process divisible into three distinct states: sense, intelligence, and emotion — not regarded as independent faculties, nor, as Lalo does, assigning to feeling a representative or intellectual significance, but rather associating these two phases of aesthetic activity, the emotive, synthetic or unitary phase and the representative, analytic or manifold one. For Fanciulli, beauty is not merely a system of parts (unity and variety), excessively complex, but has a significance derived from its reflecting all the deepest aspirations and demands of the human soul. Now this «significance» of beauty, this profound life, cannot be perceived by any intellectual process; the soul of the thing and the soul of the spectator are fused through a medium that is the more indistinct the more intimate it is: through a feeling. And naturally this emotive activity likewise presupposes the intellectual one; but the presupposition, the necessary antecedent, is not always the cause.

Analyzing the aesthetic phenomenon more particularly, Fanciulli distinguishes the following factors: intellectual factors and emotive factors.

[p. 98]The aesthetic object, like all the others of external reality, reveals itself to the subject through a series of sensations of diverse order. Sometimes the process, together with the feeling that is its consequence, is exhausted in this initial moment; one then has an elementary aesthetic feeling. But in the greater part of cases the sensory data undergo a more or less complex elaboration, by means of an analysis and a successive synthesis which man performs upon the impressions offered by nature. Pure beauty is an abstraction, and as such perhaps does not exist even in the mind of the creating artist; it becomes associated with impure, non-aesthetic elements when it leaves the domains of the spirit to turn into a real fact.
