Consequently it is necessary that the spectator should always repeat that process of analysis and synthesis, in order to find, in the material object, the imaginative conception that the artist has wished to express. When this fundamental process is not carried out, the work of art remains «not understood»; and this may happen sometimes through the intellectual insufficiency of the spectators, and at other times, on the contrary, because the artist has not known how to transfer his mental synthesis into the matter and presents a mere material fact beneath vain aesthetic appearances.

Nevertheless, the most notable factor of the whole aesthetic process is feeling, the emotional state: if only for the field it occupies in consciousness. In this respect Fanciulli establishes the following schematic classification: 1st, the simplest emotive states are those which correspond to the perception of the sensory data; 2nd, there comes next a group of emotions which, common as they are, are considered extra-aesthetic by most psychologists. In the first rank stands the peculiar pleasure introduced by the satisfaction of the tendency [p. 99]to imitation, which afterwards, as an appreciative feeling, resolves itself into the nature of the representation and into admiration for the artist's skill; in the second place stand the «sympathetic emotions», which arise when the work of art is conceived merely as the representation of a real object or state. Lastly, there is also a characteristic pleasure which in a certain manner accompanies the whole psychic labor of contemplation: it is the pleasure of activity. All these elements are found upon the confines of the aesthetic field, without yet penetrating into it; 3rd, once these preparatory or accessory stages are surpassed, one arrives — when the process is not exhausted in them — at the true and highest aesthetic enjoyment. And here too a further subdivision and a kind of hierarchy may be established: there is a feeling that penetrates the representation, which arises after the elaboration of the sensory data (the pleasure of rhythm, harmony, contrast, proportion, etc.), and there is afterwards the autonomous feeling which, in the absence of any clear representation, surpasses formal beauty and takes possession of the complex, indistinct life of the aesthetic object.

It has been seen how the aesthetic process is excessively complex, inasmuch as each of its factors decomposes into diverse elements. It is understood, however, that not in every particular case do all these numerous elements find a place; aesthetic objects, though they have deep bonds of kinship, are grouped into several categories, which are precisely the arts, and therefore require, in order to be understood and felt, a peculiar activity of the psyche, different for each category.

This leads Fanciulli to investigate and describe the psychic modifications of the individual, effected before the objects of the several arts; to which end he studies [p. 100]the elementary aesthetic feelings, in the lower and higher sensations, the intellectual factors that intervene in the higher processes of thought, and the emotive factor, so as to apply this analysis to the representative and expressive arts.

Fanciulli begins his analysis with the organic sensations, which are the most elementary, and to which he denies aesthetic value, regarding them only as concomitants or, if one will, as motives that have facilitated the production of art. «In order that the impression of beauty may be produced, it is necessary, as Souriau says, that a judgment upon its quality be associated with that sensation. Only a reflective spirit will be able to make of its states of consciousness an object of contemplation and to receive, by reaction, an aesthetic emotion». Fanciulli observes, however, that the thing added is not simply a judgment upon quality; for the judgment is at most the exponent of an elevated process which unfolds in the psyche, the exponent of the synthesis that precedes aesthetic creation; only that, in this case, the elements of such creation all remain internal; they do not go beyond the pure imaginative conception. Such a process, far from being «elementary», is possible only in refined consciousnesses. The organic sensations, therefore, do not enter into the aesthetic domain.

Fanciulli then analyzes the higher group of the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile sensations, and pronounces against their aesthetic character, departing from the opinions of Guyau, Groos, and Witasek. Fanciulli affirms that the sensation may have an affective tone, but that it will always remain confined within the realm of pleasure. This established, he adds that theoretically every sensation may undergo a special elaboration and assume [p. 101]an aesthetic value — which demands an exceptional temperament.

The higher sensations of sight and hearing, considered in themselves, likewise have no aesthetic value. In order that they may have it, it is necessary that the subject associate them with something different, or come to project them before himself in order to contemplate them; otherwise one remains within the limits of pure pleasure.

The expression «elementary aesthetic feelings» is therefore exact and acceptable if by it one means that there are aesthetic feelings of very poor content; but it has no sense when one wishes to affirm the existence of aesthetic sensations.

Having made this affirmation, Fanciulli analyzes the true aesthetic feelings, beginning with the representative arts, Architecture, Sculpture, and Painting.

Sight is the sense that offers the first revelation of all the aesthetic objects existing in space; with sight are associated the tactile and motor sensations, as necessary elements, and even the organic sensations, vague or indistinct, which reveal themselves better in the contemplation of works of architecture than in those of sculpture and painting.

The sensory elements are therefore many and complex, even more so than at first sight appears; but they would remain in large part sterile if they were not promptly elaborated by mental processes of a higher order.

The sensations begin, as in every other case, to organize themselves so as to offer the complex representation of the aesthetic object. In the first moment one has [p. 102]only the representation of the real object, which immediately — though not in all persons — may also be perceived as «aesthetic». A first step toward this end consists in certain sensations arising above the others, or rather in effecting a recognition of relations among these more salient sensations. The relations may be perceived with the aid of memory, following a series of movements (the case is typical in music), or, with greater exactness, are perceived simultaneously through the plurality of the impressions upon the retina. Since antiquity it has been recognized that the aesthetic relation par excellence lies in perceiving unity in variety; and it does not seem that one ought to discard the old formula out of a mere love of the new; it contains a great fund of truth. This principle is applicable above all to architecture, whereas for pictures and statues it remains secondary, subordinate to other factors of beauty. Variety is perceived easily, being part of every figure circumscribed by lines; unity may be taken according to three different schemes: a) there may exist a continuous reciprocity of the several parts; b) or else there is a common correlation of the parts with a dominant, ordinarily central, element; c) or, finally, likeness and equality are perceived among the parts. To this last associative type the sense of proportion approximates.

This sense, most often, consists in a vague appreciation of one magnitude with respect to another; and even when this relation is not numerically valued, it is nonetheless estimated in a very exact manner. The highly intellectual nature of this sense is discovered when one considers that it implies, above all — as Sully observes — a recognition of the correspondence of perceived relations with certain granted relations, which are furnished by an ideal type of proportion. This men[p. 103]tal type may rest upon a sense of utility or of the correspondence of the several parts to a certain end, or upon habit, or, for the freer forms, upon a vague feeling of the relative aesthetic importance of certain lines as parts of an agreeable or well-balanced whole. This elaboration of visual sensations certainly does not take place without the important aid of the tactile ones; it is fitting, rather, in order to have an adequate representation, that there be a complete fusion of the sensory (visual) elements and the reproductive (tactile-motor) ones, as Groos demonstrates.

Yet this full fusion has an ephemeral existence (only for one incapable of feeling the beautiful will it be permanent, and it will then be a mere psychic correlate of a real object); it is replaced by a new intuition; one passes from the pure representation of reality to the state commonly called aesthetic illusion, because proportion, symmetry, harmony, etc., from the aesthetic point of view, exist more in our mind than in the real object.

A first observation, even a superficial one, allows us to recognize that not everyone can contemplate the work of art in the same way. It is not difficult to indicate the various types. a) In a first type, the sensory data inherent in the aesthetic object remain such as they are, or rather confine themselves to giving the representation of what is commonly called «reality». The phenomenon, it is understood, is rather rare, possible only in the lowest savages or in children in the first periods of life; for these the statue will always be simply a piece of marble, and the picture a variously colored surface; b) But a fairly low mental level and an artistic education more than rudimentary suffice for one to recognize in the work of art [p. 104]«something represented»; and sometimes the recognition is so intense or so sudden that a veritable hallucination is engendered; that is, all the notes of the aesthetic object corresponding to real data arise and triumph, so that in the end that aesthetic object is regarded as though it were the corresponding represented object; c) But the more common case does not reach such an extreme, neither the brute perception of the matter nor the hallucination; the mental process begins to be a little more complicated.

In the aesthetic object, in effect, the representation of a real object is clearly perceived, but there are also present in consciousness all the notes that contradict the «reality» of that object; and one then has the sure conviction that the work of art is an imitation, a more or less felicitous copy. This mode of conceiving belongs to the greater number; d) On the contrary, only in superior consciousnesses can that admirable imaginative fusion be realized which is the true aesthetic creation. Even here consciousness seems to present a doubling: there is a nucleus of images which gives the impression of reality and another which draws away from it; and moreover, in place of the predominance of one part or of contrast, the most perfect accord reigns, and from the whole of the impressions there emerges the complete representation of a reality sui generis. We feel that the statue is not a piece of marble, nor a person, nor even the image of a person; but that it is simply a statue — that is, an object that has the notes of the marble, of the person, and of the image gathered together, interpenetrated, admirably fused, an object that therefore leaves the world of common reality to place itself in another wholly created by man, in the world of aesthetic reality.

It is here that the aesthetic process reaches its last [p. 105]and highest phase; for besides perceiving and conceiving, consciousness feels what the object truly is, in a manner at once more indistinct and more clear, more vague and more irrefutable. The mind must here work with the sensory data far more than for the perception of other objects; but the mental synthesis does not develop arbitrarily; that feeling is not a dream or a delirium; on the contrary, it reflects with all fidelity the total image of the work of art — so surely that, were the work modified, the synthesis too would be altered and in certain cases would disappear, the object descending from the height of the realm of aesthetic reality to the field of pure matter. It is true that with that feeling we see in the statue or the picture something that does not seem to exist materially; but even here we do not invent, we do not delude ourselves; above all because, through the interpretation of the material signs, we only come to find again the spiritual content, the soul that the artist infuses into his own work.

Fanciulli thus places himself within the domain of feeling and studies more closely the emotion which is the fundamental element of the whole aesthetic process.

As has been said, aesthetic feeling is, in part, the necessary product of sensory or intellectual phenomena and, in part, autonomous — a typical attitude that the psyche assumes where intelligence, by itself alone, seems insufficient.

Fanciulli returns to this matter, developing it further: a) As to the emotion of the first type — that is, as to the elementary aesthetic feelings — this emotion is aesthetic in a minimal degree; it may be experienced even by one who in the work of art sees only the pure matter, the marble of the statue and the color of the picture: children, savages, and even certain animals. Not for [p. 106]this is that ingenuous form of enjoyment to be despised: when the aesthetic process continues and rises, it remains, fused with other elements, in proportions not negligible; considered in itself, it may attain notable degrees of intensity, while, being infinitely simple, it remains for us a mystery.

b) To this first nucleus is very closely joined the emotion dependent on the recognition of the aesthetic relations that exist among the sensory data. Unity and variety, symmetry, proportion, etc., are perceived with an immediate and evident pleasure; ordinarily the ultimate reason escapes us; we can recall only that the ascertaining of those relations corresponds to tendencies which we have seen assert themselves far back in the aesthetic evolution of the species and become, with time, ever more imperious. These tendencies, which also assert themselves in practical life, seem to find their full satisfaction in the work of art.

c) Yet this emotive base would still remain rather poor if more complex elements were not added. It must be confessed, says Fanciulli, that in the greater part of cases what is added is a mere verbal exaggeration, or else all those emotions which have been regarded as extra-aesthetic. When the work of art is conceived as an imitation or copy, it is natural that above all the thing represented should interest us. The strong emotions that the work expresses are those which are most easily transmitted by sympathy; it suffices to cite the whole group of diverse feelings inherent in the sexual instinct. But even imitation, taken in itself, can arouse a special complacency. From this one naturally passes to admiration for the skill of the artist, who has also known how to imitate; many times this skill is known more theoretically than recognized in the fact, and so it can still always arouse a notable emotion; on the [p. 107]other hand, it is undeniable that we are all disposed to judge a canvas differently if it is signed by Raphael or by an unknown. The man is understood and admired through his work, already consecrated by glory; the work has then an importance more historical than otherwise. The mystery that envelops the origin of a work of art and its composition produces a poetic feeling that becomes associated with the others. The «reverie» may arise, and consequently determine an emotion, even independent of this fixation of the past; it suffices that the content of the work of art be not very clear and demand a long imaginative elaboration on our part, completely free. Lastly, the emotive state may be determined, and with great vivacity, when special, personal associations become knotted about a work of art as about any object whatsoever: the old and faded engraving upon which a dying man's last glances were fixed may be dearer and more apt to move us than any masterpiece of art. But it is needless to observe that this emotion has nothing to do with aesthetics.

d) Apart from all this, in the fully developed consciousness we find that emotion is not limited merely to corresponding servilely to the data of sense or of intelligence, but arises free and victoriously surpasses the limits to which the psyche has arrived by other means. Besides all the emotive elements already set forth, there is a vast residue, a quid, which at first sight seems inexplicable and which can come to be, to a certain point, justified only when an autonomous function is granted to feeling.

The principle of imitation, thus accepted in antiquity and even among modern aestheticians such as Lange, is today shown to be insufficient, seeing that the work of paint[p. 108]ing or sculpture is not a simple copy of reality, and that the bonds of architecture with real objects are so remote that they escape simple contemplation altogether.

Fanciulli here combats the theory of the North American aesthetician Berenson, who explains aesthetic emotion by an exaltation of the consciousness of the self, which might be interpreted as the moment in which intensity produces the autonomy of feeling, but which Fanciulli confounds with the feeling of self-love that becomes associated with many other emotions.

For Fanciulli no theory is, in substance, true so long as one does not cease to regard feeling as a mere resonance of pleasure or of pain inherent in the course of the intellectual operations; where intelligence appears insufficient and disconcerted, feeling substitutes itself for it and victoriously arrives at its final term.

The great role of feeling lies wholly in offering to the psyche the synthesis or the intuition of «aesthetic reality»; that fusion is effected upon intellectual data, but is not itself a phenomenon of intelligence: the intellect does not admit the coexistence of contradictories. It is true that something highly mysterious, which escapes analysis and almost expression, takes place within us while we contemplate beauty; the discordant perceptions and conceptions persist, no doubt, but notwithstanding all this, and through all this, we see something unique, something living, which is precisely the aesthetic object; we feel rising from the depths of the soul, like a fire that fuses all the materials offered by the senses, we feel arising, from the first instant of disturbance, the harmonious representation, the warm vision of Beauty. What really happens, we do not know, says Fanciulli.

[p. 109]It is, in short, very natural, however, that this «feeling» should be an exquisite and most lofty enjoyment; it is already a noble pleasure — the effort which with apparent ease the psyche makes in order to arrive at that synthesis; at last we enter a new world, we ascend to the contact of a life that transcends all the pains, all the miseries and basenesses of our life. Inert matter expresses all that a man has seen, has thought, has felt of the most beautiful and the most intense; all things great and powerful it expresses with a single form. The artist, no doubt, will be the first to feel the beauty of his creature; but even we, humble spectators, can recognize in it the higher life and enjoy it, since, after all, all men are a little «man».

We feel, moreover, gratitude toward one who has labored for us; all the vague impressions, the confused or useless tendencies find in the work of art a full satisfaction; the statues and the canvases offer an appearance of life, such as we would wish it to be and such as it is not.

### IX. TEORÍA DE LA INTUICIÓN DE CROCE — IX. CROCE'S THEORY OF INTUITION

The theories of Lalo and Fanciulli tend to explain the aesthetic phenomenon by an interpenetration of the intellectual and affective factors of consciousness, even though the former grants the principal role to thought and the latter to emotion. But other theories are exclusivist, and either make of feeling a power of knowing the beautiful, like the Einfühlung, or absolutely eliminate that factor, like Croce, making aesthetic intuition a purely theoretical operation.

According to Croce, feeling can be, and has been, understood in various ways. In the first place, the word «feeling» has been adopted to denominate a class of psychic phenomena, constituted according to the naturalist and psychological method. Thus it has happened that, according to the times and the authors, the name «feelings» has been given to all the most rudimentary, tenuous, and fugitive manifestations of the spirit: the small intuitions (or sensations, as they are called), not yet transformed into perceptions, the small perceptions, the small tendencies and appetites — in sum, all that forms almost the ground of the life of the spirit. So too, on the other hand, that name has been given to psychic processes and conditions in which, with respect to an empirically limited matter, various forms follow one another or alternate, such as the so-called feelings «of [p. 111]the fatherland», «of love», «of nature», «of the divine».

Nothing prevents the forming of such classes and the use of those denominations; but they are of no use to philosophy, which not only does not receive them into its scheme but does not even occupy itself with them, save to reject them, as when they present themselves as psychological philosophy or philosophical psychology. To classify is not to think philosophically; and philosophy, on the one hand, knows no criteria of small and great, of weak and strong, of more and less, and a small or minute thought, a small or minute tendency, is for it thought and tendency and no longer feeling; and on the other hand, it does not admit complicated processes which it does not resolve into their simple components; whence the feeling of love or of the fatherland and the others adopted as examples present themselves to it as a series of acts of thought and of will, variously combined.

Another meaning of the word «feeling», which likewise is not here considered, at least for the present, is had when it is taken to designate the «state» of the spirit or of one among the particular forms of the spirit; thus one would say more correctly, the states, since in that case it polarizes, as is well known, into two opposed terms: pleasure and pain. That these two terms can also be conceived psychologically, as in the preceding case, is beyond doubt; whence it comes that pleasure and pain are presented by the psychologists as the two extremes of a continuous series, in which one passes from one term to the other by imperceptible increments and gradations. But that this psychological representation is not the only possible one, and is not the truly real one, and that the two terms have their own place and meaning in the philosophy of the spirit, must also be recognized. They are, as has been said, opposites, and they differ[p. 112]entiate themselves, no longer by a more and a less, by a maximum and a minimum, but by the character proper to distinction that opposites possess.

But the doctrine of opposites, and of opposites in the practical activity of the spirit, Croce rejects. In denying feeling, what is denied is not the doctrine of opposites and the psychology of the states of the spirit that is founded upon it, but the doctrine of feeling considered as a peculiar form of activity.

For Croce, the conception of feeling as spiritual activity has imposed itself as a necessity of research, which may be called the provisional choice. Each time one has found oneself before a form or subform of spiritual activity which one could not manage to eliminate or to absorb into the already recognized forms, the problem to be solved has been marked with the word «feeling», which afterwards has by many been mistaken for a solution. Feeling has been, in sum, in the history of philosophy, the indeterminate, or rather that which is not yet fully determined, the semi-determinate.

Thus, when a special aesthetic function was not recognized and one attempted to explain it from the intellectual point of view as an inferior form of philosophy, or from the historical point of view as a reproduction of the historical and natural datum, or almost as the satisfaction of certain volitional needs (the hedonist theory), it was a progress that art should be considered not as a form of intellect, nor of perception, nor of will, but of feeling, and that, in order to recognize and judge it, appeal should be made to men of feeling. By reason of such insistence, one ended by discovering a theoretical form, exceedingly simple and ingenuous, deprived almost of content, whether intellectual or historical: the form of pure intuition, which is that of [p. 113]aesthetic and artistic activity.

Once the discovery of pure intuition has been made, whoever returns to treating art as a product of feeling falls back from the determinate into the semi-determinate and remains exposed to all the perils that arise from it.

Croce declares that in History, as in philosophical Logic and in the Philosophy of the practical, feeling performs the same transitory role, and he concludes by maintaining that the theoretical and practical forms suffice to comprehend the whole of psychic activity. Every phenomenon of the spirit — that is, every manifestation of activity — examined not superficially, reduces to an act of fantasy, of intellect, and of perception, that is, of theory, or else to an act of utilitarian or ethical volition, unless they be regarded as an abstraction or a psychological class.

Having excluded feeling, Croce makes the aesthetic phenomenon consist in intuition, placing it in the category of the theoretical and not of the practical, wherein reside the economic and ethical phenomena. From not having exactly recognized the theoretical character of simple intuition — distinct alike from intellectual knowledge and from the perception of the real — from believing that only the intellectual, or at most the perception of the real, is knowledge, there has arisen the affirmation so many times repeated, that art is not knowledge, that it does not offer truth, that it belongs not to the theoretical world but to the sentimental one, and others of the like.

For Croce, intuition is knowledge, free of concepts and simpler than what is called the perception of the real; and therefore art is knowledge, is form; it does not belong to feeling and to psychic matter. If so many times and by so many aestheticians it has been insisted upon that art is appearance, it has been precisely because the need was felt of distinguishing it from the more complicated fact, [p. 114]perception, by affirming pure intuitivity. And if it has been insisted that art is «feeling», it has been for the same reason; for, the concept being excluded as the content of art, and historical reality as such being excluded, there remains no other content than reality apprehended merely in its ingenuousness and immediately, in its vital impulse, in its feeling — that is, pure intuition.

Croce associates, however, with this theoretical concept another more important one: that of art as a liberator. In elaborating the impressions, man frees himself from them. In objectifying them, he detaches them from himself and makes himself superior to them. The liberating and purifying function of art is another aspect and another formula of its character as activity. Activity is liberating precisely because it eliminates passivity. This explains why one is wont to attribute to artists at once the greatest sensibility or passionateness and the greatest insensibility or Olympian serenity. Both qualities are reconciled because they do not fall upon the same object. The sensibility or passionateness refers to the rich matter which the artist absorbs into his psychic organism, the insensibility or serenity to the form with which he subdues and dominates the sensational and passional tumult.

These ideas being established, it is understood that Croce combats the theory of the aesthetic senses, as well as aesthetic hedonism.

He recognizes feeling as a special activity, of a non-cognitive nature, which has its positive and negative poles, pleasure and pain; but if the activity of feeling is activity, it is nothing but economic activity. The activity that is called that of feeling is none other than the most elementary and fundamental practical activity, distinct from the ethical, and consisting in the appetite for and voli[p. 115]tion of any individual end whatsoever, foreign to all moral determination.

If feeling has sometimes been considered as organic or natural activity, that has come about because it coincides neither with logical activity, nor with the aesthetic, nor with the ethical; and, considered from the point of view of those three, which were the only ones admitted, it appeared outside the true and proper spirit — the spirit in its aristocracy — and almost as a determination of nature and of the psyche insofar as it is nature.

But if the activity of feeling, in the defined sense, ought not to be substituted for the other forms of spiritual activity, this does not mean that it cannot accompany them. It accompanies them necessarily; for all of them stand in close relation among themselves and with the elementary volitional form, whence each has as concomitants the individual volitions and the volitional pleasures and pains that are called feeling. Nevertheless, economic or hedonistic satisfaction, ethical satisfaction, aesthetic satisfaction, and intellectual satisfaction are always preserved as distinct within that union.

Thus there is resolved, in Croce's view, at the same time, the question whether feeling and pleasure precede or follow, whether they are cause or effect of the aesthetic phenomenon — a question which must be enlarged into that of the relation among the various spiritual forms, and resolved in the sense that one cannot speak of cause and effect, nor of a chronological before and after, within the unity of the spirit.

So too, the indicated relation being established, there is no point in the investigations that are wont to be made concerning the nature of the aesthetic, moral, intellectual, or even economic feelings, as has sometimes been done, because the differences derive not from the feeling but from the substantive that lends it its color.

[p. 116]In the same way we can free ourselves from the distinction between values, or feelings of value, and merely hedonistic feelings deprived of value, and from other similar distinctions, such as that between disinterested feelings and interested feelings, between objective feelings and the others that are non-objective, simply subjective, between feelings of approbation and others of mere delight. Those distinctions had for their object to save the three spiritual forms that had been recognized — as the trinity of the True, the Good, and the Beautiful — against confusion with the fourth form, still unknown and for that very reason insidious in its indeterminacy and the mother of scandals.

In conformity with this conception of feeling, considered as economic activity divided into two poles, positive and negative, pleasure and pain, Croce translates them into the useful and the useless or harmful. If each of these is a value, each has before it the anti-value or non-value. For non-value to obtain, it does not suffice that there be a simple absence of value; rather it is requisite that activity and passivity be in struggle with each other, without the one vanquishing the other: whence arise the contradiction and the non-value of activity hindered, opposed, interrupted. Value is activity that unfolds freely; non-value is its contrary.

The aesthetic, intellectual, economic, and ethical values and non-values have various denominations in current language: beautiful, true, good, useful, fitting, just, exact, which designate the free development of spiritual activity — the action, the scientific investigation, the artistic production well achieved; and ugly, false, bad, useless, unfitting, unjust, inexact, which designate the hampered activity, the product ill achieved.

[p. 117]Consistent with these ideas, Croce condemns hedonism in general and the particular aesthetic hedonism, which regards, if not all the other activities, at least the aesthetic one, as a mere phenomenon of feeling, and confounds the pleasure of expression, which is the beautiful, with pure pleasure, with the pleasure of any other kind whatsoever.

He condemns also, as forms of aesthetic hedonism, the theory of play, the theory of sensuality and of triumph, and the aesthetics of sympathy: the first, which derives art from the exuberant nervous activity that is exercised without useful end; the second, which has attempted to deduce the pleasure of art from the resonance of the pleasure of the sexual organs, or from the pleasure of overcoming or triumphing, from the need of the male who desires to conquer the female; and the third, less gross, which regards Aesthetics as the science of the sympathetic, of that with which we sympathize — without considering that the sympathetic is nothing but the image or representation of what pleases, and as such is a complex phenomenon, resulting from a constant element, which is the aesthetic element of representation, and from a variable one, which is pleasure in its infinite appearances, arising from all the various classes of values.

### X. TEORÍA BIOLÓGICA DE BASCH — X. BASCH'S BIOLOGICAL THEORY

If Croce removes from the aesthetic conception the function of feeling as a rudimentary practical activity, other psychologists affirm it, giving it a biological or organic character and building upon that basis the structure of the aesthetic phenomenon. Such is the case with Basch, the critic of Kantian aesthetics.

For Kant, this phenomenon is a state of contemplation; it is at once a state of knowledge and a state of feeling; it consists in the harmonious activity of the imagination and the understanding, and it is the consciousness of this harmony that constitutes aesthetic pleasure par excellence, the common aesthetic feeling, for which Kant claims universality and necessity, and which he distinguishes from the other forms of feeling, from the agreeable, logical, and moral feelings. This feeling is an intellectual feeling, a feeling of reflection, a feeling of judgment. It accompanies the work of the imagination and the understanding, and since this work consists, on the one hand, in the representation and reproduction of the multiple elements of knowledge, and, on the other, in the reduction of those multiple elements to a conceptual unity, it is properly the intellectual feeling of unity in multiplicity, or, according to the consecrated formula, of unity in variety. It is the translation, in subjective terms, of the theory of Leibniz and Baumgarten, who made the beautiful consist in perfection, and which Kant had combated.

[p. 119]Basch declares it incontestable that this feeling of unity in variety, of the union of the multiple, is one of the essential elements of aesthetic feeling in general; but that it does not constitute aesthetic feeling par excellence, nor the whole of the feeling of the beautiful; because, since that harmony between the understanding and the imagination is a necessity for all knowledge, everything would be beautiful and the ugly, or the indifferent, could not be explained. Moreover, if it were true that the feeling of the harmony of the imagination and the understanding, of the union of the multiple, sufficed to give us the feeling of the beautiful, one would not understand why the mere juxtaposition of any elements whatever, having some points in common, could not cause us an aesthetic pleasure; one could not explain why geometrical figures and arithmetical and algebraic formulas would not constitute works of art. Kant, then, has studied only the intellectual aspect of aesthetic feeling, notwithstanding that this passes through successive moments, which constitute its diverse forms.

According to Basch, the first of these forms is incontestably the sensible shock, produced by the sensible elements that compose the aesthetic object. Without that shock it would be incomprehensible that we should pause to contemplate the beautiful. The pleasure that beautiful forms offer us is a pleasure of touch and a muscular pleasure. The first form of aesthetic feeling is sensible pleasure, what Kant calls the agreeable; everything that is beautiful must, of course, be agreeable, without the converse being true, without everything that is agreeable being necessarily beautiful.

Once this first form of aesthetic feeling is recognized, the intellectual form must be joined to it. With the pleasure that the intrinsic quality of [p. 120]sensations causes in us there comes to be combined the intellectual pleasure of their grouping, of their form, a pleasure that reduces to the pleasure of unity in variety, of the union of the multiple. This pleasure is much more complex than the first. It does not spring from a simple process of peripheral nervous stimulation, but always implies memory, attention, and comparison; that is, an activity of the higher nervous centers. Nevertheless, even in those intellectual pleasures there is a sensible element whose importance must be recognized.

To these two forms of feeling, sensible feeling and formal feeling, a third is joined, one extremely important. The first two being direct feelings, the third is indirect, an ideal feeling, an associated feeling. Association, with its two great forms of contiguity and resemblance, plays, in effect, a considerable role, not only in the representative life, but also in the life of feeling. Given a joyful or painful state of soul, we can associate with it all the joyful or painful elements that offer points of analogy with the first or that we have experienced at the same time as the first. This admitted, one understands how profound is the modification that our associations make our feelings undergo. If the associated feelings, when compared with the sensible feelings and the formal feelings, may be called indirect aesthetic elements, it is necessary to distinguish, among those associated feelings, the feelings associated directly from those associated indirectly. Alongside the feelings identical in all, which the contemplation of a determinate object awakens, there are some that belong to us exclusively and that constitute one's own emotional coloring. But here it must be observed that what is evoked before beautiful objects is not the associations themselves, not [p. 121]the distinct representation of all that refers to those objects, but the feelings of those associations, which come to fuse into a single feeling, which constitutes one of the essential elements of the aesthetic impression.

Aesthetic feeling would be, then, according to Basch, above all, the feeling of an activity at once intense and free, of a favorable stimulation of the nervous substance. It would be, moreover, formal feeling par excellence, the feeling of the union of the multiple. If one passes, next, from that feeling to the external objects that cause it or in connection with which it is awakened, it can come to be the associated feeling of a subjective finality, by virtue of the consideration that the objects seem as though predisposed to produce the harmonious activity of our faculties of knowing. To that feeling of subjective finality there may, moreover, be associated another or many others more elevated and more profound. We can, in this particular harmony, realized between an object and our faculties of knowing, see as it were a reflection of the universal harmony, and experience the metaphysical and moral feeling that the conviction inspires in us that the abyss between the world of phenomena and the noumena is not impassable, that the intelligence which has created the universe has had in view our faculties of knowing and has endowed the world with organism and beauty, as a pledge, as a symbol of the reconciliation between the world of knowledge and the suprasensible world of freedom; and that would then be the aesthetic feeling of the beautiful in its supreme form, as Kant seems to believe.

There is not, then, according to Basch, a single aesthetic feeling. There are innumerable forms, which reduce to three types: of sensible feeling, intellectual or formal feeling, and associated feelings.

The beautiful object is, [p. 122]for us, above all, the object capable of awakening in us, at once, those three orders of feelings in all their intensity and in proportions that vary to infinity. It must satisfy, at once, our intellectual nature and our moral nature. The harmony that it realizes is not only a harmony between our imagination and our understanding, but addresses itself to all the living forces of our individual being, in its indissoluble unity of corporeal being and spiritual being. Above all, it provokes in us a favorable stimulation of our nervous substance; it is a feeling of life at once intense and easy, at once active and passive, at once creative and receptive. Next, it is the feeling of an intellectual life, easy and harmonious, capable of embracing without fatigue a multiplicity of elements converging toward a unity. It is, moreover, the feeling in which come to fuse the feelings of all the direct and indirect, necessary and contingent associations, which the intuitions of objects of nature and of art provoke in us, insofar as these have, not only a sensible and formal value, but also, above all, a representative and expressive value of their nature, of their content, of real or ideal forces that constitute them. Before a beautiful object, we experience a single impression of confused joy, into which the elements we have enumerated all enter, at once, in different proportions, without distinctly reaching consciousness, without being able to be analyzed or expressed, and which is the more intense the more all the essential feelings that constitute our life are found as though crystallized within it.

The feelings of the agreeable, the intellectual feelings, and the moral feelings differ from aesthetic feeling in that the latter is a resultant of the former; but the true differential character [p. 123]lies in the disinterestedness of aesthetic feeling, which Kant has not demonstrated, although he established it, grounding it in the fact that this feeling depends solely on the mere representation, contemplation, or intuition of the beautiful object. To explain it, the English aestheticians have grounded themselves on the theory of play; Kirchmann on the absolute separation between real feelings and ideal ones; and the idealists, from Vischer to Hartmann, by subordinating disinterestedness to the concept in the aesthetic appearance.

Basch rejects these explanations and replaces them with psychological analysis, which shows that the sensations of the higher senses of sight and hearing are naturally disinterested — and for this reason they are called the aesthetic senses — and, in functioning, impress upon the emotion those proper characters which distinguish it from those produced by the lower senses, which are directly destined for the functions of conservation and reproduction.

Recapitulating his observations, Basch defines the aesthetic feelings as the immediate feelings due to the higher senses, which refer neither necessarily nor directly to organic functions, which emanate only from appearance, from images of things; which have for their end nothing but the immediate pleasure produced by this appearance, nor are subject to the degrading conditions that accompany the satisfaction of organic pleasures; which are, in general, less intense than the greater part of the other emotions, which exercise, consequently, a less profound action upon our will, and can therefore be more easily eliminated and coexist, in greater number, with more rapid and more abrupt variations; which are, in short, sympathetic and social feelings.

[p. 124]Given these characters, Basch seeks to know whether among them one dominates the others and is the cause of them all, and he establishes that this character is that of sociability, that of sympathy, to which Kant attributed a great importance and which is correlative with that of disinterestedness.

Basch believes he finds in sociability and sympathy all the particular characters enumerated as distinctive of aesthetic feeling. The sympathetic feelings, in effect, refer neither directly nor necessarily to the organic functions, are not subject to the denigrating conditions that accompany the satisfaction of organic pleasures, are less intense than all the egoistic emotions, arouse a less profound action upon our will, can be more easily eliminated, and coexist in greater number with the more rapid and more abrupt variations. Finally, one of the essential ends of the pleasures of sympathy is, precisely, the pleasure that it makes us experience. For the reduction to be complete, there remains a last character, the peculiarity of aesthetic feeling of being caused, not by the essence of things, but by their appearance, their images — which does not seem to us deducible from the character of sympathy, and which will serve to differentiate the aesthetic sympathetic feelings from all the other sympathetic feelings.

For Basch, the feeling of sympathy is, in the last analysis, the feeble revival of an affective state by the intermediary of a presentation. A presentation awakens in our organism the reactions that primitively corresponded to it, though all sympathy is, at bottom, an imitation. To explain the origin of the sympathetic feelings, it is necessary to appeal to the indissoluble relations between mother and child.

[p. 125]The aesthetic feeling being reduced to a feeling of sympathy, the antinomy vanishes between the interest that every agreeable feeling entails and the disinterestedness that is one of the necessary characteristics of the feeling of the beautiful. Aesthetic feeling, like every feeling of sympathy, is at once interested and disinterested. It is interested in this sense, that when we enjoy beauty we feel the sensual pleasure of the normal and adequate play of our higher senses, a maximum of stimulation with a minimum of fatigue, and the psychic pleasure of a prolongation of our life, of an energetic development of our intellectual faculties — since this enjoyment is ours, forms part of our self, and we cannot, consequently, but hope for it, desire it. But, on the other hand, it is disinterested, in the sense that the enjoyment we experience we do not isolate from the complex feeling of which it forms part, we do not seek it for itself, it is not the end of the feeling of the beautiful.

Examining, next, the nature of the symbol, whose concept he believes necessary to explain aesthetic feeling — as Kant, Vischer, and Groos have believed — Basch holds that the symbol, as an aesthetic act, is reduced to the feeling of sympathy. In effect, this act, by which we go out of ourselves to merge with things, to attribute our feelings to them, to confer upon them a personality analogous to our own, to mingle ourselves so intimately with the objects and movements of the external world, is nothing but the phenomenon of sympathy, which has its degrees, from the simple sentimental contagion, which is no more than an imitative reproduction of external movements, to sympathy properly so called, which is the intense and intimate participation of our self in the life that exists in, or that we offer to, another self.

[p. 126]Basch concludes from this analysis, definitively, that aesthetic feeling resides essentially in the act of sympathizing with things, or rather with the appearances of things. Basch's conclusion is the Einfühlung of Lipps and Volkelt.

Basch reduces to sympathy likewise the direct sensible factor, the direct intellectual or formal factor, and the associated factors. According to him, for the feeling of the normal exercise of the higher senses to become aesthetic, it is necessary to add to it the instinctive symbolization, which engenders a bond of sympathy between our nervous system and the external excitations; it is necessary to attribute our feelings to them, to associate our personality with them. Moreover, every aesthetic sensation, even an elementary one, is like the symbol of the universal harmony. In the aesthetic feeling that a beautiful color or a pure sound causes in us, it seems to us that there necessarily enters the presentiment of the universal order, and that it allows us to penetrate, through our sympathy, to the movements of the most tenuous elements of things, to identify ourselves with them, and to find in them the image of the movements of our soul. Kant had well observed that harmony was one of the essential conditions of all aesthetic feeling; but this harmony he had reduced to the conscious and logical accord of the imagination and the understanding. According to Basch, one has only to broaden that conception, one has only to join to this harmony that which exists between the laws of our physiological organization and those of the physical world, in order to arrive at the theory of sympathy.

In the formal factor, as in the direct sensible one, it is symbolization, sympathy, that explains aesthetic feeling; for forms, as Lotze and Vischer believe, show that their rhythmic impression is nothing [p. 127]more than the delicious total impression of a harmonious series of self-movements which fulfill their end, and sympathy truly explains the pleasure that the forms and contours of the external world cause in us.

As for the associated factor, Basch begins by showing that symbolism necessarily presupposes the work of association; but it is necessary to investigate whether that work of association, which is an indispensable condition of the aesthetic act, is the sufficient condition, whether it is not necessary that something else come to join it in order to give birth to the feeling of the beautiful. To this end Basch distinguishes the phenomenon of association from that of symbolism. For him, sympathetic symbolism resides in the semi-unconscious and semi-conscious, semi-voluntary and semi-involuntary act by which we offer ourselves to objects, merge with them, confer upon them a personality, transforming them into states of soul. For Basch, as for Fechner, Siebeck, Hermann, and other associationists, association is a necessary condition of aesthetic contemplation and feeling, but it is not a sufficient condition of aesthetic feeling, because that association is necessarily realized in the beautiful as in the ugly and the indifferent, because it is an operation that precedes the aesthetic act, as Volkelt affirms. What applies to direct association may be applied also to indirect association, which has greater relations with the aesthetic state.

The great difference between association properly so called, direct or indirect, and sympathetic symbolism, consists in this: that in all association there is an operation which is not immediately intuitive and sensible, but is a memory, a determinate experience, in a word, a knowledge, whereas in the act of symbolization we never leave the sphere of spontaneous intuition, of immediate feeling.

In aesthetic [p. 128]vision the union of the elements is so perfect, so complete, that there is truly fusion, and that it is absolutely impossible, even to the most penetrating analysis, to dissociate the sensible element and the intellectual element. Whereas in association we always know, very distinctly, that there is an object and a subject, in aesthetic vision we do not know it, nor do we care to know it. What distinguishes, in short, association from aesthetic symbolism is that, if symbolism necessarily presupposes this association, it cannot be reduced to it, and that association is absolutely incapable of explaining what constitutes the properly aesthetic element of the contemplation of the beautiful and of the feeling bound up with it — the act by which we metamorphose dead things, making them ours, transubstantiate them, making them persons, living souls in our own image.

The three elements of all aesthetic feeling — the direct sensible factor, the direct intellectual or formal factor, and the associated factor — are explained, then, by the feeling of sympathy, and reduce to it. The feeling of the beautiful is, above all, a sympathetic feeling, and the aesthetic act consists, essentially, in the act of conferring upon external objects life, personality, of lending them a soul, our soul.

The aesthetic state being reduced to a state of sympathy with things, it is necessary to seek the first source of the feeling of the beautiful in the movements of sympathy, as irresistible, spontaneous, and natural to the human soul as the egoistic movements. And this Basch does, rising from animal sympathy to intellectual sympathy and to aesthetic sympathy.

He accepts at the origins the activity of play, with which Spencer occupies himself, but denies that it is identical to aesthetic [p. 129]activity. He accepts also the elementary aesthetic feelings; but if every feeling must be agreeable, the converse is not true, and in any case it is necessary that the phenomenon of sympathy present itself in order for the feeling to be aesthetic. It is in the feelings of higher sympathy that the origin of the aesthetic feelings must be sought, and these could not have developed except by virtue of a slow evolution, after the egoistic feelings and the feelings of instinctive sympathy innate to human nature.

What differentiates aesthetic judgment from every other judgment is, consequently, its dependence upon feeling.

As one sees, Basch's theory is that of German sentimentalism, with a biological basis.

### XI. TEORÍA POSITIVISTA DEL JUEGO — XI. THE POSITIVIST THEORY OF PLAY

Although the biological theory of play no longer has the importance it enjoyed during the predominance of Spencerian positivism, it is worth knowing, because it still exerts an influence upon recent aesthetic theories, as is the case in those of Lalo and Basch.

Under the title of aesthetic feelings, Spencer comprehends states of consciousness of every degree of complexity, from those which, like the sensations, have their origin in purely physical conditions, to those which are representative in the most extreme degree. In all these states, Spencer attributes aesthetic pleasure to three sources: the primary source is a combination of such a nature that the faculties are exercised as completely as possible, with the least expenditure. To this source comes to be joined a secondary one, the diffusion of the normal stimulus, that is to say, diffuse nervous discharges, in great proportions, which develop a wave of agreeable feeling, faint and indefinable; and to these two sources is joined a third, the partial development, through the effect of these discharges, of various particular attractions, bound up, in experience, with the combinations of the given species.

For this philosopher, the aesthetic character of the psychological phenomenon is determined by its remoteness from [p. 131]the functions that serve life. The aesthetic consciousness is, essentially, that in which the actions themselves constitute the object, abstraction being made of their ends; aesthetic activity is an activity of pure play, without any tendency toward a practical or positive end, without any useful end. Aesthetic excitation is that which is produced when there is an exercise of certain faculties, with a view to those faculties themselves, abstraction being made of all utility.

Consequently, the aesthetic feelings and emotions do not differ, according to Spencer, from the rest, either in their origin or in their nature. The same energies are set in action; the difference lies in the attitude of the consciousness with respect to the states that result from that action; it lies in its disinterested character. But this makes of the aesthetic emotion a unique case, which differs from the other emotions, whose origin and reason for being lie, as Ribot says, in the conservation of the individual as such or as a social being, in that the activity which produces them has for its end, not the fulfilment of a vital or social function, but the very pleasure of exercising itself, having served only accidentally as a social factor of the second order.

According to this biological explanation, it is necessary that the human organism should reach such a development that it can emancipate itself from the practical necessities of life and enter into that activity of pure play, in order to experience the aesthetic emotion.

Spencer, in explaining in this manner the nature of the aesthetic emotion, revived the theory of play initiated by Kant and developed by Schiller and others of his disciples; only that Spencer transferred the phenomenon from the logical order, in which it was defined by Kant, who considered it as the consciousness of the free play of the cognitive faculties, or as a finality without an end, [p. 132]to the biological order, as a nervous energy developed in all its plenitude, with the least possible expenditure and without any practical end. What for Kant was a judgment, for Spencer is a feeling. The aesthetic phenomenon thus ceased to move solely within the domain of pure contemplation, in which it had been placed by the formalists, who considered in it only the element of quality, leaving aside that of intensity.

Ribot, who accepts this theory, recognizes that, in effect, the aesthetic feeling is necessarily bound to physiological conditions, as Spencer defines it. There are, he says, in the constitution of that feeling, two factors: one direct, bound to the sensations and perceptions, and another indirect, bound to the representations (images and associations of ideas), the one or the other predominating according to the different species of beauty and the moments of the emotion.

For Ribot, the origin of that feeling is likewise an excess of activity, which is spent in a particular direction, under the influence of the creative imagination in artistic production. Its characteristic is disinterestedness. The more directly a tendency is bound to life, the more necessary, exacting, and serious it is, and the less it lends itself to aesthetic emotion, Ribot repeats; because it lacks an excess of activity to be spent freely.

The predominant character of the aesthetic emotion, according to this doctrine, is its disinterestedness, its uselessness. Aesthetic emotion and art, consequently, are nothing but a form of play. Play, as Ribot says, is a genus of which aesthetic activity is only a species; it is distinguished from the other forms of play only by the materials employed, images in this case, and by the direction followed.

[p. 133]But not all the aestheticians who are partisans of the theory of play accept uselessness as the essential characteristic of the aesthetic phenomenon, establishing a radical opposition between the beautiful and the useful.

Groos substitutes for the thesis of a superabundance of energy that of a primitive instinct, of which play, under all its forms, would be the expression. According to Spencer, Sergi, and others, play is explained thus: the higher animals, thanks to a better nutrition, and thanks also to a greater division of labor among the organs, which permits some to rest while the others are in activity, produce more nervous force than they expend. When the excess reaches a determinate quantity, the organism experiences the imperious need to discharge it; if, at that moment, no real, serious end solicits it to act, its activity will be spent without object, for the pleasure of spending itself, and in this consists play. On the other hand, since the acts useful for the existence of the individual or of the species are the most habitual, they are also those which offer the easiest slope; and that is why play consists in the functioning, without burden, of the most important instincts, in the stimulation of the principal acts of life.

Karl Groos combats this explanation at length. An excess of energy is, according to him, a circumstance that favors play, but it is not absolutely necessary to it. Play is, above all, a preparation for the serious life: such is its reason for being and its biological utility. Given the complexity of the instincts in the higher beings, it was very useful that the animal should be able to execute them in a non-serious manner, before the moment when those instincts became indispensable to its existence; that is to say, to exercise them without running the risks that clumsiness or inexperience would later produce. This prepa[p. 134]ratory exercise attenuates, moreover, the mechanical rigor of the instinct, permits a more adequate adaptation to the infinite variations of the environment and, a thing more important still, makes possible the gradual substitution of intelligence, the fruit of individual experience, for the reflexes transmitted hereditarily by the ancestors. Hence the appearance and the development of the play instinct, or, more exactly, of the tendency to satisfy, through games, the inclinations that cannot yet be manifested seriously. Other instincts, the instinct of imitation for example, may moreover combine with that one in certain particular forms of play.

Groos has analyzed profoundly this activity of luxury, which man, as a higher animal, would have been able to develop amply, refining it more and more until arriving at the constitution of a superior play sui generis, which is art. If play and art differ notably today, it is because these two orders of facts, joined primitively, have followed a separate line of development; but between the two there exist numerous and evident points of contact. Play, says Groos, is a species of activity which, without being motivated by exterior ends, exists solely for the enjoyment it produces. The same is the case with aesthetic pleasure in general. It too is autonomous; that is to say, independent of every exterior end; and even when the individual devotes himself to an occupation that produces aesthetic enjoyment for an end other than the enjoyment in itself (for example, in order to learn), this end remains always as something absolutely secondary, which neither augments nor diminishes the aesthetic enjoyment.

Play arises from the need of activity of the nervous system and takes place when every more serious mode of acting is wanting; analogous is aesthetic enjoyment. In play there are distinguished two culminating aspects of pleasure, the [p. 135]pleasurable and the intensive. The first is obtained when to psychic reactions of weak or mediocre intensity there corresponds a sweet and pure well-being, full of harmony; while the second takes place in correspondence with violent and impetuous reactions, in which one has the feeling of an excitation, generally not without some slight disagreeable feeling being mingled with it. This distinction can be repeated even in the world of Art. Finally, common to play and to aesthetic enjoyment is the feeling of freedom, that is to say, of liberation, in daily life, from the mean preoccupations of existence. And this is obtained in various ways: first, the voluntary and free entrance into the field of play and of enjoyment; second, the voluntary submission to the norms that regulate those facts and that would be difficult to obtain in the field of man's ordinary activity; third, the voluntary illusion they entail; fourth, the voluntary dedication, without reserve, with which man abandons himself to play and to aesthetic enjoyment. Setting out from these analogies, Groos believes himself authorized to conceive the aesthetic phenomenon, in its substance, as a form of play, albeit the noblest.

Groos shares the aesthetic ideal of Schiller, introducing into play and into art the principle of the autonomy of the real self, which feels itself to be the cause of the pseudo-representations and pseudo-feelings that it draws freely from itself and transports unconsciously into the world of appearance. In the play of aesthetic appearance, he says, man is free; that is to say, he is entirely free only where he plays, because there is no real freedom in the domain of experience. Groos finds that Schiller was perfectly right in saying that the feeling of freedom was the most elevated and most precious result of play, a feeling of freedom that is closely bound to the feeling of necessity. We [p. 136]feel, in effect, that we are forces and by that very fact free. Such is the intimate nature of the state of the soul in play; we feel ourselves constrained, because pseudo-activity has this in common with the hypnotic states, that they treat pure appearance as if it were reality. We are constrained because we are in the power of an illusion, and we are free because we ourselves have provoked it.

One may, then, affirm that nowhere do we feel ourselves as free as in play; because, making abstraction of all transcendental determinism, one may say that, psychologically, if we feel ourselves free to act, it is because we feel the power to act, because it pleases us to act, and this without other reason; and, on the other hand, we feel the power to interrupt the action, from the moment it pleases us to do so. One may, briefly, characterize the feeling of freedom in the following manner, according to Groos: when we feel ourselves free, it is that we feel ourselves the absolute cause of our states. This may be an error for the metaphysician and for the theorist of knowledge; but it is a psychological fact that we can have that feeling, and there is no doubt whatever that this fact has an infinite practical importance. To say that we feel ourselves the absolute cause signifies, of course, that we have the impression of being determined completely by ourselves, by our present will; no non-self seems to influence us, neither the present objects, nor the idea of our anterior or future experiences. It seems as though we were separated from the causal nexus and realized only what we have the desire to realize, without concerning ourselves with conditions or effects. It seems as though we were, as Kant says, the beginning of a series of causes and effects.

The feeling of freedom is, moreover, augmented by the impression that we can, at each instant, stop ourselves and not finish an action. Here too the [p. 137]feeling of freedom is identical with the conviction of being the absolute cause. The instinctive impulse of every living being, to conserve its independence, to prevent invasion, attains its psychic form, the most elevated, in the aspiration toward freedom. The pleasure that the feeling of freedom offers is the most elevated degree of this joy of being a cause, which has long been familiar to us. Now, the feeling of freedom, the purest and the most intense, is found only in the domain of play. In real life we are, on every side, under the empire of objects and under the double pressure of the future and the past. The joy of being a cause finds its summit in the most elevated and most delicate pleasure, in the feeling of freedom contained in the appearance we have ourselves created. Groos thus finds the most important factor of aesthetic enjoyment, giving to freedom a psychological foundation that Schiller does not examine, dominated as he was by his metaphysical orientation. Only that Groos does not distinguish play from art, which have radical differences.

Ribot and Bray believe that the theories of Spencer and Groos concerning play do not exclude one another, but that, on the contrary, they presuppose and complete one another reciprocally. That of Spencer, says Bray, makes known to us only the physiological conditions of play, without elucidating its biological signification, as Groos observes; but one may, with the same reason, reproach the latter with seeing only this last and disdaining the physiological aspect of the question. His theory, adds Bray, explains well to us why selection must produce the development of the play instinct, but does not teach us how this tendency could have been born.

With the object of combining both explanations, Bray proposes the following. The production of an excess of nervous force must have made, simultaneously, its [p. 138]appearance by way of several means of discharge; among these means, selection must, naturally, have favored those which, like games, present the inestimable advantage of preparing the organism for the struggle for life. By mutual action and reaction, at the same time that this preparation permitted the perfecting of the instincts, their more exact adaptation to the variations of the environment, and the introduction of intelligence into the domain of the reflex act, its importance went on growing with the contemplation of those instincts. Thus, from the role of a useful accessory effect, it has passed, little by little, to the rank of an indispensable factor. Play has come to be an integral part in the development of the animal; a period more or less long of its life has adapted itself to that genus of activity, and at present an imperious tendency, an inescapable force impels the young mammal to play, spending its nervous reserves. The absence of games and of youth properly so called in other classes of the animal kingdom, whose instincts are nevertheless comparable to those of the higher vertebrates (for example, in the insects), seems to militate in favor of this manner of seeing. If one holds strictly to the opinions of Groos, says Bray, one cannot understand how selection has not brought the play instinct to birth in the cases in which there was the same utility for doing so. The theory of Spencer offers a satisfactory answer: selection has developed nothing, because the indispensable original variation does not present itself; games do not appear because their physiological base, that is to say, the excess of nervous force, is wanting.

Be that as it may, concludes Bray, in the one as in the other explanation, play is the manifestation of a tendency to simulate the essential acts of life, without any immediate practical end, without other object than the activity itself, at least in appearance. This tendency engen[p. 139]ders, according to Ribot, the need for physical exercise, the taste for adventures, the passion for games of chance, and the aesthetic emotion.

Sergi, who likewise accepts this theory, believes that the first manifestation of aesthetic pleasure is found in the imitation of the useful acts of life. The transition between pure play and aesthetic activity, which is play as creation, is the pantomimic dance. Primitively, the dance represents two capital facts in the life of man: the struggle against other men and sexual love. It becomes, thereupon, a representative art, extending itself to the representation or simulation of all the acts of social life. This art is, then, primordial, without direct and immediate end, universal and symbolic. Ribot goes so far as to maintain that painting and sculpture have issued from it.

From this theory it is deduced: that imitation is the fundamental aesthetic principle, which attains its perfection with creation in art; that if the beautiful is nothing but a play and art an imitation, there is an irreducible divorce between the beautiful of art and the beautiful in nature; and that, if the beautiful and art are nothing but an activity without end, there is excluded all that is useful, all that supposes a need or a desire.

To explain the beautiful in nature, Sergi appeals to an obscure and unconscious memory of feelings experienced in the prehistoric epoch, when men enjoyed fully the state of nature, when they were adorers of nature, out of fear or terror, when their joys, their hopes, and their sorrows were associated with the contemplation of nature in its primitive state. Ribot makes it derive from an increasing extension of sympathy, which sets out from man to reach the whole world.

[p. 140]Ribot appeals to indirect social utility to explain how the aesthetic emotion could have evolved in the absence of direct utility. Alongside the dance, which has played the role of discipline, of collective action, of school of war, the arts in repose have offered adornments, converted thereupon into social signs; besides, they supposed and perfected the visual memory and the manual habit, two faculties eminently useful to primitive men. The evolution of the aesthetic feeling presents itself under two distinct aspects: strictly social in its origin, it tends toward individualism through three successive phases; in the first, pleasure coexists with the useful, is enclosed within it, in a common state of consciousness: the agreeable; it was necessary, in order to be felt, that it should possess some individual or social utility; in the second, the relation relaxes; what nature had made for use became adornment, according to Emerson's word; in the third, finally, there was absolute independence, expressed in the thesis of art for art's sake, which appears only very late in mature civilizations. Strictly human in its origin, it tends more and more to comprehend the whole of nature by the natural extension of sensibility and of sympathy, under the influence of civilization: man has admired his fellow, his bodily adornments, then his arms and his utensils, the animals, and, finally, nature, first in reproduction and more or less humanized, and, in the last place, savage nature.

This notion of the beautiful, pure of all utility and of all interest, derived from the theory of play, is none other than that of Kant. If we emancipate it, says Bray, from the forms proper to the philosophical system of the author, in order to reduce it to its essential principles, the theory of Kant may, in effect, be enclosed in the following propositions: the judgment of taste is entirely disinterested; it has [p. 141]no end, neither objective nor subjective; it has not for motive attraction or emotion, although these be among the things that may mingle with the satisfaction of the beautiful; neither is it founded upon any interest, which distinguishes it from the good, the agreeable, and the useful; but nothing prevents that, once acquired, it should be joined indirectly to an interest, and it is precisely social life that brings this to birth and gives it its power; a man isolated on an island would not think of adorning his dwelling; it is society that produces in his spirit the idea that he is not merely a man, but a man distinguished within his kind, which constitutes the beginning of civilization; it is society that has given importance and a great interest, first, to things that were no more than simple attractions, that is to say, the colors with which one painted oneself, or to flowers, shells, feathers, and afterward, likewise, with time, has given it to beautiful forms (in canoes, for example, and in garments, etc.), which of themselves offer no enjoyment.

If one separates from the work of Kant, on the one hand, all that the progress of experimental science renders unacceptable, such as the concept of the beautiful stripped of all attraction and of all emotion, and gives, on the other hand, a physiological base to the psychological principles he has brought into relief, there would be effaced, says Bray, even the shadow of a difference between the thesis of the Critique of Judgment and that of the psychologists whose opinions have just been expressed. When Spencer defines the aesthetic consciousness as that in which the actions themselves form the object, abstraction being made of their ends, he does no more than reproduce, almost in the same terms, the famous formula of the Critique of Judgment, that «finality without an end», that «causality which consists in conserving, without further object, the state of the representation itself and the play of the faculties of knowing».

[p. 142]Bray combats this theory, which makes the essential characteristic of the subjective aesthetic phenomenon consist in disinterestedness, in its opposition to the useful, considering it exaggerated and incomplete. That our aesthetic emotions, the most elevated, should be exempt from every interested motive cannot be denied, although the importance of that character has been much exaggerated; but what Bray does not admit is that, from this, it must be concluded that disinterestedness is, always and in every degree, the essential thing in aesthetic activity, and much less that it should be so in its obscure and distant origins, more animal than human, in which it is possible to object to the utilitarian character attributed to the intellectual and moral feelings. Bray does not believe that there is reason to deny the beautiful to what is attributed to the good, to truth, to art, to morality, and to science, which are equivalent means with a view to the single end: the common happiness of the greatest number.

In his conception, the analogies that have been sought to be established between the aesthetic emotion and the pleasure of play do not derive from experience, but rest exclusively upon an aprioristic conception of play and of art considered as essentially disinterested; a conception to which Spencer has given a physiological base. The opinion that makes of play the type of disinterested activity is not, on the other hand, sheltered from all criticism, as Souriau demonstrates in his work «The Aesthetics of Movement». According to Souriau, in play we are always preoccupied with the result of our activity, whatever, for that matter, may be the intrinsic value of this end, which may be nothing but the honor of winning; in play it is essential, in order that it produce pleasure, that it exalt the imagination; for one who had in it no interest, for one who remained indifferent before loss or gain, play would be only a motive of fatigue and of tedium; the true player takes an in[p. 143]terest in his game and frequently grows passionate over it. Besides, very frequently play has for its object to make us stronger or more skillful, and in that case disinterestedness would not be intelligible.

Finally, it is an observed fact that man does not truly amuse himself, does not truly deploy all his activity, save when there is emulation, and this, in its turn, excludes disinterestedness. Disinterested play, says Groos, making his own an expression of Souriau, encloses a contradiction, because the enthusiasm experienced derives essentially from the joy of being a cause, of being power, of feeling oneself strong, which, at bottom, is nothing but the joy of conquering, as may be observed in all the games of animals. Now, this joy of conquering supposes necessarily a difficulty to be overcome, and, this being admitted, one cannot say that play is an activity without object.
