If this is so, if, at least in the greater part of the cases, play is not, properly speaking, a play, that is to say, a pleasure, save when it excites a real interest, distinct from that which consists in an expenditure of forces effected simply with a view to the expenditure itself, then the whole system that makes of play the point of departure of aesthetic evolution, solely because it believes it stripped of all interest, is without base, as is the erroneous conception that has given it birth.

Bray examines also the characters upon which Groos founds himself in order to refer art to play and to deduce from the latter the origin of the former. Those characters, which have nothing to do with that pretended disinterestedness, may be reduced to two principal points: first, the pleasure of art, like that of play, is, in the last analysis, nothing but the pleasure of deploying one's power, of extending one's sphere of action, whether by creating, or principally by acting upon the spirit of the spectator or of the audience; second, in art, as in play, there exists the consciousness of an ap[p. 144]parent activity, which implies two things: a doubling, more or less profound, of the consciousness, and a feeling of freedom, which proceeds from the fact that we feel ourselves the cause of the appearance and masters of making it cease when it pleases us.

Bray considers these two propositions as almost incontestable, but does not believe that they have the importance Groos attributes to them so as to consider them a sufficient demonstration of the kinship between play and art. For Bray, the first of those two analogies proves absolutely nothing; because one may conclude from the very categorical terms of Groos that the joy of power is inherent in every activity that supposes a difficulty overcome; that is to say, as much, if not more, in real activity, which has a practical end, as in the conventional activity in play; whence it follows that there is no more reason to apply art to the second than to the first, from this point of view at least.

There remains, then, only the analogy founded upon the apparent character of the activity. The conscious illusion that exists in the artist, as in the player, supposes necessarily a doubling of the consciousness; in other terms, it implies that, alongside the self of appearance of play and of artistic production, the real self persists and influences the former by ways probably unconscious. But this phenomenon of doubling does not neatly separate art from reality, nor does it create between it and play an indisputable kinship. Let us not forget, says Bray, that this doubling is far from being rare; that it is met with even in the most ordinary circumstances of daily life, and that, from the fact of that phenomenon being found in the player and in the artist, one cannot conclude that art is a form of play.

[p. 145]Neither does Bray believe that the simultaneous existence, in play and in art, of a feeling of freedom is more demonstrative of that relation; because, according to Groos himself, that feeling has its origin in the combination of two preceding factors: the pleasure of being a cause and the doubling of the consciousness. We, he says, feel ourselves the cause, and the absolute cause, of an appearance, that is to say, of a thing which it depends upon us to produce and to make cease at will, and it is in this that the feeling of freedom consists. Bray recognizes that, both in play and in art, that feeling exists as a common character; but he does not believe that such an analogy, which may be explained by a phenomenon of convergence, signifies filiation.

Bray rejects also the evolutionary process according to which Spencer as well as Sergi and Ribot explain the transit from the useful to the beautiful. The attentive study of the evolution of the beautiful leads the theory of play to an embarrassing dilemma: either it is necessary to reject the picture that Ribot has traced of the aesthetic development of humanity, or it is necessary not to admit a conception which not only does not explain it, but raises, at every step, inextricable difficulties.

If beauty, adds Bray, is nothing but an activity without object, as it is without interest, then the capital role of fitness in aesthetic production is not explained; if the expenditure of forces in play is the root of aesthetic emotion, it is not explained why not all games are beautiful; the condition of disinterestedness does not give that explanation, because precisely Spencer, like Ribot, makes of disinterestedness the essential characteristic of the activity of play; neither does the greater or lesser expenditure of superabundant forces that the various games provoke give it, because then the most violent would be the most aesthetic. [p. 146]If, then, one establishes among games a perfectly founded distinction; if some are aesthetic and others indifferent in this respect, that proves that the idea of beauty is anterior and superior to that distinction; in a word, that it is foreign to the notion of play, as it is to the notion of harmony, of perfection, of relation, of order, of grandeur, and of so many others that have been invoked successively to explain it.

One may admit, with Guyau, adds Bray, that every play encloses aesthetic elements, but without concluding from that to a pretended identity, which the facts do not absolutely justify. Finally, Bray observes that this theory does not explain moral beauty, which exists notwithstanding the efforts made to deny it.

Bray opposes to this explanation by play that of the aesthetic feeling and of the beautiful as the result of the original tendency existing in man, as in all organisms, to distinguish himself from his fellows, in order to attract attention: a tendency bound, like others, to the reproductive function.

Bray, like Ribot, accepts in substance the theory of Grant Allen concerning the influence of the sexual instinct in the formation of the feeling of the beautiful.

Grant Allen maintains that the objects which man, from the beginning, has esteemed beautiful, have been his fellows. The Australian man admires the Australian woman. In that period, human aesthetics is not distinguished from the animal, if the animals too have an aesthetics. The dances of the animals, their music, their adornments are directed only to an individual of the species and have for their end generation. Man would have issued immediately from this cycle with the adornments added to his person. This addition may seem futile; but in reality it was the decisive step for surpassing nature. In the [p. 147]colors and in the designs applied directly to the body, and fixed later by tattooing, one already notes a selection, a symmetry, an artistic disposition.

After the human person, the aesthetic instinct extends to what touches him most closely; it externalizes itself, it is applied to arms, to garments, to utensils. Architecture itself, strictly speaking, may be assimilated to an extension of clothing. It is to be noted that, from the epoch of the lake dwellings, there is verified a special taste for symmetry; that taste is spontaneous, innate.

The poetry of the first times is not differentiated into epic, dramatic, and lyric; it has all those characters united, but its essential character is that of being exclusively human, destined for man, for his undertakings and for his feelings.

Music presents itself joined to the dance, first under its vocal form, that is to say, translating human emotions with a human organ. Almost suddenly it externalizes itself with the coarsest percussion instruments, which serve also, however, to mark rigorously the rhythm or the measure, and even to produce upon the senses a certain physical excitation. Afterward comes the imitation of the human voice with the flute or some other instrument of wind or of string, and one arrives, little by little, at the constitution of a true orchestra.

Very soon, aesthetic activity extends to the animals in order to make them enter into its domain, above all to the domestic animals, companions or servants of man, as the paintings and sculptures of India, of Egypt, and of Assyria prove. In poetry, the horses and dogs of the warriors come to be personages; they enter into art by their moral qualities: bravery and fidelity.

[p. 148]Finally, and very late, the aesthetic feeling surpasses man completely; it no longer refers only to men or to animals, but to the vegetable and inorganic world; there arises the feeling of nature.

To this theory, which has for its point of departure the sexual aesthetics and which does not truly explain the genesis of that feeling which obliges primitive man to adorn himself, is related the theory of Bray.

In his conception, human beauty is the consequence of this tendency, which impels a being to distinguish himself from his fellows, in order to triumph over them in the sexual struggle; the aesthetic emotion is the pleasure or the pain that results from the satisfaction or non-satisfaction of that need; the idea of the beautiful is born from the verification of that pleasure and from the comparison of the elements that give it birth; the pleasure of the beautiful is, in principle, that which derives from the perception of a distinction of visual or auditory origin.

The hypothesis of Bray, like that of play, has the defect of proving too much and, by that very fact, of not being able to give a specific explanation of the aesthetic phenomenon; because if in the feeling of distinction lay the origin of aesthetic pleasure, one would not explain the purely contemplative character that the beautiful has in its aesthetic form, nor why many acts that reveal that feeling of vanity are not beautiful, and, on the other hand, the aesthetic phenomenon would finally be reduced to a logical phenomenon.

### XII. TEORÍA DE LA LIBERTAD ESTÉTICA — XII. THE THEORY OF AESTHETIC FREEDOM

The theories set forth, in which the essential character of the beautiful is sought in technical judgment, in feeling, or in the biological tendency, discuss at bottom the question of aesthetic value, considering it solely from the subjective point of view, as in the sentimentalist theory, or from the twofold subjective and objective point of view, as in the other two. All three theories, however, make of pleasure the essential condition of the beautiful; for even though Lalo aspires to create an integral aesthetics, with his critical intellectualism, his so-called technical feelings seem to reduce to a logical feeling, to a feeling of perfection. The biological theory, founded on the activity of play, makes the beautiful consist in the development of that free activity, but at bottom characterizes it by the agreeable feeling, faint or indefinable, produced by the nervous discharge, associated with other, different attractions, as Spencer analyzes it, or by the feeling of the pleasure of being a powerful cause or of freedom, on which Groos founds it. Those who follow Grant Allen make of sympathy, as Basch does, the nature of the beautiful, reducing it to pleasure. Croce, on the contrary, radically rejects aesthetic hedonism and the theory of the sympathetic, in order to place the beautiful in the pure theoretical order, as the intuition [p. 150]inseparable from adequate expression. For Croce, it is a manner of knowing what for the others is a manner of feeling: disinterested feeling, that which is opposed to the useful for the Kantians.

A contemporary psychologist, Pujo, departing from those tendencies in whatever they have of the intellectualist, regards as the root of aesthetic emotion the pure feeling, active, free of all representation and, for that very reason, purely happy. For Pujo, the feeling of freedom engenders the aesthetic life.

This hypothesis agrees with the ideas put forward by two philosophers, Fouillée and Fonsegrive, in treating of the role of freedom in the generation of the beautiful. For both, the beautiful and grace are one and the same, and grace is the form of freedom.

According to Fouillée, grace, from the mechanical point of view, presupposes movement easily performed and easily perceived; it presupposes the greatest employment of force with the least possible loss and expenditure; from the physiological point of view, it excludes everything that feels effort, the labor of reflection, the subjection of the will; it demands natural well-being, the greatest effect with the least means; in a word, inspiration, spontaneous in appearance, which finds without seeking. Grace is the superabundance of an activity that has more than it needs to perform a movement or to attain an end, and that seems to wish to extend beyond itself —that image of the infinite—; and this is what causes it to be called divine. From the moral point of view, freedom being the principle of liberality, grace is a gift, and a disinterested gift; the gracious is gratuitous. Lastly, gratuitousness being the superabundance and creative fecundity proper to love, grace is loving or [p. 151]seems to love, according to Schelling's thought, and this is what makes it lovable. Kant used to say that beauty was the symbolic representation of morality; one may say that it is so more particularly of grace; that grace is, from the moral point of view, the symbol of loving goodness.

Grace, which the ancients did not separate from love, is, according to Fouillée, that which, in the very bosom of a really necessary mechanism and of an organism in which the parts really depend on the whole, expresses and lets glimpse, as in a dream, a principle free of all material or formal necessity: grace is thus the aesthetic expression of ideal freedom.

For this reason Fouillée, in agreement with the Platonic school, finds the good in the beautiful. It is not by itself alone that the beautiful form has the power to excite love; for, while the gaze of the intelligence embraces this form, the will passes beyond its limits and sets within the form, as the ground from which it derives, a living will that aspires to act, to expand, and to love.

Beauty, and principally grace, invites us, then, to conceive a principle of spontaneous action and determination, superior to the mechanical faculties; it is the intermediary between the material world and the moral world. It seems as though it figured the ideal freedom of the will, at the moment when the will delighted in itself, before imposing upon itself a law and a necessary rule, a limit and a sacrifice; for this very reason, beauty is an expression of the happy life, of felicity. When, later, by a final effort, freedom seems to rise above every limit and every sacrifice, in the plenitude and the infinitude of love for another, it gathers in itself moral sublimity and moral grace. If there is grace and beauty in the spontaneous expansion of innocence, [p. 152]there is grace and sublimity in the effortless disinterestedness of charity.

According to this analysis, grace is the aesthetic expression of ideal freedom, although it is not freedom itself, nor does it, of itself alone, demonstrate the existence of freedom. But, with this limitation, grace is the attribute that expresses that inner freedom of the beautiful, which is born of harmony and which corresponds to the characters of the harmonious, the disinterested, and the free that the aesthetic feeling offers in the plenitude of its development. Man finds grace beautiful and loves it, because it faithfully renders the state of his spirit: that state of felicity in which, filled with harmony, he tends to rise and does in fact rise to a world in which Kant placed his pure and free beauty, emancipated from all physical necessity, whether final or moral, exaggerating the disinterested character of the beautiful.

Fonsegrive expresses the same ideas. Grace, he says, is not an element of beauty: it is beauty itself, that which it has of most intimate and most enchanting. And since grace can receive its full and entire meaning only from moral considerations, and since it implies freedom, we may say that beauty is the reflection or the symbol of freedom; not, doubtless, of all freedom, but of that freedom which recognizes reason, freely accepts its laws, and easily fulfills them. Things, adds Fonsegrive, are beautiful in the proportion in which they manifest the more the harmony of freedom and of reason. Beauty, consequently, ought to express not only freedom, but also the reconciliation between it and an ideal order determined by reason.

Referring to aesthetic pleasure, Fonsegrive adds that what pleases us is the independent, that which is free of its end, without there being any need that it contradict that end. Beauty consists in realizing that end with fa[p. 153]cility, without constraint. This freedom of the means, with respect to the end that has to be realized, is what constitutes the pleasure of the excess it offers us and for which we are grateful to it, what, so to speak, constitutes its grace; grace being understood as that radiation of a force which does more than it is strictly destined to do and which could do still more than it does, or, what is the same thing, a free force, of an unlimited fecundity.

Bergson, in his book on «Laughter», expresses ideas analogous to those of Fouillée and Fonsegrive. «In every human form —he says— the imagination perceives the effort of a soul that informs matter, a soul infinitely flexible, eternally mobile, withdrawn from gravity, because it is not the earth that draws it. Of its winged lightness, this soul communicates something to the body it animates; the immateriality that thus passes into matter is what is called grace». The comic, for Bergson, is the opposite of grace, because it is a tendency toward inertia and automatism; the comic is opposed to the serious, and all that is serious in life proceeds from our freedom.

This explanation of aesthetic value by freedom may be reduced to the formula of appetition, applied to all value.

Freedom, considered as a need of expansion and of creation, takes on the form of appetite with that infinitude and plenitude which Fouillée recognizes in it, when it expands and creates in the world of the ideal, which is the world created by the imagination under the stimulus of that appetite. Whatever satisfies it engenders the feeling of freedom and aesthetic pleasure, because it is a harmony, and a harmony is the absence of constraint.

But since freedom is not a reality that has its measure in itself, but rather in the resistance of the medium [p. 154]and in the reaction of the subject, it is not possible to separate it from representation and from feeling, which are its inseparable symbols. Hence the intellectualist and sentimentalist theories of the aesthetic phenomenon. Ideal freedom, which informs the beautiful, is appraised sometimes by the qualities of its artistic expression, which are intelligible and submit to criticism, or by the intensity and purity of the aesthetic emotion, which is the result of the beauty contemplated.

On the other hand, these two moments of the aesthetic cycle, that of contemplation and that of creation, are separated so as to constitute isolated states, or an attempt is made to reduce them to the second, so as to subordinate the affective moment to the cognitive or operative one.

An integral theory of aesthetic value ought to comprise all the successive moments of the aesthetic process, or aesthetic emotion, bringing into play all the elements of consciousness that contribute to the valuation of beauty.

Aesthetic emotion is not, in its origin, a pure sensation, nor an instinct, nor a tendency, nor an isolated feeling, but rather the complex of these psychological elements, inseparable in the reality of consciousness. This synthetic conception of the emotion of the beautiful is founded on the study made of the nature of all emotion, whose components are a representation, a feeling, and a tendency, associated with one another and with concomitant physiological phenomena, which are their expression. The aesthetic judgment has for its base that affective state; it is a judgment of value, having for its cause freedom felt and expressed as spontaneity.

Let us see how the beautiful acts upon us so as to produce that valuation.

[p. 155]Taccone explains the first moment of aesthetic generation by attraction. The beautiful acts upon our aesthetic senses, but, at the same time, it exercises a special action upon the faculties of our spirit, in such wise that the pleasure resulting from it could not be attributed to the senses, nor to the intelligence alone, but to a secret and mysterious harmony that unites sense and intelligence in a single whole, in which sensation loses something of its materiality and intelligence something of its spirituality, without the eurhythmy that constitutes the aesthetic type being thereby broken. This harmonic synthesis would be the remote cause generating the pleasures of the beautiful, without being, however, the motor of the aesthetic sensations.

In effect, says Taccone, sensation is produced by the tendency of the sense toward a given object, which impresses upon the sense a determinate modification. Now, in order that any force or power whatever should move or be modified, two things are necessary: a movement impressed upon the force, and a power of attraction concentrated in an exterior object. Hence it comes that, in the apprehension of the beautiful, one seeks the movement impressed upon the sense and the intelligence, and the power of attraction deposited by nature in the object that is beautiful. In a word, one endeavors to account for the subjective movement and for the objective attraction, because, when it is a matter of aesthetic sensations, the expansive force of subjectivity cannot be separated from the attractive force of objectivity without destroying sensation itself.

Taccone thus establishes, in this law of harmony, the motor of the aesthetic sensations, as the bond that unites subjectivity —that is, the expansive force of the spirit— to objectivity, or attractive force. That bond would be sympathy, considered not only as a movement of cognition, but also, and above all, as a movement of satisfaction essential in sympathy.

[p. 156]This relation of sympathy would prepare aesthetic admiration, according to Krause—the first moment of emotion, which Jandelli regards as the specific character of the beautiful, even though not all admiration is aesthetic, it being necessary, according to Paulhan, that the object of admiration be considered in itself in order that it may take on an aesthetic character.

Soret claims to give a scientific explanation of this relation between subject and object at the beginning of aesthetic emotion. According to Soret, the analysis of aesthetic pleasure, in its most elementary form of symmetry, shows that it has its origin in the repetition of one and the same sensation. But since there are cases in which those repetitions are not accompanied by an aesthetic feeling, he believes he finds the cause of that pleasure in the satisfaction which the spirit experiences on discovering a law, a relation among the objects that impress it; yet not in view of reasoning, but by means of intuition. Whenever a law entails as its consequence the identity of two or more sensations —that is, a reiterated impression— we have the immediate intuition of the existence of a relation and, consequently, we experience an aesthetic enjoyment.

According to this, the aesthetic phenomenon requires from its very beginning that the intelligence freely perceive a certain relation of harmony. Without it, the feeling of aesthetic admiration does not present itself, and aesthetic valuation is not possible.

Admiration coincides with the phenomenon of surprise in this case; but the shock of the first instant, the arrest of the existing tendencies, is very slight, owing to the fact that the new sensations adapt themselves very easily to the system formed by our habits. Sympathy is a harmony rapidly realized. To [p. 157]this joyful adaptation there contribute the degree of aesthetic education of the subject and a certain predisposition of the spirit to enjoy. The more familiar the spirit is with aesthetic knowledge and enjoyment, the more rapidly and with the greater intensity is the harmony realized, hastening the evolution of the phenomenon and diminishing the duration and intensity of the first moment, so as to pass to the second, that of aesthetic emotion, in which it halts if the faculties of the subject do not powerfully feel the need to create, which Ribot regards as the essential characteristic of aesthetic emotion in its plenitude.

In that second moment, of pure and serene enjoyment, there is realized the systematization and the harmony to which Paulhan and Brunschwigg refer in their description of the aesthetic life. It is then that consciousness and the contemplation of the inner harmony —fruit of the harmony perceived by intuition, freely and intimately bound to it— produce that feeling of absolute liberation, of disinterested satisfaction, which is content with itself and which extends, without limits, in the world of the imagination, free of all constraint. It is in that state that one best observes the absence of every practical end; the tendency is not directed toward the act; the Platonic contemplation of the beautiful prevails. As Brunschwigg says, this is a moment of absolute satisfaction, in which man isolates himself from all that he has done until then, forgets what remains for him to do, so as to taste, in all its plenitude, the joy of the present hour. Before him there is an object which he contemplates, but this contemplation provokes no effort, whether to analyze its conditions or to follow out its exterior consequences. Between him and what he contemplates there is a perfect unity, and this unity is not a result laboriously obtained, but rather acquired at a stroke, as though by the chance of a [p. 158]discovery; it is the perfect harmony, naturally felt as profound, almost as eternal, which emancipates man from every desire, which makes him taste the plenitude of his own life, engendering a special joy, capable even of transforming pain, and which escapes all scientific analysis. The aesthetic life thus envelops the content of the human spirit, but invests it with a characteristic form, suspending, for a certain time, the effort of reflection and the struggle to live, banishing the memory of the past and the disquiet of the future.

To this state Pujó also refers when he gives to aesthetic emotion an infinite, or rather an absolute, character, as a pure feeling, free of all positive representation. This state can thus produce the aesthetic ecstasy, which has so much analogy with religious ecstasy and which may be confounded with it, if the artist succeeds the contemplator and divinizes his images. It is at this moment too that inspiration presents itself, as a need to create, in souls predisposed to artistic activity.

But although this moment of the subjective aesthetic process is not one of pure and exclusive aesthetic contemplation, but rather is translated into organic phenomena with which it is associated, it is not the creative moment of aesthetic activity, which presents itself only in natures endowed with artistic aptitudes. In a third moment, the most important and the most fecund, the soul, in the plenitude of its forces and with an excess of energy that has no practical application or that cannot develop in acts of positive life, by reason of the nature of the subject, feels the need to create and engenders the work of art, after conceiving and informing the ideal of its creation.

This moment of creation comprises the two phases of internal creation, or formation of the ideal, and that of [p. 159]artistic expression in outward sensible forms. Croce excludes this second phase, whereas Lalo makes of it, essentially, the specific characteristic of the beautiful. Aesthetic activity, for the former, is purely theoretical activity, while for the latter it is purely technical or practical. Croce and Lalo thus reproduce the old question of knowing whether the beautiful ought to be classified in the domain of the theoretical or of the practical.

The truth is that the aesthetic phenomenon embraces the whole of psychic activity and, consequently, both the theoretical, as intuition, and the practical, in its creative function, in which the element of the will predominates, with the vehement desire to produce. Thus, upon the simple contemplation of the beautiful object there follows an intense love for that same object, idealized by the powerful force of artistic imagination; the intensity of the love develops an excess of energy and spiritual activity, which demand a more extensive and fecund systematization and which develop a vigorous tendency toward the act of artistic creation. Under the pressure of this need, that state of pure, static, and joyful contemplation disappears, and upon the tranquil aesthetic pleasure of the second moment there follows a certain uneasiness, which is not extinguished by the creation of the ideal aroused by the beautiful object, even though that ideal is the symbol of its inner freedom; rather, the soul aspires to free itself of that excess of psychic activity developed by inspiration, which it achieves by means of that kind of spiritual bringing-to-birth that constitutes the creation of the work of art, the outward symbol of that freedom, conquered by the imagination in the world of the ideal.

By virtue of this bringing-to-birth the spirit recovers its equilibrium; the inner harmony, enriched by the acquisition and expression of the ideal of the contemplated object, [p. 160]forms part of another, vaster harmony, in which the artist associates his freedom with that of humanity. Then emotion, objectifying itself in that form, takes on that sociological and utilitarian, educative and teaching character which Guyau attributes to it in examining the transcendence of the work of art. In this way the aesthetic phenomenon is realized in all its integrity; objective beauty, the origin of the aesthetic process, after transforming and enriching itself in the soul of the artist of genius, reappears in reality so as to continue the same evolution within the bosom of human society, as a close and powerful bond of solidarity.

But the process is not always initiated by the contemplation of the beautiful work. Sometimes the creative process feeds solely on the elements scattered in reality and gathered by the artistic imagination; but, in this case, the internal contemplation of one's own work precedes its expression in external form. This process, which may have been frequent in the beginnings of art, would be exceptional now, when a generalized artistic culture puts the artistic spirit into early and immediate relation with the beautiful work.

The subjective aesthetic phenomenon being thus understood as a process, one may reconcile its characters of the disinterested and the utilitarian, the contemplative and the active, the sensible, the intellectual, and the volitional, which predominate successively in its development, although it possesses, without differentiation, those three elements at its root. A biological, psychological, and sociological phenomenon, it must be regarded as the most complex and most perfect synthesis of human activity, as the most attractive human system and the one that possesses the most powerful systematizing action. In its evolution it offers those three characters; endowed with a great variety by the elements of its psychological composition, its variety increases to the point of the incomprehensible under [p. 161]the action of the diverse causes that operate in the physical and social medium in which it is produced and developed. This explains not only its immense complexity and the difficulty of its analysis, but also the diverse manner in which it is observed, in which it is explained, and in which its laws are established in constructing the psychology of the beautiful and founding the bases of artistic criticism.

Notwithstanding that complexity and the concurrence of all the elements of consciousness in the valuation of the beautiful, it is discovered that what determines aesthetic value is freedom. Without the presence of that factor, neither is the thought aesthetic nor is the emotion aesthetic; sympathy, which initiates the aesthetic phenomenon, is explained by freedom, because man loves the latter, whatever be the form under which it presents itself, and he loves objects in so far as they reflect that freedom, which is the fundamental appetite of consciousness, without which the expansion of the spirit is not to be explained. Wherever we suppose a freedom, a causality, a movement that are in ourselves alone, there is beauty, says Volkelt. Perception, in order to be aesthetic, needs to be free; for this reason Kant defined aesthetic taste as the free play of the cognitive faculties, and the senses of sight and hearing are qualified as aesthetic by reason of their relative emancipation from matter. The aesthetic feeling is a feeling of liberation, which rejects every imperative and withdraws itself from all law; the creative power of the artistic imagination is characterized essentially by that absolute freedom which Pujó recognizes in the aesthetic feeling. It is in the domain of the creative imagination, as Krause says, that it is possible to satisfy the appetite for infinite freedom that informs the spirit and characterizes its essence. Expression is artistic when it reflects freedom. The theory of play aspires to explain it only through that concept. What for Kant is the free play of [p. 162]the cognitive faculties is, for the physiologists or biologists, the free play of the vital forces.

All the theories take into account this principle of freedom, though expressed under diverse forms: it is harmony, which signifies equilibrium or non-constraint, that is, a static or passive freedom; it is the feeling of being able to be a cause in the domain of appearances, of which Groos speaks; it is the desire to triumph and to distinguish oneself, to which Grant Allen and Bray refer; it is the intuition that meets no obstacles in expression, that is identified with it; it is the liberating and purifying activity in the conception of Croce; it is the feeling of harmony that Lalo includes among the truly aesthetic feelings; it is, in fine, the grace of which Fouillée and Fonsegrive speak.

For this reason many philosophers and aestheticians have defined the beautiful by freedom, even though they did not have of the latter a positive and dynamic conception.<sup>1</sup> For Kant, the sympathetic emotion of the beautiful is a principle of freedom; the beautiful is a finality without an end, and the most free that can be conceived within a finality; men feel themselves united and free through the principle of the beautiful, which speaks to them in the language of the pleasurable, of the disinterested, the good, and the free; the beautiful is morality with sensible representation; the pleasure of the beautiful consists in the free play of the intellectual faculties. For Kant, only the pure and free beauty of nature is beautiful; art will be beautiful when the final artistic form appears as free of all constraint of arbitrary rules as if it were the effect of nature alone.

<sup>1</sup> See, in the second part, the exposition and critique of the systems that have considered freedom as an aesthetic factor.

For Schiller, the beautiful resides in the freedom derived from the play instinct; beauty is nothing other than [p. 163]freedom in the phenomenon, freedom in willing and not in knowing, as Kant thought in his logical formalism. To give freedom through freedom is the fundamental thing of the aesthetic state, says Schiller.

Fichte did not distinguish aesthetics from morals, because he absorbed both into that same principle of freedom, carried to its utmost limits in the artistic humor derived from irony, the expression of an art free of all constraint, of all ordering or regulating law imposed by reason or by tradition.

The very objective aesthetics, called forth by the subjectivist idealism of Fichte, proclaims that principle of freedom, essential in the beautiful. Art expresses, according to Schelling, the infinite of beauty in finite forms; art does not receive rules, but rather itself imposes them, because genius, which creates art, is the supreme and absolute reality, which never comes to objectify itself, but which is the cause of all that is objective.

The most elevated faculty that the subject can possess is freedom, says Hegel. Freedom is the most elevated destiny of the spirit, and consists in this, that the subject finds nothing foreign, nothing that limits it, nothing that is not in harmony with it and that does not satisfy it. Man, according to Hegel, can attain this complete harmony only in the region of the absolutely true, within whose bosom freedom and necessity, spirit and nature, science and its object, law and thought —in a word, all contraries— are absorbed and reconciled. Man reaches that region by means of philosophy and of religion; but art, which occupies itself equally with the true, as the absolute object of consciousness, belongs also, says Hegel, to the absolute sphere of the spirit, and under this title places itself on the same level as religion and philosophy. Art is, then, the sensible ma[p. 164]nifestation, in individual form, of that region of absolute truth which realizes absolute freedom.

The contemplation of the beautiful, adds Hegel, is a liberal contemplation, which leaves the object in its independent existence and excludes from the subject every desire to possess it and to convert it into an instrument for his ends. Beauty, in living and animate beings, is not the mere regularity of the parts, nor the mere conformity of the movements to an end, but the total form revealing the force that animates it; it is the force manifested by an ensemble of forms, of independent and free movements, it is the inner and living harmony which reveals itself outwardly, without our pausing to consider the relation of the parts to the whole, nor the equilibrium of the functions, as the naturalist does. Art expresses the free development of life, and above all of the free life of the spirit.

For Schopenhauer, it is only in art that one sees the pure will and life free of all torment; art realizes that ideal of freedom which man will never be able to attain in nature, which offers only struggle and pain as its consequence. The beautiful in art realizes that harmony between the real and the ideal which freedom needs in order to satisfy man and make him happy. Schopenhauer, as is known, finds a true analogy between the noumenon of Kant and the Platonic Idea, which he identifies with the will. This Idea is an attempt at freedom; hence the disinterested character of the art that expresses it.

According to Krause, the character and the general form of the beauty of the spirit is ideal freedom; that is, the power of determining oneself by oneself in conformity with eternal ideas.

Contemporary aesthetics has pronounced this characteristic more strongly. The most profound element that has been [p. 165]discovered in the pleasure of the beautiful, says Fouillée, is the voluntary element, which completes the sensible and intellectual element.

Chaignet defines the beautiful as the conception of the force whose freedom seems unlimited, in which one does not see the limits, although one knows that it must have them; as an individual and ideal form of the active force in the indefinite development of its freedom.

When, as the substance develops, its element of quantity can conform to the notion of order and its element of activity can expand freely, then beauty will be found, says Voituron.

According to Lemcke, freedom and order, in right harmony, engender the impression of the beautiful. In the purely beautiful there reigns the free harmony between the phenomenon and our representation; we feel ourselves before it pure and free, without further desires or passions, satisfied and happy. The free spirit has the power to escape from objective reality and from the seriousness of life, taking refuge in the realm of fantasy and forming this realm for itself, according to the measure of the desire or of the power to unite fantasy with activity. This latter is what happens in play properly so called, in which the forces, both spiritual and bodily, are occupied and exercised, for distraction and pleasure.

This same principle of freedom, which arises from harmonic integration, also explains the sociological character that is attributed to the aesthetic phenomenon. The more numerous and sympathetic are man's relations with nature and society, the greater is the integration of his being, the more powerful and fecund his freedom. Happiness increases in proportion, and with it the beauty of sympathetic objects grows and is accentuated. The beautiful is, for this reason, a sympathy symbo[p. 166]lized, as Basch defines it, and what Léveque regards as fitness among the external characters of the beautiful is no more than a limited aspect of that law of association, according to which beings complete one another reciprocally by a sympathetic affinity, increasing the richness of their harmonies, so as to be better known in their greater integrity, better relished by feeling, and more beautiful in their appreciation. Sociological aesthetics, consequently, does no more than confirm the principle of freedom as the essential characteristic of the beautiful, as that which constitutes aesthetic value.

This same principle is found in the psychological explanation of Einfühlung, as we have seen. «For Lipps —as Basch says— the psychic element that penetrates the beautiful object is activity, force, life, inner activity, the force that unfolds without hindrance, the profound life of the personality that realizes and satisfies itself fully and entirely. Beauty is a free affirmation of life, felt in the contemplation of an object and bound to this contemplation in a sensible manner». «The beautiful is free life, vital energy, the personality in all its richness».

But if freedom, as an appetite of expansion, determines aesthetic value, since freedom cannot present itself in isolation from representation and from feeling, which are its indices, in external reality it is the form that contains and reveals it by means of certain special characters that reduce to order, and in internal reality it is the feeling that impresses upon it a consciousness of its own; hence the aesthetic consciousness, as valuing, is reduced, in the last term, to a judgment of value, an intuitive judgment and one of feeling, which affirms in objects the quality of the beautiful and its contrary.

### XIII. LOS SENTIDOS ESTÉTICOS — XIII. THE AESTHETIC SENSES

With the characterization of the aesthetic consciousness is connected the debated question of the aesthetic senses and of the elementary aesthetic feelings derived from the aesthetic sensations or aroused by them.

In the view of some aestheticians, only the senses of hearing and of sight can offer us isolated representations of aesthetic effects. Almost all psychologists are in agreement upon this point. Nevertheless, the contrary thesis, which is found in germ in the eighteenth century, in the system of Burke, has been maintained by other psychologists, who believe that the domain of the beautiful does not belong exclusively to those senses, called aesthetic par excellence, but that the others too can offer elements for an enjoyment of an aesthetic nature.

The idealist psychologists, who found the notion of the beautiful upon the a priori concept of the ideal, give the greatest importance to the sense of sight, and admit the aesthetic emotions acquired through hearing; but they absolutely reject the aesthetic character of the other senses, separating, in a radical manner, the agreeable from the aesthetic.

The positivist psychologists, and all who find only a difference of degree between agree[p. 168]able sensation and the intellectual enjoyment of the beautiful, affirm the possibility of acquiring aesthetic sensations through all the senses. Guyau is of this opinion.

Every agreeable sensation, whatever it may be, and when it is not, by its very nature, bound to repugnant associations—writes Guyau—can take on an aesthetic character, acquiring a certain degree of intensity, of resonance in the consciousness. Guyau distinguishes three phases in sensation. In the first, the being registers a shock, slight or violent, and distinguishes, more or less vaguely, the specific quality and the intensity of the impression, without yet knowing whether the sensation will be agreeable or disagreeable. In the second, the sensation becomes definite and acquires, where there is occasion for it, a clearly painful or agreeable character, resulting from its being harmful or useful. Finally, when the sensation of pain or of pleasure is not extinguished immediately, so as to give place either to an indifferent act or to another sensation, it spreads through the nervous system, after the manner of a wave, awakens, by association or suggestion, a multitude of complementary ideas and feelings, and invades the entire consciousness.

At this instant, the sensation, which at first seemed no more than agreeable or disagreeable, tends to become aesthetic or anti-aesthetic. The aesthetic emotion—adds Guyau—thus appears to us to consist, essentially, in a prolongation, in a kind of resonance of the sensation throughout our whole being, above all through our intelligence and will. It is an accord, a harmony among the sensations, the ideas, and the feelings. Hence this definition of the beautiful: a perception or an action that stimulates in us life under its three forms at once—sensibility, intelligence, and will—and produces pleasure through the swift consciousness of this general stimulus. The beautiful is enclosed in germ within the agreeable, the agreeable being reduced to [p. 169]the consciousness of unimpeded life; it is there too that the true principle of the beautiful must be found. Every pleasure thus tends to become aesthetic; the one that halts at the agreeable aborts, so to speak.

Mario Pilo goes further still. We call beautiful—says Pilo—pleasure, and ugly pain, exclusively, or, at least, essentially and principally sensory. The beautiful is, then, what pleases us, but what pleases, first and above all, the senses. For Pilo, a thing has no need, in order to be beautiful, save that the nervous current it determines in us should propagate beyond the zone of the senses. That it should arouse emotions, confirm theories, evoke visions—all this is no more than an excess for aesthetics, a luxury for the beautiful. The sole essential condition is the production of an image in this zone of the senses; thus one may declare the perfume of jasmine beautiful. Nevertheless, if the nervous current is sufficiently intense and penetrates cerebral strata higher and higher and above the purely sensory beautiful, one will have, successively: in the zone of feeling, a sentimental image or emotion, which will combine with the first, that is, the sentimental beautiful; in the zone of the intellect, an abbreviated notion, a schema or, often, a mere sign of reality, which will be superimposed upon the other two, that is, the intellectual beautiful; finally, in the supreme zone of the ideal, the current will be perceived in a manner still more immaterial, in the form of a vision, of an essence, of a symbol, in which reality is found transfigured and made a new creation by our spirit; that degree, the most elevated, or the ideal beautiful, contains, in its turn, the three that have preceded it.

This theory, like that of Guyau, takes from the senses of sight and hearing the monopoly of beauty and, consequently, that of art. All our senses are [p. 170]capable of offering us aesthetic emotions, says Guyau. «I assign—writes Pilo—in the hierarchy of the senses, the lowest place to the visceral sense, which yields enjoyments often intense but always confused and rarely conscious; I place next the muscular sense, already more psychological; then touch, taste, smell, and so forth—all of them being, though in diverse proportions, rich sources of aesthetic enjoyments», which another Italian physiologist, Mantegazza, has described in his Physiology of Pleasure.

Sully Prudhomme denies to the sensations of taste and of smell all aesthetic quality, because the successive sensations experienced through these senses are not kept isolated by the memory, so that the intelligence might discover their relation, as happens with the other senses, but combine to form a single sensation, or else the second destroys the effect of the first—whence results the impossibility of combining flavors and odors into an aesthetic harmony.

In the view of Soret, of the three senses—taste, smell, and touch—taste is the least apt to develop aesthetic sensations; its role in our organization is reduced, almost exclusively, to accompanying with a sensual enjoyment the act of nutrition, in order to incite man to eat and thus to maintain life. Beyond this, taste serves us very little to teach us the function, the nature, and the characters of objects. The reiterated impressions that taste can make us experience have not the aesthetic character; because, in the succession of flavors, the intelligence does not acquire the knowledge of that law which explains aesthetic satisfaction, according to this psychologist. The role of taste would be completely null in aesthetics, if it did not sometimes awaken in us memories, impressions entirely independent of the sensual effect, agreeable or disagreeable, that it pro[p. 171]vokes—a property enjoyed by the other senses. According to Soret, that mode of reiterated impressions, after a long interval of time, that recollection of an idea provoked by a physical sensation, has an aesthetic character of the intellectual order.

Smell, although it resembles taste in many points, is much more apt to put us in relation with the exterior world, and often completes, in this respect, the senses of hearing and of sight. Its aesthetic role is, for that reason, in Soret's view, a little more important than that of taste. Smell, more than taste, has the property of evoking memories: a perfume recalls to us old impressions, causing a picture of the past to arise. Education might perhaps obtain from it more frequent aesthetic sensations, in the view of this psychologist, who affirms the aesthetic character of the sensations of touch.

Soret, in effect, shows that the sensations of rhythm, perceived through hearing, can be accessible through touch, whether associated with hearing or functioning in isolation. He observes that those who listen to a piece of music have very generally the tendency to mark the rhythm by sensations of touch, which result from cadenced movements; the pleasure of the dance and of other bodily exercises, in which music is wholly foreign—such as horsemanship—being founded upon the same phenomenon. He observes, likewise, that persons absolutely deprived of hearing also experience a very positive impression of rhythm which, for them, results solely from the sensations of touch, this sense performing an important role in the appreciation of the forms of objects among the blind, who, according to experiments made by Soret, can appreciate, through touch, symmetry, repetition, and continu[p. 172]ity, and, consequently, be impressed by form in the decorative arts, limiting their judgment, naturally, to objects whose dimensions are accessible to them.

Souriau, in his treatise on rational beauty, likewise attributes an aesthetic value to the interior senses of touch, taste, and smell. The sensations they produce, considered in themselves, have no determinate aesthetic character; but placed in their natural milieu, in the whole of which they form part, they acquire, in his view, an undeniable aesthetic value, because they then enter into the judgment we form upon the beauty of things and contribute, for their part, to determining it. Upon those primary data, which are like the immediate apprehension of the simplest beauties of nature, there is produced a whole mental labor, which tends to give them a greater aesthetic value. By means of the imagination they undergo a kind of interior elaboration, which transfigures them in the direction of the greatest beauty. The association of ideas intervenes here in a constant manner. The lower sensations, which are found mingled and confounded with the sensations of a higher order that we receive, at the same time, from the same objects, contract with these intimate associations. To our sensations there may also be joined pure feelings, which give them a particular tinge.

The mere fact—adds Souriau—that the lower sensations pass through our imagination suffices to idealize them. All those lower and accessory sensations, to which one is willing to grant no more than a superficial and adventitious charm, reveal to us, on the contrary, a profound, intimate beauty, the true vital beauty, because they are the sensible expression of life freely developed—young, powerful, healthy, and pure—and it is for that reason that we make them enter into our ideal of physical beauty. Following this same order of ideas, Souriau sees no [p. 173]reason to refuse an aesthetic value to the things that offer us an agreeable impression, when this agreeableness proves to us that they are healthy and good for us.

Bray combats these theories, which confound and absorb the beautiful into the agreeable, demonstrating that the only aesthetic senses are those of hearing and sight. Between the sensations acquired through these senses and the others he establishes differences founded: first, upon the conditions of their functioning; second, upon the form of the excitation; third, upon their affective tonality; fourth, upon their power of association; and fifth, upon the role they perform in the life of man. These differences are clear as regards taste and smell. As regards touch he observes that the distinctive characters are much less marked. This intermediate position is explained if one takes into account that the tactile sense has served as the base for the evolution of four special senses, the mutual aid that eye and hand lend each other in the first experiences of the child—which tends to confound, more or less, the two orders of perceptions—and the feeble differentiation that touch presents with respect to the general sensibility.

But if Bray rejects the aesthetic equivalence of the senses, combating the opinions of Guyau and of Pilo, he does not absolutely deny all aesthetic function to the senses of taste, smell, and touch. If they are incapable, he says, of awakening by themselves the emotion of the beautiful, they can, nevertheless, in combination with the visual and auditory impressions, reinforce or weaken the aesthetic effect of the latter, according as their sensations produce in us a state of well-being that favors it or repulsions that thwart it. Their function is, then, secondary, indirect, and by association. The eye and the ear are, as Bain says, the two avenues by which aesthetic influences penetrate to our spirit. These senses reveal themselves to us as the aesthetic senses [p. 174]par excellence, or rather as the only ones capable, in the normal state, of provoking the emotion of the beautiful—provided one does not lose sight, as Bray says, first, that their perceptions are not possible save with the intervention of muscular sensations, and second, that those perceptions can be reinforced or thwarted by those which derive from other modes of the sensibility.

Croce, in his revolutionary aesthetics, combats radically the theory of the aesthetic senses. In his view, that theory has had its origin in not having established well, or in having lost sight of, the character that distinguishes expression from impression, form from matter—which reduces to the error of wishing to find a passage from the quality of the content to that of the form. To ask, in effect, which are the aesthetic senses is tantamount to asking which sensible impressions can enter into the aesthetic expressions and which must enter of necessity; to which one must answer, at once, says Croce, that all impressions can enter into the aesthetic expressions or formations, but that none must enter of necessity.

To believe, he adds, that the impressions of sight and of hearing enter as direct into the aesthetic phenomenon and the others only as associated, is to establish a wholly arbitrary distinction; because aesthetic expression is a synthesis, in which it is impossible to distinguish the direct from the indirect. All impressions resemble one another in expression, once they become aesthetic. He who receives the image of a painting or of a poem no longer has before him this image as a series of impressions, some of which possess prerogative or precedence with respect to the others; of what happens before he has received it nothing is known; just as the distinctions made afterward, in reflecting, no longer correspond to art.

[p. 175]For this reason Croce excludes the theory of the aesthetic senses, even when presented as the attempt to establish the physiological organs necessary for the aesthetic phenomenon, which has no relation whatever with expression, which constitutes, for Croce, the aesthetic phenomenon.

This theory of the aesthetic senses answers chiefly to the intellectualist or physiologist conception of the beautiful, which attribute a decisive role to the phenomenon of aesthetic sensation and to that of the sensory feeling immediately bound to it. On that ground it is a question of distinguishing the agreeable from the beautiful; but even on that same ground the distinction between the sensations of hearing and sight and the other sensations does not definitively resolve the question relative to the difference between the agreeable and the beautiful; because that difference presents itself within the very feelings aroused by the sensations of hearing and sight.

In answer to this question, Bray declares that there exists between the agreeable and the beautiful no difference of nature. Agreeable, he says, is a term as extensive as that of pleasure itself; now, pleasure and pain are general forms, applicable to all the emotions, including the aesthetic emotion. The agreeable is, then, a genus of which the beautiful is a species. But if everything that forms part of the species also and necessarily forms part of the genus, the converse does not hold. Everything that is beautiful is, by itself and necessarily, an object of pleasure; but it is not true to say that everything that is an object of pleasure is beautiful, or that it can become so through a certain degree of intensity, of resonance in the consciousness, as Guyau affirms. It is thus that the distinction established between the beautiful and the agreeable must be understood.

Bray finds this distinction justified by the very analysis of the perceptions of hearing and of sight. [p. 176]In his view, not all our luminous or acoustic impressions have as their result the offering of a representation of the exterior world; rather, a certain number of them make us know scarcely more than the state of well-being or discomfort of the eye or of the ear, provoked by the excitation. The objective element is then not wholly wanting; but it presents itself in a subordinate place. Those impressions resemble those of the lower senses; intimately bound to the present state of the organ, destined to enlighten us as to the danger or utility the exterior irritant offers it, they too do not pass beyond the sphere of the vegetative functions, and we see no reason to raise ourselves to a higher level.

In sum: in the whole of our sensations, Bray distinguishes the existence of two well-distinct classes. The ones depend essentially upon the normal or pathological condition of our sensory apparatus; they reveal to us a simple state of well-being or of discomfort, but without offering us, as a general rule, any precise notion of the objective causes of those phenomena. In the others, on the contrary, this wholly physical and subjective impression is null or very accessory, and the sensation is transformed immediately into a mental and objective image. To the first would correspond, accordingly, the usual terms of agreeable and disagreeable, and only the second would be susceptible of beauty. According to this classification, the term agreeable would apply exclusively to the sensations of taste, smell, and touch, to the organic and visceral sensations, and to the muscular senses. Abstraction made of abnormal cases, in which the muscular sense is called upon to supply the absence of other senses, the impressions it communicates to us are eminently subjective, and their combination with the visual or acoustic perceptions can alone confer upon them [p. 177]objectivity. The sensations of sight and hearing would belong chiefly, but not exclusively, to the second class, which admits at once the beautiful and the agreeable.

Bray restricts this classification to man alone, who is organized to judge of the world, above all, by luminous and sonorous vibrations. It is not impossible, he says, that other beings, endowed with other senses or whose most developed senses correspond to those which in us are least so, should form of the world a very different conception and possess a rich treasure of tactile, olfactory, and gustatory notions—even veritable arts of which we can have not the least idea.

Founded upon this analysis, Bray establishes the following differences between the beautiful and the agreeable. Physiologically, the agreeable or disagreeable tone of a sensation depends solely upon the constitution and the state of our organs, upon our bodily habit; our mentality enters there for absolutely nothing. Custom can modify it in a certain measure, but education properly so called would be impotent. Hence this psychological consequence: that our judgments upon the agreeable have no pretension whatever to universality; our appreciations are, in this respect, eminently personal; they lie within the domain of egoism. Aesthetic pleasure and displeasure, on the contrary, derive essentially, but not exclusively, from our mental régime; the influence of education is enormous in this matter. It is for that reason that our aesthetic judgments aspire to a universal value, which Kant has set in relief as the character of the aesthetic judgment.

These distinctions, Bray adds, are not absolute, because the pleasure of the beautiful is but one of the forms of pleasure in general; the beautiful has issued from the agreeable by a slow and gradual evolution, which implies between [p. 178]them the existence of transitions. But they suffice to justify a specific distinction between the two concepts, in conformity with current language, and to condemn every theory which, far from explaining, claims to see between them no more than a simple difference of intensity or of extension.

At the bottom of this distinction we may observe that it is reduced to this: that certain senses, such as hearing and sight, offer isolated, independent representations, freely perceived and freely combined by the imagination, which are the most apt not only to make us feel what there is of the free in the expressions of objective reality, especially of the artistic, but also to express, in free and consequently beautiful form, the expansions of our psychic life.

The question of the aesthetic senses, reduced to these limits, has not, consequently, the importance that the intellectualists and biologists have attributed to it, who have treated it considering agreeable sensation as the characteristic of the beautiful. This does not mean that the sense which serves us as the avenue of the acquisition and production of the beautiful is without importance; but however great that real importance may be, the aesthetic question it has raised does not possess so much.

### XIV. CLASIFICACIÓN DE LOS SENTIMIENTOS ESTÉTICOS — XIV. CLASSIFICATION OF THE AESTHETIC FEELINGS

If sensation has been analyzed with care, in order to discover the specific character of the so-called aesthetic sensations, as much—and more—has been done in the order of aesthetic feeling, which has been the matter of general treatises of psychology and of aesthetics and has been the object of special studies such as that of Lalo.

Among these studies the important one is that of Wundt, who establishes the generally admitted classification of the aesthetic feelings into elementary and superior. The elementary aesthetic feelings are those which are bound to isolated representations and are the product of combinations of sensations. The superior aesthetic feelings are much more complex than the former and accompany all representations, developing with a more intense energy or fusing with other feelings of a less simple origin.

The elementary aesthetic feelings, as Wundt defines them, offer us representations of space or of time. The compound feelings, which belong to the domain of the senses of hearing and of sight, are ordinarily, says Wundt, designated as elementary aesthetic feelings—an expression which, in and of itself, embraces all the feelings bound up with compound representations, and which are for that reason compound.

These feelings can serve as the model of all the ulterior compound feelings that arise in the course of the intellectual pro[p. 180]cesses—that is, of the logical, moral, and superior aesthetic feelings, or those of a more elevated nature, in which the elementary aesthetic feelings are linked with feelings and emotions that arise from the complex connection of the psychic processes.

According to the analysis made by Wundt, the elementary aesthetic feelings rest, essentially, upon the relations of representations in time and in space, which correspond to the senses of hearing and of sight and which fuse in the phenomenon of movement.

To the sense of hearing correspond two fundamental forms of aesthetic feeling: harmony and rhythm. The fundamental basis of harmony is the coincidence of determinate partial tones, which correspond to diverse sounds. Harmony alone satisfies the ear; and if we bear disharmony, it is solely as a transitory disposition, founded upon harmony itself, whose satisfying effect it throws into relief with greater purity. This effect is reinforced by dissonance, which adds to the immediate disturbance of the sound-sensations the disturbing action exercised upon our consciousness by the irreconcilable character of the isolated representations.

Rhythm excites pleasure by means of impressions that have a kinship among themselves through intensity or quality and which, in the succession of diverse auditory representations, are repeated, most frequently, after regular intervals of time. Equal impressions, manifesting themselves at equal pauses, produce a fatiguing effect, which is never rhythm. For an aesthetic pleasure to be produced, it is necessary, at the least, that there be two different impressions, corresponding to the rise and the fall of the sound, and alternating regularly. The rhythmic feeling can also be wanting when the series of heterogeneous impressions is [p. 181]so great that the mind cannot perceive its unity, or when the rhythmic forms overstep the limit that the mind can easily embrace.

The rhythmic feeling is susceptible of extending to more considerable successions of sounds, joining the elementary measures into rhythmic series, the series into periods, and the periods into vaster divisions. Rhythm rests, consequently, like harmony, upon the concatenation of representations, which our mind is capable of perceiving easily. In the whole of a musical effect, it is harmony that gives direction to the disposition of the soul, and rhythm that describes the alternation and the undulation of the feelings.

As regards the visual representations, there has been attributed to the combination of diverse colored sensations, produced simultaneously, a particular effect, analogous to the combinations of sounds. Wundt believes, nevertheless, that, aesthetic feeling being taken in its psychological sense, it is independent of color and of brilliance, even though these play a great role in the production of the complex aesthetic effect. To the sense of sight corresponds the aesthetic effect of forms.

Taking, first, as a point of departure in this analysis the simplest things of geometrical beauty, which reduce to mathematical relations, one observes that their aesthetic effect is very mediocre. There are generally distinguished two conditions in this elementary aesthetic effect: the disposition or arrangement of the forms and the direction of the lines of the contour or profile. Observing the disposition or arrangement of the simple forms, one notes that we prefer regularity to irregularity. The simplest case of regularity, which is symmetry, shows itself, then, in all the forms in which one seeks to realize a certain aesthetic effect and in which [p. 182]a deviation from this regularity is not the copy or the imitation of asymmetrical forms of nature. With the impression produced by the arrangement of forms is associated the other factor: the direction of the lines of the profile, which comprises perspective.

Symmetry is by preference horizontal. Frequently, other relations of magnitude, which present themselves in the vertical direction, are substituted for the horizontal direction, owing to the habit we have of observing natural forms in which this horizontal or bilateral symmetry predominates. The repetition of homologous parts, which in the vertical arrangement produces a symmetry of a more complex kind, contributes to making us perceive aesthetically the human form and the animal and vegetable forms. Consequently, the aesthetic effect of organic forms depends especially upon a symmetry consisting in the repetition of homologous parts; but it depends also upon the perfecting of the structure of the forms, which, in this case, reveals itself simultaneously. If from here we pass to the examination of the beauties of landscapes or of works of sculpture, we observe, likewise, that the relations of the dimensions and of their parts depart greatly from the monotony offered by complete symmetry and from the limit of incommensurable proportions.

If the relations of representations in time and in space can explain the intensity of aesthetic pleasure, they cannot explain the qualitative diversity of aesthetic feeling, which receives its specific character only from the particular content of the representations. Harmony, rhythm, and symmetry please us because the laws of multiplicity they enclose awaken in our spirit innumerable representations of aesthetic objects. These abstract relations of forms [p. 183]are aesthetic objects of an indeterminate content, but they are not devoid of a content. For that reason they are apt to become the factors of complex aesthetic effects; and, in such a case, in order that our feeling be satisfied, the form must correspond to the content. Consequently, in a total effect of that kind, those abstract relations of harmony, of rhythm, and of symmetry are, at the same time, the external conditions of form, which make possible the union of diverse parts of the aesthetic content.

All the representations that constitute the content of aesthetic effects are always, in the first place, isolated representations. They excite our pleasure or our displeasure, subordinating themselves to certain general representations which are at the disposal of our consciousness. When the complex aesthetic object arouses a series of representations, bound among themselves, which are rendered under the form of a thought in which all the parts are connected, that is what is expressed in this familiar rule: «the aesthetic object must be the bearer of an idea». Even the simple beauty of measure or of geometrical regularity is not absolutely without idea. Now, this regularity suggests the idea of a harmonic proportion—an idea which, in the higher transformations of beauty, is reproduced only in more developed forms.

And since the ideas awakened in us by an aesthetic object depend not only upon it but also upon the momentary disposition, as upon the permanent disposition, of our consciousness, this explains, on the one hand, the indetermination of aesthetic ideas and, on the other hand, their dependence upon the object of observation. The same object is susceptible of awakening, in different persons, ideas that vary in a mani[p. 184]fold manner; just as the spirit of the individual cultivated from the aesthetic point of view will be able to combine diverse ideas with the same object.

From this analysis Wundt deduces the following conclusions: that aesthetic feeling always emanates from the immediate effect of isolated representations upon the consciousness; that this effect reveals itself on the occasion of the arrangement or ordering that the isolated representation offers within the existing store of general representations; that the intimate motive of pleasure consists always in the ease with which the object of our perception adapts itself to the prepared forms of the intuition of time and of space; and that the uniform cadence of rhythm, as regards time, and the relations—easily visible to our spirit—of the symmetrical and proportional arrangement, as regards space, enclose the simplest conditions of aesthetic pleasure.

It is inferred from this that into the elementary aesthetic sensation or feeling there enter, as conditions of pleasure, a principle of order, another of easy adaptation, and, finally, another rational one, which serves as the content of the feeling—which confirms the belief that unity and variety, as well as harmony, that is, the law existing between unity and variety, are the fundamental conditions of aesthetic pleasure in its most elementary forms.

It is a character inherent in our physiological nature, says Soret, that every sensation which is prolonged or which is repeated indefinitely ceases to be perceived by us or comes to be painful. Variety is absolutely necessary to reanimate our impressions and to prevent the effect of dulling—often of pain—that the monotony of our sensations produces, whether in the physical or in the intellectual order.

In [p. 185]the perception of the beautiful, variety is, then, a necessary condition of pleasure, though a negative condition, according to Soret, since for him the pleasurable satisfaction of the beautiful is born of a principle of equality or of unity, that is, of a reiterated impression, whose law or relation we can acquire by means of an immediate intuition—which happens in harmony, in rhythm, symmetry, and proportion, elementary forms of aesthetic feelings, according to the philosopher Wundt.

The superior aesthetic feelings appear, generally, as complex resultants of all the forms of feelings that Wundt calls intellectual, as the most developed and most complicated forms of these feelings. They are the products of the concatenation of elementary aesthetic feelings with forms of intellectual feelings; that is, with logical, moral, and religious feelings, sensory feelings and diverse emotions also forming part of their constitution.

Aesthetic feeling, thus comprehending all the other feelings, takes possession of the whole life of the soul. A finished work of art puts our logical feeling into a state of tension, excites the ethical and religious feelings, engenders emotions and sensory feelings, and adds still to that combination, in the capacity of essential constitutive elements, the elementary aesthetic feelings, which proceed from the concatenation of successive representations or of parts of a simultaneous representation.

Now, all those elements excite a superior aesthetic feeling, on the sole condition that they unite to produce a total effect that is harmonic and full of measure or proportion. The elementary aesthetic feelings, joined to this complex representation, are, [p. 186]chiefly, those which favor this harmonic union, becoming, for that reason, the base of the total aesthetic effect.

Consequently, the psychological analysis of the superior aesthetic feelings has a double function to fulfill: first, it must give account of the manner in which the particular forms of feelings are bound together to produce a total aesthetic effect; and second, it must ascertain the intimate motive by whose aid the elementary aesthetic feelings are especially fitted to become the factors or bases of the total aesthetic effect.

Under the first aspect, the diverse species of aesthetic production differ from one another in the most varied manner. Each aesthetic form directs itself, first, toward a determinate form of feeling, which then sets the others in movement.

Thus, music engenders emotions by describing them through the sensory coloration of sounds and their succession. But this description or sensory painting of emotions does not yet produce the aesthetic effect of music, which results from the satisfying development and the final resolution of the emotions, for which these have need of the elementary aesthetic feelings, which are born of rhythmic and harmonic combinations of sounds. Nevertheless, that satisfying resolution of emotions cannot be realized in our soul save through the appearance of logical, ethical, and religious feelings, in the capacity of secondary constitutive elements of the musical effect.

Architecture, which among the plastic arts is the freest and the most akin to music, reveals to us clearly that the feelings of simple or elementary aesthetic forms—symmetry, proportional arrangement, and so forth—manifest themselves there and are the most intimate effects. Those [p. 187]feelings are born, whether from relations of magnitude or from the absolute magnitude of the forms. Now, the conception of relations of suitable magnitudes satisfies, at the same time, the logical feeling and excites besides the religious feeling, under certain conditions, chiefly if the forms are found within the limits of our faculty of perception.

The other plastic arts are bound, more than architecture, to forms that exterior nature offers to our senses or that are provoked by the variable taste of the epoch, such as the considerations and habits of practical life. It is for that reason that, in those arts, the associations of representations occupy the first place. Thus, for example, in a historical painting it is the intellectual, moral, and religious relations that immediately excite the corresponding feelings. But beyond those movements of the soul, provoked by association, the feeling of the elementary aesthetic form constantly preserves its importance, since it must already contain a general indication concerning the direction of those intellectual feelings.

In those diverse forms, poetry directs itself, in the most immediate manner, to the intellectual feelings—wholly the contrary of music; for if in poetry the intellectual feelings constitute the most special content of the work of art, music must engender those feelings by the movement of the emotions.
