The aesthetic spectator, like the tragic artist, shares with the Apollonian artistic sphere the complete pleasure in appearance and in beholding, and, at the same time, denies that pleasure and has a satisfaction even greater in the destruction of the visible apparent world. The content of the tragic myth is, in the first place, an epic event with the glorification of the combating hero. But whence proceeds that trait, enigmatic in itself, that there should be represented the suffering within the hero, the painful victories, the most tormenting contradictions of the motives, the ugly and inharmonious, in short, in forms so innumerable, with such predilection, ever anew and, precisely, in the freshest and most youthful age of a people, if there be not perceived, in this whole, a loftier pleasure? For him who wishes to derive the tragic effect from moral sources alone, says Nietzsche, the explanation cannot present itself. For the explanation of the tragic myth one must seek, precisely, the primitive requirement and the pleasure proper to it in the purely aesthetic sphere, without entering into the domain of compassion, of fear, of the morally exalted. How can the ugly and inharmonious, content of the tragic myth, produce an aesthetic pleasure?

Thus, then, in Nietzsche's view, it is necessary to rise to a metaphysics of Art, repeating the sentence that existence and the world appear justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon; in which sense the tragic myth, too, must convince us that even the ugly and inharmonious is an artistic play that the will plays with itself in the eternal plenitude of its pleasure. This primitive phenomenon of Dionysian art, difficult to comprehend, is made comprehensible only in the marvelous signification of musical dissonance; just [p. 234]as, in general, only music can give, placed beside the world, an idea of what is to be understood, under the justification of the world, as an aesthetic phenomenon.

The pleasure produced by the tragic myth has a common homeland with the pleasure-filled sensation of dissonance in music. The Dionysian, with its primal pleasure, perceived even in jest, is the common birth-womb of music and of the tragic myth.

Nietzsche believes that by this means, taking as an aid the musical relation of dissonance, the difficult problem of the tragic effect has been essentially facilitated; for now we understand what it means to wish to behold, at the same time, tragedy and to long beyond beholding; a state which, in relation to the artistic dissonance employed, would have to be characterized as if one wished to hear and to long beyond hearing, at the same time. That tendency toward the infinite, the fluttering of longing, in the greatest pleasure, in reality clearly perceived, recall that we must recognize, in both states, a Dionysian phenomenon, which ever anew reveals to us the playful building up and tearing down of the individual world as the emanation of a primal pleasure.

Music and tragic myth are thus, in like manner, expression of the Dionysian aptitude of a people and inseparable one from the other. Both proceed from an artistic domain that lies beyond the Apollonian; both glorify a region in whose chords of pleasure dissonance, as well as the horrible image of the world, are extinguished full of enchantment; both play with the sting of displeasure, trusting in their excessively powerful magic arts; both justify, by means of this play, the existence even of the worst world. Here the Dionysian shows itself, measured by the Apollonian, as the eternal and primitive artistic power that calls com[p. 235]pletely into existence the whole world of phenomena, in whose center a new radiance of glorification is necessary in order to keep alive the animated world of individuation.

This theory of Nietzsche's concerning the tragic still preserves its importance, notwithstanding its obscurity, accentuated by the intervention of the mythological, and even after the abandonment that Nietzsche made of his sympathies for Schopenhauer and Wagner, in whose doctrines he found his inspiration; and that importance depends on the fact that it is an aesthetic explanation, and not a moral or merely psychological one, that he gives of the pleasurable effect of the artistically tragic, comparing the tragic myth with dissonance in music. Applied to the study of Hellenic tragedy, it has a special importance for the interpretation it attributes to the artistic divinities Apollo and Dionysus; and even considered in relation to the problem of the tragic, it contains, within that mythological symbolism, an explanation that does not differ from those given previously.

In effect, if one considers the satyr as the incarnation of life in the plenitude of its freedom, as the expression of its blind and free will, stimulated solely by pleasure and pain, which longs to live and struggles with the limitations that Nature offers it —that pessimistic will of Schopenhauer, condemned irremissibly to pain by the absolute necessity of its determination and individualization, a will necessarily tragic from the moment it is set in action—, we may consider the Dionysian element as the element of freedom, which all recognize as the principal source of the tragic; only that here, as in Schopenhauer, that freedom is not moral, but purely instinctive; it is the creative expansion of psychic life, which, like all life, harbors that germ of freedom, as Berg[p. 236]son demonstrates.

That principle of the tragic is sympathetic, because it is the true value; and even when it struggles against the opposite principle and succumbs, that sympathy does not disappear—it joins itself to pity and to resignation and maintains itself as the true value; but it is necessary that this Dionysian principle express an absolute, embody an eternal idea, in order that the event be tragic, because only then does it emerge from the sphere of the purely criminal to rise to what Nietzsche calls the metaphysical consolation, the existence of a higher ideal order in which the spirit of the spectator may find a possible reconciliation.

Dominated as Nietzsche was by the determinism reigning in his age and by the value given to the phenomena of Nature, he symbolized that principle of freedom in the satyr; but, deepening that symbol, he found what is today considered a truth: that that primitive impulse of freedom constitutes the musicality of the spirit, the source of the tragic myth expressed through music.

The opposite principle—of order, of measure, of rational construction, of law, of artistic form—is the Apollonian principle, without which man cannot live, because it signifies the idealization of human efforts to constitute a civilization against which it is not possible to struggle, because it represents intangible justice. The struggle between these two elements and their purely ideal reconciliation in the spectator thus constitutes the tragic, both for those who follow Fichte and for Nietzsche, who, poet and philosopher at once, gave to his theory this double character.

In the incessant struggle between the free spirit, which tends to expand and to reintegrate the ideal with elements of reality, abandoned notwithstanding that they are loved, and the order conquered after so many sacrifices and represented by the precepts of morality, of [p. 237]politics, and of religion, man feels a horrible fear that this good may disappear before the titanic effort of a free and sympathetic character, whose ruin he accepts with resignation under the sway of the traditional precept. This sad feeling of moral satisfaction undoubtedly produces the tragic, which some aestheticians, such as Herckenrath, cited by Faguet, seek to explain as an atavistic feeling that renews the primitive instincts of ferocity, which took delight in the suffering of one's fellows—to which Faguet joins a little love of truth and an invincible preoccupation with serious things.

It might be affirmed, finally, that the simple spectacle of a free power, struggling with forces infinitely superior to its will, suffices to explain the pleasure of the tragic.

### XVIII. EL SENTIMIENTO DE LO CÓMICO Y LO DRAMÁTICO — XVIII. THE FEELING OF THE COMIC AND THE DRAMATIC

If an irremediable conflict, when it is real, produces the feeling of the tragic, when it is apparent it has an opposite result and occasions in us a wholly joyful feeling, imparting to the beautiful a special characteristic, the modality of the comic.

In the comic, says Lemcke, freedom triumphs over the contradictions of life, and, making itself superior to them, it can convert the serious side of life into mere appearance, thus stripping it of its importance and re-establishing harmony by the simple destruction of that appearance, without any effective evil, without true disaster, as in the tragic, and leaving in the soul the pure pleasure of harmony, without the shadow of sadness or of compassionate pain. Even there, where our spirit dies away, through sympathy or antipathy, at the moment in which we consider the thing as null, as appearance and mere play, we give ourselves over to joy, being able to laugh at it or at our error in taking it seriously.

The emotion of the comic is thus opposed to that of the tragic; both are born of a contradiction, of a conflict, of a contrast, but in place of terror there arise from the comic conflict joy and laughter, instead of seriousness and compassion, and a game for our understanding, so far as possible always at another's expense; and this happens because in the tragic the conflict cannot disappear, harmony cannot be re-established without the actual ru[p. 239]in of a power; whereas in the comic, by reason of the appearance of the conflict, equilibrium is re-established with nothing more than the destruction of that appearance. Freedom triumphs without true struggle, without any sacrifice, producing a wholly joyful harmony.

This very thing explains the transition from one aesthetic modality to another; it suffices that the conflict lose its real truth, becoming an appearance, for the tragic to be converted into the comic or the laughable, as happens with parodies of tragic struggles, and, conversely, the comic can be converted into the tragic by a conversion of the apparent into the true and real.

Basch distinguishes three moments in everything comic: the object begins by seeming to us quite natural; this observation is not accompanied by any appreciable sentimental tone; afterward, we perceive that it is absurd, which causes us a disagreeable feeling; and finally, there is a third moment, which is accompanied by a feeling of pleasure, but in which it is more difficult to distinguish the causes. On the one hand there enters, as an essential factor of that feeling of pleasure, as Hobbes would already have observed and Bacon maintained, the feeling of our own superiority. We know full well, adds Basch, that we have discovered the absurdity of the comic thing, and this consciousness of our penetration, which is but a form of the most powerful feeling of human nature, the feeling of egoism, the feeling of self-preservation, evidently fills us with pleasurable satisfaction.

This feeling grows still more when the object that seems absurd to us is not a phenomenon of Nature, but rather when the absurdity has been intended. In the [p. 240]comic, which Basch qualifies as voluntary, the contrast that forms the soul of the comic springs from the difference between the illogical world, toward which we have let ourselves be dragged for an instant, and the logical world, which recovers its titles and strongly opposes the first. When the comic is involuntary, that is, when it is offered by natural phenomena, something similar is produced; there too the feeling of our superiority and the feeling of the logical constitution of the Universe make themselves felt. In Basch's view, when we observe an absurdity outside ourselves, we begin by experiencing a disagreeable feeling; we feel disoriented; afterward, the final feeling of pleasure, which is as characteristic in the comic as in the sublime, definitively absorbs it. We realize, of course, the absurdity of the phenomenon, and at once we know that this absurdity is only apparent, that, at bottom, the being that makes us laugh is but a very contemptible derogation of the essential laws of Nature, that these laws hold good, notwithstanding some exceptions and some monstrosities, and that their existence in no way impedes the natural and necessary order of things.

Basch recognizes three great causes of the comic, which he considers synonymous with the laughable: physical well-being, absurdity or the coexistence of two irreconcilable concepts, and finally, the consciousness of our superiority. Basch believes that, besides these causes of laughter, others intervene which diversify the comic and complicate its nature.

Masci declares that one of the most difficult points in the psychology of the aesthetic feelings is the psychology of the comic. Sensations, by themselves, do not produce it, nor do combinations of simple sensations. A dissonance or a disharmony of [p. 241]colors is disagreeable, but they are not comic if they are not referred to a representation of which they form part; for example, dissonance in a well-known aria, disharmony of colors in the decoration with which it contrasts. Comicality derives, consequently, in general, from a contrast of intellectual nature; only that with these two elements alone one is still far indeed from comicality. In order that the intellectual contrast be comic, the synthesis of the contrasting representations must be possible and, moreover, must be suggested; but, in the act of the repulsion's being realized, it needs to appear clear, and the attempt to resolve itself into nothing. Without this suggestive life and without this failure there is no comicality, according to Masci.

But, in his view, the foregoing does not suffice to define the comic; for the logical absurd has the indicated characters and does not produce the comic feeling. It is necessary that the subject of the contrast be the same, that the same subject appear as the knot of the antithesis, as great and small, as wise and stupid; it not mattering that the subject of the antithesis be inanimate and know nothing of what we discover in it: because, in the excitation of comicality we instinctively transfer our consciousness to the object and, for that reason, we find comic the mountain that gives birth to a mouse. It is necessary, moreover, that the contrast be represented in a sensible form; otherwise, it would be foreign to art; that it be a sophistication, not of the intellect, like the logical absurd, but of fantasy; and finally, it is necessary, as Spencer has noted, that the contrast be descending, a concept consigned by Kant when he says that comicality derives from the sudden resolving into nothing of an expectation. The comic feeling proceeds, consequently, according to Masci, from that form of the intellectual contrast in which the small is compared with the [p. 242]great and takes its place.

And the small is always the second element, not that from which it proceeds, but that at which the intellectual contrast arrives. The ascending discordance, says Masci, would produce the contrary effect, wonder. Moreover, the small, at which the comic contrast arrives, must not be dishonest or very bad, to the point of engendering disgust and hatred, nor atypical, in such a way that it comes to be indifferent. For this reason Aristotle said well when he affirmed that comicality derives from a harmless absurdity, from an ignominy without pain.

However complex and profound this analysis may be, Masci finds it still insufficient; because in truth, if the comic is a typical absurd in sensible form, we ought to expect that the repulsion which bursts forth with the suggestion of accord does not annul the tendency to think it again, as happens in the purely logical contrast. And so it happens, in effect; the form being typical, it comes to be a source of pleasure in itself and induces one to admire it. The comic contrast, says Masci, is repeated in the fantasy a certain number of times, rapidly, in the form of alternation or oscillation; and the greater the alternation of the intellectual ricorsi, the greater the feeling of comicality, and it is null if the alternation is null. The clearer the fusion of the hostile elements in the form is to the imagination, the more difficult it comes to be to think of them separately, and the more the play of the tendencies and repulsions of intellectual fantasy grows. From there derives, according to Masci, what may be called the suggestive power of the comic, which is the soul of the words of esprit that are truly effective, because, the greater the number of the relations knotted and almost intricately bound in a single group, the more numerous the directions of attention which the image stimulates, and its returns, the greater the fantastic activity.

[p. 243]These two characters, the descending but not painful contrast, and the rapid alternation, the succession of the fantastic-intellectual ricorsi, explain two properties of the feeling of the comic: the feeling of superiority, which derives from the first, and the feeling of free movement, which derives from the second. The first property was demonstrated by Hobbes, when he says that laughter is a sudden pride, which is born of the sudden perception of a superiority of ours over others or of our past weakness. And that this form of the feeling of self enters into the excitation of the comic is true; but it is not true that it is the exclusive factor or even the sole principal one. For Masci it is a secondary and concomitant factor, and one that explains two things: first, that we hardly laugh at ourselves, and that, though we gladly take another as a comic subject, we do not want another to take us ourselves as such; second, that comic existence is never solitary, save the exception of humor.

The feeling of freedom, which is another property of the feeling of the comic, may be defined, according to Masci, as the feeling of reaction against seriousness. Truly, seriousness, intimately felt, does not admit comic reactions; the believer does not laugh at profane incidents in Church. Nevertheless, the reaction against seriousness is a natural feeling in every man who is not, by his nature, condemned to sadness and pain. Parody presents itself spontaneously, in the midst of seriousness; because the serious and the laughable are in perpetual contrast in life and in daily experience. And since joy corresponds to comicality, to freedom, to abandon, to unconcern, and since seriousness is labor, difficulty, the obstacle to be overcome, so it is always agreeable to pass from the severe aspect of life to the easy; and the comic conjunc[p. 244]tion of the two aspects is the aesthetic form of this transaction. The comic temperament is determined, probably, says Masci, by a certain ineptitude for remaining in the serious and the solemn, which makes one feel pain at maintaining oneself in it and take joy in freeing oneself from it. Children are the most common example of the comic temperament; they suffer greatly under gravity, which for them cannot but be forced, and they are very ready to rid themselves of it as soon as they can do so.

Summing up what has been set forth, Masci establishes that, in every manner of comicality there are at least two contemporaneous and opposed representations, fused in the same form, and mutually repugnant and, for that reason, not fixed, but alternating in a more or less brief series of inverse transitions from one to the other, and almost of transformations and metamorphoses. The contemporaneity and the perspicuity of the contrast, in the simulation of unity, constitute what is called the point of the comic. But since two opposed representations cannot easily coexist, on account of the narrowness of consciousness, we must understand contemporaneity as rapid alternation, as a rapidly inverted succession, which simulates coexistence. Now then, from this near-gymnastics, to which comicality constrains the intellectual fantasy, there derives a feeling of pleasure so intense that it reaches almost the tone of the sensory feelings and resembles what is piquant in the gustatory sensations, the slight sting and tickle in the tactile, and the sensation of the brilliant in the visual.

Some have maintained that the feeling of the comic is a mixture of pleasure and pain; but if one reflects, says Masci, that if pain sets in comicality is destroyed, it does not seem that this opinion can be accepted. The [p. 245]pleasure of comicality, very intense in itself, offers no negative compensations, in his view. The ugly, which exists in the comic, does not produce pain, as, in general, the representation of the ugly in art does not produce it, because the ugly that art represents is the characteristic and the interesting. Art must reproduce living individuality and, for that reason, must admit that proportion of ugliness which serves to reproduce it and to characterize it. Art knows no ugliness that is not dissolved.

The causes of the pleasure of the comic, according to Masci, are various. First, that alternating transit of the intellectual fantasy from one to another of the contrasting representations; then, that play of knotting and untying relations, that alternation of tension and of release of energy, that feeling which frees one from the submission and the bond of seriousness. There is still the stimulus of the feeling of self; but referred, principally, to intellectual superiority, to bravura, to the triumph of critical and penetrating reason. This species of critical vanity is one of the reasons for the fact that the pleasure of comicality is hardly enjoyed by itself alone, that it intensifies in company, and that, for this reason, we do everything to excite the attention of others upon the comic object and that we never employ esprit against ourselves. Finally, the intensity of the pleasure develops also through the complete absence of negative compensations; because, if any value whatever appears, the comic effect is instantaneously destroyed. However little comicality contradicts piety, affection, respect, pride, the relative feeling is not produced or, once produced, is extinguished.

A notable philosopher, Bergson, has occupied himself with this aesthetic modality, seeking to know its profound signification. According to Bergson, the comic requires, in order to produce all its effect, something like a momentary anesthesia [p. 246]of the heart, addressing itself to pure intelligence. For Bergson, as for the earlier aestheticians, the comic and the laughable are the same thing; hence he attributes to the comic the conditions and characters of the laughable. The comic or laughable responds to a need of social life, it is translated where a certain mechanical rigidity is found, in place of flexibility, and it offers the character of the accidental, remaining, so to speak, on the surface of the person, as happens with the phenomenon of distraction, which, if it is not in the very source of the comic, permits us to infer its nature. What makes us laugh, says Bergson, is a kind of automatism; the comic is unconscious. Laughter is a kind of sanction, and from this it results that laughter pursues, in many cases, a useful end of general improvement and that the comic oscillates between life and art.

The automatism and the rigidity that make one laugh produce a more intense effect when they refer to a certain fundamental distraction of the person, as if the soul let itself be fascinated, hypnotized, by the materiality of a simple action, thwarting its natural dynamic tendency, its infinite flexibility, which imparts to the body the seal of grace. Wherever matter, with its tendency to inertia, succeeds in condensing externally the life of the soul, in fixing movement, in thwarting grace, it obtains from the body a comic effect. If, then, one wished to define the comic here by approximating it to its contrary, it would be necessary to oppose it to grace rather than to beauty, says Bergson; because it is rigidity rather than ugliness. The attitudes, gestures, and movements of the human body are laughable in the exact measure in which that body makes us think of a simple mechanism. For this reason, to imitate someone is to bring out the part of automatism he has let introduce itself into his person; it is, by very definition, to make him comic, and it is not [p. 247]astonishing that imitation makes one laugh. The inflexibility of life, in the mechanical direction, is thus the true cause of laughter or of the comic.

Bergson insists on this idea, confirming it in diverse directions: the mechanization of life is the origin of the laughable or comic, which is a sanction of social character. Hence the comic addresses itself to pure intelligence and laughter is incompatible with emotion. Unsociability of the character, insensibility of the spectator, such are the two essential conditions of a comic character, to which is added a third, implied in the other two, automatism or distraction. Bergson thus recognizes, through this analysis, that what is essential in the comic is the lack of freedom in the comic character, which is not in contradiction but, on the contrary, confirms the feeling of freedom which arises, by reaction, in the spirit of the spectator.

According to a modern theory, the essence of the laughable is found in freedom. Laughter, says Penjon, is nothing but the expression of freedom felt or of our sympathy for certain real or imagined manifestations of an alien freedom; it is the sign of freedom, freedom made visible, the freedom that, in its turn, is the essence of play. But the freedom that constitutes play and gives laughter occasion to burst forth is that which surprises, that which intervenes, in a certain manner, in spite of the rule, mocking it and reason. At bottom, the impression of the comic always has the same origin. The disagreement, the disproportion, or the impropriety, imagined or real, appear as the work of a spontaneity that plays with order, proportion, and rule, that hides them from him who might have found and observed them. For this reason, laughter is not explained: because spontaneity, freedom, considered in itself, as nature, is attested but not defined.

[p. 248]This theory, which makes the laughable and the comic consist in that unreflective freedom, playing with the rules established by reason to regulate it, comprehends also, as its foundation, the notion of a slight disorder, of a disorder that surprises but that produces no serious consequences. Freedom, by itself alone, engenders grace, which is one of the characters of beauty; but not the comic, nor the ridiculous. In order for it to produce the laughable, it needs to be considered as a disturbing principle, as a deviation from the rule, effected by an activity of play, as a trick played on reason.

But not all disorder is laughable, even though it be slight; it must offer the form of an opposition, of a contrast, that makes the spirit oscillate, with vivacity and freedom, between the appearances of the beautiful, the true, the good, the correct, or the simply ordinary, which reason loves, as Lévéque says, and the true forms to which those appearances correspond and with which it is found in effective contrast. The opposition between what things are and what it seems to us they ought to be, that conflict, without serious consequences, excites the feeling of love of freedom and produces, as its effect, an interior harmony, wholly joyful and of great vivacity, translating itself into the biological phenomenon of laughter, on account of the intensity of the transition between the apparent and the real and, also, of the complete dominion of pleasure. The comic, says Lemcke, shows the freedom of the spirit, which can treat everything as appearance and play, and it raises us to the pleasure of pure harmony, and, to a certain degree, makes the worst expiate its malice.

This opposition of the true with the apparent, of the real with the ideal, is not, as Soriano Sánchez says, [p. 249]a total, absolute opposition, but a partial and relative one; it is not a negation of ideality, to the point that reality should seem superior to the idea; because, if it were so, the feeling of the comic would not be, as it is, wholly joyful, but would be accompanied by the sadness inseparable from the ruin of the ideal. On the contrary, all the comic, of elevated style, presupposes that the ideal is known, whose abandonment is shown in a ridiculous and condemnable manner.

Freedom and order explain, consequently, this aesthetic modality of the comic, opposed to that of the tragic. In the tragic, the reconciliation of freedom and of nature is realized in the absolute order, in the domains of reason; in the comic, that reconciliation is effected in a relative and finite order; in both, the objective element is a disharmony and the subjective one a harmony, effected, in the tragic, by an effort of reason, and in the comic, by imagination, which engenders and resolves the visible contrasts.

The multitude of circumstances that influence whether an action seems comic, says Revilla, gives a certain inconstancy and variability to the notion of the comic and makes its appreciation vary greatly, according to the cases in which it is produced and according to the criterion and the state of mind of him who contemplates it. The comic, like the sublime, is always in the subject, never in the object, observes Jean Paul. Objects in no way comic in themselves come to be so, insofar as they give matter for an imitation or mimic reproduction. Even to laugh at one's own actions, it is necessary to make oneself another self and to be able to attribute to the first the thoughts of the second. Jean Paul deduces from this that every definition of the comic founded solely on a real contradiction is faulty at its base; because the comic requires, at the least, an appearance of free [p. 250]subjectivity.

Thus, we laugh only at animals that have a certain degree of intelligence and to which we can attribute an anthropomorphic personification; the comic increases in proportion to the intelligence of the comic person, and the man who knows how to raise himself to the cause of life gives himself the spectacle of the best comedy, because he can attribute the most elevated motives to the basest actions, thus engendering the absurd. Nature in itself is not comic; but we can, says Soriano Sánchez, conceive as comic certain forms with a certain apparent contradiction.

Because the comic presents itself accompanied, almost always, by laughter, the laughable has been confused with the comic, the former being defined by the latter and thus confounding the genus with the species. The comic, in effect, is a species or particular form of the laughable; but it is not all the laughable; because laughter, as a biological phenomenon, can be associated with the beautiful as with the ugly, with the serious as with the comic, with pain as with pleasure. It has been observed that there are bitter and violent laughs, as well as spontaneous and sincere laughs, innocent laughs as well as malign ones, laughs born of a normal state of the organism as well as laughs provoked by a pathological state, laughs engendered by true comic situations as well as laughs without explanation, such as those that become a habitual state, in servile natures or in infantile characters; that there may be, too, spirits that preserve, by habit, seriousness, in the presence of the truly comic, in which case the comic can exist without laughter; that some creative geniuses of the artistic comic were serious spirits and that many produce more effect, in expressing it, by preserving seriousness. Serious nations are those that have the most elevated and profound feeling of the comic, says Jean Paul. In [p. 251]his view, seriousness is a condition of the comic, even in individuals; for this reason the ecclesiastical estate has produced the greatest comic writers, Rabelais, Swift, Sterne, and Tirso.

From not considering the comic as a species of the laughable, derived from an opposition in beautiful reality, which produces in our soul an innocent and pure joy, there has arisen the confusion of the comic with the ridiculous, which is a form of the ugly. The ridiculous also produces laughter and is engendered, like the comic, by a contrast; but this is not of the same nature as the contrast or disagreement of the comic, nor does it produce the same feeling. The feeling of the ridiculous is bound to contempt for the being in which it is realized. The ridiculous is not sympathetic; the comic is. Don Quixote takes possession of our sympathy from his first adventure, and that sympathy grows throughout his entire comic history; his follies make us laugh, with that innocent and benevolent laughter of the truly comic. The same does not happen with the Tartuffe of Molière, who displeases us, even though he provokes our laughter. This depends on the fact that the comic is explained by the tragic and the ridiculous by the ugly, of which it is an attenuation. In the contrast or the disorder of the comic, the real is inferior to the apparent, as power, value, or freedom, and in the contrast of the ridiculous the true or real is superior to the apparent. In the first it is ascending and in the second descending.

It pleases us, says Soriano Sánchez, that inferiority should take on the appearances of superiority, as play or with a noble end, as when we see a child disguised as a warrior or a sincere man sterilely undertaking an enterprise beyond his powers; but the contrary displeases us, much more so when the man avails himself of the forms of the good in order to degrade his nature. The comic is an opposition that is verified in a [p. 252]beautiful reality, in such a way that, if this reality is lacking, as is fundamental, the comic disappears and the ugly or the ridiculous presents itself.

Not all the arts can express the comic directly, as Poetry can. Certain lines can perhaps determine contrasts that produce, by association, the idea and the feeling of the comic in Architecture; Sculpture can reproduce comic or tragic types that Poetry and Painting have personified, engraving them upon the imagination; Music, with its dissonances and imitations of sounds, can also awaken the idea of the tragic and of the comic, as well as their respective emotion, but the true domain of the tragic and of the comic is found in Painting and more especially in Poetry, in the forms of drama and of the novel, without the epic and lyric genres being foreign to them.

The aestheticians make diverse classifications of the comic, as of the tragic; but the species they establish are fragmentary forms, indefinable by their subjective character and their expression, subjected to a conventional criterion. To those forms correspond the objective or burlesque comic, the subjective or witty comic, and the subjective-objective or humoristic comic, of which Soriano Sánchez speaks; the high, middle, and low comic, which Lemcke describes; the involuntary and voluntary laughable of Dumont's classification, which comprise three genera and varied species; the ingenuous comic and the comic of imposture of Philbert; the benign comic and the malign comic of Lemcke; parody, the tragicomic, and irony; humor being the most important of these forms.

The dramatic, the third principal modality of the aesthetic feelings of contrast, is the beauty of action, as Masci defines it. In order that the action be [p. 253]dramatic, according to this psychologist, it must result from an interlacing and a contrast of human actions significant for the moral life; it must present, in a conflict of actions, the personal agents as conscious, emotive, closely characterized; that is, having a pronounced form of moral or amoral will and being, for that reason, the object of the purest and most vivid aesthetic sympathy.

The feeling of the dramatic is the most eventful and the most agitated of the aesthetic feelings, because it does not proceed in a single direction, but rather resembles a converging and an interlacing of waves, each of which acquires greater intensity through the shock of the others, whether by addition or by repulsion. The elements of the dramatic are, then, these two: contrast of the actions significant for the moral life of man, and representation of characters, of intentions, of situations, with that multiplicity and seriousness which the reality of life presents. The dramatic must be polychrome. For this reason the uniform, the indifferent, are the opposite of the dramatic, which does not harmonize either with the idyllic feeling and requires the shock of the passions that contrast. Another direct enemy of the dramatic, adds Masci, is the conventional in the characters, in the situations, and in the solutions. Drama, as a reproduction of real moral life, though idealized, does not much admit that which contrasts with real life.

Masci finds that the great emotive efficacy of the dramatic has its reason in the nature of feeling, which is much less agile than the representative faculty. For this reason, when, as in drama, the exciting representations are various and opposed, and such that they interest in the highest degree, because they represent directly the pains, the joys, the hopes, the despairs, the loves, and the hatreds, th[p. 254]en the things of human life, the feelings that are engendered, are fused into a mixed feeling, whose intensity is not only the sum of the elementary excitations, but even the product of mutual reinforcements and of the secondary re-excitations of one by another. Easily influenced by the direct and unobstructed action of sympathy, the dramatic feelings find another coefficient of force in the excitation of the formal feelings; because just as the dramatic is, essentially, an art of the successive, even when its representation is entrusted to the figurative arts, in which case by suggestion, so uncertainty, anxiety, curiosity, expectation, doubt, etc., are strongly stimulated and in turn stimulate the quantitative feelings, which are the effect of the nature and quality of the representative action.

The foregoing description refers to the artistic form of the dramatic, which is that which is preferentially studied by the aestheticians, taking the experiences of drama in its diverse forms, in tragedy and comedy, which are the expression of dramatic poetry, and in drama, properly so called, which is distinguished from the other two, because its harmonic denouement is neither tragic nor comic. But the tragic, the comic, and the harmonic dramatic present themselves also in real life, and it is from there that the poet takes them in order to clothe them in artistic forms, prescribed by the respective technique, modifying reality in order to perfect it. Then, to the feeling of the dramatic, of the tragic, and of the comic in social life, there is associated a special aesthetic feeling, a feeling of pleasure, with which Nietzsche explains the association of joy with the feeling of horror that the tragic simply produces. This feeling is bound to the pure form of the representation; it is the Apollonian form with which the Dionysian content is represented, which is the nucleus or tragic myth.

### XIX. EL SENTIMIENTO DE LO HUMORÍSTICO — XIX. THE FEELING OF THE HUMOROUS

If it is difficult to determine the nature and forms of the feeling of the comic, it is much more difficult to specify the meaning of humor, because the aesthetic category, in which one attempts to comprehend it, has no fixed limits, nor are the forms in which it is exhibited so alike that its common and specific characters can be determined, nor have the artists who are called humorists had the same psychology, analogous methods, and produced works susceptible of being grouped in one and the same genre.

A symbol of an age of skepticism, in which human values lose all their prestige, humor is a work of dissolution, in which the subject predominates as the sole moral power, attributing to itself a unique value, before which the objective ideals file past like decrepit entities, condemned to death, under the anathema of a disdainful irony, which assumes the most varied forms, from the pious smile to the gesture of implacable satire.

That radical subjectivism explains its great variety, the absolute freedom of its means of expression, and its affinities with all the artistic modalities, into which it penetrates with its dissolving weapon of aesthetic irony.

The diversity of its meanings begins with the sense of the word humor. What the English call [p. 256]humour has meant, primitively, liquid, and, in particular, the liquid elements of the bodies of animals. The hypothesis long in vogue, says Dumont, that the state of the different humors of the organism was the cause of the different temperaments and characters, has extended the name of humors to the different dispositions of the soul. One may call humor, he adds, the phenomenon by which a single particular quality so completely possesses a man that it drags, in a single direction, all his feelings, his spirit, and his faculties. Thus Ben Jonson defines it; but independently of this general acceptation, the word humor has since been employed, especially, to designate two different things: first, the state of a soul that has the habit of abandoning itself entirely to its humor or, rather, to the different humors or natural dispositions that succeed one another within it, and second, humor par excellence, that is to say, the exceptional humor which is distinguished from the rest.

In the first sense, in which humor yields to all the movements of spontaneity, one calls a humorist a writer who lets his imagination wander over the most diverse objects, from the sad to the merry, from the low to the sublime, joining together, consequently, the most disparate things and producing works that do not have beauty as their end. In the second sense, humor may be merry or sad. Merry humor merges with jocosity; sad or melancholy humor is the melancholy of a superior soul, which laughs at human imperfections. The first Lemcke calls good humor and the second bad humor.

Good humor preserves its cheerfulness and its inner freedom in all relations, even the most serious, and knows how to see the merry side, even of the worst things. Bad humor is that of the weak spirit, which does not [p. 257]succeed in bearing or enduring any sensation. It betrays a nervous weakness that carries the one who suffers it from one extreme to another, involuntarily, without his being able to master himself. Soriano Sánchez, who regards the humorous as the form of the subjective-objective comic, derives it from the conditions of the subject and from the consideration of the object; it is the comic of the general, in which the effort of wit is superior and must be compared with the general conditions of life. For this author, this form of the comic comprises simple humor, in which the individual, seeing everything under its gloomy aspect, wishes to look at things in a comic relation, believing himself free of the world's pettinesses, and it is he who turns out to be comic; dissolved romantic or satanic humor, in which, weary of society and of himself, the individual mocks everything and even himself; and free or reflective humor, in which the artist, contemplating human frailties, does not deify himself, but sets against them a lofty ideal of reform and a hope of improvement, attempting to raise up a decayed society. Jean Paul adds to the modality of humor, as a subdivision, the laune, which is the humor that principally wishes to laugh and to make others laugh; it is humor belittled and imprisoned, which presents itself as the esprit of the domestic hearth or of the countryside and which approaches the burlesque.

Notwithstanding this dispersion, this elasticity, humor receives the influence of its social milieu, which imprints a certain homogeneity upon its works, permitting classifications which, even though they lack logical rigor, derive from the particular orientation offered by the psychology of the races. Thus one speaks of English humor and of German humor and distinguishes them from Latin humor by characters that derive from the predominance of the ordering reason or of free feeling in the con[p. 258]sciousness of the race, from the empire of classicism or of romanticism in the artistic attitude of the milieu.

Firmery insists on this distinction. «In English», says this critic, «humor designates everything that is opposed to the grave and the serious. From the moment gravity is set aside and the most discreet smile is made to arise, by means of fine irony, or the most uproarious laughter is excited with the liveliest and maddest jocosities, there is, for the English, humor. In this sense humor is a general form of the laughable». «The Germans, who often employ the word humor in the English sense, have distinguished, at least in theory, humor properly so called, from the comic, from the irony of esprit, and from satire». For the Germans, according to this author, who takes his inspiration from Jean Paul and Laube, true humor «expresses the feeling of the contrast between the finite and the infinite, the real and the ideal, under all their forms; it expresses the opposition between the subject and the object, between nature and civilization, between the small and the sublime, between Ormuzd and Ahriman, always ending in the feeling of nothingness, even when the humorist, philosopher and merry, seeks to reconcile us to that state of things and invites us to consider the world such as it is».

The French signification of the word humor is not the same for Firmery. According to him, «the French understand by humor a particular character, a kind of indefinable savor, which makes its impression in the greater part of witty works; in a word, it is the esprit that is distinguished from the Germanic esprit»... «What dominates in the French esprit is reason, and in German humor it is imagination, fantasy; the esprit is calm and serene, humor restless and agitated; the esprit is healthy and humor more easily sickly; the esprit escapes more from the analysis of criticism; it is difficult to enumerate the means of which it makes use and to note the tenuous and delicate expression in [p. 259]which it conceals itself; on the contrary, it is easy to point out all the sources of which humor makes use. The esprit is easily superficial and almost always light and merry; humor is more profound and at bottom melancholy». The esprit would have more relation with the classical form of art, and humor would be a romantic expression of the comic contrast which sad reality offers.

This analysis, however exact it may be, when it comes to distinguishing three diverse forms of humor as modalities of the comic, is nevertheless not in harmony with the appreciation of the works regarded as types of humor. England offers humorists such as Shakespeare, Swift, Sterne, and Carlyle, who differ radically in their psychology and in the purpose of their works. «Hamlet has his soul laden with a very heavy enterprise; impotence makes him a humorist», says Barthélemy; «Swift has frightful personal hatreds to sate; the desire for his vengeance forms his genius as a humorist; Carlyle has overwhelming thoughts to carry through life; that preoccupation inspires all his humor. The first is the humor of the despairing man; the second, of hatred; and the last, of the intellect, considered as synonymous with moral speculation». Swift is thus a spirit opposed to that of Carlyle, as unbridled passion and serene judgment are opposed in the resolution of a problem; but their opposition is not so great as that which exists between interest and disinterest, between the satirical writer, who lashes out of hatred, and «the one who has the habit of abandoning himself entirely to his humor, yielding to all the movements of spontaneity and letting his imagination wander over the most diverse objects, from the sad to the merry, from the low to the sublime, thus joining together the most disparate things and producing works that do not have beauty as their end». This merry humor, this good humor is not that of Swift, [p. 260]nor that of Carlyle.

Swift's humor is bad, and Carlyle's, without having that impassioned character, is not absolutely disinterested; it is, as Barthélemy says, a mixture of humor and of the ideal, of realism, tinged with the thousand colors taken from things themselves, and of a transcendental idealism which, retaining those hues, pursues a moral end. There is in Carlyle's humor a metaphysical background, which leads thought toward the contrasts that the immediate perception of existence encounters in analyzing human miseries. Swift is a perverse critic, whom the philosophy of life does not raise above the purpose of his passions. Taine judges him thus. «If there was ever a soul that glutted itself with the delight of tearing, of outraging, and of destroying, it was Swift's», says Taine. «His mockery is funereal, his gaiety is always tragic», he adds. He is the type of bad humor, he is the genius of insult, opposed to that of Voltaire, with whom that writer compares him. And yet, Barthélemy finds in Swift's «Tale of a Tub» and Carlyle's «Sartor Resartus» the same spirit. Taine does not distinguish them profoundly, even though he characterizes Swift as a completely English genius and Carlyle as the representative of the Germanic spirit, of that nebulous and metaphysical spirit, openly opposed to the realistic and utilitarian positivism of the English character.

One must grant, notwithstanding the affinities found between the two English humorists, that their purposes and methods are different. Carlyle underwent the influence of the great German humorist Jean Paul Friedrich Richter, whose psychology was openly opposed to that of Swift. His humor is disinterested and merry, to judge by the appreciation Henrich makes of him. The work of Cervantes seems reflected in the novelistic compositions of Jean Paul. The mysterious Siebenkäs, who fig[p. 261]ures in his tragic poem «Titan», as a transformation of the old pessimistic and mad Schoppe, friend and defender of the hero Albano, resembles a Germanic Don Quixote, who fulfills his protective, disinterested mission, in the service of justice alone. Bertrand, in his study on Cervantes and German romanticism, referring to Jean Paul, says: «It is Cervantes who conquers Jean Paul, and among his works, Don Quixote. He himself had the double character of the Spanish novelist; the unshakeable and mystical idealism and the sense of practical life; and the humor of his work reached out its hand, across the centuries, to the irony of Cervantes».

The genius of Cervantes, who is also regarded as the greatest humorist, was able to inspire that ingenuous humor which departs from satire, without losing its tragic character, and approaches the pure comic, in which irony loses the force of a moral and social sanction. Jean Paul finds in him the fundamental traits of humor. His humor is universal and subjective. Cervantes offers the spectacle of the struggle between realism and idealism, the antithesis between the soul and the body; the comic lies there not in the object, but in the subject; it lies in the contrast between what Don Quixote believes to be the truth and what we know to be madness. The opposition is always resolved in the annihilation of appearances, considered as absolute realities. Jean Paul, in his enthusiasm for the humor of Cervantes, wished to revive his hero on German soil and wrote his Komet, in which Nikolaus Marggraf is considered, by many, to be the Don Quixote so long awaited.

Schelling and Solger characterize the irony of Cervantes as humoristic. «The laughter that Cervantes provokes, says Schelling, is not degrading; it is the divine irony that the poet lets hover around his creations». Sol[p. 262]ger, who makes irony the center of his aesthetic system, characterizes the Quixote as a work of the purest irony or of the purest humor.

That humoristic form also constitutes the charm of Sterne's work in his «Tristram Shandy», the history of the life of his father, dominated by traditional philosophical ideas, and that of his uncle occupied exclusively with military exploits. That double preoccupation, which reflects that of the social milieu, offers very comic contrasts, which involve a social critique, but which do not have this as the purpose of the work, which thus belongs to the genre of good humor, departing absolutely from the works of Shakespeare, Swift, and Carlyle.

Jean Paul calls Rabelais the greatest of humorists and the precursor of Sterne; but Marty-Laveaux characterizes Rabelais as a great satirist, who mocks everyone, not excluding his readers. «One recognizes Rabelais, says that writer, in that he is a profound philosopher beneath a mocking appearance». Rabelais, in his history of the exploits of Gargantua and his son Pantagruel, reveals himself also as a humorist of a festive bent, who, even though he satirizes the friars and criticizes scholasticism in order to exalt the value of enlightened paganism, has as his purpose to make others laugh, employing comic irony. The tragic factor, introduced by romanticism, does not determine the nature of his genius. Rabelais is classical like Swift, like Sterne and Voltaire. Romanticism produced in literature that sad note which makes of the comic a sui generis modality and which produces «that laughter in which a grief and a grandeur are mingled», as Jean Paul observes. Romantics were Shakespeare and Cervantes, Jean Paul and Carlyle, philosophers of intuition, who annihilated decrepit ideals, whether to reconstruct them or only to stone them with the Fichtean irony, which proclaimed the supremacy of the ego, or to [p. 263]give fuel to their humoristic faculties, creators of contrasts, in order to give themselves the pleasure of destroying their elements.

How is one to define humor in the face of this diversity of models that reveal creative and therefore original artistic consciousnesses? Intellectualism loves definitions and classifications, because it does not comprehend the infinite complexity of the moral life, which overflows all the logical categories. Hence the Babylonian confusion that Pirandello points out in interpreting the word humor. «For the greater number», he says, «a humoristic writer is one who makes others laugh; the comic, the burlesque, the satirical, the trivial, caricature, farce, the epigram, the calembour are baptized with the name of humor, just as one is accustomed to call romantic everything that is most Arcadian and sentimental, most false and baroque».

An indirect way of marking out the imprecise limits of this indefinable artistic modality would be to distinguish it from those with which it is confused, and, within those limits, to indicate its essential characters. This is what Jean Paul has done in his Introduction to Aesthetics, even though inverting the terms and setting out from the concept of the romantic comic.

Humor fluctuates between the tragic and the comic, but it is neither the one nor the other. Humor seeks contrasts in the essence of things, principally, and, regarding them with a criterion steeped in pessimism and skepticism, it takes pleasure in annihilating all the objective realities: grandeurs above all; so that it may properly be said that it is the contrary of the tragic in this sense. The tragic, in effect, resolves the irremediable con[p. 264]flict of two absolute realities by means of a victim; the dramatic resolves the conflict of two opposed realities which can, however, be harmonized without any catastrophe by virtue of their relative character; the comic opposes a reality to an appearance and destroys the opposition by destroying the appearance; but the humorous reduces all realities to mere appearances and takes pleasure in thus opposing them, in order then to annihilate them in that opposition. «In Don Quixote, as in Hamlet and Faust, we have found the tragedy of our own nothingness», Heine has said.

For the humorist there exists no other reality than the free ego, than the reality of grief in melancholy and pessimistic humor, which has lost faith in finite things as in infinite and absolute ones. The humorist, as Jean Paul says, «places himself in that opposition without setting himself in a strange place, as happens in comedy, and divides his ego into two factors, the finite and the infinite, and makes the latter issue from the former. Man laughs, then, because he says to himself: this is impossible! this is absurd!»

In humor, for this reason, the ego plays the leading role. It is the ego that creates the contrast and it is the ego itself that destroys it. Objectivity is merely an instrument. Humor enters the domain of the tragic only through the annihilation of ideals, and that of the comic through the liberation of the ego.

Irony is the principal instrument of humor; but it is not to be confused with it, nor does it assume the form in which it presents itself in comedy and in satire. «It has been wished, says Pirandello, to substitute for the word humor that of ironism, derived from irony, notwithstanding that, if irony contains a fictitious contradiction as a rhetorical figure, contradiction, on the contrary, is essential and not fictitious in humor; [p. 265]it being possible, indeed, to admit a certain kinship between humor and irony, such as the German romantics understood it, although they cannot be confused, because irony, even employed with a good end, is inseparable from a certain mockery and mordancy, which are not essential in humor».

In this precisely is distinguished classical irony, proper to comedy and to satire, from romantic irony, peculiar to humor. The first is aggressive and tendentious; the second is innocent and disinterested; the first pretends to moralize, the second lacks any didactic finality and contents itself with destroying only, without aspiring to a reconstruction, nor even to a restoration of the ideal. When, in humor, that pedagogical aspiration is pronounced, it turns into a means of strange objectivity.

Romantic irony, defined by Friedrich Schlegel, consists, for the poet, as Basch says, «in raising oneself above a subject and above oneself, in hovering infinitely above the events one represents and the characters one sketches; in never founding oneself upon one's work; in never losing, even in the most pathetic moment, the consciousness of the unreality of one's creations; in never being deceived by the illusion of the phantoms one has oneself evoked, but in always knowing how to split oneself in two, to watch oneself live and create and to smile at the reader, who lets himself be caught in this game, and at oneself, who consecrates one's existence to playing».

There is thus, at the bottom of humor, a profound philosophy, a transcendental philosophy; not an abstract philosophy of thought, but a philosophical intuition of lived reality and of its irremediable contrasts, which superficial optimism resolves by means of rash hypotheses, the product of desire. «The humor[p. 266]ist», as Pirandello says, «is a philosopher-poet, who analyzes all reality with the criterion of a skeptic and a pessimist, not in order to laugh, with the laughter of the comic, nor to grow indignant, like the satirist, but in order to deny all objective value to that reality and to smile at those who believe in it».

Humor, which is philosophy at bottom, is free art, the freest in its form; but it is not a constructive art, but a dissolving one, proper to abnormal epochs, in which skepticism and pessimism destroy the values maintained as absolute by traditional conformism. This character distinguishes it from all the other forms of art and lends merit to the disdainful appreciations of those who understand art with a classical or objective criterion.

Such is the criterion of Hegel, who condemns the humor of Jean Paul, characterizing it as an excrescence of art. True humor for Hegel «must unite, to a great richness of imagination, much sense and profundity of spirit, in order to develop what seems purely arbitrary as really full of truth and to bring forth from the bosom of those accidental particularities a substantial and true idea». For Hegel the disorder of ideas of humor is opposed to art. «For the very reason, he says, that they are traits which spring up at random and without order, the inner concatenation must be all the more profoundly marked, and in the midst of these particularities the luminous ray of the spirit must penetrate». Hegel wishes, in this way, that the ideal should not disappear from humor, so that it may preserve its artistic character; classical unity is for that philosopher the type of art, and for that reason humor, which runs counter to that type, is the final term of romantic art and the last stage of aesthetic evolution. The absolute, which informs art, disappears, and the realized or longed-for harmony is replaced by the dispersion of the spirit into capricious and [p. 267]lawless forms.

The criterion which flees from the subjectivism of Protagoras, in order to construct its absolute unity in the thought of Plato, returns to Protagoras, in order to proclaim the exclusive empire of the free consciousness. In that exchange of the absolute for the relative, art finds the dissolving form of humor, which prepares the constitution of new values, values that respond to the conquest of experience and better satisfy the tendency toward the free life. Humor contemplates and dissects reality with its contrasts, without affecting a militant attitude, and that contemplative and descriptive attitude, in which it reveals the force of its intuition, suffices to imprint an artistic seal upon its works.

Humor is, consequently, philosophy and art at the same time; but it is not a philosophy of the absolute, nor an art in which subject and object interpenetrate to constitute a harmony, or in which that fusion is sought in an infinite ideal; humor is a philosophy of intuition, in which the freedom of the ego penetrates reality and expresses its profound oppositions, as the lyric poet reveals the agitations of his soul; it is a philosophy such as Simmel understands it. The force, the intuition, and the unity of the artist are its only elements. If in that expression the logical categories disappear, it is because thought is there subordinated to the intensity and variability of the feeling with which the freedom of the artist merges and realizes itself; and that feeling is annihilating, because every absolute norm is repugnant to its nature, simply for being a norm. That sentimental criterion explains the enigmatic and often unintelligible quality of humoristic expression.

Jean Paul was right, therefore, to point out as essential characters of romantic humor the annihilating idea and the romantic infinite, which ends in a negation of the infinite. Referring to those [p. 268]ideas, Stapfer says, interpreting the thought of Jean Paul: «At the bottom of the humorist's spirit there exists the idea of universal nothingness; he despises everything, men as well as things, without anger, without bitterness, without passion, with the laughter of Democritus. Nothing, in his eyes, deserves to be distinguished in that great heap of vanities; above all he makes no distinction between folly and wisdom. There are no wise men; the whole world is mad, and the humorist himself is no less so than the rest; for he no longer takes inspiration from what remains to him of the serious in the Universe, one of his most characteristic traits being the perpetual inner mockery which has for its object his own person». Only, this mockery is not bloody, as in satire; it is the gesture that the divinity would have in contemplating the vanities taken seriously by men; it is a paternal, innocent, pious mockery, which provokes a reflective smile before those who struggle for the irremediable.

This good humor has developed greatly in modern times, after positive science has dispelled so many illusions with which humanity believed it had conquered the future. The moral values having been absorbed by the pseudo-value of the economic, and this same value having been discredited by the social struggles, humanity marches heedlessly amid the ruins that egoism and war have scattered everywhere. Without any foresight of the future, it squanders its forces in the whirlwind of the reactions of feeling, without escaping the bitternesses that memory renews for it and without orienting its consciousness toward a new ideal.

A Spanish humorist called attention to the growing development of works of this genre and found their explanation in grief. «When Spain laughed at the humor of Goya it was not fruitful. But the scenery has changed. Today there are many people who do not live; [p. 269]many who eat in abbreviation and who drink by the dropperful. Politics is marking the critical period of its decadence. Spain has become serious. And humor, child of seriousness and of grief, has spread through art. The numerous salons of humorists reveal it». The uncertainty which paralyzes the energies destined for practical life produces that form of resignation, which finds no other defense than the disdainful smile against human vanity.

Civilizations have a fixed art which reflects their definitive ideals; but the fugitive and transitory forms, which translate decadence and disorder, have also their art of disorder, in which ideal constructions are impossible and the ugly acquires a destructive supremacy. Humor is that art of disorder, in which freedom loses itself in vain expressions, which signify only a squandering of psychic energy. For that reason pure humor is very rare, because it can hardly emancipate itself from that aspiration of thought to order reality in some fashion.

«Art, like all ideal or illusory constructions, says Pirandello, tends to fix life; it fixes it in one moment or in several determined moments. Art in general composes; but humor decomposes. Art abstracts and concentrates, takes and represents the essential and characteristic ideality of individuals as of things. Now then, to humor it seems that all this simplifies nature too much and tends to make life too rational or, at least, too coherent. It seems to it that art does not hold in great consideration, as it should, the true causes that many times move this poor human soul to the most ill-considered acts, absolutely unforeseeable. For the humorist, the causes in li[p. 270]fe are never so logical, so ordered as in our common works of art, in which everything is, at bottom, combined, ordered, in accordance with the ends the writer proposes to himself; it seems to it a vain pretension, that of ordering, when we have four souls in struggle among themselves, the instinctive soul, the moral soul, the affective soul, and the social soul; and according as this one or that one dominates, our consciousness takes an attitude, and we consider valid and sincere the fictitious interpretation of ourselves, of our inner being which we do not know, because it never manifests itself entire, but now in one manner, now in another, as the things of life will have it».

### XX. EL SENTIMIENTO DE LO FEO — XX. THE FEELING OF THE UGLY

The aesthetic phenomenon comprises not only value but also its opposite, aesthetic non-value; that is to say, its domain includes not only the beautiful, which produces a pleasure, but also the ugly, which produces a displeasure. What is the nature of this feeling? This is a question that cannot be resolved merely by turning into negatives the positive data that enter into the beautiful; for the ugly, reproduced as a factor in a work of art, produces a feeling of pleasure that is born solely of artistic conception and production, modifying the feeling that the ugly produces in the reality which is not artistic.

Hence the study of the ugly holds an important place in aesthetics, apart from its consideration as a psychological phenomenon. The artistically beautiful comprises the beautiful, as it does the ugly and the indifferent, without its being possible to say, as Croce does, that the ugly is only failed expression, for the ugly can exist independently of its artistic expression, the pleasure of the latter being a concomitant of the aesthetic pleasure offered by the content in itself. The value of the artistically beautiful may or may not be joined to the value of the beautiful as a reality separate from art, and in some cases value needs to be associated with non-value precisely in the service of the former.

[p. 272]This is why Fanciulli regards the ugly as the origin of aesthetic feelings different from those produced by the beautiful, and admits two fundamental types: one corresponding to the apprehension of sensory data and to the processes of intellectual elaboration, and another that refers to autonomous feeling.

In the first type, the cause of non-value may reside in the quality of the sensory data and of the intellectual processes, as happens in disharmonies, or in the quantity, as when one perceives defect or excess in the perceptions. In the second type, the feeling of the ugly arises when the object is at odds with the feeling of the beholder, when he desires and expects to find in the work of art the beautiful creature, the creature of the higher world, and finds himself surprised by what is mere delight of the senses, or intellectual play, or a pale copy of reality.

But Fanciulli does not thus explain the nature of the ugly, which it is necessary to determine by distinguishing it beforehand from other analogous forms.

The ugly is distinguished from the laughable. The feeling of the ugly, observes Dumont, is purely painful, whereas that of the laughable is purely agreeable. We experience the feeling of the ugly when our understanding cannot refrain from investigating a relation of unity among the different parts of an object, but finds itself, on the other hand, so hampered in this investigation that its energy succumbs after much time and fatigue; we feel, then, the sorrow that results from the impossibility of exercising our activity. We experience, on the contrary, the feeling of the laughable, Dumont adds, whenever an object leads our understanding to form a relation and to destroy it immediately within itself, substituting for it [p. 273]another; we then experience a pleasure that results from the activity of the understanding, which is exercised doubly and in opposite directions upon one and the same object. This object, Dumont continues, may be at once ugly and laughable; but these two qualities cannot occupy us at the same time, because the two feelings can only follow one after the other. The festive quality of an object, by drawing our attention upon it, may make us laugh first, and afterward make us perceive its ugliness, which had been hidden from us without that attraction. Laughter, Dumont concludes, far from being one of the forms of the feeling of the ugly, stands in opposition to it.

It is well to recall that Dumont distinguishes laughter from the feeling of the laughable; laughter is a phenomenon that may be associated with very diverse feelings, as it is with the feeling of the laughable, which, for Dumont, is purely joyful, without any admixture of a more or less intense sorrow. The laughable, for this reason, differs as much from the ugly, which produces repugnance, as from the ridiculous, which involves a censure and provokes mockery, and which may be regarded as a transition between the comic and the ugly, as a mere semblance of the ugly, as Lemcke thinks.

We accept this difference, and also that the opposite of the laughable or of the purely comic is the serious and not the ugly; but we believe that the feeling of displeasure which the latter produces does not proceed from an intellectual function, as Dumont affirms, but from a violent and profound disharmony between the subject and the object contemplated, felt with the same instantaneousness as the emotion of the beautiful.

In the ugly, our feeling of freedom does not succumb after much time and fatigue, but suffers an abrupt opposition, producing, if it is fleeting, the fee[p. 274]ling of the ridiculous, and, if it is permanent, that of the ugly and repulsive. The disorder, in this case, is neither unlimited nor overwhelming, as in the sublime, nor does it end, as it does there, in a subjective reconciliation; rather, it is permanent for the subject who contemplates it, yet produced by a limited force that the imagination is able to grasp and represent.

Freedom and order, in right harmony, engender the impression of the beautiful; consequently, caprice alone without order, or order without freedom—that is, coercion—are ugly and repugnant, says Lemcke. Chaos is odious, as are slavery and tyranny; so too anarchy, as well as every model and pattern devoid of spirit, and every dead form; arbitrariness, as well as pedantry. Beauty demands unity and variety. If the impression of unity is suppressed, one obtains a chaotic mass, a confused hubbub, an arbitrary plurality, which can awaken nothing but distaste. Thus it is, Lemcke adds, that a cluster of worms crawling one alongside another, whose bodies cannot be coordinated even once, is one of the things that cause the most disgust. In the same way it happens with a heap of rags and tatters from a refuse-heap, piled up without order or concert, with a dunghill, and with every dismembered plurality that appears to lack unity.

These examples, valued by Lemcke, nevertheless confuse the ugly with the repugnant, which are distinct. In the ugly there is always an ideal element that can be made artistic; in the merely disgusting that element does not exist. The ugly and the disgusting may be joined in reality—they almost always are—but in Art the same does not occur.

The ugly may be associated with the characteristic, and then produce a feeling of intellectual pleasure that [p. 275]must not be confused with the aesthetic one. A typical monkey may afford the naturalist a pleasure; but that pleasure of the perfect in its kind, even when it contains a realized ideal element, is not to be confused with aesthetic pleasure, which subordinates the real to the ideal, the latter being informed freely, without subjection to predetermined objective ends. The order of the perfect in reality is not the order of freedom.

Just as the lack of unity is disagreeable, so unity without plurality, without variety, or unity with a false plurality within it, are also disagreeable. Always the same form, the same idea, and, in general, always the same repetition of something, everything extended without interruption or change—in a word, every deficient unity produces in us a disagreeable impression. And this applies as much to the phenomenon in itself as to the idea and to the character.

The lack of regularity, of symmetry, of proportion, of harmony, of order—in a word—consequently awakens sensations opposed to the beautiful, which vary according to their intensity, their content, and their forms of expression, from the disgusting and repulsive to the merely ridiculous that makes one laugh; from the physically ugly to the morally ugly, and from the ugly in Nature to the ugly expressed artistically.

The ugly, for Rosenkranz, is a relative idea that exists only by virtue of the beautiful, which it presupposes; but it is not the pure and abstract negation of the beautiful, but rather a negation in sensible form. Neither is the ugly the imperfect. For Rosenkranz, the ugly is scarcely to be discovered in the inorganic realm; it does appear, however, in organic nature, where it becomes accentuated by degrees, as the individual principle and the intensity of life increase. In plants it is manifested only through the obstacles that thwart their development. In the animal [p. 276]kingdom, the ugly is produced chiefly in the species of transition, true equivocal species, in which one might say that Nature proceeds in a hesitant and irresolute manner.

Passing from the realm of Nature to that of the spirit, moral ugliness appears. But here Rosenkranz makes an essential distinction. In the moral order, the absolute end is the true or the good; only in a subordinate manner can the beautiful be so. From this he infers that the ideal of spiritual life, although it is never ugly, may very well not be beautiful in the classical manner—that is, with the beauty of physical forms—and for this reason the idea that Jesus Christ was not comely in the eyes of the flesh was so common among the Fathers and Doctors of the early ages of the Church. The element of holiness here overrides the aesthetic element and may be manifested in a body that is not at all comely, and even ugly. Nevertheless, in a general sense, it is true that virtue beautifies and vice makes ugly, a principle that Rosenkranz expresses in the following terms: «The consciousness of free and harmonious development beautifies; unfreedom—that is, the impossibility of determining oneself in an infinite manner—makes ugly. This influence of freedom is transmitted to the body; thus the aristocratic races are more beautiful, because they are more emancipated from the necessities of life and can employ their activity in play, in love, in poetry.» Ugliness, therefore, is the absence of freedom, the servitude of the spirit, which is manifested even in the movements and attitudes of the body.

There exists for Rosenkranz another kind of ugliness, that of vice, of perversity. The perverse man is not incapable of all beauty, for other good qualities may coexist with evil moral ones—the generosity of certain bandits, for example. Moreover, the body having only a symbolic value in its relations with [p. 277]the spirit, it may acquire, even while being ugly, a certain aesthetic charm by virtue of expression, as is reported of Socrates and of Mirabeau. But the general effect of perversity, being as it is by its essence a negation of true freedom, of the freedom of the good, consists in disfiguring the features of the human countenance. The internal contradiction between the will and its idea must necessarily manifest itself outwardly in a determinate physiognomic contradiction. It must be noted, nevertheless, that habitual and systematic perversity is wont, by a strange circumstance, to produce a certain equilibrium, and even a certain detestable harmony in the will, transcending to the features of the countenance. For this reason, the expression of absolute perversity and of habitual crime is not usually as violent as that of the momentary aberration caused by passion.

The ugly, according to Rosenkranz, does not enter into Art as a mere contrast to the beautiful. Contrast can add nothing to the divine serenity of beauty, and besides, there may be contrast without the ugly intervening. The true reason is more essential and more profound: it consists in the necessity that art has of manifesting sensibly the totality of the idea in all its free development. The idea, says Rosenkranz, appears and moves amid agitation and disorder, amid the conflicts of reality.
