If art wishes to represent the idea in its totality, it cannot dispense with the ugly, with the diabolical, with the negative element, alongside the pure ideal. Even the purest aesthetic sense of the Greeks admitted harpies, chimeras, satyrs, and a lame god. The Christian religion, accustoming us to scrutinize the roots of sin and to conquer it, has come to give a new importance to the ugly in the world of Art.

But the ugly can never claim more than a secondary and relative place; it can never aspire to the inde[p. 278]pendence enjoyed by the beautiful, which is precisely the only thing that legitimizes, in the aesthetic sense, the right of the ugly to exist in Art.

The ugly has, then, a merely accidental value, contrary to what some romantics taught and what the naturalists teach and practice. Art ought not to beautify but to idealize the ugly; that is, to treat it in accordance with the rules of the beautiful.

The theory concerning the pleasure that the ugly causes may easily be inferred from all that has been set forth. This pleasure may be of two kinds, according to Rosenkranz: healthy and unhealthy. The impression of the ugly is healthy when it contributes to the triumph of the beautiful; unhealthy when one wishes to give it a value of its own, as happens in decadent and corrupt periods, in which art flees from truth, from simplicity, and from naturalness, to fall into the unheard-of, the outrageous, and the extravagant. The ugly may enter into aesthetic conception as a means of deepening a contrast or of making it more vivid, in order to enhance and render more pleasing the beauty that is opposed to it, or it may also enter as a means of expressing the sorrowful forms of life and the sad feelings joined to them.

Rosenkranz considers as forms and categories of the ugly deformity, incorrectness, and disfigurement, subdividing the first into amorphousness, asymmetry, and disharmony. Disfigurement embraces the common, the repugnant, the caricature, and so forth. As higher forms there appear the criminal, the spectral, the diabolical, the demoniac, sorcery, the satanic, and so forth—all that Rosenkranz calls the aesthetic hell, where Satan reigns, the ideal of evil and the culminating point of the ugly.

As is evident, according to this theory, which Lemcke adopts, the ugly is explained, like the beautiful, by the ideas of freedom and of the order in which that freedom develops. An order [p. 279]opposed to freedom, which is a disorder for the feeling of freedom, is ugly; as is ugly a freedom that upsets an order accepted as absolute. In the one case as in the other, it is the coercion experienced or expressed in beings that constitutes the essential characteristic of the ugly; for freedom alone is lovable, even in the form of repose, and the order in which that freedom develops agreeably is always relative, inseparable from freedom, of which it is the form and direction, and inseparable from the individual and collective ideal, which synthesizes the concrete form of possible happiness.

In the beautiful, freedom and Nature are reconciled without effort, in an ideal order, informed by the imagination and expressed through graceful sensible forms; in the sublime and in the comic that reconciliation is always achieved, after an effort, in order to overcome a conflict; in the ugly, reconciliation is impossible; the adaptation of the subject to the ugly reality is not achieved even ideally, because freedom succumbs before the coercion of Nature, which imposes upon it its disordered forms, whether as physical laws or as passions rebellious to the discipline of an absolute moral order, rendering grace unrealizable. We feel, then, as Dumont says, the sorrow that results from the impossibility of exercising our activity.

The ugly, thus considered, is distinguished from the merely disagreeable, which is repugnant to the senses: into the ugly there necessarily enter forms, colors, or sounds, associated with representations of other kinds, but in a certain relation capable of being appreciated by thought, even if intuitively. There are no ugly odors, nor ugly flavors, nor ugly tactile sensations. The ugly, like the beautiful, refers directly to the sensations belonging to the domain of sight and hearing. For this same reason, the ugly must not be confused with the evil, which requires no sen[p. 280]sible forms for its realization. The ugly exists only in physical nature or in Art.

Art, it is said, is wont to convert the ugly into the beautiful. This assertion must not be understood in the sense that the ugly loses its nature by the effect of its artistic expression. The ugly expressed by Art is always ugly, and even uglier than it is in Nature, in which the artist finds his inspiration, idealizing it, accentuating its characters; what, in that expression of the ugly, causes us pleasure is the soul of the artist, who freely chooses the elements of his work and orders and combines them in harmony with his artistic idea. The ugly enters here as contrast or as symbol, whether to contribute to the realization of the beautiful or to express a state of the artist's soul.

What makes possible, and even to a certain point necessary, the representation of the ugly in works of art is a well-known law, the law of contrast, says Basch. It is entirely true that the artistic representation of things solely beautiful would fatigue us, and that this is the essential reason why academic painting and a certain idyllic literature weary us so quickly. There have been and there are schools that have exaggerated that principle and that have seemed to make of the minute representation of the ugly the essential labor, the sole end of Art, just as there are schools that, on the contrary, have excluded from Art everything that wounds, everything that reveals to us the irremediable sickness of the human body and spirit. It is in the middle term, says Basch, that the truth is found: Art must always take its inspiration from Nature, which offers neither the purely beautiful nor the ugly exclusively; for to idealize is not to mutilate, but to express reality with more truth, with more purity, and above all with more intensity.

Bray, consistent with his aesthetic theory of dis[p. 281]tinction as the characteristic of the beautiful, regards the ugly as every disagreeable emotion that results from the perception of a distinction, and distinguishes the negative ugly from the positive ugly; the former deriving from a very weak excitation, and the latter proceeding from an excitation that exceeds the maximum. This separation does not appear well founded, because the nature of the feeling of the ugly demands a certain degree of violence, an abrupt shock, as the beginning of the respective emotion. A weak excitation can produce only monotony and indifference, if it is not repeated for a long time. The ugly, then, though opposed to the beautiful, is as positive as the latter, being indeed more subjective than it, owing to the lesser determination of its elements.

In Bray's conception, the ugly evolves in this manner: at the beginning there is no other ugliness than that which results from a repulsion of organic origin; negative ugliness does not yet exist, so to speak; it appears only with the voluntary investigation of the sources of aesthetic enjoyment—that is, with the birth of the arts.

The introduction and the preponderance of the intellectual and moral factors in the formula of the beautiful come next to multiply considerably the causes of positive distaste, and to give, on the other hand, a more and more extensive basis to the negative ugly. But, in exchange, the progress of reason and of the social feelings ceaselessly eliminates the purely physical repugnances and fears.

Finally, in the state which the most advanced spirits reach, thanks to their superior power of inhibition, the influence of these latter is reduced to so little that, very often, they are no longer an obstacle to aesthetic admiration. In this state our aversions are essentially of an intellectual and moral order; that is why [p. 282]sympathy and scientific admiration then triumph so easily. This demonstration Bray considers of the highest importance, because it alone permits us to explain the considerable role that the positive ugly tends to play in artistic creations.

It does not appear that the aesthetic feeling of the ugly derives, as Bray believes, primitively from the organic reflexes, even though the repugnant is confused with the ugly in that first moment. The aesthetic phenomenon of the beautiful, as of the ugly, is a synthesis from its origin, into which there enter a tendency, a representation, and a feeling, associated with concomitant physiological phenomena. There, it is true, the lower and organic sensations corresponding to all the senses play a considerable role; but not all of them have an aesthetic value, as Bray supposes, nor are they alone, as psychological elements, nor, still less, do they exclusively explain that intellectual feeling which distinguishes the aesthetic from the other feelings by referring it to freedom. It is true that, in the evolution of the ugly, the intellectual and moral feelings must have developed with human culture, widening the domain of the ugly and purifying its special feeling; but this does not signify the exclusion of all the radical elements of consciousness in the first moment, nor does it explain the reason why the ugly in Nature does not produce in Art the same feeling.

Bray asks whether there exists an ideal of the ugly, and answers, against Léveque, in the affirmative; because the ideal is, by its nature, relative and progressive; because it is, in each genus, that which best answers to the idea we form of that genus. This ideal will vary with the culture of him who pursues it, rising from the purely sensible disorder to the moral disorder and adapting itself to very diverse arbitrary expressions. Nevertheless, si[p. 283]nce disorder is indeterminate, the creation of its types is much more difficult than in the beautiful, for that reason and because the pure ugly does not enter into the aesthetic domain except as a contrast to the beautiful and in the service of it, or as artistic representation, and consequently subject to the laws of the beautiful and to the disorders produced by human freedom.

Not everything that exists is beautiful or ugly; there exists also, and on a vaster scale, the indifferent, which produces no aesthetic emotion whatever, owing to its insignificance. The domain of the insignificant, says Lemcke, lies outside all that which seeks to awaken our aesthetic interest; at most, it serves to set off forms superior to it, forms full of significance.

Art can, nevertheless, raise the indifferent to the category of the beautiful, by imprinting upon it a profound significance or by expressing it with the attractive forms of grace, which expresses freedom. Such is the case with the painting of the Low Countries, in which vulgar scenes express the joy and the freedom of living.

### XXI. LA CONCIENCIA ESTÉTICA SUPERIOR (EL ARTISTA) — XXI. THE HIGHER AESTHETIC CONSCIOUSNESS (THE ARTIST)

Aesthetic activity is not confined, as has been said, to the receptive and static moment of emotion, as happens in common natures, which possess only the aesthetic criterion of the sensory feelings, and as happens also in certain elite spirits, capable of a higher appreciation and of an aesthetic criticism, but rather it ascends and develops in a sphere of more intense and profound activity, which takes possession of the will and engenders a work of art, with the concurrence of all the human energies.

This aesthetic activity is called artistic, and he in whom it is realized is an artist.

The artist is not, in truth, a man fundamentally different from the rest, but his organization differs from the common one by the intensity of his life and the harmony of his functions. What is spontaneous in Nature is more perfect in the artist than in any other man. The artist, says Sully Prudhomme, is distinguished from other men, above all, by an eminent aptitude for feeling the agreeable or disagreeable qualities of visual or auditory sensations, and for establishing, in all the arts, the intimate subordination of those sensations to certain laws demonstrated in the exact sciences. The power of perceiving forms and sounds, of combin[p. 285]ing them harmoniously, and of expressing those combinations in fitting forms, is much greater in the artist. For this reason it is said that the artist is born; because, in effect, the possession of an excellent sense is chiefly the result of heredity.

But this necessary condition is not sufficient, as Sully Prudhomme himself observes, because this quality, purely passive, which may be perfected through artistic education, does not explain the power to create, although it may be the reason for the necessity or tendency to create, born of an excess of energy and of psychophysical activity.

The faculty of creating involves elements of sensibility, of intelligence, and of will, without which invention is impossible or barren. This ensemble of conditions is what constitutes the temperament of the artist, the original seal of his aesthetic personality.

The temperament of an artist is his very physical and moral nature, in all its complexity, operating a selection among the harmonious combinations proper to his art. The artist conceives his work, invents it, and executes it according to his temperament and under the influence of his milieu, impressing upon it the seal of his personal originality, if he is a true artist.

Invention adapts the materials of perceived reality to the needs and aptitudes of the artist's temperament, which combines them according to the conception he has of freedom and of Nature. The artist, proceeding in this way, creates a new order, and in impressing it upon an artistic reality, it may also be said that he creates a new being, even though he does not engender the sensible materials he employs, nor the laws that govern harmony.

[p. 286]But this adaptation between Nature and the artist, between the objective and the subjective; this exterior and interior systematization, cannot be realized without the ideal taking form and without the forms of the objective being modified in some way and in some measure. In this double labor, which involves a series of instinctive and conscious actions and reactions between the subjective and the objective, the reconciliation of the beautiful is practiced; the ideal and the real interpenetrate; the real forms, modified incessantly by the imagination, which selects and combines them according to the feeling of love of freedom, integrate the conception of the order that is proper to it and determine it, thus producing the aesthetic satisfaction of the artist, who sees his aspiration to the better fulfilled in an ideal order, in which the exterior, idealized, adapts itself completely to his physical and moral nature.

This satisfaction is of a high degree of fecundity in the artist, whose activity necessarily passes from the contemplative state to the state of creation, by effect of a double necessity: that of producing, which is inherent in every powerful force that develops an excess of energy, and that of sociability, which partakes of the spontaneous nature of the first, but which is characterized chiefly by the free choice of a spiritual end, which involves the free choice of an artistic subject, in harmony with that end; that is, of an idea which, embodied in an imagined form, may serve as the motive for the production of a work of art.

There are, then, necessary to the artist native and special aptitudes of feeling, of intelligence, and of will, with harmonious, constant, and invincible tendencies toward a determined end, which constitutes the artistic vocation. A consequence of those aptitudes is that of executing, with the materials proper to each art—it is the dexterity in that execution, called virtuosity in art.

[p. 287]As Seailles says, the artist presupposes, above all, delicate and easily impressionable senses, a vast memory, an imagination at once lively and tenacious, which leaves the sensations their freshness and their intensity, and an exquisite sensibility that vivifies nature. But of all these aptitudes the creative imagination is the essential one and that which synthesizes all the rest. Without imagination there are no artists; neither reason nor the understanding takes its place, even in those genres in which Art is put at the service of science, as Revilla observes.

The creative imagination is of an extreme complexity. It not only fuses the subjective and the objective in an inseparable interpenetration of the elements of the exterior world and of the spirit, but, as Ribot demonstrates, it is, in the intellectual order, the equivalent of the will in the order of movements; it is the will itself in its function of apperceptive association, according to the psychological analysis of Wundt.

The imagination, says Ribot, resembling the will, tends to exteriorize itself, to affirm itself in a work that exists not only for the creator but for all the world. The imagination reproduces forms, maintains them with vivacity, dissociates them, associates them, combines them and affirms them in a determined order, impressing upon them an ideal unity; it awakens the tendency to objectification and develops it, presiding over, directing, and sustaining the will in the external realization of the ideal.

In the creative imagination there exist, for that very reason, several factors. Ribot considers three: the intellectual factor, negative, of dissociation, and the positive one of association; the emotional or affective factor, which comprises the motor, impulsive, or inhibitory element; and the unconscious factor called inspiration.

[p. 288]Considered under its scientific aspect, inspiration has, according to Ribot, two essential characters: its instantaneity and its impersonality, the latter being more profound than the former. Inspiration reveals a power superior to the conscious individual, foreign to him, though acting through him, and which may be reduced to intellectual or affective processes whose preparatory labor is unknown, being an unconscious labor that penetrates into the domain of consciousness, suddenly, after that preparation.

Guido Villa, following Wundt, reduces the latent psychic life to dispositions, to aptitudes of the psychic elements for returning to consciousness and recomposing themselves into complex forms, more or less similar to those in which they have already presented themselves, rejecting every hypothesis that would invalidate the existence of an unconscious or subconscious life, which psychological experience does not demonstrate and which is placed arbitrarily between the physiological and the psychological phenomena.

To these characters of instantaneity and of impersonality, which Ribot derives from the subconscious life, another must be added, that of freedom, which Joyau attributes to it. In the conception of this philosopher, inspiration, far from being originated by the tyrannical domination of a power exterior and superior to the soul, as the ancients believed, is, on the contrary, a more independent and freer unfolding of human thought and the temporary triumph of a personal tendency over the antagonistic influences. This development, the most autonomous of our intellectual activity, explains, according to Joyau, the pleasure of incomparable intensity that inspiration produces. Although inspiration is unconscious and impersonal, because it does not respond immediately and directly to the stimuli of the will, it is, neverthe[p. 289]less, the triumph of the nature of the superior man, who, under the direction of an ideal, dissociating, associating, and systematizing elements, and at the impulse of a most vivid emotion, works secretly and by itself that work of freedom or of emancipation from routine, translated into a new and superior form of the spirit, unexpected for consciousness.

The three factors considered by Ribot in the imagination do not function in isolation and by their own virtue in the elaboration of the work, but rather converge toward one and the same end: invention, under the discipline of a fixed idea or of a fixed emotion, which are not absolutely distinct, because they are inseparable and almost equivalent. This principle of unity, this center of attraction and point of support of all the work of the creative imagination—that is, of a subjective synthesis that tends to become objective—is the ideal, a construction of images destined to be objectified, as Ribot defines it.

Since the imagination is the fruit of the artist's temperament, it is understandable that it varies according to his nature. But in this immense variety of the imagination, derived from the personality of the artist and giving rise to the diversity of arts, of styles within each art, and of manners within each style, science endeavors to generalize by making classifications of great comprehensiveness.

Ribot reduces the types of imagination to seven: the plastic imagination, the diffluent, the mystical, the scientific, the practical and mechanical, the commercial, and the utopian, the first two belonging to the artistic order.

The plastic imagination employs in art, first and above all, visual images, and afterward motor images; it depends on special conditions and is directed principally to sensation, giving little and passing room to the affective element. Clarity [p. 290]within complexity is the characteristic of this type of imagination.

The diffluent imagination is the antithesis of the plastic and consists of images with vague, indistinct contours, which are evoked and gathered according to the less rigorous modes of association. The affective element predominates in this type of artistic imagination.

But it may happen that the plastic element and the emotional one present themselves with equal power in the artist; then arise the exceptional types, which unite to the intense and adequate vision of reality a profound emotion, like Dante, Shakespeare, and Goethe.

It might be said that all classical art answers to the first type of imagination, and romantic art to the second type; but whatever be the type considered, the creative imagination offers, as its essential characteristic, that spontaneous tendency to transform and to produce.

That spontaneity is not sufficient, however, for the development of the artist's aptitudes; it is required, moreover, that they be cultivated by a special education, proper to the art of his preference; because in the creation of the artistic work there enters not only invention, but also, in addition, routine and imitation, as Paulhan demonstrates. This education must comprehend the artist, both as a man and as a professional; it must be, for that reason, general and special or technical, the latter being more important than the former.

Technical education comprises the study of the laws of the art to which the artist devotes himself, that of the history of that art, the practical knowledge of the properties and laws of the sensible material he must employ, and the study of the great models of art.

### XXII. LA CONCIENCIA ESTÉTICA SUPERIOR (EL GENIO) — XXII. THE HIGHER AESTHETIC CONSCIOUSNESS (GENIUS)

[p. 291]When the power to create rises to a high degree, then it is said that the artist has genius, that he is a genius. Genius is determined in art, as in all human activity, by the superior forms of invention or creation.

The nature of genius has been explained by two theories: one pathological and the other physiological. The first, initiated as far back as Aristotle, treated afterward, incidentally, in comparing inspiration with madness, has obtained its complete expression in the famous formula of Moreau de Tours: «Genius is a neurosis». Neuropathy was for him the exaltation of the vital properties and, consequently, the most favorable condition for the creations of genius. Later Lombroso, seeking to make that formula more precise, substituted for neurosis in general a determinate neurosis: disguised epilepsy. That theory has been victoriously combated by the alienists, who have not failed to recognize, however, that in the greater part of geniuses there are found caprices, eccentricities, and physical disorders of every kind, which lend much verisimilitude to the pathological theory.

There remain the healthy geniuses, who could not be included in the preceding formula and who have made it possible to establish a contrary theory. Thus Nordau, reject[p. 292]ing the doctrine of his master Lombroso, has maintained that the essential elements of genius are judgment and will. According to this definition, he establishes among superior men the following hierarchy: in the first place, those in whom judgment and will are equally powerful: men of action, who make the history of the world, like Alexander, Cromwell, Napoleon, who are the tamers of men; in the second rank, the geniuses of judgment, but without a development of the will amounting to genius, like Pasteur, Helmholtz, Röntgen; and in the third rank, the geniuses of judgment, without an energetic will, like the thinkers and philosophers. Nordau does not consider the emotional geniuses, the poets and artists; because, according to him, they are not geniuses in the proper sense, since they create nothing new and exercise no influence over phenomena.

Without discussing the value of this classification, says Ribot; without examining whether it is even possible, since there is no common measure between Alexander, Pasteur, Spinoza, and Shakespeare, and whether, on the contrary, the common opinion is not right in placing on the same line the great creators, whoever they may be, merely because they surpass the middling level; it is indispensable to observe that in the aforesaid definition the creative faculty par excellence, the imagination, necessary to all inventors, has been totally omitted.

The theories indicated do not explain, then, the whole nature of genius, because the pathological cannot comprehend the healthy and balanced geniuses, and the physiological does not explain the special group of the emotional geniuses, in whom creation requires a great nervous excitability and a predominance of the affective states, which rapidly become morbid, as Ribot observes.

[p. 293]This psychologist reduces the characters of the greater part of the great inventors to three: precocity, the fatality of creation, and the clear, profound individualism of the great creator.

Precocity is the sign of the true vocation and develops in a preparatory period of imitation. The character of necessity, which produces in the genius the consciousness of a mission, is one of irresistible impulsion, which does not proceed from a creative instinct in general, but from particular tendencies, oriented in a determined direction, yet resembling instinct in many aspects. It is contrary to experience and to logic, adds Ribot, to admit that the creator of genius could follow any path whatever of his own choosing. That is true only of talent, the work of education and of circumstances. Genius is always, as Schopenhauer says, monstrum per excesum. The excess of development in a single direction, the hypertrophy of a special aptitude, often makes geniuses, in all else, men inferior to the middling; and even those very ones who by exception have given proof of multiple aptitudes have always had a preponderant tendency in which the common opinion sums them up.

The character of individualism is indisputable: what has been disputed is its origin, in determining the influence of race and of epoch on the work of genius.

The question of the individuality or originality of genius has been posed in two ways: for some, the representative character of genius must be sought in his nature; for others it is found in the milieu. For Schopenhauer, Carlyle, and Nietzsche, the great man is an autonomous product, explained neither by heredity nor by the milieu. For Taine, Spencer, Grant Allen, what is important lies in the race and the exterior conditions.

Ribot inclines toward the thesis of pure and [p. 294]simple individualism, for the very powerful reason that, the same milieu acting upon all the men of an epoch, the genius is nevertheless exceptional, which leads one to believe in the personal ferment. Moreover, he adds, that against the exclusive theory of the milieu one may urge this well-known fact, that the greater part of innovators and inventors provoke, from the outset, the opposition of the milieu. The misoneism of the multitudes is, then, one of the most powerful arguments in favor of the individual character of the invention of genius.

But however individual creation may be, it always involves a social coefficient. In this order, no invention is personal, in a very rigorous sense; because there always exists, as Ribot says, a little of this anonymous collaboration, whose mythic activity is its most elevated expression.

Genius does not always proceed in the same manner in invention. That mechanism always demands a natural disposition; but it varies in its origin and its development. Ribot distinguishes in this respect two general procedures for the development of the conceived ideal: one complete, whose phases are these: 1st the idea and its special incubation, more or less long; 2nd the invention or discovery; and 3rd the verification or application; and another incomplete, whose phases are these: 1st the general preparation in an unconscious state; 2nd the idea, the inspiration, and the eruption; and 3rd the period of constitution and development. The first corresponds to reflective spirits and the second to intuitive ones, without there being between the two a profound difference, since in both the essential moment, that of the imaginative synthesis, constitutes the second phase. The second process is, consequently, nothing more than the abbreviation of the first.

Pure intuition and pure combination are exceptional; in invention there is ordinarily a mixed proce[p. 295]dure, in which one of the elements prevails and permits it to be characterized. The difference lies not in the nature of the creation, but in the mechanism, which is accessory.

By reason of this difference, Ribot classifies the inventive spirits into two groups: 1st improvising spirits, who excel in conception, which they produce almost at a stroke, by means of a labor principally unconscious and abrupt actions; and 2nd spirits of logical development, who excel in development, whose preponderant role is patience, their labor being conscious and their actions slow. Without bringing in the unconscious, this same classification could be made by attributing to the will a more or less important role in relation to thought.

According to Paulhan, all intellectual creation resides in the birth of a synthetic idea, formed by the new combination of elements already existing, at least in part, in the spirit. Invention appears as the last moment of a more or less long process, in which, under the impulse of a dominant tendency—or, what amounts to the same thing, in order to complete a system sketched out but imperfect, whose force is already considerable—diverse elements attempt to combine, combating one another, modifying one another, evoking other psychological phenomena according to their own affinities, in conformity with the known laws of the activity of the spirit, until the idea or the image capable of satisfying the intellectual tendency and of perfecting the incomplete system presents itself and realizes, at last, the new and systematic synthesis that is intellectual creation, in which there are useful the influence of the unified intelligence, of the dominant tendency, of the directing idea, and of the independent play of the psychic elements.

[p. 296]But if the work of genius requires this labor of preparation, the characteristic of the genius of Art, principally, is improvisation, intuition, which does not exclude that slow labor, but rather reduces it to the sphere of the spontaneous.

In the artistic genius it may be said that the spontaneous predominates in the first moment of artistic generation; not because invention is given over to chance, as Souriau affirms, but because inspiration, which impresses that character of spontaneity, essential in the artistic work, predominates in the emotional geniuses. For this reason spontaneity is made the essential condition of genius, because that quality involves all the others.

Genius, in the most extensive sense of the word, says Seailles, is the fecundity of the spirit, the power to organize ideas, images, or signs spontaneously, without employing the slow procedures of reflective intelligence and the successive developments of discursive reasoning. That spontaneity is derived, however, from an innate tendency, tenacious and vigorous, to break with routine, to emancipate itself from the existing forms, and to modify them according to an idea of its own, suggested by those very forms, but born of the autonomy of the genius, of his nature, more perfect than observed reality.

That radical tendency, which escapes psychological analysis, engenders the new work, which is not the result, consequently, of a collision between external causality and internal finality, as Souriau would have it, but of the latter aided by the former. With much reason Kant believed that genius is not an arbitrary product of human subjectivity, but something objective, springing from the very depths of things, revealing and realizing the essence, the content, and the laws of that depth—or, what amounts to the same thing, the most elevated and perfect reconciliation of nature and freedom, of the phenomenon and [p. 297]the noumenon.

The genius, dominated by that creative tendency which has its explanation in freedom and which sums up his nature, dissociates and associates the external forms; and in that double labor of systematization he shows himself disordered and ordered according to the mechanism or process of his spirit. Invention, says Paulhan, requires at once, or at least recognizes as very favorable conditions, a certain disequilibrium of the spirit and also a very strong equilibrium, whether of the spirit in general or of certain tendencies. That disequilibrium favors invention and explains the analogies of genius and of madness, according to this philosopher, because of a certain independent and irregular activity of the psychic elements that is necessary in order to impress novelty upon phenomena.

That irregular functioning—illogical, revolutionary—which Paulhan finds in the first moment of the general spontaneous process, obeys the autonomic tendency, which we consider as essential. The freedom of the genius, of which that tendency is a primitive, instinctive, impulsive form, sets him at variance with observed reality and impels him irresistibly, with the powerful and ample force of his synthetic nature, to revolutionize what exists and to engender a superior order, a new synthesis, in harmony with his own nature, or to complete and perfect a system whose germs are found in his spirit.

Without that powerful and invincible tendency toward freedom, dissociation in the psychological process would not be realized, nor would the spirit, consciously or unconsciously, submit itself to imitation and routine; but without a nature better systematized than exterior reality, association would likewise be impossible, because the directing idea, the unifying and systematizing ideal, would not present itself to the spirit in the form of inspiration. Chance may enter, and does enter [p. 298]in effect, into invention; but chance, as Ribot observes, depends, in a broad sense, on circumstances completely exterior and purely psychic, and, in a strict and limited sense, is a happy accident that depends on the convergence of two factors: the one internal, the individual genius, and the other external, the fortuitous event. The nature of genius is, consequently, determined by that double power of destroying and of creating, which are explained by his psychological organization.

The genius, an organism endowed with a vigorous, free, and systematizing force, concentrated in one tendency, on entering into relation with the exterior world, experiences the need to modify it and reveals that need, like his aptitudes, in the phenomenon of precocity, which stimulates the process of spontaneous elaboration and prepares the phenomenon of inspiration, which produces the directing idea or the ideal and determines the logical process of the spirit in the realization of his work.

There is, then, as Paulhan says, a double process—illogical and logical—in the spirit of genius, which are explained, respectively, by the free force of the creative tendency, turned in its turn into a disturbing and disordered one, and by the ordering force of that same tendency; a double process necessary in order that the nature of the genius, better balanced in a certain sense, in the sense of his culminating tendency, may set itself in harmony with existing reality.

The labor of the genius is also one of true adaptation; only that the genius tends to adapt, and does adapt, the objective to the subjective, modifying the former by means of a new synthesis; whereas the vulgar man submits himself to the laws of routine, adapting the subjective to the objective. The autonomy of the genius, his individuality, thus explain his na[p. 299]ture.

The complete genius is power and harmony, says Guyau: genius, we say, is freedom and harmony; genius is systematizing freedom, which acquires through education greater elements for satisfying the tendency to create in which its activity is summed up.

The artistic genius is not, for that reason, radically distinguished from the artist, who is the genus; his difference lies in the intensity of his creative power, in his force of emancipation, which leads him to create new models, overturning or completing the existing forms. It is clear that in the genius there enter the same fundamental conditions of the artist, though in a much greater intensity, determining a creative power more synthetic, more efficacious, more rapid, and above all more fecund. By the fecundity of the work of art the power of the genius may be judged.

The simple novelty of the idea does not distinguish him, as Paulhan says; amplitude, power, and fecundity have the same importance as the novelty of the idea of genius; but it is the genius himself who forms his fecundity; it is the force of his freedom.

As Seailles demonstrates, the spontaneous genius, by means of a new effort of his fecundity in harmony, subjects to reason what seems to contradict it, concentrates in an ordering idea both beauties and ugliness, finds unity in its oppositions, and thus forces the very discordances to resound in the universal concert; all by means of the idea of progress, which places in the present something of the future, which permits the good to be presented in the evil, freedom in constraint, we would add, and which imposes itself upon the spirit as the necessary solution of the problem it must resolve.

Genius is, consequently, a spontaneous, free, powerful activity, whose natural law is the effort [p. 300]toward harmonic synthesis; freedom and harmony characterize its creative power and explain it. Genius is free, but it is also the living law; it reconciles the spirit and nature, says Seailles; reason in it is an instinct; it has its logic, but a superior logic, imposed by its own systematizing nature. In the genius, the free play of life realizes, without effort, an accord that the logic of the understanding, reduced to endless calculations, could not attain by its learned combinations. In this consists precisely the autonomy of the genius; and in this infinite freedom of his power lies the cause of his fecundity and the reason of his originality.

It being in the nature of the genius to create freely, the same nature that gives him aptitude for intellectual and imaginative production gives him the easy handling of the materials with whose aid the various arts are formulated. There is in this no extraordinary phenomenon that should impose admiration, but a natural phenomenon that reveals the application of a very general law: the relation of excitation to movement, as Seailles demonstrates. The aesthetic conception is an ensemble of images, combined according to the vital laws; it is transformed into an ensemble of movements that imitate its relations and harmony, under the empire of the feeling and of the tenacious desire that evokes and combines them.

The genius thus proceeds like Nature, and in this sense he may be compared with free life, as Seailles does; but he differs from Nature and surpasses it, in that in the latter the principle of causality predominates, which determines the blind mechanism of its activity, whereas, in the genius, it is the principle of finality, of freedom, that acts as the determining cause of his action. The ideal is the result of the autonomy of the genius and the final cause of his systematizing and creative activity.

Genius is spontaneous and reflec[p. 301]tive activity at the same time; it is the success of Nature, but attained through the triumph of freedom over necessity; it is the spirit reaching its apogee, not in the moment in which it surpasses reflection and becomes Nature, as Seailles believes, but in that in which it raises Nature to the height of its ideal conception.

Genius is defined, then, not by life, but by freedom: only thus can it be brought about that beauty depends on genius and not the latter on an arbitrary function of beauty, founded on the exclusive influence of the objective. What is proper to the artistic genius consists, as Guyau says, in emancipating himself from all constraint, exterior as well as interior, and in coming to be the primitive spark of life and of will.

There has commonly been given to the faculty of invention, when it is developed in a notable manner, the name of genius, and to the faculty of expression the name of talent, says Souriau. There are men of genius who, lacking talent, pass their lives in conceiving grandiose projects which they never execute, and men of talent who, notwithstanding their devotion and their skill, cannot rise above mediocrity, and, lacking genius, execute nothing but banal works. Talent is thus considered secondary, for the sole reason that it is study that gives it. Souriau, like Hirth, Ribot, and Paulhan, combat this separation between the inventive and the expressive faculties, affirming that genius is explained only by the harmony between the two.

Genius and talent are nothing more than one and the same faculty applied to discovering, whether ideas of the whole or ideas of detail, says Souriau. One cannot recognize the artistic genius without a power superior to that which is characterized as talent and which is revealed in the specific art, writes Hirth.

According to Ribot, invention—that tendency to variation—is fundamental or slight; the funda[p. 302]mental corresponds to genius and survives, by analogous procedures, natural selection, that is, by its own force; the slight corresponds to talent, survives and prospers principally by the aid of circumstances and of its milieu; here the orientation comes from without, not from within; which signifies that a good part of the force of talent lies not in the aptitude for invention, but for imitation. Paulhan believes that invention is inseparable from routine and from imitation. According to these psychologists, the difference between genius and talent is one of degree and not of nature.

But if genius represents a superiority not of nature but of degree, since that degree may vary considerably, it is impossible to say where genius begins or ends. Hence the diverse criterion by which geniuses are classified, when these do not stand in the first rank by the creation of models or of viable types, consecrated by the constant admiration of the public. Nevertheless, the predominance of imitation over invention may serve to characterize talent, which always shows itself reflective and laborious; genius reveals itself in the spontaneity of its work, in the superior degree of freedom for conceiving the ideal and realizing it. In that harmonic interpenetration of the subjective and the objective which constitutes art, genius is distinguished by the predominance of the subjective, and talent by that of the objective.

### XXIII. LA CONCIENCIA ESTÉTICA SUPERIOR (LA CREACIÓN ARTÍSTICA) — XXIII. THE HIGHER AESTHETIC CONSCIOUSNESS (ARTISTIC CREATION)

Given the richness, complexity, and autonomy of genius, it is impossible to make a detailed and precise analysis of its artistic activity. Even in natures that do not rise to the height of genius, the process in the creation of the work of art varies considerably according to the temperament of the artist. For this reason the psychologists confine themselves, in this matter, to characterizing that process in a general and vague manner.

Seailles, who identifies the work of genius with that of Nature, attributes to the creative action of the artist the character of simultaneity. The work of art ought to issue forth at a single stroke, says Seailles; but the impossibility of saying everything at once, or the difficulty of expression, compels the artist to a successive labor, in which the conception, like the living being, grows in all its parts at once, and the execution, for that very reason, becomes simultaneous.

According to Paulhan the form of the whole is not drawn with clarity, in many cases, until after the invention of the details, and then it is not the nature of the ensemble that determines the nature of the details, but rather the nature of the details, evoked at times, a little by chance, that comes to determine the nature of the whole and to fix the [p. 304]orientation of the spirit. But, in any case, the primitive tendency that impels the creation of the work is always, according to Paulhan, an abstract and general disposition, a kind of permanent possibility of this or that class of phenomena. That tendency consists in a set of physio-psychological ways of being which, without being actually manifested by any fact of consciousness, preserves its reality and, when the occasion presents itself, determines systems of ideas and of acts, always variable in some degree, but always of the same nature.

In the view, then, of this philosopher, the first perceptible phenomenon in the preparation of a work is not a specialized tendency, nor a guiding idea, but an impression of a general order or an abstract idea, a tendency that manifests itself through a general expression, as happens with the organic tendencies. The process of creation proceeds, according to this analysis, from the abstract toward a concrete that is ever more complex and systematized, and not the contrary, as those think who admit at the beginning of creative activity a tendency specialized toward a concrete object.

G. Finnbogason, in his book on sympathetic intelligence, seems to be in agreement with Paulhan. Studying the manner in which literary characters have arisen in the soul of the author, he holds that the poetic gift of forming new individualities is not merely a further development of the faculty, possessed more or less by every man, of comprehending the individuality of others. In his view, the germs of literary characters may have the most varied origins. In every man, in a poet more than in any other, there reside varied tendencies that are never expressed in actions, different possibilities that are never [p. 305]realized; these tendencies and possibilities vegetate, in the form of vain desires, only to be thrust back into the depths by the iron hand of reality. It is possible that we give preference to a desire and that the phantom of a personality is evoked which bears a resemblance to the self and which, in reality, is nothing but one's own personality. But Finnbogason thinks that it does not happen thus with all the characters that literature presents to us, with respect to which the poet knows that they are foreign to him, as happens with the historical characters he chooses. Sometimes the poet sets out from a psychological problem or from an abstract situation. He knows then, perhaps, what class of characters he proposes to describe, and he has the feeling of the general orientation of his work, but he does not yet know his heroes personally. These figures, which cast their shadow into the soul of the poet before presenting themselves, become individualized by means of images that come from the external world.

As to the manner in which the first idea of a work is born in the soul of a poet, that manner varies in the extreme, according to the case, and often the author himself does not perhaps know it. That idea may present itself in the waking state or in dream. It has been observed, moreover, that the memories of childhood play a great part in the productions of many authors. Everything seems to tend, in the soul of the author, toward the same direction, when he sets himself to create a work. Just as a melody forms around a motif, as a plant sprouts from a small seed, so in the soul of the author a new person is born out of certain isolated traits, out of certain manifestations of the soul, which carry within them the intimate law of this person. Consequently, no conception of literary production could be more false than that which consists in believing that the poet simply copies reality.

[p. 306]All the psychologists agree, however, in accepting the existence of a guiding idea, engendered by the preparatory labor of inspiration, with the concurrence of the intellectual and affective elements of the creative imagination. This idea is what is called the ideal, taken in its psychological and not its metaphysical sense. The ideal, which is also called the thought, the essence or ground of the work of art, contains its intelligible elements. The forms that express that ideal constitute its sensible conditions, elements which reality does not separate, but which abstraction can present in isolation for its analysis.

The ideal is informed, in effect, by the simultaneous concurrence of intelligence and sensibility. Without the primitive, spontaneous, and irresistible tendency to dissociate the forms and then at once to associate them, the ideal would not arise in the soul of the artist; without the pleasurable or disagreeable emotion produced by the activity of that tendency, there would exist no criterion for the systematization, which is a labor of adaptation of the objective to the subjective; and without the perception of the relations that reality offers, the systematization of the ideal would likewise be impossible.

For this reason the ideal, as Ricardou shows, is neither an absolute idea, nor an abstract idea, nor a general idea that remains in the indetermination of the abstract, nor the greatest perfection possible in general; but rather our perfection, immediately possible, that which we attain by suppressing the obstacles that reality offers to our tendency toward a greater freedom; nor is it, finally, the fiction that dissociates and associates forms without subjection to a possible order.

The ideal, thus considered, is determinate, individual, particular, manifold, and variable; it involves an indefinite number of modes and of degrees; in all its moments and directions it is a tendency and a thought [p. 307]that fix themselves, by means of a concrete and living image, in harmony with feeling and as the object of the will. Although engendered by the whole being, its directive character predominates in the ideal, and for this reason Ricardou had defined it as the progressive conception, under a determinate form, of the perfection that a being can realize at a given moment; a vague definition, because it depends upon the vague idea of perfection, but one that becomes precise when we consider that perfection is relative to freedom in an order suited to its nature. The concept of a possible better, with which Ricardou means to fix the nature of the ideal, can refer only to that idea of relative freedom, which determines in man the ideas of the better and of the more perfect, through the satisfaction they produce in him.

Thus Ricardou understands it, when he explains the mechanism in the formation of the ideal and defines progress. Whether it be a question of the psychological form of the better, as of any other, the mechanism of its formation implies, according to Ricardou, free activity, tending toward moral perfection. In the generation of the aesthetic ideal, he adds, we wish to escape from the tyranny of things, taking refuge in a creation in which matter docilely expresses our soul and where we can freely deploy our activity; fascinated by the vision of infinite freedom we tend toward it, we make an effort toward an inner life in which the subject may dominate being absolutely, we diminish the servitude of the exterior, and realize progressively our human and partial freedom. The aesthetic ideal results from reconciling order and freedom, says Ricardou; in our view, that reconciliation of the aesthetic ideal is realized between freedom and nature, in an order suited to freedom. The ideal lies, then, neither in nature nor in man alone, but in the reconciliation of these two elements, the subjective and the objective, through the action of the subject [p. 308]upon the object; it partakes, for that very reason, of the forms of reality and of the modalities of the being that thinks and feels; the tendency toward freedom engenders the ideal, imagination offers it forms taken from external reality, and reason impresses upon it the relations of an order more in harmony with feeling, which is the regulating power in the generation of the artistic ideal.

It may be said with Bénard that the true ideal in art is composed of two terms united by a relation of unity or of identity: first, the idea that the artist conceives and that must appear and be realized in his works; second, the form he gives to this idea in order to express or represent it; and third, the relation that unites the two terms, which is an intimate bond that makes of the whole a living ensemble, a true symbol.

The artist, who informs the ideal, realizes the intelligible conditions of his work. But this reconciliation of freedom and Nature, as Hegel observes, can take place in two ways: either Nature, at peace with man and as his friend, herself offers him liberally what he asks of her, and, instead of binding him, of hampering him, goes everywhere anticipating his desires; or man has needs and desires that Nature is not in a condition to satisfy immediately, and then he must procure for himself, by his own activity, what is necessary to him, seize upon things, appropriate them to his designs, smooth away obstacles through the skill of his genius, and thus transform the external world so that it becomes a means serving the fulfillment of all his ends. The most perfect mode of reconciliation is found at the point where these conditions are joined; that is to say, when the action of man is seconded by Nature and, in place of a violent struggle in which their mutual dependence would shine forth, [p. 309]both offer the spectacle of a happy accord and of a harmonious concurrence.

The artist finds the ideal, then, in Nature or outside of it, or he rises above Nature in order to obtain in the divine principle a reconciliation of an absolute character. The artist thus draws his inspiration from the divine, the human, and the reality that forms the world inferior to man. The divine offers him the religious ideal, the human the moral ideal, individual and social, and external nature the ideal of physical or physiological force, developing with the appearance of freedom, in graceful forms: the mathematical ideal, as Ricardou calls it.

Art, in its history, has evolved from the religious ideal to the mechanical ideal of Nature. Subordinated to the sentiment of the divine in its beginnings, it became humanized in Greek anthropomorphism; collective and social, in its confusion with the useful and in the subordination of thought to the religious idea, it afterward became individualized and was dispersed with the freedom of the artist and the infinite diversity of the forms of Nature.

In this evolution of the aesthetic ideal, which answers to that of the aesthetic emotion, Hegel has found three particular forms, which he has named symbolism, classicism, and romanticism, and which he considers as successive moments of the development of the idea or of the ideal. In the symbolic form, the idea seeks, but does not find, a form that suits it; in the classical form, the idea finds that form, man; but in the romantic it surpasses it and strips itself of the sensible forms. Consistent with this distinction, Hegel classifies the arts as symbolic, classical, and romantic; and the very history of art into three periods: oriental art, Greek and Roman art, and Christian art. Architecture is the symbolic art, which predominates in the Orient; Sculpture is [p. 310]the classical art, which predominates chiefly in Greece; Painting and Music are romantic and Christian arts; Poetry likewise forms part of the romantic series, especially lyric poetry; but in the universality of its forms it contains also the symbolic and the classical. Architecture, Sculpture, and Painting may equally partake of the other forms, but these are not so essential to them.

The ideal, in its generality, becomes particularized by means of the form that contains the sensible conditions of the work of art. This form is internal and external; the first is the image; the second is the sensible figure given to the image by the matter chosen to reproduce it. All the arts partake of both; the internal form is the ideal artistic form; the external is born of the instrument that each art employs, namely: stones, marbles, colors, sounds, words. The internal form is inseparable from the ideal; without it the ideal would cease to be what it is, because it would lose its individuality and be confounded with the general or abstract idea; but neither is it the whole of the ideal, for then it would be confounded with the forms of reality perceived and preserved by memory. When one speaks, then, of the artistic form, as a term opposed to the ground of a work, reference is made to the external and sensible form that expresses the individual ideal.

Form in art, as De Coster says, embraces all the elements that contribute to the complete expression of the thought, with all the dispositions and developments that are taken from nature or that are created with a view to the realization of the ideal. Each branch of art, according to the exigencies of the material means at its disposal, has recourse to particular forms, which are classified into forms of space and forms of time. The first comprise: first, lines and figu[p. 311]res or surfaces; second, light with its effects of shadow and of chiaroscuro; third, colors and tints or shades; and fourth, movement, locomotion, gesture, and physiognomy. The forms in time comprise: first, sound, timbre, and harmony; second, movement and rhythm; and third, articulation, the word, and language.

Against what De Coster maintains, we believe that Nature is the principal source of the artistic forms; not only by reason of its inexhaustible variety, of the life it encloses, and of the force with which it impresses the artist, but, moreover, because only in that source can the imagination develop with ample freedom and find the originality that characterizes true artistic production.

We do agree, indeed, with idealism in denying to form its exclusivism in the characterization of art. Just as the beautiful is not pure emotion, neither is art pure form, without an ideal content. Art, reduced to a combination of forms, would not fulfill the sociological end that its nature likewise imposes upon it, through the intervention of the milieu as an important factor in artistic generation.

Croce is in this respect more radical. One of the most debated questions in Aesthetics, he writes, is the relation between matter and form or, as is ordinarily said, between content and form. The question is to know whether the aesthetic phenomenon consists in the content alone, or in the form alone, or in the one and the other at the same time. In Croce's view, the question is not susceptible of doubt, if by matter is understood emotionality not aesthetically elaborated, or the impressions, and by form the elaboration, that is to say, the spiritual activity and its expression.

Croce rejects the thesis that makes the aesthetic phenomenon consist in the content alone, that is, in the simple [p. 312]impressions, as well as the thesis that makes it consist in the addition of form to content, that is, in the impressions plus the expressions. In the aesthetic phenomenon, the expressive activity is not added to the phenomenon of the impressions, but rather these arrive already elaborated and formed by it. The aesthetic phenomenon is, for this reason, form and nothing but form; which does not mean that the content is something superfluous, but that from the quality of the content to that of the form there is no transition. The aesthetic phenomenon is ground and form at the same time, because it is intuitive knowledge, which is knowledge and expression at the same time. But the aesthetic phenomenon is not practical for Croce, but purely theoretical, so that it is exhausted in the internal form alone. The aesthetic phenomenon, he says, is exhausted entirely in the expressive elaboration of the impressions. When we have conquered the inner word, conceived clearly and vividly a figure or a statue, found a musical motif, the expression is clear and complete; there is no need of more. External expression is an added phenomenon, which obeys other laws; it is a practical phenomenon, or one of will; the aesthetic work is always internal, and what is called external is not a work of art.

This theory, which can be applied only to the poetic work, in which the form is purely internal, does not apply to the other arts, in which objectivity seems inseparable from sensible expression. To deny to the external form its role in the constitution of the aesthetic phenomenon is to disregard every end of art, to forget the reciprocal influence existing between the two forms, which correct and complete each other, and to sacrifice aesthetic value to the purpose of making of Aesthetics a Philosophy. Lalo, in opposition to Croce, makes of technique, precisely, the content of the aesthetic phenomenon, a thesis equally inadmissible, since it constitutes the opposite extreme, it being worth [p. 313]noting that both theories, that of Croce as well as that of Lalo, are intellectualist and combat aesthetic sentimentalism.

The ideal does not derive, then, exclusively from an intellectual function. The study we have made of creative aesthetic activity shows, on the contrary, that the will plays the principal role in the formation of the ideal, considered as an organism that answers to a need of that autonomous feeling which constitutes the ground of the aesthetic consciousness.

The spirit, which feels the need of progress in the form of a greater expansion, within the limits of the reality in which it acts, satisfies that need, first, through imagination, recomposing reality, and, afterward, through action presided over by that new conception of life. When renovation is impossible, because the effort is rendered sterile before an adverse or deficient reality, then it concentrates itself in imagination, and for the happiness of doing there is substituted the happiness of contemplating the new order created by the spirit in the service of freedom. Thus is formed the ideal with a practical end. Realized through action, it constitutes a norm, and if it is not renewed it becomes a routine.

But outside of practice, the ideal may be created solely for the pleasure of contemplating it; for, freedom being the supreme good of man, its pure contemplation, in adequate and expressive forms, satisfies the spirit, which thus emancipates itself from the representations that are repugnant to its nature.

In any case, the creation of the ideal supposes a perfecting of the real, obtained with the criterion of feeling; it supposes a free choice, which cannot submit itself to the canons of reason. Its unity does not depend on the associations of thought, but on the u[p. 314]nity of feeling and of willing, which is the unity of the self. This explains how the collective ideal exists only in moments when feeling gives uniformity to the social consciousness, and why the ideal has become individual, through the complexity and heterogeneity of consciousnesses.

The ideal may be elaborated with the representations that the spirit chooses among those offered to it by physical or social reality; but it may also be informed with the data of internal reality, and then it becomes a work of subjective penetration, in which the spirit lives or aspires to live completely of itself, reaching to the very root of consciousness, where the spirit has not yet suffered the servitude of the intelligence, which enslaves it with its motives of action; that is to say, in the domain in which Bergson places that «élan that each individual retains from the global impulse of life», at that point where we feel ourselves most inward in our own life, in the domain of pure spirituality, of the duration of the profound self, of immense virtuality, of the creative power, of absolute freedom.

The ideal thus offers two fundamental forms, like the imagination that creates it: one principally objective, which corresponds to plastic imagination, and another principally subjective, which is engendered by the diffluent imagination, whose characters Ribot has marked out, and which refer respectively to the arts that Hegel has classified under the denominations of classical and romantic. But both types have in common that their content is freedom, considered in its static form of equilibrium, of eurythmy in the plastic ideal, and of free movement in the diffluent or dynamic ideal.

The ideal, as Ricardou says, is essentially a qualification ever more concrete and more perfect; it is the notion of a higher degree of concrete reality. [p. 315]It implies, in the midst of its individual, particular, manifold, and variable determination, the idea of possible perfection, an image that unites the representation under a determinate form, incarnating itself in a living individual aspect, so as to constitute a model that imposes itself upon our activity.

In a broad sense, the ideal is the idea, as Plato and Schopenhauer regarded it, an eternal archetype, an order of relations with a metaphysical content. Plato said: just as God is the author of the essences and has created the world, which is the image of his ideas, so the human artist conceives an ideal of beauty and imitates it by means of elements offered by Nature.

The ideas of Schopenhauer are the Platonic ones and, in the particular form they acquire, resemble rather those of Schelling. The ideas are objectivations or representations of the will. All the degrees of objectivation of the Will, says Schopenhauer, are nothing other than the ideas of Plato. I understand by Idea every determinate and constant degree of objectivation of the Will, insofar as this is the thing in itself and, consequently, stripped of all multiplicity.

According to Schopenhauer, art conceives and reproduces, by means of pure contemplation, the eternal Ideas, that which is essential in all phenomena. Its sole origin is the knowledge of the Ideas, and its sole end to communicate this knowledge; its object is the essence, the Idea. Schopenhauer defines the aesthetic work by saying that it is the contemplation of things independently of the principle of reason, in opposition to that other contemplation which is subjected to the said principle and which is that of experience and of the sciences.

Schopenhauer differentiates the Idea from the notion. The notion is abstract, discursive, indeterminate [p. 316]in its comprehension, but perfectly limited as to its extension; to be perceived it needs nothing more than reason; words suffice to communicate it, without other intermediary, and its definition exhausts completely all its content. On the contrary, the Idea, which might be defined, strictly, as the adequate representative of the notion, is essentially intuitive and, although it takes the place of an infinity of things, is absolutely determinate; it lies not within the reach of the individual, but only of genius.

The Idea, in this sense, that is, the Ideal, is distinguished both from the individual and concrete idea—the synthesis of representations produced by the perception of an individual, in which are combined all its sensible and logical properties, in the same order offered by perceived reality—and from the general and abstract idea, called the concept, in which the synthesis excludes the sensible properties, leaving only the common or logical ones, that is, a mere system of relations, an empty order. Virtue, as Kant says, and with it human wisdom, in all its purity, are ideas, but the wisdom of the Stoics is an ideal. The ideal is confounded, sometimes, with the idea of genus and at other times with the idea of species. The Platonic ideal was generic, more abstract than concrete; that of Schopenhauer was specific, more concrete than abstract. The first makes of order the formative principle of the Idea; the second makes of the Idea a representation of the Will, as «thing in itself», as noumenon, as a free, omnipotent, and creative will.

It is in this sense that the aesthetic ideal must be considered. Whether it be a question of the psychological form of the better, that is to say of the ideal, as of any other form, the mechanism of its formation implies free activity, [p. 317]tending toward moral perfection, as Ricardou affirms. In the aesthetic ideal, we wish, escaping the tyranny of things, to take refuge in a creation in which, docilely, matter may express our soul and where we may freely deploy our activity, because we aspire to infinite existence.

The means of realizing the ideal form is the artistic procedure, the artistic technique. Every matter has its laws and can be employed only in certain cases, in a certain manner, and up to a certain point. The science of those laws and of their consequences forms the basis of the procedures in all the arts and all the crafts; it is acquired through the education of the artist.

The procedure may be considered in itself, and then it is not distinguished from the craft; but considered in its relation to art, it creates the style and the manner of the artist. By referring the execution of the artistic work to its conception, which the execution continues; by referring the procedure to the feeling that creates it, and the form to the ground of the work, one obtains the notion of style, says Seailles. In general, style, which is always the style of some one, is thought made visible in its expression; it is the law of expression that the artist establishes between his work and the reality it represents. The proper manner that each artist has of conceiving art, according to his particular character—such is the principle which, developed freely and consciously, comes to be for him his practical system, or style. For this reason style refers to the manner of conceiving an object and to that of executing it; it has something objective, by the forms the artist acquires, and something subjective, by the manner in which he combines and expresses them. Style is not, consequently, abstract, but a vital, concrete, and spontaneous phenomenon, as Seailles shows.

Manner, which is distinguished from originality, is a way of conceiving and of executing that is purely acciden[p. 318]tal, proper to each artist and that may be carried to the point of standing in direct opposition to the true principle of the ideal. Manner thus considered is a vice or an infraction of style, inasmuch as it may be referred also to the thought and to its execution, says Nuñez de Arenas. The true manner, according to Hegel, ought to withdraw from a narrow particularity, purely personal, and take a higher flight, if one does not wish it to end in a routine. The artist ought to keep himself in perfect conformity with the nature of the subject he treats, comprehend its spirit, and observe its law in employing a particular procedure in expression.

The ideal, the form, the style, and the manner, as is seen, are not purely subjective; the artist, in conceiving the ideal, in informing and expressing it in a special style and manner, undergoes the influence of the milieu in which he exercises his activity. The same causes that influence the aesthetic emotion and determine its relativity influence also the creation of the artistic work. The ideal is modified according to the force and the culture of the intelligence, character, and education; in a word, according to all the internal or external influences that can act upon the intellectual and moral principle. Thus it assumes in every man, as De Coster observes, a particular character in relation with individual tendencies, ideas, and feelings. And since epochs and nations, just like persons, have their own character, their tendencies, their aim, the ideal for societies, just as for individuals, depends on the current of ideas that result from religion, from philosophy, from political institutions, from the degree of civilization, from intellectual and moral culture, from the passions, from race itself, and from climate; and thus the individual reacts upon his nation and upon his century, as his century and his nation react upon him, engendering an [p. 319]ideal that develops, transforms itself, perfects itself, grows, and declines, according to the times, the places, and the individuals, taking on in the diverse epochs, in the different countries, and in each artist in particular, a special character, without losing, in the midst of that great variety, the unity impressed upon it by the fundamental unity of man.

The physical and social milieu influence with the same efficacy the materiality of the form, with its elements, its models, and with the taste of the public that judges the work of art.

This influence has been exaggerated to the point of maintaining that the ideal is engendered by the social action upon the individual, determining in him his aspirations. The concept of the ideal implies the idea of progressive evolution, of harmonious adaptation, of perfection, and of a foreseen end. The feeling of the ideal is the complex and confused impression that we have of the course of real evolution: a very particular emotion that accompanies the vision of the evolutionary process, above all when it is realized in ourselves. Our discontent with the real and the effort to change the real—such is the ideal and the creative activity of the imagination; but that state of instability of the soul is produced entirely by social transformations. The more extensive societies are, the denser is their content, the more complex and unstable is their life, and the more changing and idealizing is their spiritual life. And since the extension, the volume, and the density of societies are indefinitely variable elements—for history shows us only peoples that grow or diminish, that expand or contract, that intensify or grow rarefied—the spirit of the men who form part of them follows the same infinitely unstable movement. Such is precisely, says Draghicesco, the origin of all ideal creation.

[p. 320]The effort to surpass oneself infinitely, as well as that characteristic tendency of man to believe himself different from what he is—which constitute the essence of the ideal—translate, in fact, the infinite mobility of the spirit and, indirectly, the indefinite variability of social groups, their tendency to grow and to extend themselves indefinitely. Not only does the ideal have this origin, but its own mechanism is created and modeled by the general needs of collective life, which tend to extend and to deepen themselves. Consistent with this thesis, Draghicesco maintains the social origin of aesthetic inspiration, to which he recognizes the function of liberation from reality, but leaving aside the subjective factor of the creative will.

This sociological and determinist explanation is in contradiction with the fact of the great innovating geniuses, who have rebelled against social tyranny, opposing their individual ideal to the collective one of society. This contradiction proceeds from substituting for the generating cause of freedom the occasional cause of the influence of the milieu, which modifies the ideal but does not create it. Changes in society certainly reverberate in consciousnesses; but when these are not purely receptive, but forces capable of a free interpretation of those changes, the ideal arises as an individual, spontaneous, original work—not by reason of the representations aroused in the consciousness, but by reason of the syntheses formed by the will, which places the self in those organisms and communicates to them an ideal life.

### XXIV. CAUSAS DE LA RELATIVIDAD DEL FENÓMENO ESTÉTICO — XXIV. CAUSES OF THE RELATIVITY OF THE AESTHETIC PHENOMENON

According to Mario Pilo, the causes of the relativity of the aesthetic phenomenon reside in two fundamental biological and psychological laws: the law of heredity and the law of the environment, inertia and mobility, the fixity and the variability of the world that lives and thinks.

We have, indeed, with respect to the beautiful, says Pilo, the tastes that our ancestors have transmitted to us, and of those tastes, some are common to all or to a part of animal beings, and others are individual. Sounds, colors, and forms may afford common elementary aesthetic feelings, which are nevertheless diversified by the diversity of the senses.

Race is another element of variety and of relativity. The perfecting of the races, from the twofold biological and psychological point of view, determines differences as regards the perception and comprehension of the beautiful, as well as with respect to the intensity, vividness, and complexity of aesthetic emotion.

Within the limits of a single race, each people has its own special taste. With the passing of the centuries the taste of a people is purified and transformed by progressing, or it evolves in a regressive direction, passing into a period of decadence.

But within one and the same people, and even within one and the same period of its historical evolution, not all the social classes feel the beautiful equally. And within the same social [p. 322]classes, certain families are endowed with a more refined and more complete feeling, owing to fortunate hereditary combinations or to an accumulation of effects, due to their particular conditions.

The two sexes likewise have diverse tastes, and not only in appreciating the beauty of the other sex, complementary to that of each of them, but also in matters that have nothing directly to do with sex.
