There is no longer, for this dogmatism, an absolute and invariable essence of beauty, of beauty in itself, of an immutable archetype, but only laws of beauty—that is, an ensemble of determinations and of conditions perfectly flexible and in perpetual evolution, in no way universal, consequently; general, in the precise measure in which their conditions are repeated.

Lalo comprehends that, in this form of dogmatic criticism, freedom is suppressed, as much as in the absolute dogmatic criticism; but, according to Lalo, true freedom does not consist in having no laws, but in obeying only the interior laws; and the laws of our actions are not truly interior to us, that is to say, personal, except when our character obeys this internal logic, which really constitutes «a theorem that marches» and not a pure series of caprices at the mercy of all external accidents. Now, Lalo adds, it is precisely the just proportion of this relative autonomy and of the influence of the external milieu that measures the ever-variable degree of our freedom.

[p. 367]One form of relativist dogmatic criticism, the most humble and yet the richest in future, is, for Lalo, the one established by contemporary experimental aesthetics, which devotes itself to establishing aesthetic laws, starting from aesthetic experimentation upon a determined number of interrogated subjects and which is valid only for those subjects and cannot be generalized except with a hypothetical character. Aesthetic experimentation is a consecration, at once, of impressionism and of dogmatism, because the generalities at which it arrives are, for it, only a sum of individual facts. The essential object of this method is to form this sum of subjective impressions, which absolute dogmatism disdains and which the more moderate dogmatists suppose realized confusedly under the names of taste, of good sense, of common consent, or of established and definitive opinion in humanity; which the impressionists likewise note, though ridiculing it, as a tradition or a coarse and scarcely respectable routine. The adepts of aesthetic experimentation occupy themselves with methodically establishing these special facts of aesthetics, which are called «judgments of value». It results therefrom that the «objective criticism» of a work of art is a synthesis of all the aesthetic judgments formed upon it by humanity.

What, in Lalo's conception, is fecund in the impressionist and dogmatic systems and that wherein they concur, when they are well understood, is the idea of relativity. The one conceives it in a more strict manner; the other in a more ample manner. Impressionism studies only the relativity of works in an individual and even under its most subjective form of our own individual. Dogmatism in no way suppresses this investigation; on the contrary, it adds to it others very similar; it comprehends it and surpasses it. It is no longer, solely [p. 368]in relation to ourselves, but in relation to a given time or a given milieu, or even, if possible, in relation to all men and all times, that it establishes the universal relativity of the values of art. If, in the end, this value appears to be an approximation of the absolute, there is nothing more in this; for the absolute is not, in art, as in all else, anything but a more ample relativity, the mathematical or ideal limit of all possible relativities, which, consequently, we shall never attain, but toward which we shall always tend.

Impressionism establishes a psychological relativity, still but mediocrely understood, and dogmatism establishes a sociological relativity, often still very abstract. But nothing prevents the better understanding of the one and the «concretizing» of the other, and in this case they coincide. Reduced to these terms, the two systems in no way contradict each other; they complete each other, they presuppose each other; each has its value and its legitimate role. Each is only a necessary phase, through which the other must normally pass in order to conclude its integral development, and through which the thought of each critic passes with respect to each of his judgments, whether or not he is conscious of them.

According to Lalo, there are, then, two dogmatisms, the absolute which rejects and the relativist which accepts; and within this modality there is still the semi-absolute dogmatism, which admits that all values are relative, but which wishes, nonetheless, that the criticism of these values be absolute. And, on the other hand, there is also the fully relativist dogmatism of the experimental school, for which everything is so relative that the absolute, representable by us, is only the sum or the synthesis of the greatest possible number of relativities, and dogmatism, more objective, the combination of the greatest possible number of subjective impressions. Dogma[p. 369]tism, well understood, is nothing but an organized impressionism, as impressionism, well understood, is only a relativist dogmatism. Thus the experimental method of contemporary aesthetics is the synthesis of dogmatism and of relativism.

The conclusion at which Lalo arrives, after this ample study, he sums up thus: in our scientific age, aesthetics, this philosophy of art criticism, will not exist, or, surpassing impressionism, will be dogmatic. Dogmatism will be nothing but a retarded survival of traditionalism, unless it comes to convert itself, from absolute, into relativist. Aesthetic relativism, finally, will not be complete unless it extends itself truly to all relations, unless it implies, necessarily, more and more, the sociological point of view.

The problem of critical aesthetic activity refers, as one sees, to that of «aesthetic value», in which it is a question of knowing whether, in the appreciation of the phenomenon of the beautiful, there predominates the psychological factor of harmony, the psychological factor of the aesthetic emotion, or the logical factor of rational knowledge. As the critical function of consciousness is exercised upon the judgment of appreciation or of aesthetic value, in order to demonstrate or justify it, two factors enter into it: the aesthetic and the logical, whose confusion has given rise to the impressionist and dogmatic systems that Lalo analyzes.

The first of those factors, that is to say the judgment of aesthetic value, is complex also, because in the aesthetic phenomenon, as in every psycho-social phenomenon, there intervene perception, feeling and the will, which synthesizes them and properly determines their value; there arising, from that conjunction, the necessity of determining which of those psychological functions predominates and explains the judgment of aesthetic value, and there being derived from it the three theories—hedonist, intellectualist and voluntarist—which dispute that predominance and which decide, respec[p. 370]tively, the question relative to the critical function, which reduces itself to adopting one of those three criteria: that of the pleasure of impressions, that of the absolute or relative canon which serves as a model among the dogmatists, and the criterion of free activity, reflected in the artistic work, upon which the integral appreciation of aesthetic voluntarism is founded.

This criterion surpasses the other two, not only because the function of the free will comprises and impresses its character upon the other two psychological functions, but because it investigates in the artistic work the essential aesthetic factor of freedom, without which artistic creation is incomprehensible and aesthetic value is indemonstrable. Every dogmatism, however relativist it may be considered, suppresses the source of aesthetic creation, because it suppresses the free expansion of the spirit, which is incarnated in the work of art and is its sole form of valuation. Impressionism tends toward that freedom; but in making of the immediate and psychological effects of aesthetic contemplation the criterion of value, it chains art to those effects.

If the logical or demonstrative phase, which predominates in the critical function, has given primacy to dogmatism, it has had the tendency to convert the aesthetic phenomenon into a scientific phenomenon, changing its nature. That is the error of Lalo's aesthetics and of all who persist in making of aesthetics a logic. If impressionism aspires to make of the aesthetic function an artistic function and dogmatism a logical function, it is because the singular nature of aesthetic value, informed by psychological freedom, has been misapprehended.

The true critic must be artist, philosopher and man of science, at one and the same time, and if he is not capable of creating, by his own effort, a work of art, he must be capable of reconstructing, by means of the imagination, the [p. 371]artistic work he appreciates, discovering in it all that its author wished to put and did, in effect, put there, and of forming thus aesthetic judgments of value, which, as philosopher and man of science, he must demonstrate and justify. Only by forming judgments of value can the critic communicate with the creator of the work and be in a condition to criticize it; that is to say, to reveal its qualities and deficiencies.

But the critic, in proceeding in that manner, discoursing upon the basis of judgments of value acquired as a spectator, does not proceed as a mathematician, nor as a physicist, deducing conclusions from immutable categories, imposed upon reason, or from organized sums of impressions, subjected to a law, but as an aesthetic consciousness, guided by that criterion of freedom, proper to the aesthete, who cannot emancipate himself from feeling and enter into the domain of the purely abstract; his demonstrations bear no resemblance to those which rational science employs in the purely logical order. Aesthetics itself, as philosophy, departs from this logism.

From the exclusive consideration of the logical factor are born the qualities that are demanded of the critic and the precepts to which he is subordinated. The critic must have the following qualities: science, artistic feeling, good taste and impartiality—qualities that are acquired by means of a special education. Only the critic who possesses those qualities demonstrates in his labor a profound and detailed knowledge of the work he analyzes; only then is he just in his appreciations, benevolent in the revelation of defects, fecund in the demonstration of qualities, independent in the examination of the conditions of production, and impersonal in rendering his verdict upon the merit of the work.

The true critic is not, nor can he be, consequently, the mere erudite, however great he may be. His [p. 372]science. The true critic is an artist, in his own way, and, at times, is a veritable creator of beauties, who reveals his temperament and defends his ideals in criticism. Thus do philosophical criticism with Taine, the eclectic with Brandes, the subjective with France and Capuana, the impressionist with Lemaitre, Arnold and Desjardins, and the experimental with Spronck and Tellier, demonstrate it. The decadent critics themselves are, at once, poets and novelists, like Moréas and Plessys, Morice, Vanor, Baju and Verlaine.

But if the critic is not capable of producing beautiful works, of the kind of those he criticizes, he must, at least, have educated his sensibility in the contemplation of art, in order to possess, like the artist, that physiological and psychological aptitude which gives to feeling the exact measure of what is beautiful. Without that fundamental condition, the critic will be incapable of divining the process followed in the elaboration of art, of analyzing its moments, of comprehending all the harmonies enclosed in that complex synthesis which is called the work of art, of determining the value of its components, of demonstrating its excellences, of knowing the social influence of the work he examines.

### XXVII. LA DEFINICIÓN DE LO BELLO — XXVII. THE DEFINITION OF THE BEAUTIFUL

Across the immense variety of aesthetic feelings, which engenders a great variety of ideals of beauty, philosophy seeks to find common characters that may allow beauty to be defined objectively, in order to establish general laws that may direct aesthetic taste and justify the verdicts of artistic criticism.

The difficulty of finding such a definition is readily understood; a difficulty that arises not only from the complexity of the aesthetic feeling, even in its most elementary form, but from the diverse importance assigned to the subjective and objective factors that enter into the aesthetic phenomenon, and from the special character of the psychological doctrine that serves as the basis for the analysis of the subjective phenomenon. Those who believe that there is no objective beauty, properly so called, but solely and exclusively an aesthetic feeling that serves as a criterion for classifying objects as beautiful, ugly, or indifferent, give a subjective definition, which may take as its basis the idea or representation, the feeling, the tendency or instinct, or all these elements simultaneously. Those who deny the autonomy of feeling and of the will and reduce them to a resultant of the environment will define it objectively, even when their definition has the characters of a scientific one, as happens in the positivist aesthetics of Taine, and departs from the metaphysical method, which regards the beautiful as an absolute entity, wholly independent of man, to which he adapts his aesthetic feelings.

[p. 374]Without failing to recognize this difficulty, we believe that the analysis we have made of aesthetic activity allows us to establish that what is essential in it is freedom, felt in harmony, conceived in artistic activity, and expressed in its works. This concept can serve as a criterion for explaining the objective characters attributed to beauty and for giving a definition that comprehends these characters; a definition applicable not only to static beauty, a beauty foreign to all disharmony, to all struggle, to all disordered movement, but also to dynamic beauty, the beauty of free action, which realizes an ideal once a painful struggle has been consummated, a struggle into which disharmony enters as a means. This double aspect will make it possible to reduce classical beauty and romantic beauty to a single criterion, explaining, through the development of freedom, aesthetic evolution in the history of art.

Grace has been regarded as the expression of that freedom in beautiful works. Grace encloses two elements and, for that very reason, two different ideas: the idea of freedom and that of the order within which that freedom is realized, ideas that correspond to the subjective and objective factors of the aesthetic consciousness. This is why Lemcke defines beauty, in general, as freedom in order, given in representation; understanding by freedom the capacity of a being to develop according to its own intimate essence, without suffering any disturbing or harmful influence from without.

The idea of freedom we acquire directly in the state of movement and indirectly in the state of repose; both states suggest, by induction, that idea through the effect of a negation: the negation of resistance.

The idea of order is obtained by means of an idealization of reality. The spirit rises to the idea of order by idealizing the state within which [p. 375]freedom develops, so as to attain a higher state that offers greater enjoyment and happiness through the unfolding of greater energy with the least resistance, combining new forms that constitute that higher state or order, which it qualifies as more perfect.

Order is a certain accord between the subject and the object, says Bergson. It is the spirit finding itself again in things. But the spirit, according to this philosopher, can direct itself in two opposite senses: either it follows its natural direction, and then it is progress under the form of tension, continuous creation, free activity; or it inverts that direction, and this inversion, carried to its term, leads to extension, to the necessary reciprocal determination of exteriorized elements, and finally to geometrical mechanism. Now, whether experience seems to us to adopt the first direction, or whether it is oriented in the sense of the second, in both cases we say that there is order, because in both processes the spirit is found; but the two orders are different: the second, which is the geometrical order, evokes ideas of inertia, of passivity, of automatism; the first is the vital order, the order of what is desired, the free order.

This free order of life and of the spirit in its creative evolution is the one contained in the idea of grace. This idea is formal; but the element of freedom is the real element that serves as its content, because it is inseparable from spirit and from life. It is the element that refers to activity, to movement, as much to biological energy as to the psychological energy that is concomitant with it.

The real is also the resistance that limits this activity and that thus determines, by reaction, that instinctive aspiration toward the better, that creative activity of the spirit. The imagination, in suppressing that resistance [p. 376]by means of a spontaneous or reflective abstraction, invents and creates an order or state within which it judges possible the disappearance or diminution of that real resistance, and, consequently, the expansion of energy, making happiness consist in this, and it sets out to realize that better state or limits itself to contemplating it with enjoyment.

In this consists the process of idealization. Man is born with an innate tendency toward movement, which engenders an aspiration to freedom without limit and the desire for the most complete systematization of the external world, in harmony with his needs and enjoyments. Since this desire is unrealizable in the reality of Nature, man amply satisfies that instinct for the better in the world of the imagination, creating forms that contain the greatest freedom through the most perfect systematization of the elements offered in perceived and felt reality. Thus is born the ideal, as has been seen, the expression of a freedom engendered by a harmony between the Spirit and Nature, and which is offered as the most perfect integration of the elements favorable to progress.

This idealization is practiced by a double mode at the same time: by the suppression or setting aside of the real factors that oppose the expansion of energy, and by the exaltation or alteration of the favorable positive factors, which determine what man considers as the characteristic of the ideal. It is a double process of integration and adaptation, on the one hand, and of disaggregation and rejection, on the other, which have as their governing interest the feeling of pleasure or of pain. What pleases in the object constitutes a positive factor; what displeases forms a negative factor.

The ideal is thus engendered by a psychological [p. 377]evolution, not as Bray understands it. According to this aesthetician, every excitation provokes a manifestation of energy; this is produced, naturally, on the side of least resistance and there realizes, naturally also, its maximum of effect; such is, according to Bray, in its simplest form, the general fact that translates the law of the minimum of expenditure. In the inorganic world, nothing conceals the simplicity of that phenomenon; but in organized beings, on the contrary, two special phenomena, irritability and, in certain cases, consciousness, singularly modify its aspect. Thanks to their irritability, organisms very often react in a manner disproportionate to the initial excitation and apparently spontaneous; hence, according to Bray, the illusion of a force that would be proper to them, of a tendency to action. From this point of view, it seems to Bray that the being sets itself, in each case, the solution of this problem: to economize effort while increasing the result.

When, later, consciousness appears with those two so energetic stimulants, the whole life of the being turns around them; effort, for it, is confounded with pain, the growth of its energies with pleasure, and the phenomenon once again changes its aspect: the tendency is converted into a need and an aspiration; everything thereafter proceeds as if, by its own movement, the being strove to avoid pain and to give birth to pleasure. To increase the sum of enjoyments, to diminish that of pains, such are for it the two possible forms of the better. In man, at least in the higher spheres of his mental, aesthetic, moral, scientific, and other activity, this aspiration, objectified by the procedure familiar to the metaphysical spirit, has received, according to Bray, the name of ideal. But the phenomenon is far from being proper to our species; in his conception, the search for the better is a [p. 378]fact as commonplace as it is general; it is found, conscious or not, in all organized beings.

This theory does not accord with the specific nature of psychological phenomena, which cannot be explained as an evolution of biological phenomena. The formation of the ideal, moreover, must be regarded as an invention, as an act of the creative activity of the imagination, which cannot be attributed to all organisms, nor even to the higher animals; for it requires a certain degree of development in the apperception of forms and in their free choice, a development not found in instinct.

The instincts, as Wundt says, may be regarded, in general, as impulsive acts that are born of sensations and of sensory feelings, and even the most complex ones may be explained as products of originally simple impulses, which are constantly differentiated in the course of numerous generations by means of individual habits that, little by little, are gathered, consolidated, and transmitted by heredity. In man himself, the tendency toward the better does not attain the conception of a true ideal at any period of his development. In children, the intentional movements of imitation appear only after a certain degree of development of the will; the impulse to play, a product of the imaginative activity, develops still later, and among savages imitation repeats the forms without creating anything that reveals a subjective progress.

The expression of the ideal coincides with the appearance of free art, which emancipates itself from the mere imitation of isolated representations; and, as Bray himself says, it is progressively purified and ennobled as the evolution of beauty itself is pursued, ever advancing beyond and surpassing it, offering to the spirit the clear or confused image of a higher beauty; for, however great the pleasure born of a [p. 379]new or revived perception, however exact the concordance of this with the whole of our psychic states, there subsists, almost infallibly, a deficiency, an imperfection, which awakens, by elimination, the idea of a more complete enjoyment. Moreover, as Bray also observes, once this appearance becomes fully conscious, reasoning must necessarily lead to supposing it without limit, because it is impossible to imagine a motive for it to be otherwise.

Consequently, the ideal is always a resultant, whatever its value; it represents the maximum of aesthetic perfection, of aesthetic order, that a man, an epoch, or a race is capable of conceiving; it is, as Bray qualifies it, the crowning or, more exactly, the becoming of evolution, and not the inaccessible end toward which it tends; hence the absolute of the metaphysicians is a pure hypothesis, born of the impossibility of assigning a limit to progress by means of a process analogous to that which leads to the mathematical infinite.

From this also arises the relativity of the ideal, founded on the relativity of the aesthetic feeling, which disposes the order of individual freedom, not as a teleological judgment, but as an aesthetic judgment, according to Kant. The accord of ideas among men afterward synthesizes those individual ideals, and thus collective ideals are formed, following the same process as in the formation of general ideas or of genera, from the least general up to the universal.

In his relation with nature, man can form his ideal, rising from the most rudimentary biological needs up to the higher feelings, in a prolonged progressive evolution; but in that labor he finds a powerful auxiliary in the environment [p. 380]that surrounds him, which offers him natural or artificial combinations that economize his efforts of idealization.

Man, at birth, not only has inherited tendencies that imprint a certain direction upon his energies; he also finds types already formed, models elaborated by man in all the spheres of his activity, which the childish spirit assimilates easily, owing to its adequate human organization and to the education it receives. In the generality of cases, the spirit accepts without reflection those models consecrated by a secular civilization as the expression of truth, of the good, or of beauty, joining to them a presentiment of happiness; but sometimes the human spirit, endowed with the independence or freedom of genius, conceives new forms, which it judges more perfect in relation to the happiness of man, and imposes those forms, whether by substituting them for the existing ones, or by merely modifying them, in harmony with the philosophical environment, or by creating new models that become associated with the accepted ones.

Habit joins with education in this labor of the formation of types. By virtue of habit we easily adapt to our spirit the forms or combinations with which we are familiar; we comprehend them without any effort; we feel them without disturbing the systematization of our emotions, and we associate, moreover, with those combinations agreeable ideas and feelings that facilitate and perfect their adaptation. In this way we form models that we regard as expressions of beauty, until the empire of other forms, overcoming the malaise produced by contrast and by the disaggregation of psychological elements rooted by habit, reorganizes the harmony of [p. 381]our soul—a result not obtained save after a profound change in ideas and feelings, one that operates very rarely in the history of humanity; for, as Lemcke says, from the total sum of the singular representations and of the corresponding sensations, of the judgments and of the volitions, reason forms the typical total concepts and the imagination engenders typical forms, the ideals or types being thus organizations of such complexity and unity that they express the entire soul and resist the changing influence of the environment.

By this the form and the richness of the ideal vary extraordinarily, by reason of the multiple personal and hereditary factors that enter into its composition and of the differences that exist in the means of imagination or of ideation from individual to individual, as Bray observes. At first it presents itself under the concrete form of a more or less clear image. At the lowest point, this is confounded almost with certain enjoyments of which the spirit has preserved a memory; it is incapable of imagining new or more elevated ones, but, as a general rule, Bray adds, it derives from more or less original combinations among the elements accumulated by memory, in which the spirit strives to condense the greatest sum of aesthetic qualities.

According to this psychologist, very often the ideal is reduced to a pure abstraction, to an idea; above the most beautiful things known, we conceive the mere possibility of greater beauties, without being in a state to imagine in what they might consist. But this mere possibility, although it is joined to the constant tendency toward progress, cannot constitute an ideal, a new type, a higher imagined order informed by the spirit, but only a logical conception, a geometrical order.

[p. 382]It may be said, as a consequence of what has been set forth up to here, that the element of order constitutes the characteristic of the ideal, and that, in order to appreciate that element, it is necessary to refer it to a determinate type, to a genus, within which the object is classified by means of experience. Lévêque is therefore right in considering the idea of genus, or of a certain typical order, to be included in the conception of the beautiful; only that the idea of genus is the idea of a form that needs to be penetrated with freedom in order to constitute a type of beauty.

Freedom, then, essentially characterizes the aesthetic order, but it also characterizes the moral order, although freedom plays a distinct role in each. In the moral or practical order, freedom is limited by an objective principle, superior to it and subordinating it, with an imperative, categorical character; whereas, in the aesthetic imaginative order, on the contrary, freedom tends toward the infinite; but, being unable to satisfy its aspiration in the reality of nature, it satisfies it in the free world of the imagination, thus realizing the beautiful, which is, in consequence, a conciliation of freedom and of nature, by means of an ideal order created by the imagination; a conciliation felt and not merely perceived, real and not formal, as Kant thought. This conciliation is, then, a demand of feeling, which finds beautiful every object in which freedom is expressed through grace, a grace that is born of an innate need of harmony with nature, as a means of attaining greater freedom, and that is resolved in the harmony and freedom of feeling, as in the harmony, freedom, and fecundity of the work of art.

Into this conciliation enter three elements: Na[p. 383]ture and Freedom as real elements, and the Order in which they are conciliated, as the formal or ideal element; the first refers to our sentimentality, the second to our will, and the third to our intelligence. Intelligence informs the ideal with the data of nature, chosen by feeling in its intuitive function and in the service of the free force. This conciliation, expressed through grace—which, in its turn, is an ordered and free form—realizes the beautiful, which may therefore be defined as the ideal and felt conciliation of nature and of the free force expressed through grace.

The mere ideal conciliation between freedom and nature, however vivid the image that realizes it, does not fully correspond to the nature of aesthetic pleasure—which excludes all feeling of displeasure. In bringing all our faculties into accord, the beautiful reconciles nature and spirit, says Séailles; but the conciliation merely imagined, and still more, imagined in individual form, awakens the vehement desire for its external realization; such is the property of every vividly felt image, as Ribot demonstrates; that disturbing desire, which characterizes the need to create and which grows during artistic activity, is opposed to the harmonic satisfaction of aesthetic pleasure, which is reestablished as soon as the sensible artistic forms represent that imagined conciliation which is called the ideal. For this reason, without the external forms realized by nature in an apparently free manner, or invented by the free and conscious energy of genius, there is no beauty.

It is deduced from this that there is no beauty save where there is freedom, whether this be expressed by a force in movement or simply by a harmony or equili[p. 384]brium that suggests the idea of freedom, whether it be a really free force, such as the spirit, or one that has the appearance of freedom, such as physical force under special conditions. It is also inferred that the beautiful is not the ideal order alone, as the idealists maintain, heirs of classical aesthetics, nor is it exclusively free life, as the realists affirm, enemies of the classical beauty of pure harmony; but rather free life within an ideal order forged by the imagination for freedom and realized in nature or in art.

The beautiful is not the pure ideal, even considered in the sense that Chaignet gives it. The conception of a wholly free force, escaping the restraints that impede its course and lower its flight; this creation of an individuality, if not all-powerful, at least independent and developing in a sensible form and in visible acts, will be the ideal of the beautiful; but it is not the pure ideal, which, in order to exist, requires only imagined forms not visible or sensible to the ear, nor is it the beautiful, for whose existence the free force expressed by a harmony suffices, as happens in the beauty of nature, which Chaignet does not admit, logically reducing, by his doctrine, the domains of aesthetics to the circle of the artistic representations of human freedom.

It is deduced, finally, from the analysis made, that the ideal, the type or order of the beautiful, is not innate, although man is born with tendencies or dispositions to follow a certain direction, the direction imprinted upon the tendencies of his progenitors. Order results from combinations imposed by the representations of the external world and afterward modified by the aspirations of life toward a free movement, without constraint, in the efforts of [p. 385]adaptation and assimilation that maintain and develop its expansive force. Education and habit direct that operation in the totality of cases.

From the isolated consideration of these two elements, the real and the ideal, which enter combined into the concept of the beautiful, have come the different definitions of this quality of objects.

Ancient philosophy, objective, founded on the idea of order, like the classical civilization incarnated in equilibrium, defined the beautiful by the perfect, the good, or the true—diverse manifestations of the absolute order—dwelling upon the analysis of the external characters of the things called beautiful. Modern philosophy, daughter of a civilization informed by the idea of free movement, has defined the beautiful by referring it directly or indirectly to the notion of freedom and analyzing the effects that the beautiful produces in the soul.

Ancient philosophy did not set aside the aesthetic feeling and even gave subjective definitions of the beautiful, just as modern philosophy of positivist tendency has given objective ones; but it is observed that the objective method predominates before Kant, and the more marked tendency of the subjective method after this philosopher, who consolidated the bases of aesthetic psychology with the laws of aesthetic taste.

### XXVIII. EL ARTE — XXVIII. ART

When one approaches, in a philosophical spirit, any question relating to art—however simple and plain it may present itself at first sight—it raises, as soon as one probes a little, a complication of questions that lift the spirit to the study of the gravest problems of life.

Being a synthesis of all the psychic energies, in its twofold function, subjective and objective, art penetrates every domain of theoretical and practical activity, and is nourished, in its turn, by all the productions that constitute the reality felt, perceived, and enacted.

Hence the indeterminacy of its limits, the vagueness of its definitions, the confusion of its nature with that of other realities related to it, the arbitrariness with which it is judged, the variety of doctrines that claim to discover its essence and to prescribe rules for its functions, and the diverse value at which it is appraised—from its condemnation to its exaltation as the principle of all truth and the source of all morality.

Its mere enunciation already poses questions that have not yet been able to be resolved, not even with the aid of the progress acquired by human thought.

What is Art? The art called beautiful—how is it derived from that generic concept? Artistic activity, in this last and restricted sense, is it a cognitive [p. 387]activity, or a practical activity, or the synthesis of the one and the other? And, in these cases respectively, in what does it differ from science, from morality, and from religion? And even once that distinction is made, is art a purely subjective activity, the exclusive fruit of individual freedom, or is it a slow assimilation of social activity, which imposes ideals upon the individual as the effect of the fatal action of the physical environment?

These questions are bound up with these others, no less grave and subject to debate: does the concept of the beautiful inform that of art, or does the contrary occur? And, in this latter case, what does the so-called beauty of nature signify, and what value has the principle of imitation on which the nature of art has been founded?

Even once these intricate aesthetic problems are resolved, others arise concerning the essence of the beautiful. Is the beautiful an objective reality? Is it, on the contrary, a purely subjective reality? And if the beautiful exists only because man exists, what is it that characterizes this aesthetic activity? What role do the nervous system, the intelligence, feeling, and freedom play in the conception of the beautiful? Can the aesthetic phenomenon be explained by only one of those factors of consciousness, or is the concurrence of them all necessary? Will that subjective synthesis suffice to explain the generality of the aesthetic phenomenon and the common criterion by which its realization in art is appraised?

This series of problems grows far more complicated still when one attempts to determine the nature of one of the arts. Then the diversity of its components creates new divergences. Into every work of art there enter as factors the artist, with all his psychic and physiological energies; the external environment in which he acts, and which offers him as materials ideas and emotions, models, [p. 388]schools and styles already formed; and, lastly, the technique of art—the body of procedures created and slowly perfected by the artistic milieu, and which the artist applies as the instrument of his imaginative activity.

Which of these factors constitutes the essence of art, distinguishing it from every other human function? Is art pure emotion, pure imitation, pure technique, or the synthesis of these three elements? What difference is there, then, between science and art? Can art, like science, establish laws or fixed norms for its activity, deriving them from other sciences; or is art, as the realization of absolute freedom, opposed to all law?

To this analysis and opposition of elements refers also the debate provoked by the study of the finality of art, considering separately the substance, content, or object of the artistic work; the form, by means of which that content or idea is expressed; and the style, or the relation freely established by art between substance and form. What is essential in art? Is it the idea expressed, which sets the spirit of the artist in communication with other men? Is that content a matter of indifference? Is it only the form that matters in art? And, within the choice of the diverse forms to which the content adapts itself, is it not the style that essentially constitutes the characteristic of the work?

This complication of problems becomes greater still in the case of music, by reason of the profundity of the emotion it produces, the immateriality of its form, the complexity of its elements, the vagueness of its images, and its special relation to the world of thought.

Aristotle, in explaining the nature of art in [p. 389]general, affirmed that art arises when, from a body of intuitions furnished by experience, one obtains a general knowledge applicable to all similar cases. This with respect to art as knowledge of things. As action, it would seem that experience is not different from art. Experience is knowledge of particular facts, while art, on the contrary, is knowledge of what is general; but every action or productive process, observes Aristotle, must be carried out with particular things; and although he who knows art knows the causes, the empirical man does not know them. Aristotle thus establishes the distinction that exists between experience and art, the latter being identified with the rule formed from experience and applied to action. Art is inferior to experience as action, as practice; but it is superior in the scientific order: the man of experience knows only the fact, the what; but the man of art knows the why; he can teach, which constitutes the character of science: wisdom.

As is known, according to Aristotle there are three possible modes of development of an intelligent being: to know, to act, and to produce—science, practice, and art; the science of speculation, or speculative science; the science of action, or practical science; and the science of production—which constitute the threefold division of philosophy. The concept of art, here, is opposed to that of science; the poetic and practical sciences have for their object that which may be, different from that which is, and which, consequently, depends more or less upon the will; the speculative sciences have for their object that which is necessary, at least in its principles, and which the will cannot change. Nor is art to be confounded with practice; for it has its end in a thing placed outside the agent, and in which the latter must realize his will: the end of practice lies in the willing itself and in the inner action of the agent.

[p. 390]For this reason Aristotle distinguishes art from the theoretical function and from the practical function of thought, placing it in the productive function and thus clarifying the foregoing concepts of art. He distinguishes it also from nature. For Aristotle, nature is not, like art, an independent activity exercised indifferently upon every kind of matter. Nature, like art, directs itself to its end without being constrained; but nature is a concrete activity, a form in a matter. Its end is not, like that of art, a conception, an idea, an arbitrary type that exists only in thought and that the will realizes.

Developing this Aristotelian conception, art has been defined as everything that is distinguished from nature. Art and nature are the two most comprehensive genera formed by the human intelligence; but the one as much as the other is indeterminate and variable. Thus it is common to designate as nature all that exists independently of study and labor, or, in other terms, the phenomena just as we find them; whereas we designate as art all that we do not find but produce with invention and effort. It is added to these designations that they are not used, in every case, in a constant manner, for at times an arbitrary line is drawn in the action of individuals and societies, and so it is said that such a law, such a practice, such an industry is natural or artificial, according as it appears to arise spontaneously or to require reflection and effort. Finally, there is no lack of cases in which art is included within nature, which in this case embraces the phenomena of the universe, considering them as natural. It is affirmed, lastly, that in an absolute manner and by opposition to nature, art embraces all that, in order to exist, has required the intervention of the hand, of the [p. 391]spirit, and of the will of man; but this expression has been reserved, above all, for the manifestations of human activity in the order of feeling and of imagination, art being understood essentially as the five great arts.

This lack of precision, in which science, nature, and art are at once distinguished and confounded, has given rise to inexact and deficient definitions of art, and to the inclusion, within the artistic discipline, of teachings that are foreign to it.

Art has been defined by Aristotle as the faculty of producing works that have their principle of activity not in themselves but in him who produces them. The object of art is to produce a work that subsists after the act which has produced it. In art, the principle is foreign to nature; it resides in the artist; in the works of nature the contrary is the case. The work of art is reasoned and reflective; that of nature is instinctive. Art is, then, the faculty of realizing the true with reflection. This definition comprehended all the arts—the manual or useful ones, like the rest of the arts; the servile arts, like the liberal. The sciences themselves were comprehended within them, such as Logic, Rhetoric, and Grammar.

By this same criterion art has been defined as every regulated operation by means of which organized beings pursue an end known to them, together with the rules and the result of that same operation. The idea of art thus implies a body of procedures, a method for obtaining determinate results. For this reason Littré could define it as the manner of doing something according to a certain method, and Joubert as skill reduced to theory. Hence there has been talk of the culinary art, the surgical art, the agricultural art, as of the pictorial art and the dramatic art.

[p. 392]On the other hand, although distinct from science, there has been attributed to each science an art, which may be called instrumental and which refers to the methods for arriving at the results proper to it. By this same extension the name of art has been applied to every body of rules that govern a determinate class of knowledge for its study; save that science consists in knowledge and art in action; science teaches what one must do in order to know, and art what one must know in order to do.

This great diversity with which the concept of art has been considered—derived from ignorance of aesthetic psychology, in which the true foundation of artistic activity is found—gave rise to numerous classifications of art that did nothing to fix its nature.

Art is, above all, an inner work of the will, which aspires to objectify itself in the most intense form—which is also the freest and the most fecund and creative. But since the will, blind and unreflecting, cannot satisfy that aspiration, it employs the intelligence in its service, which offers it, together with the representations of reality, the order or system of relations that unite those representations or images and form the world of personal activity. The labor of art consists in combining those images in such a way that they constitute an ideal order, superior to reality, as a means of free existence. To realize the greatest sum of freedom in an imagined order—such is the value of an artistic ideal.

This finality of art imposes the necessity of establishing a twofold accord: first, among the representations that serve the feeling of freedom; and afterward, between the system of representations, or order, and the free [p. 393]activity of the artist—accords that are realized through the unity of the representations and their expressive power. The disaccord of the representations would produce the ineptitude of the medium destined to realize the idea conceived by the artist; the disaccord of the representations with the artist's activity would destroy his freedom, inasmuch as the expressive power of the representations arises only from their capacity to translate the expansive force of the spirit that conceives them. Hence it is that the artistic function consists, precisely, in the power to choose representations by the criterion of feeling, which is not subject to the logical laws of the intelligence and which possesses an innate character.

This power to choose representations expressive of an ideal presents itself as an instinct susceptible of education, and reveals an interior freedom that has been compared to divine grace, and whose movement bears the seal of an originality opposed to the life of habit—the expression of a true autonomy. For this reason Gaultier has defined the work of art as the manifestation of a spontaneous activity that unfolds of itself; pure of every extrinsic end and effortless, for pure pleasure and as a play.

According to Gaultier, art is not, however, to be confused with play; nor does it proceed from imitation; art has its own beauty, independent of the things it takes as its themes; it is emotion par excellence; what constitutes its value is the personality of the artist, the style; freedom is its law; originality its rule; the aesthetic ideal is the effective ideal. The work of art is the ineffable synthesis of the subject and the object, of the person of the artist with living beings and with the things that move him. Art is nature interpreted by [p. 394]man, penetrated and expressed by him; it is the aesthetic emotion solidified and crystallized in linear, colored, and sonorous forms. Its efficacy depends on its power of communicating that emotion to others.

This same subjectivist and idealist conception is found in Udine. For this critic, who leans upon the aesthetics of Griveau, rhythm, which engenders the aesthetic emotion, is the essence of art. The true beauty of the work of art is the spontaneity of feeling, joined to the precision of the synthesis. Virtuosity, or skill of execution, is its worst enemy. What is essential in art is not its object, substance, or content, nor its form, but its style. What makes a work of art interesting is its property of provoking, in certain individuals, human emotions of the same order as those felt by its creator. Art might thus be defined as the transmission of any emotion whatever, through the medium of a stylized natural rhythm, without there being anything fixed or absolute in this transmission. The latter depends less upon the work itself than upon a physiological concordance, a kind of resonance between each creator and the individuals attuned to the same pitch as he.

Reacting against this subjective conception of art, which assigns it as its sole end the expression and communication of the aesthetic feeling, Boutroux attributes to art, as principal ends among the many that pertain to it, the following: first, to eternize the forms that interest it; second, to create an ideal world that may help to forget the miseries of the real world; third, to express that which admits of no adequate expression or translation, and thus to make souls communicate in what they have of the intimate and the profound; and fourth, to offer living representations of beauty. In these diverse ends, art seems to submit to a twofold law: first, it must at once [p. 395]conserve and innovate; second, it must gather and combine individuality and universality.

These ends are clearly subordinated to the second of those indicated; that is, to the creation of an ideal world—not with the object that Boutroux indicates, which is the same that Schopenhauer assigns to art, but with that of conquering a greater happiness; not only through the contemplation of that ideal world, but through the communication of that world to others. All the ends of art are comprehended in that one, for it is the forms of that world that art is concerned to eternize, that it aspires to communicate to others through its own elements, and that comprise living representations of beauty.

It is the creation of the ideal world, consequently, that constitutes the nature of art. Its expression and communication determine its efficacy. From the theoretical point of view, art fulfills its whole end with that creation; from the practical point of view, art needs to realize itself in the world of matter and to communicate itself to other men in order to engender an artistic solidarity.

For those who characterize the artistic phenomenon by considering it as cognitive only, that external realization is foreign to art. According to Croce, artistic activity is purely theoretical; practical activity is economic or moral. The artistic phenomenon is identified with intuition; but intuition and expression are the same thing; the spirit does not proceed by intuition, but by doing, forming, expressing. The beautiful is the expression that succeeds; or rather, it is expression alone; for the expression that does not attain its object is not expression. The ugly is the expression that has failed.

[p. 396]But this expression is limited to the pure image. Croce rejects external expression as belonging to the practical order, to technique; he denies that the physical phenomenon penetrates the spirit as image; expression, considered in itself, is pure technical activity and, as such, precedes practice and the intellectual knowledge that illuminates practice; expression lacks means, because it has no end; it knows something by intuition, but it does not will, and therefore cannot be divided into means and end; the beautiful, consequently, has no physical existence. It is pure internal form, without content separated from it. It is emotion transformed, but without external expression.

But is it possible in art to separate theoretical activity from practical activity? Croce himself denies the absolute separation between the theoretical and the practical, between the work of the intelligence and that of the will; and if knowing entails willing, that knowledge, in which the fantastic intuition and the expression are identified, cannot escape the function of the will, which, as pure activity, is already comprehended in all knowledge. To claim that the aesthetic phenomenon is pure image and nothing more than image is to reduce all art to Poetry, which, properly, lacks physical form, and is even to exclude Music and the Lyric, in which the intuitions have their immediate expression in sounds. The creation of the ideal world must, then, be integrated with the choice and application of the forms, colors, and sounds that are destined to serve it as exteriorization.

But that ideal world, which embraces the existent as well as the possible, the present as well as the past and the future—the whole of reality—how is it created? in what does it consist? Is the ideal a purely intellectual formation? Is it the [p. 397]opposite of the real perceived by the senses? Is it an imaginative formation, in which the intelligence associates present and remembered images, without the intervention of the will and of feeling; or is it a free synthesis wrought by feeling upon the images associated by the intelligence? Contemporary psychology gives answer to these interrogations, making of the ideal a product of the total activity of the aesthetic consciousness, in which the function of freedom predominates.

Freedom is what is essential in art, as much in that content as in its expressive forms, as much in the work as in the activity of its creator. We may, then, define art as the expression of the ideal conceived by intuition and formed by the elective action of autonomous feeling. This definition does not differ, at bottom, from the one that regards art as the graceful expression of the conciliation between nature and freedom—a conciliation imagined by the artist and rendered by means of adequate or expressive forms. That conciliation is the ideal of equilibrium or of movement, which come to be incompatible, growing accentuated in a certain period of the evolution of life, but which complete each other in an embryonic state, as Bergson says; in that global state of life in which the intelligence has not yet imposed fixed norms upon psychic activity.

In this conciliation nature is subordinated to freedom, which is the essence of art. The work of art, Fechner has said, is a free manifestation of the spirit; and even though not every manifestation of the spirit is a work of art, as Riemann observes, Fechner has designated very well, in his conception, by those words, two of the essential qualities of every true work of art. The notion of freedom, as well as that of [p. 398]homogeneity, which the word manifestation encloses, are distinctive characters of art.

But this conciliation of nature and freedom, in which the élan vital of consciousness triumphs—does it signify a static conception of art? So it might be inferred from the limited concept that Bergson has of art in his study on spiritual energy. If in all domains, he says, the triumph of life is creation, must we not suppose that human life has its reason for being in a creation that may, unlike that of the artist and of the sage, be pursued at every moment in all men—in the creation of oneself by oneself, in the aggrandizement of the personality by an effort that draws much from little, something from nothing, and adds without cease to what there was of richness in the world? To that interrogation Bergson responds by exalting moral value, as a dynamic form superior to the artistic form of life, as a definitive point of view that the artist's vision does not attain.

In his conception, the richness and originality of the aesthetic forms symbolize very well an expansion of life; but in this expansion, in which beauty signifies power, life also manifests an arrest of its élan and a momentary impotence to press farther. Superior is the point of view of the moralist; for only in man, and above all in the best of us, does the vital movement pursue itself without obstacle, casting through this work of art that is the human body—and that it has created in its passage—the indefinitely creative current of the moral life. Creator par excellence is he whose intense action is capable of intensifying also the action of other men, and of kindling, generous, foci of generosity. The great men of goodness, and more particularly those whose inventive and simple heroism has [p. 399]opened new paths to virtue, are revealers of metaphysical truth; they have reached the culminating point of evolution and are nearest to the origins, making sensible to our eyes the impulse that comes from the depths.

Bergson, who has declared that art is nothing but freedom and that every free action is a true creation—and consequently a true work of art—could not deny that the moral ideal, created by the perfect man of goodness, likewise accomplishes a work of art; for wherever there is creation, whenever the imagination invents an ideal, a work of art is created, save that instead of choosing forms, colors, and sounds to express that infinite aspiration toward the free life, one chooses actions, elements more perfect and more expressive of that aspiration. The moralist is, consequently, the greatest artist, when he opens new paths to virtue, discovering higher ideals to illumine and guide humanity.

But moral ideals also crystallize, and then they become empty dogmas, with their norms and their imperatives that eliminate freedom and suppress the élan of the spirit. Religion or science seizes upon them and introduces into their construction a more or less rigorous determinism. The works of art that embody an ideal, by contrast, do not lose but increase their educative influence; freedom animates them always, for only in art do the norms and their imperatives lose their coercive force. Aesthetic value thus comprehends moral value and surpasses it.

In this direct expression of the freedom of the spirit, reflected in the work of art and beautifying even what lacks aesthetic value in reality, consists the [p. 400]superiority of artistic beauty over natural beauty, which offers only appearances of the freedom felt and embodied in art. This same thing explains why a proper aesthetic value is denied to Nature, and why it is maintained that the soul, in being moved by the spectacles of reality, transmits to the latter the feelings that art has created through the joyous contemplation of its works. Those who think thus do not reflect that, in the order of the beautiful, the mere appearance of freedom suffices for aesthetic enjoyment to be produced, even when the intelligence has the conviction that the reality perceived is subject to the most rigorous determinism. To such a degree is freedom essential to the nature of the beautiful.

If the soul's aspiration to a greater sum of freedom creates the ideal world and its artistic exteriorization, the aesthetic ideal is one by its origin and its end and by the psychic energy that conceives it and realizes it in its expansion. Art, consequently, is one, and its diversity derives from the modalities in which its finality presents itself and from the means by which the latter satisfies the aesthetic consciousness. Hence the more or less restricted classifications by which men attempt to enclose, within logical categories, that which surpasses thought in artistic expression—that which, by the infinite and inexhaustible variety of its nuances, refuses the rigor of all classification.

This continuity in the manifestations of art is opposed to the static conception, which supposes the crystallization of its moments of development, and it gives an idea of its dynamic unity, in which the separations are not radical, as though they were degrees or types with unmistakable limits. Art penetrates and diffuses itself throughout all reality, availing itself of the creative imagination, whose intuitive and synthetic [p. 401]activity permits it to discover the essences of objects, to invent forms as new substances, to arouse fundamental ideas and unknown combinations, to provoke superior actions by a movement of disinterested sympathy, to resuscitate and embellish extinguished worlds, as to prophesy worlds to come, to see into the depths of impenetrable consciousnesses, and to create psychological and moral types not furnished by experience.

Art invades everything, in order to idealize it, to embellish it, to reveal the profound qualities that determine the essence of realities, to simplify complicated expressions by realizing the cardinal functions, to unite the ease and efficacy of action, to bring to light models or guides that may preside over civilization. Nothing escapes its dominion: science, industry, philosophy, morality, religion, law, politics, the solidary work of peace as well as the destructive work of war, receive the action of the creative imagination, which produces artistic works that widen, to infinity, the already very ample radius of the arts called beautiful in the narrow sense. Nature herself practices a work of art in her creations, which it is not possible to explain without the intervention of that élan vital on which Bergson founds his grandiose cosmic conception. Schelling was right to make of art the expression of the absolute, which may be symbolized by that creation of the universe, drawn from the substance of the creator.

This universality of art is not opposed to the profundity of the artistic work. Genius puts its whole soul into its creation; it sacrifices neither the details to the unity, nor the latter to the minute forms of its work; the interpenetration of the parts and the whole, of the ends and the means, is such that there is produced the most [p. 402]perfect individuality in the ensemble, as is realized in the human person ideally conceived. But, in reflecting his whole soul in his work, the artist impresses upon it that seal of universality which every living type reveals, however great its originality. It is proper to art to reconcile those two phases of the perfect life which, logically considered, are irreconcilable.

It is understood, after this, how destitute of importance are the theories that dispute the finality of art, restricting its limit to the theory of art for art's sake and to that of pedagogical or didactic art; for if by the finality of art one understands the creator's aspiration to the construction and realization of an ideal that may express his longings for freedom, that finality surpasses the ambit of both theories; that aspiration to the ideal is aspiration to the universal, whose nature depends neither on the narrow limit that technique imposes upon artistic expression, nor on the effects that the work may produce in the education of man. That aspiration might be qualified as absolute, for in the spontaneity of artistic creation nothing governs or determines it. The work is born because its creator so wills it, and nothing more. There may be associated with that act of free will any interests whatever, but none of them will be able to explain the aesthetic value of the work or to fix itself beforehand as a special finality.

The work is beautiful because it expresses the free and communicative expansion of the spirit, and nothing more. Consequently, to suppose that the finality of art is subordinated to pleasure, or to utility, or to a value opposed or foreign to freedom—which is its own value—is to make of beauty a pure form, indifferent to its content or destined to serve as a means to the realization of values that are not aesthetic; an assertion that can be sustained only upon an intellectualist concept of the beautiful, which converts aesthetic [p. 403]knowledge into logical knowledge. To suppose, on the other hand, that the entire content of a superior aesthetic feeling, produced by a work of art, is a logical, moral, or religious feeling, is to reduce art to a means of expression of those feelings—which may serve to diversify the aesthetic content, but not to substitute for it. Content, like form, in art responds, essentially, to that need of the creative spirit to reflect its aspiration toward an ideal of freedom.

## PARTE SEGUNDA · CUESTIONES ESTÉTICAS — PART TWO · AESTHETIC QUESTIONS

### I. EL VALOR ESTÉTICO — I. AESTHETIC VALUE

[p. 406] The historical development of aesthetic ideas shows that the fundamental concepts relating to the aesthetic phenomenon, in its twofold subjective and objective aspect—of feeling and of work of art—have not had an intimate relation such that a system could be established among them like that of the other philosophical sciences.

The notions of the beautiful and of art were primitively independent, and if that independence has disappeared in the form of concepts derived from different principles, it has always subsisted in the form of a reciprocal indetermination and in the maintenance of the naturalist theory, which persists in attributing to the imitative function the nature of aesthetic art. The question of the primacy of art—from which one claims to deduce aesthetic feeling, in opposition to the artistic tendency or to innate aesthetic feeling—involves that separation of the two fundamental concepts, which respectively engender the sociological and psychological directions adopted in contemporary aesthetics and which begin with Kant. Almost all agree in recognizing in the aesthetic phenomenon this twofold subjective and objective aspect. But some seek in the analysis of consciousness the explanation of contemplative and creative aesthetic activity, making of the work of [p. 407] art an expression more or less closely bound to that activity, but subordinate to it; and others give little importance to that analysis, claiming to find in the physiological or psychological function, determined by the external milieu, the exclusive cause of aesthetic feeling. For some, there exists a pure beauty, created by innate aesthetic feeling, which differs radically from the artistic beauty produced by biological exigencies or by intellectual values; for others, art, in its evolution—from its practical finality to its purely contemplative form—comes to create that aesthetic feeling which allows us to appreciate pure beauty in art as in nature.

As a consequence of this double direction, aesthetics has tended to become a philosophy of spirit or a sociology, a pure psychology or a pure science, confounding itself with metaphysics, with logic, with morality, or else with physiology and with technique, which aspire to establish invariable scientific norms.

This disagreement comes from the influence exerted by the philosophical and scientific movement upon the ideas of value. Aesthetics, like morality, like the other sciences of norms, has followed the fortunes of the reigning philosophical ideas. Intellectualism, maintained throughout the course of those ideas up to contemporary times, has made of aesthetics a metaphysics of the knowledge of the beautiful or a science of aesthetic phenomena, making both revolve around the idea of order—an idea essential to the logical or noetic problem. Aesthetics acquired its independence as a propaedeutic of sensory knowledge, as a logic of that knowledge. Its tendency was to become confounded with logic, save for the rare atte[p. 408]mpts to include it in morality when the idea of freedom insinuated itself as the guiding idea.

In aesthetics, as in the whole of philosophy, there is observed, for this reason, the predominance of the idea of order—although it is understood, or rather is known by intuition, that the aesthetic order is not a logical order, wholly destitute of freedom, but a harmony in which the freedom of the spirit throbs beneath the images that express artistic beauty. This intuition, however, has not influenced the abstract concept of the aesthetic phenomenon except in recent times, when psychology ceased to be a metaphysics or a pure science subordinate to physiology, to become a positive philosophy of the spirit, a philosophical science of psychic phenomena regarded as phenomena sui generis.

Only then has the whole importance of the imaginative function in the constitution of the aesthetic phenomenon been understood. The imagination having been eliminated from science as a factor hostile to order, opposed to reason—reason being regarded as the essential element of philosophical and scientific activity—it was logical that aesthetics should not study that function with the aim of finding in it the explanation of aesthetic value, and that the influence of the creative power in artistic activity should be kept as something mysterious, or that there should be attributed to aesthetic pleasure a distinctive character setting it apart from mere sensory pleasure, founded solely on the logical value of the idea joined to that pleasure.

The intellectualist concept of the imagination—even after its false disordering power was corrected, even raised to the heights of metaphysics—always had the fragmentary character of a cognitive function [p. 409] more or less important, but different from the other faculties of the same kind. The limit of its activity has been extended only in recent times, so as to embrace completely the whole psychic activity and to reflect its influence into domains from which it had been systematically excluded. The nature of the spirit being affirmed as essentially a creative power, the nature of the imagination was implicitly affirmed as that power, establishing an equivalence between spirit and imagination and, consequently, between integral psychic activity and aesthetic activity. Hence a theory of the imagination may lead to a true aesthetic theory, which, at bottom, would be a true immanent philosophical theory, destined to give an explanation of the whole of reality, as metaphysics aspires to do.

If that theory has not been clearly formulated, after the attempt of Frohschammer, this has depended on two causes: the disdain for metaphysical studies, accentuated by modern and contemporary science, and the introduction of the pseudo-scientific hypothesis of the unconscious, which has made it possible to obtain, conveniently, all the solutions desired by the spirit and not attained even by theological metaphysics—which is more rational than that hypothesis.

Nevertheless, it may be said that this theory is found in germ in the Bergsonian ideas on memory and creative evolution, which rest on an empirical foundation, on the psychological analysis of activity. For Bergson, as for contemporary psychology, memory does not repeat the perceived image, as the intellectualists believed; it does not reproduce in consciousness the immortal images deposited in the unconscious, as Herbart affirmed, but re-creates the ima[p. 410]ge, converting into actual and real the virtual energy of the forgotten image. This creative function is pure imagination; it is the simplest and most elementary form of imagination, into which enters the whole activity of the spirit; it is the entire spirit that evokes that remembered image. Spirit and imagination are equivalent in this primordial function, without which neither the inner life nor the outer life could be explained; for if the spirit were not capable of creating, from the very first instants of its action, it would not be distinguished from inert matter: life would not be change, would not be progress, would not be life.

This shows why vitalism necessarily becomes a panpsychism, why the philosophy of life is a derivation of the philosophy of spirit, and why invention—incessant creation, more or less durable and multiform—extends the domain of art toward confines that artistic beauty, restricted to the sphere of the old aesthetics, cannot reach.

The aesthetic concept being extended to all invention, the artistic domain must extend to every work in which the imagination produces something new, eliminating only what repeats itself, what repeated movement transforms into habit and replaces consciousness by an unconscious movement, destitute of freedom. The aesthetic concept thus extended, its positive form embraces all living reality, in which creation reveals itself and in which it supposes a freedom more or less intense and disinterested; and its negative form, all that is mechanical, all that is inert, all that does not admit the hypothesis of free creation. The aesthetic concept takes, in the first sense, the expression of Art, and in the second, of Science, and in the comprehension of both [p. 411] it formulates a universal, metaphysical explanation, in which, to the principle of freedom, or aesthetic principle, is opposed the principle of order, or scientific principle.

The aesthetics of the future must set out from these bases in order to reach a more satisfactory solution of its fundamental problems. Without a study of the creative imagination, in which interior freedom is presented as the essential character, aesthetic psychology cannot arrive at conclusions solid enough to explain the domain of art in all the spheres of life and to comprehend the intervention of the fantastic in the artistic emotion of the beautiful and in the production of works of fine art that presuppose inspiration. And since the creative imagination is inexplicable without the freedom of the spirit, the aesthetic postulate is that freedom, and aesthetic value is that same freedom.

The aesthetics of the future must build upon those bases, in order to be a philosophy of spirit and not an empty metaphysics, as it was before the positivist period, nor a science of phenomena, as it has claimed to be since. Aesthetics, thus regarded as a new immanent and transcendent metaphysics, will not be able to dispense with the data that psychological experience offers it concerning the creative power of the imagination, nor to withdraw itself from the metaphysical problems to which the hypothesis of creative activity in nature and in the divine Being—the latter superior to experience—leads. It will have to answer the questions about the imagination in animate nature and in God, taking as its point of departure the human imagination, and to resolve this prior and fundamental question relating to the necessity of the image for the exercise of the creative function, and to the role it plays in animal psychic life; for, if to imagine is to construct with images, as [p. 412] psychology has maintained, an activity of such a kind is inconceivable in beings without senses, which are the instruments of perception.

That problem being posed, aesthetics could not resolve it positively, but it could affirm that it does not repel reason to conceive a power that creates, by force of its expansion alone, without predetermined finality or by virtue of an immanent finality, without need of the instruments of the senses—which do not engender that power, but are its consequence, the immediate practical result of the creative activity exercised under conditions of resistance and of adaptation to the milieu. That hypothesis is not contradictory, and, far from it, it might find a certain experience in creation by types, as in the Platonic, or by internal contemplation, as in the Aristotelian, or by the mystical objectification that eliminates every image.

The formation of the senses was, no doubt, a limit upon the intensity of that power; but, at the same time, it was, by the infinite diversity of its modes, a boundless extension in the power to imagine. This power did not lose its creative nature through the intervention of the image; it preserved it, and one may say that it organized it in harmony with the nature within which it exercises its action.

To imagine is thus to create, even when creation is effected by means of abstract ideas or philosophical intuitions, which are not images; it is to exercise a free activity that produces new elements and new combinations of already existing elements. Its essential character is not the image, but freedom. For this reason, imagination is equivalent to spirit.

But, in man himself and in the animal, which cannot emancipate itself from images, that creative force [p. 413] has very diverse limits and aspects, corresponding to the degree of concentration of the spirit, on the one hand, and to that of expansion, on the other. In the animal, the concentration that produces the self-consciousness of the ego does not exist; psychic life is pure objectification; in man, on the contrary, that concentration is gradual and more or less profound, just as the expansion is more or less intense and more or less penetrated with objectivity. Instinct and reason, which pursue different practical ends—limiting freedom to the point of annulling it, or extending it to the point of making it superior to every force of objectification—create varieties as diverse as there are animate beings in the world, from the microbe to the genius.

Given this infinite variety of works produced by the psyche in its imaginative activity, one ought to conclude that all those works enter the domain of aesthetics, if aesthetics comprises the whole extent of that activity. It is not so, however. Philosophy and science have restricted that limit, without fixing it exactly, setting apart in a special group, under the denomination of beautiful or ugly works, the creations produced by determinate senses and foreign to all practical finality, giving them the title of works of art and characterizing their aesthetic value by the double criterion of the specific pleasure of the beautiful and of the external characters of those works, which have been reduced to a likewise specific quality of order, called harmony.

But this double criterion has been derived from the inexact and deficient experience of aesthetic activity, under its double aspect—contemplative and active—the very aspects that have been analyzed, now independently of the imaginative function, now with an intellectualist criterion of that function, or else bringing it in as a complementary and collateral factor; and in almost all th[p. 414]ese cases, leaving aside freedom, which philosophy has almost always studied as the moral element of action, or has eliminated as an illusion.

Hence the mistaken or deficient concept of the aesthetic phenomenon, in which there has always been maintained the traditional factor of harmony; that is, the intellectual factor of order, leaving aside the volitional factor, regarded as essential in the psyche by contemporary psychology.

Bergson has been the first philosopher to place freedom in the essence of aesthetic art, after having made of freedom the essence of the spirit, and of the spirit an incessant creative activity.
