For this reason his philosophy is a philosophy of spirit, an aesthetics, in the broad acceptation we have given to this word. Freedom is the generator of art, and every soul would be an artist if nature did not constrain it. «If reality,» says Bergson, «impressed our senses and our consciousness directly; if we could enter into immediate communication with things and with ourselves, I quite believe that art would be useless, or, rather, that we should all be artists, because our soul would then vibrate continually in unison with nature».

It is not so, because the practical or useful ends of life are opposed to that freedom, threatening it constantly with habit, which suppresses creation and condemns the spirit to the mechanical repetition of the inert mass and to pure objectification. If direct intuition of reality in itself were always possible; if the spirit could always act without the resistance that inertia offers it and without the instruments that channel its energy, limiting it toward habit, every action would be free, and the free act would constitute a work of art, capable of producing, in being realized, the double satisfaction of the [p. 415] aesthetic feeling, which delights in the contemplation of the ideal, and of the moral feeling, which delights in the realization of that ideal consecrated by history.

The ever-free soul would always be an artist; because the imagination—that power of creating, of inventing the better, without which life is inconceivable as evolution and progress, and whose true activity is exercised by means of intuition, which is its proper form—would spontaneously engender artistic forms, in which the dynamism of life, in its aspiration toward a freer organism, would be reflected in forms superior to those of imperfect and deficient reality, in which the inert and the living are confounded like coercion and freedom.

Nor is it possible here to affirm from experience whether every psyche acts guided by that conception of the better, which the imagination discovers as the spontaneous product of its own virtuality. The explanation of instinct in Bergson's philosophy, and that of vital evolution in view of an immanent end, which the biologists Driesch and Reinke adopt, agree in admitting that guiding finality in nature, which would permit attributing to it an unconscious artistic activity, author of all those marvels that life displays and whose beauties some aestheticians seek to reduce to mere appearances, similar to the creations of the human artist, which would be the real and sole object of our aesthetic admiration. The equations between spirit and freedom, between imagination and freedom, between art and freedom being admitted, it is not possible to deny the spirit that imaginative and artistic function, extensive to pure life, if it is regarded as equally creative—the profound variations offered by conscious and unconscious, reflective and spontaneous activity being sought in the formation of consciousness and its degrees, activities which asso[p. 416]ciate themselves, nonetheless, in the human psyche as thought and instinct.

It belongs to metaphysics to discuss those hypotheses that transcend human experience; but within the latter, psychological analysis finds that creative power of the imagination, which does not consist only in associating freely and according to a determinate plan the perceived images or ideas, as Wundt thinks, but which penetrates, discovers, invents, divines reality in itself, through its infinite forms, so as to intuit what there is in it of the essential and to give to that essence a concrete or abstract form, according as the will ascertains what constitutes the most perfect individuality or the most complete universality. That free and creative power is the base of artistic conception and of aesthetic emotion, of which it is at once the cause and the effect. It is not only the postulate of aesthetic philosophy, but its empirical foundation; for not only is the conception of an ideal, engendered by the imagination, indispensable in order to comprehend the aesthetic phenomenon in its total evolution, but it is necessary to set out from the analysis of the creative imagination in order to explain the very formation of that ideal. Aesthetic experience, like all scientific experience, presupposes a guiding norm, a criterion formed upon the quality of the phenomenon that is the matter of observation, and it is a vicious circle to presuppose that guiding conception—which allows the aesthetic phenomena to be distinguished and separated—only to seek afterward, by means of a pure empiricism, that norm already established beforehand as a valuation of the aesthetic consciousness. That defect of method disappears if it is affirmed that psychic activity is creative; that that creative activity is the imagination, which informs the ideal by an intuitive process proper to its nature, by which it pene[p. 417]trates reality and discovers the better; that that function is the one that realizes art, and that it is essentially freedom, because creation and freedom are equivalent.

Freedom, as the necessary mode of creative activity, is thus not a mere ideal, a metaphysical postulate of the moral and aesthetic order, as Schiller conceived it in his aesthetic system, but a reality subject to psychological and external observation, which has, like every reality, diverse forms and moments in its evolution. That free and creative activity, which has a universal significance as fact and as idea, comprises aesthetic activity, which is called the emotion of the beautiful in its subjective aspect, and the work of art in its objective expression. To establish it as a base is to prepare the solution of the problems that Lalo regards as preliminary in his Introduction to Aesthetics; because the method of investigation, the nature of aesthetic value, of the valuing aesthetic consciousness and its norm, are founded on the study of the creative imagination, whose nature was not understood until recent times—giving rise, through the errors of its concept, to the fruitless attempts of the intellectualist and sentimentalist aesthetics, which have divided between them the field of artistic criticism without attaining a philosophical organization that answers satisfactorily those fundamental problems.

To Ribot is owed the most profound study of the imagination, after that of Frohschammer, who made of it a metaphysics. For that great psychologist, as has been said before<sup>1</sup>, the imagination is, in the intellectual order, the equivalent of the will in the order of movements. The imagination, like the will, tends to exteriorize itself, to affirm itself in a work that exists, not only for the creator but for the whole wor[p. 418]ld. The imagination reproduces the forms, keeps them vivid, dissociates them, associates them, combines and affirms them in a determinate order, imprinting on them an ideal unity; it awakens the tendency to objectification and realizes it. In the creative imagination there exist, therefore, several factors.

<sup>1</sup> See the chapter on the artist.

Ribot considers three: the intellectual factor—negative, of dissociation, and positive, of association; the emotional or affective factor, which comprises the motor element, impulsive or inhibitory; and the unconscious factor of inspiration, which, considered under its scientific aspect, has, for Ribot, two essential characters: its instantaneity and its impersonality, the latter being more profound than the former. Inspiration, says Ribot, reveals a power superior to the conscious individual, foreign to him though acting through him, and which can be reduced to intellectual or affective processes whose preparatory work is unknown—being an unconscious work—and which penetrates the domain of consciousness suddenly, after that preparation. Those three factors do not function in isolation and by their own virtue in the elaboration of the work, but converge toward one and the same end: invention, under the discipline of a fixed idea or of a fixed emotion, which are not absolutely distinct, because they are inseparable and almost equivalent. This principle of unity—this center of attraction and point of support of all the work of the creative imagination, that is, of a subjective synthesis that tends to become objective—is the ideal, a construction of images destined to be objectified, as Ribot defines it.

The prestige of the hypothesis of the unconscious did not permit Ribot, no doubt, to realize that in that mysterious factor of inspiration is realized the inventive function of the imagination in what it has of the essential; for it, precisely, contains the discovery of the [p. 419] ideal, by virtue of a synthetic activity of consciousness which, by its instantaneity and freedom, offers us the appearance of the unconscious, the lack of a discursive development operating in diverse moments, like reflective association. The free act is thus also instantaneous and without determining cause; it is the product of the integral activity of consciousness, realized in an instant, as if it were a single act, like a burst of inspiration; and that act, nonetheless, is not unconscious, even when it is not scientifically explicable; on the contrary, consciousness regards it as the act most proper to it, because it is the most profound. Such is the constant character of all the productions of the creative imagination, which invents the ideal in an instant and translates it into a fact or into an essential form.

Inspiration, which is always artistic—even when the imagination adopts diverse types like those indicated by Ribot—is the product of the creative imagination as a whole, whose elements concur in that production with the instantaneity and freedom that it reveals in its entirety. It has, therefore, nothing unconscious and mysterious, even when its complexity disappears in the complete fusion of its factors and is inaccessible to the analysis that its preparation and its complete realization offer to the psychologist and to the aesthetician. Inspiration is the ideal itself in germ, which escapes decomposition in that primordial instant and remains rebellious to analysis even in the forms it animates with its spirit. The ideal may take on diverse forms, because of its objective components and its means of realization; it may be more or less profound and elevated; it may vary according to the role played by the cognitive and affective factors and by the instruments of the senses that perceive the images; but in its essence it is the [p. 420] same: it is the creative power of the imagination, which discovers an order superior to reality, in which the spirit can expand more and better, realizing a greater freedom; it is a free power that creates its own order—that is, an organism that satisfies the incessant longing of the spirit toward an expansion without limits and, consequently, without any coercion. An aesthetic formation that the imagination creates in a single instant, an intimate fusion of the cognitive and affective elements of consciousness, which the will, in a free effort, interpenetrates and orients toward a determinate finality, or offers to the spirit that contents itself with its joyous contemplation.

Such is the root of artistic activity in all its forms, and very especially in the one that is translated into a beautiful work; such must also be the character of pure aesthetic value and the norm of its special criterion. Wherever freedom presents itself, there is offered also an aesthetic form, even when an apparent disorder is associated with that expression and even when freedom is only a non-coercion, a mere appearance, an illusion of the senses, or a forgetting or abstraction of the determining cause. Freedom is what the soul seeks and desires always; it is what it loves above all; it is what is discovered at the bottom of all its enjoyments, even the most sensory; it is what Groos finds even in the play of animals; it is that élan vital by which Bergson explains the whole of creation and which, satisfied, produces that sympathetic interpenetration which the German psychologists call Einfühlung. To choose another point of departure—making of the idea alone, or of feeling alone, or of the combinations of the latter with the ideal element or with the social factor or with the physical factor, the base of aesthetic value, as is claimed by the intellectualists, the sentimentalists, or the sociologists—is to eliminate what there is of the essential in the aesthetic phenomenon, in which, freedom being destroyed, whether as [p. 421] a psychic state or as a factor of aesthetic production, that phenomenon disappears in order to become another of a different nature; it is to attribute to it a logical, economic, religious, or moral value, in which freedom does not exist, or exists in relation to a higher principle, and not with that absolute value which is presented only in fine art; it is to sacrifice the individualism of aesthetic activity to the universality of a supposed norm derived from reason, or to sacrifice the aesthetic criterion to the inconstancy and versatility of individual feeling—incapable of creating any norm, even when appeal is made, as by Kant, to the homogeneity of human nature, which lacks a norm in the pure reactions of sensory feeling; it is, in short, to fail to recognize that what truly constitutes that homogeneity is not pleasure, but freedom, the source of pleasure—that insatiable aspiration to develop without coercion and in ever-new forms, that power of creating which constitutes the imagination, free par excellence.

It is by freedom, consequently, that the beautiful is to be appreciated. It is that freedom, in effect, that analysis finds in the examination of the valuing aesthetic consciousness, under its triple aspect of perception, feeling, and artistic production—which are not successive moments, as is believed, although it is necessary to separate them in order to make their appreciation possible.

Aesthetics, as the philosophical science of the beautiful, must, then, examine at the outset, aided by the scientific methods, the content of aesthetic experience, having for its guide that criterion of its proper value, in order to know the characters presented by the elementary factors of the consciousness that valuates. An investigation without a guiding direction would be vicious, as has been said, or would not lead to the determination of any norm or law. It wou[p. 422]ld be simply a heaping-up of curious facts, interpreted arbitrarily or by using the vulgar criterion, which offers no other reason than that of a feeling of sensory pleasure or displeasure, which the empiricists themselves reject as an aesthetic norm.

It is necessary to set out from a determinate psychology that offers the direction of the scientific analysis, resolving beforehand whether in consciousness the essential is thought, or feeling, or the synthesizing and directing will. The first solution would lead to the aesthetics of order; the second, to the subjective aesthetics of pleasure, which denies the pre-existing order, loses itself in the arbitrary, and fails to recognize true freedom; and the third, to voluntarist aesthetics, which assigns to freedom the role of dominant and constitutive in psychic activity.

This last solution has over the others the advantage of comprehending and surpassing them in the explanation of the aesthetic phenomenon, as artistic activity, in the broad sense given to this phrase.

After what has been set forth, one understands the vast extension of aesthetics, which is neither pure metaphysics nor pure science, which is neither pure psychology nor sociology alone, which is not circumscribed to aesthetic technique nor fulfills its object with the history of artistic forms—even though it may set out from those offered by the spontaneous activity of vital energy. Aesthetics embraces all that, because, as a phenomenon of freedom, it finds its experience in all those domains, which explain one another reciprocally, so as to formulate conclusions that may enter as bases into the field of metaphysical hypotheses. As has been said, aesthetic feeling is cause and effect at the same time; the same may be said of the work of art, which produces aesthetic emotion and is produced by it; the experience of the one is founded on the knowl[p. 423]edge of the other, and that same experience, in order to be complete, demands the knowledge of aesthetic physics, of aesthetic technique, and of the history of art. If science establishes a succession among those factors, that depends exclusively on a logical necessity of knowledge—the same that facilitates the analysis of the elements of consciousness, notwithstanding the indetermination with which the psychic circle develops. This same thing explains the complexity of this study, its great difficulties, and the necessity of being very modest in its aspirations.

### II. LA EXPERIENCIA ESTÉTICA<sup>1</sup> — II. AESTHETIC EXPERIENCE<sup>1</sup>

<sup>1</sup> The content of this chapter is treated more fully later on. Nevertheless, it does not seem useless to reproduce it, even though it be a repetition.

[p. 424] Granting that all creation has an aesthetic value, the question concerning the nature of the beautiful is not thereby resolved; because the creative imagination is translated into diverse forms, which differ from those that are characterized as beautiful or ugly, constituting orders of phenomena separated by subjective and objective characters of their own, and which aspire to be regarded as so many human values. All the normative sciences, in effect, have an independent finality, which may claim to become a value created by imaginative intuition. Logic, economics, morality, law, and religion set out to realize, as values or ideals, truth, utility, the good, justice, and holiness; and in all these disciplines the imagination can invent, realizing an aesthetic function which, nevertheless, differs from the creation of the beautiful, which enters the exclusive domain of the emotion called aesthetic in the strict sense. The phenomenon of the beautiful, in all its amplitude—comprising the beautiful and the ugly, in nature as in art—has for its base free activity within and outside consciousness. But this same form of activity is presented also in the logical, economic, moral, juridical, and [p. 425] religious creations, which, like the artistic ones, involve a double aspect, psychic and social, and tend to construct norms of thought and of the will, criteria for distinguishing and judging, and motives for producing conscious actions.

It is disputed whether truth and utility are end-values, true values like the others indicated, or whether they are mere means of realizing the human ends regarded as supreme. Viewed from the point of view of finality alone, their exclusion might be admitted. Considered in relation to the feeling of freedom—pleasurable or painful—which necessarily enters into the constitution of value, it might be admitted as well.

The logical process, like the economic, can be carried out without the intervention of feeling and of freedom, with the rigorous determinism of science. The demonstration of truth and the calculation of interest can be conceived as pure functions of thought, as auxiliary means to end-values, but not as of the same nature as these. But such purity is only an abstraction and leaves aside the intuitions that the imagination offers in the discovery of new truths, which have, in that case, the character of true values, even when they do not have all the notes that their kindred offer. They are means-values, and for that reason they differ radically from the others, and especially from aesthetic value, which might be characterized as the value of values.

The profound difference that contemporary philosophy establishes between Science and Art—not as a result of the one established since Aristotle between the theoretical and the practical, between thought and action, but between the two activities, the ordering and the free—marks the difference that exists between truth, as a means-va[p. 426]lue, and the beautiful, as an end-value. The ordering logical activity, which eliminates freedom in order to constitute science, enters as an auxiliary of the free activity that informs the beautiful work or that is produced by its aesthetic contemplation. The beautiful is not demonstrated like truth; it is intuited, it is felt, and its nature is thus understood, because the inspiration that engenders it or springs from it escapes the exclusively logical procedure of deduction. Never will the latter be able to explain the genesis of the work of art, which is concrete, nor the aesthetic state of admiration, penetrated with freedom and with feeling.

The intelligence can collaborate in the realization of both phenomena: it can prepare the elements of inspiration and second the efforts employed by the latter in objectifying itself; but in no way can it substitute for the imaginative and free function of beautiful creation. To suppose the contrary is to admit into aesthetic activity the intervention of norms that involve imperatives opposed to freedom; it is to fail to recognize the nature of the imagination; it is to suppose arbitrarily the existence of innate types of beauty, functioning like the axioms in logic, or to attribute to the action of the physical or social milieu an imposition that psychology belies with the infinite variety of works of art and with the equally infinite variability of aesthetic emotion. The great error of intellectualism has been to assign to thought a contemplative function like the aesthetic one—a primordial and theoretical function—placing art in the domain of practical activity, subordinate to the former. Those functions being inverted by contemporary voluntarism, thought has been reduced to the role that belongs to it in the psychic synthesis: that of an auxiliary instrument of freedom in the adaptation of the latter to the milieu in which it must be exercised. Such are the relat[p. 427]ions existing between the true and the beautiful, between the logical phenomenon and the aesthetic phenomenon, between pure science and pure art.

Analogous is the one that exists between the economic phenomenon and the aesthetic, between the useful and the beautiful. So it has been recognized by all who have rejected the hedonist or eudaemonist theory of the beautiful, which makes aesthetic value depend on human happiness, founded on pleasure. The aesthetic phenomenon is essentially disinterested; it pursues no end outside itself, neither economic, nor moral, nor religious; it has its end in itself, which constitutes its essential character. In that consists its disinterestedness, because in that emancipation from ends lies its freedom. Hence it is, as Kant says, «a finality without an end». The economic phenomenon is subject to the imperative of desire, which destroys all its autonomy; the useful depends exclusively on desire. And even when the latter may present itself in the development of aesthetic emotion, it does not constitute a necessary factor, because the latter can and even must subsist foreign to the desire of appropriation—whether of the work contemplated, or of the benefits its author aspires to obtain, or even of the ends of artistic utility that the work realizes. That factor being eliminated, the beautiful does not disappear, though aesthetic emotion may lose or gain in intensity. The so-called aesthetic fitness is an associated element, but not an essential one. The freedom with which the artist produces his work may be limited by the necessity of that fitness or adaptation; aesthetic feeling may integrate itself with that element; but its subsistence does not depend on it. On the other hand, freedom being suppressed, the beautiful disappears, but the economic phenomenon persists.

If the aesthetic phenomenon differs radically from the logical and the economic, it is not the same with the [p. 428] moral, with which it has much analogy. In the moral phenomenon, in effect, freedom is an essential factor as in the aesthetic; the moral ideal may be regarded as an aesthetic creation and, in this sense, the actions that realize that ideal might be characterized as aesthetic. An action of great moral value becomes beautiful; and beauty and the good interpenetrate in such a way that it is not possible to separate the two aspects without profoundly modifying the nature of that action. Notwithstanding that analogy, the difference between the two phenomena is found in the role that freedom plays in the one and the other. The moral phenomenon involves the coercion of duty, imposed by a norm that the moral conscience finds superior to its will. That imperative of the law subsists, whatever be the character attributed to it and the influence it exerts upon freedom. Categorical, hypothetical, or persuasive, it is always an imperative that imposes a duty, to which the moral conscience feels the necessity of submitting, even when it rebels against it. The moral norm is, like the logical norm, an inescapable condition that the spirit must follow. Without the fulfillment of the first, the goodness of the action disappears; without obedience to the second, there is no truth in thought.

It is not the same with the aesthetic phenomenon, in which freedom is everything and the norm is subordinate to it. Properly speaking, there are no norms in the aesthetic order, since the feeling of freedom can create or feel beauty within an original and unique psychic state. Precisely, originality is the character of the work of art of genius. The genius can alter or destroy the existing norms, creating new ones, in offering new models of artistic production. If he does not always do so, if he employs the canons established by technical tradition, he does so freely, because he regards them as useful au[p. 429]xiliaries for the production and the intelligibility of his work, and because, those canons being results of the free activity of the spirit, they are not opposed to it save when they fix narrow limits to its expansion, crystallizing forms that do not answer to a greater ambition for freedom. The aesthetic criterion does not resign itself, as the moral one does, to the constitution of absolute and eternal dogmas; it does not feel the necessity of conserving them; it is not painfully disquieted by the substitution of some ideals for others, even when they are opposed. On the contrary, it longs for diversity as an essential condition in the phenomenon; it rejects the unity that absorbs it, and condemns that unity as anti-aesthetic when the ideal, in its process of unification, assumes the abstract form of the universal, to which the ethical criterion constantly aspires.

Aesthetic emotion, intimately associated with moral emotion in the contemplation of the beauty of actions, derives, nevertheless, from a different cause. The aesthetic consciousness delights in what the action has of the free, while the moral one delights in what it has of the ordered or of the conformed to the norm. The moral act is founded essentially on the power of inhibition of consciousness, and even in positive acts of doing it supposes the absolute inhibition of the opposite acts. It is not the same in the aesthetic act, which is essentially expansive. Aesthetic enjoyment is founded on the intuition of the ideal; moral enjoyment, on the comparison of the fact with the precept, in which the reflective function surpasses the intuitive to the point of rendering it useless. For this reason, in moral beauty there is intuition and reflection at the same time: its beauty is felt, and its morality can be demonstrated, as a logical consequence of the universal and abstract precept.

That demonstration supposes an invariable principle, a dogma, an imperative norm superior to the [p. 430] will, which in aesthetic activity does not exist, as has been said—even though one may wish to give that character to technique, as the aesthetic sociology of Lalo claims; because whatever be the influence attributed to the traditional rule, it cannot surpass the freedom of the spirit that creates the work of art, nor condemn passive aesthetic feeling to a determinate form of pleasure, nor explain its existence and its evolution while leaving aside the freedom that is its source.

On the other hand, the idea of order plays a very different role in the two phenomena: in the moral, it is the transcendent end of the freedom that must submit to it. The norm here creates the order with the characters that it has. That order is imperative, necessary, absolute, eternal; it is the very perfection of human life, which the individual does not create, though he accepts it freely as an ideal, and which constitutes an end of the will, exterior and superior to it, even in the hedonist conception of the moral law. Freedom does not create that order, because, if it created it, the norm would lose those characters and would cease to impose upon conduct a system of duties. At bottom, that submission to the norm characterizes the morality of the act. If freedom is associated with it, it is because freedom constitutes the postulate of the sanction and because, in a spiritualist conception of man, only free actions are human—whether freedom be understood in an intellectualist or a voluntarist sense. In the aesthetic phenomenon the very contrary happens: there freedom creates its own order; freedom is an end in itself; it lacks a transcendent finality; the aesthetic order is the one that best satisfies the expansion of the spirit, the one that eliminates most and best the coercion opposed to its nature. To realize that order, that ideal—therein lies the whole aspiration of the aesthetic will.

The moral order and the aesthetic order thus have very different characters. The first, in its highest degree [p. 431] of perfection, is a system of relations, of concepts, established by a normative law, even when in its origin it was an order of images. The second has been and is always a system of images. In the first, systematization is a logical procedure, which pursues the unity of the ideal and of the norm outside the individual, as in science. In the second, systematization is an intuitive procedure, which finds simultaneously unity and variety in the imaginative function that realizes it in the individual. In the first, universality is sought in the extension of the norm; in the second, it is found in the extension of aesthetic activity and in the depth of its intuition. The moral order presupposes the existence of an ideal of perfection, which it dogmatizes and imposes upon the will in its relation with the other wills; the aesthetic order is that ideal created by the spirit in the exercise of its freedom. Without that creation there would exist no imperative other than the biological; the moral imperative would be inexplicable. The moral order thus has its foundation in the aesthetic order, because only the latter is a creation.

The religious phenomenon has with the aesthetic more profound analogies. They were born together in the creation of the Myth, as Wundt says, and they have never separated completely. The religious phenomenon has always sought in the aesthetic form its most complete and efficacious expression. But their difference is no less clear, if one considers the role that freedom plays in the one and the other phenomenon. The religious state is one of liberation, of emancipation from the world, but of absolute submission to the divinity. The aesthetic state is one of absolute freedom. In the religious phenomenon, the norm dictated by the divine will and known by revelation is everything; in the aesthetic, inspiration is subject to no norm, nor does the work of art suffer its imposition, nor does aesthetic enjoyment [p. 432] mold itself to it. In both, the feeling of liberation is profound, but its cause and its tendency differ radically. Both coexist in the original myth; but the myth is, above all, the work of the creative imagination, an aesthetic phenomenon par excellence. Revelation is either an aesthetic inspiration or an inexplicable mystery. Without that inspiration the myth would never have existed. Within the limits of philosophical investigation, one must presuppose here, as in the moral order, the supremacy of aesthetic activity.

The differences established between aesthetic value and the other values do not permit us to deduce, nevertheless, that the aesthetic phenomenon exists pure, isolated from the other social facts, with which it has so close a relation.

Such purity is also a mere abstraction. In the reality of life, on the contrary, these diverse phenomena are associated so intimately that their analysis gives rise to diverse theories destined to explain the nature of the beautiful and that of art, which is its most perfect expression.

The admission of a guiding Idea—which may lead the spirit in the slow process of artistic execution, or may permit aesthetic contemplation to discern the beauty realized, in order to enjoy it merely or to make its critique—has given to logical value a great importance in aesthetic valuation, to the point of making the very nature of the beautiful, and the sole foundation of its critique, depend on the realization of the Idea. To know that idea and to realize it, or to appreciate it after it is realized, setting out from an aesthetic category established like the logical categories of thought, has been the fundamental problem for those who have confounded the aesthetic phenomenon of the beautiful with the [p. 433] logical phenomenon of the true—attributing to reason what belongs to the imagination and supposing erroneously that the aesthetic function is reflective and not intuitive, that reason has a dynamogenic power which it lacks, and that the aesthetic problem is resolved in knowing the beautiful and not in feeling it and producing it freely.

That influence of intellectualism on the development of aesthetic ideas has given rise to the dispute between idealists, partisans of content, and realists, attached to the form of the aesthetic phenomenon; the former dominated by philosophical panlogism, which has made the idea of order the axis of its doctrine, notwithstanding its sympathies for the principle of freedom, and the latter subjected to the powerful influence of artistic technique, which seeks in the scientific methods the law of its execution. More logicians than aestheticians, both have contemplated the problem of the beautiful as a form of truth, as a theory of knowledge, as a logical explanation of harmony—regarded as the essential character of the beautiful and subject, for that reason, to the methods of discursive knowledge.

This mistaken point of view has come from the systematic orientation of the whole of philosophy toward the central idea of order, which is essentially logical, and from the reduction of all knowledge to that exclusive form and of all logic to the logic of thought—failing to recognize the intuitive activity of the imagination, which penetrates reality, with all the energies of the spirit, discovering what of the essential exists through the forms accessible to sensory experience and in the very depths of the ideas elaborated by thought. That «divining sympathy» of which Bergson speaks, and which explains aesthetic inspiration, is not the idea in the Platonic sense nor in the Aristotelian; it is not the fruit of a [p. 434] fragmentary consciousness, which eliminates reality or mutilates it, but the whole consciousness, which projects itself freely toward an ideal it has formed and seeks to realize, or toward an ideal already realized, which satisfies that longing for creative expansion. In that integral activity, the logical phenomenon cannot be lacking; but, if its concurrence is necessary, it does not constitute an end, but a means; it does not impart unity and direction to the aesthetic life, but subordinates itself to the élan of the spirit, which pursues a freer reality in the world forged by the imagination, so that it may serve as a guide in its intellectual efforts oriented in the direction of practice. It is then that the guiding idea, which is already an aesthetic creation, invests with importance the logical phenomenon, the conscious reflection in the adaptation of the means to the practical end established.

The economic phenomenon concurs also, in that same auxiliary form, in aesthetic activity, notwithstanding its external finality. The idea of the useful—the foundation of that phenomenon, which in its turn derives from the feeling of sensory pleasure—is not totally excluded. It does not enter into that activity, it is true, with the overpowering force of human egoism, which destroys all solidarity and admits only the form of the false freedom that sees the effects alone and fails to recognize the slavery of the passion that is its cause. So considered, the economic phenomenon is openly opposed to the aesthetic. A disinterested activity, which has its end in itself, is not conceivable in a state of consciousness reduced to egoism, which follows a unilateral direction and excludes every affective factor that might deflect that direction or attenuate its destructive force. But a state of that nature, purely economic, would be abnormal, like that of the miser, or would have value only as a pure abstraction; in normal experience it does not present itself with that extre[p. 435]me rigor.

The useful and the disinterested are associated in diverse degrees, undergoing transformations that demonstrate the possible harmony between the aesthetic and the extra-aesthetic. Useful coordination can favor aesthetic value by the suitable disposition or placing of beautiful objects, as happens in the concurrence of different artistic objects, in architecture and in the drama, and of beautiful objects in Nature. It can produce aesthetic emotion, even as a mere useful coordination of coexistence or succession, if it can offer the spirit the appearance or symbol of freedom. The useful, then, offers the illusion of free life and loses, for the one who contemplates it, that characteristic external finality, in order to acquire the appearance of fecund spontaneity, which imprints on it an illusory aesthetic value, as illusory as is the spontaneity on which it is founded. The thesis of Guyau—which, in opposition to that of Spencer, finds in the useful an aesthetic element—does not destroy, consequently, the disinterested character of the beautiful by assimilating the aesthetic phenomenon to the economic; rather it takes from utility its proper form in order to associate it with the aesthetic form, thus confirming the belief that the useful and the beautiful can aid one another reciprocally, favoring each other without losing their proper nature—the first conserving its practical finality, and the second its emancipation from all objective finality, its intrinsic freedom. The examples offered by architecture and by oratory are a proof of this interpenetration, in which utility enhances beauty and the latter makes utility more efficacious.

The cooperation of the moral phenomenon is more intimate still. It is necessary when the aesthetic object is a human action—whether it be performed, or have been performed, or be intended to be performed; whether the imagination invent it or reproduce it, or intervene mere[p. 436]ly by coloring the real action contemplated. In all these cases, the beautiful is inseparable from the good; both values come to fuse in such a way that the aesthetic criterion becomes moral, and there arises the tendency to alter the nature of art, imposing on it a pedagogical finality as essential. The theories of didactic art and of art for art's sake—equally exclusivist and inexact—derive from that confusion, in which these two theses are respectively affirmed: the powerful influence of moral value in the appreciation of aesthetic value, and the autonomy of art; theses that, far from excluding one another, are reconciled theoretically and practically, taking into account that the moral phenomenon, by what it has of the ordered, favors aesthetic freedom, and the aesthetic phenomenon, by what it has of the free, exalts the moral order—thus concurring in the greater integrity and the greater depth of the ideal feeling that comes from both factors.

The feeling of moral value, though extra-aesthetic and merely associated, has here so great a share in the phenomenon of the beautiful that its elimination would deprive it of its object, leaving only aesthetic representations very different from those that express conscious acts of will. All poetry, chiefly the dramatic, would develop as sculptural, pictorial, and musical form only, if moral value were eliminated from the aesthetic content. Even outside art, the beautiful human action would be so only by its practical form, and in the other arts—with the exception of architecture—the complete separation of that value would alter their nature, since the feelings aroused by the expressions of the human spirit always enter the domain of moral value. This explains why the immorality of the symbol impairs the efficacy of aesthetic emotion, thwarting and weakening it, and why the contrary happens when that sym[p. 437]bol is not opposed to the moral beliefs of the aesthetic spectator, but becomes also a symbol of those very beliefs. That fusion does not prevent, however, feeling beauty as dominant, and even finding it and feeling it in the symbol when it expresses a powerful freedom, which opposes itself resolutely to morality and succumbs in that opposition, or maintains itself in that attitude as the incarnation of the aesthetic principle of freedom.

Religious value is associated with the aesthetic, serving also as content for the feeling produced by the work of art. The highest aesthetic forms of art have had for their object the expression of the divine principle. The temple, the statue of the god, the religious painting, music of mystical depth, and lyric poetry—as a revelation of what there is of the divine in the depths of the soul—have expressed a religious content more or less directly, with greater or lesser intensity. The feeling of emancipation, which characterizes the two values, aesthetic and religious, associates them in the artistic expansions of the spirit. On the other hand, religious feeling would not arise in the human consciousness if the mystical idea did not clothe itself in forms produced by the imagination, and it would not be purified if those forms were not idealized by art. Pure thought would never have comprehended the divine principle. Logic would never have substituted for inspiration in creating religious ideas and feelings. God made man is the most perfect aesthetic symbol of the religious idea.

But, just as analysis distinguishes aesthetic value from the moral in experience, so likewise it can separate it from religious value. Symbols opposed to art have had and have a great religious value for mystical contemplation; on the other hand, art can express, and does express, the divine principle in aesthetic forms that leave with[p. 438]out action the religious feeling. In the great diversity of cults, only those artistic forms have influence which are in harmony with the religious beliefs of the one who contemplates them. They can be admired only aesthetically by those who profess different religious beliefs. On the contrary, among those who profess the same cult, the religious symbol, joined to the aesthetic form, may be adored as a symbol of the divinity, but not comprehended nor judged as an expression of the beautiful. The aesthetic form may even be condemned if it opposes the religious belief—there resulting from that relation a consequence similar to the one deduced from the association between aesthetic value and moral value.

The aesthetic phenomenon is not, then, isolated in reality, but combines with the other phenomena that derive from the same creative activity and concur in the realization of the aesthetic ideal of freedom. The spirit tends toward a movement without coercion and toward a fecundity without limit; but if free activity is conceived thus, logically eliminating all resistance, in lived reality it could not create, nor even subsist, without that opposed reality of coercion, which produces, in the development of the psyche, the consciousness of the ego. Birds, it has been said, would believe themselves freer in their flight if the resistance of the atmosphere disappeared, because they do not know that without that resistance they could not fly. The same happens with the flight of the spirit. If external coercion did not exist as an inertia that must be penetrated and ordered in the service of greater freedom, of the amplest and most efficacious creation, psychic virtuality would exhaust itself in an instant, would cease to be activity in order to become inertia, would no longer be spirit, but matter, as Bergson maintains.

Free activity struggles with the obstacles that its environment offers it. In opposition with external natu[p. 439]re it vanquishes it, employing the intelligence, and, having vanquished it, obtains from it all the material means it uses for the realization of its ideal. Thus are born logic and economics in intimate consortium; thus is formed science, which fecundates the production of wealth and destroys the slavery of physical reality; but thus too is fortified and crystallized that utilitarian ideal which, absorbing at last the inner freedom, makes of egoism the exclusive criterion of happiness.

Free activity struggles, on the other hand, with the social milieu penetrated with egoism, and triumphs over it by means of moral solidarity, which abandons the biological procedures of conquest and finds, in the free concurrence of free beings, a mesh of threads of a boundless flexibility, which orders the function of the will, integrating freedom as pure expansion. The ideal of expansion without norm, which constitutes the ground of the creative imagination, becomes an ideal of solidary activity and creates morality in human coexistence, in the service of that same inner freedom; and with morality spring up the juridical and political values, which are of the same kind.

Free activity, finally, incarnates in a divine personality the aesthetic ideal not realized in human morality. It effaces the limit that marks every work of man and raises creation to an infinite and absolutely free power, placed in the region of the mysterious and inexplicable, and thus engenders religion, which feeds on a supernatural inspiration.

But, notwithstanding these expressions, free activity never renounces its essential and supreme function—the creation of the ideal and its contemplation without any practical end, its pure aesthetic function, the production of fine art, in which the spirit aspires to realize that [p. 440] creative ambition capable of producing what the coercion of the milieu makes impossible. This function constitutes, therefore, the source from which the other values drink their inspirations. It is not exaggerated, for this reason, to call this disinterested and pure activity the «value of values».

The distinction established among the diverse human ends or values does not leave resolved the question relating to the nature of the aesthetic phenomenon. The negative analysis must be completed with a positive one, which studies that phenomenon in the double experience, subjective and objective, that it presents—seeking to isolate it, by abstraction, from the other associated forms that make aesthetic activity so complex. Only after this analysis will it be possible to define the beautiful and to explain its diverse modalities in consciousness, in nature, in art, and in history.

### III. LA ACTIVIDAD ESTÉTICA — III. AESTHETIC ACTIVITY

Since the aesthetic phenomenon offers to analysis a double aspect, subjective and objective, the theory of the beautiful has oscillated between those extremes, making the objective face of the phenomenon depend upon psychological activity or the reverse; and from that oscillation there derive two opposed criteria, founded respectively upon aesthetic feeling and upon the aesthetic idea, which, under the names of impressionism and dogmatism, Lalo examines and condemns in his «Introduction to Aesthetics».

The fundamental error in that analysis has consisted, on the one hand, in founding aesthetic value upon a passive element, which explains neither artistic creation nor pure aesthetic emotion, and in attributing to the subjective aesthetic state a purely contemplative and receptive quality; and, on the other, in including, as a product of the dynamic function of every image, the special and characteristic content of aesthetic feeling. In the first case, the attempt has been made to draw activity out of pure passivity—freedom, which is the soul of artistic creation, out of the instinctive and even unconscious movement of the creative spirit—and in the second, aesthetic emotion has been made a mere reflection of the object, an adaptation, a coordination, a fusion equally instinctive and necessary between object and subject, brought about by the attraction or sympathy that the object provokes. Freedom, as creative activity, as the imagination that engenders the ideal, has been excluded, set aside, [p. 442]regarded as the ideal of the perfect, confused with the feeling of non-coercion, or taken, as Groos does, in the Kantian sense, as the absolute beginning of action, as the feeling of being a cause in the activity of pure play.

In the disagreement in which the psychologists still remain concerning the very nature of feeling, it is logical that the analysis of the aesthetic phenomenon should suffer the consequences, and that, under the still-subsisting sway of philosophical intellectualism—which has found strong support in psychophysics—one should persist in observing the subjective aesthetic phenomenon, whether through its expressive and immutable symbols or with the instrument of scientific experiment, in order to discover aesthetic laws under the obsession of science, which tends toward the immobility of life.

Feeling, reduced to a mere reaction of consciousness against the image, likewise does not explain, by that single fundamental character, its two opposed modalities of pleasure and pain, which are effects of that cause but which presuppose fusion with, or contrast to, the perceived image. Hence Wundt finds in pleasure an aspiration toward the object and in pain a rejection of it, introducing the dynamic factor of the will into this phenomenon, to which all contemporary psychology attributes the value of a stimulus. But the characteristics established by Wundtian voluntarism seem to explain the opposed effects of feeling and not its causes. Pleasure tends toward fusion and pain toward separation from the image, yet it is not explained why that double function is brought about, why feeling does not remain indifferent to the presence of the image, or limit itself to defending consciousness by reacting against the new image without fusing or combining with it, and without producing pleasure or pain.

This diver[p. 443]sity might be explained by starting from the principle that the spirit is freedom, expansion, and that it turns into pleasure whenever that expansion is satisfied, as happens when sensation and feeling harmonize and fuse, and turns into pain when feeling is thwarted by the image and either eliminates it through forgetting or associates itself with it through the repetition of habit, which attenuates the expansive force of the spirit and brings about a conciliation that at last permits the immediate fusion of pleasure. Joy, according to Bergson, expresses the triumph of free life; the conquest of freedom is the symbol of a creation. «Wherever there is joy, there is creation: the richer the creation, the deeper the joy.» Thus, by way of freedom it would not be impossible to find a solution to all the problems raised by the complex activity of consciousness, in which the will performs the double synthesizing and directing function that contemporary voluntarism recognizes in it.

Psycho-aesthetic activity, the imaginative and free activity of consciousness, finds its explanation, in effect, within that dynamic theory of feeling which the psychological aesthetics of Einfühlung has analyzed profoundly, as an activity that tends to objectify itself, departing from the passive conception of the aesthetic state—the conception that explains the pleasure of the beautiful by a harmony of consciousness produced from without and that leads to a negative freedom, to the emancipation of the self identified with the harmony of the beautiful object. But the theory of Einfühlung is an obscure and vague sentimentalism which, though it is expressed through a phenomenon of sympathy or of imitation accessible to psychological analysis, has its root in a vital feeling of the self—an obscure matrix, as Lalo says—in which the unity of consciousness is realized, and intuition discovers the will as an immediate and irreducible datum, as a tendency to produce, to rea[p. 444]lize; but not as a free activity, rather as an instinctive activity, biological more than psychic. «For aesthetic Einfühlung,» says Lalo, «all beauty is the symbol of a personal life and of an expansion of our own life.» «This aesthetic vitalism,» he adds, «is the confused form, par excellence, of sentimentalism; it is the aesthetics of intuition»; it is a mysticism for which everything is beautiful and every man may take delight in every beauty, being for that very reason arbitrary in its norms and opposed to a scientific conception of the aesthetic phenomenon.

Lalo's intellectualism, which condemns aesthetic sentimentalism and rejects the «certainty of the possibility of exercising each one of our faculties» that Volkelt supposes in Einfühlung, logically condemns as well the theory of Bergson, which makes the subjective aesthetic phenomenon derive from creative freedom.

Bergson, in effect, in explaining the progressive intervention of new elements—visible in the fundamental emotion, and which seem to grow in magnitude even when they merely modify its nature—offers, as very notable examples, the aesthetic feelings, analyzing the simplest among them, the feeling of grace. What characterizes this feeling is, first, a certain ease in the outward movements; next, the fusion of that perceived ease with the pleasure of arresting, in some fashion, the march of time and of possessing the future in the present; and, finally, a kind of physical sympathy, derived from the rhythm of easy movement, which is associated with moral sympathy and with many other factors. Bergson thus makes of rhythm the symbol of pleasurable aesthetic feeling. Rhythm, the expression of inner freedom, contains the constant renewal of psychic elements which offer the appearance of [p. 445]a progressive intensity, but which mark new and therefore incommensurable feelings. According to Bergson, there is in the affective aesthetic process an incessant creation, in which psychic activity presents itself as a feeling of freedom that, in its expansion, creates art.

But Lalo himself, who calls that theory mystical and does not accept the idea of play interpreted as an absolute freedom, as a true creation of the imaginative activity that engenders art, finds himself nonetheless forced to accept that essential factor of freedom, though subjecting it to the discipline of artistic technique, which for Lalo has an imperative character, even though aesthetic duty is not to be confused with moral duty—which aspires to dominate the whole of life and to present its laws as absolute, unlike aesthetic duty, which is relative and guarantees only the morality of art, saving it from egoism and giving it a social function.

In his theory Lalo confuses the aesthetic value of the beautiful with the value of the perfect, attributing to it a logical finality which by its nature it lacks. That confusion, which converts the technical criterion into an aesthetic criterion, destroys the importance of the affective factor, to the point of regarding its elimination as necessary for a serene and exact judgment upon the artistic value of a work. It is the old Platonic intellectualism, clothed in the forms of sociological science, which puts in the place of the Idea the canon imposed by artistic tradition. To judge beauty, one must submit to the imperative of the recognized canon; to be understood and appreciated aesthetically, it is a duty to produce in accordance with that canon. Lalo thus affirms its imperative force, but does not inquire into the origin of that human value; for in that inquiry he would necessa[p. 446]rily come up against freedom, unless he accepted as his basis Plato's innate Idea.

Only fantasy, by its free and creative character, can explain the nature of the aesthetic phenomenon in all its breadth. An original and global activity, as Croce considers it, its value derives from freedom alone, even when the affective and cognitive factors enter into its content. The higher aesthetic feelings are not such because logical, moral, or religious feelings serve them as their object, but because the imagination exhibits them penetrated by freedom and as its symbols. Even the elementary aesthetic feelings, which contain sensory and affective factors, take their value not from these but from the harmonic unity that the imagination constructs with them and that enfolds the static freedom of non-coercion, the most elementary form of equilibrium of inner freedom.

Aesthetic activity is always free activity, whether it be regarded as contemplative or as projected outward. It is the «free play of the cognitive faculties» established by Kant; it is the play instinct that expresses that same harmony in Schiller's aesthetics; it is the expenditure of excess biological energy, the free play of that force, as Spencer thinks; it is the free simulation of practical activity, which delights in that freedom, in the feeling of being able to be a cause, as Groos interprets play; it is the exclusive fruit of free inspiration, as Leopardi thinks; it is, in short, in all aesthetic ideas, free order, even though freedom does not surpass order by creating it freely and without any practical finality.

Witasek, analyzing the feelings of value derived from a judgment of appreciation—which he calls feelings of judgment, to distinguish them from the purely [p. 447]sensory ones—establishes that in all cases in which they are associated with a moral approval or disapproval, persuasion may be replaced by a fiction, in which case they attach not to «real feelings» but only to analogous states of mind, which he terms «feelings of fantasy». Aesthetic feeling, which forms the center of aesthetic activity, does not fall into the class of the logical feelings, or feelings of thought, derived from intellectual premises, but belongs to that of the feelings of fantasy. Persuasion does not enter into it as an essential element, the representation being a sufficient premise of that feeling. Aesthetic feeling is a feeling of intuitive representation and not of logical judgment—to which there is afterward joined a judgment that determines the class to which it belongs; that is, a judgment of value, in which the aesthetic representation is compared to a norm.

The feeling of value that derives from that judgment is, for that very reason, very different from the aesthetic feeling that serves as its basis; for it is by force of this feeling of pleasure that value is attributed to the object. The feeling of value has nothing to do with aesthetic qualities; and if one passes from this feeling to the aesthetic one, it is by virtue of the transposition of feelings—an activity of great importance in the psychic life of man, by which a logical feeling of persuasion is changed into an aesthetic one of representation. But representation, though intuitive, does not contain the whole premise of aesthetic feeling; it must also be, essentially, expressive of psychic phenomena, as artistic representation is.

Witasek accords great importance to fantasy in the analysis of expressive beauty. «It is true,» he says, «that to represent psychic phenomena intuitively is a matter of inner perception; but the totality of psychic phenomena can be divided into two classes, such [p. 448]that every phenomenon entering into the one has its reflection in the second, so that, in given circumstances, it can take its place. To perceptive representation there corresponds a representation of fantasy; to persuasion, a fiction that has the same object; to real feeling, a feeling of fantasy; to real desire, a desire of fantasy. If one must form the intuitive representation of any state of mind whatever that is not present, nor can exist in the soul of the subject, the corresponding state of fantasy will replace it; and so long as inner perception is directed to it, the required intuitive representation will be formed.»

Witasek finds an analogous relation between persuasion and fiction; the latter is a special psychic act, even though it has in common with persuasion its being directed toward an object. «Fiction is a psychic phenomenon, in all respects similar to judgment; only that it leaves the subject's persuasion indifferent, coming to stand with him outside the field of believing and knowing, and reducing itself, so to speak, to a judgment of fantasy»—although both persuasion and fiction are capable of arousing feelings. Witasek observes, moreover, that the pure emotional factor of the feelings aroused by fiction, of these feelings of fantasy, is identical to that of the feelings of reality aroused by persuasions or representations, even though the intensity is not the same. «Nevertheless, taken as a whole, they differ essentially from real feelings; for, as the designation of feelings of fantasy gives to understand, they produce neither pleasure nor pain»—a difference that proceeds from the premises: when it is a question of feelings of reality, the premise is a persuasion and is directed to things that really exist, but when it is a question of feelings of imagination, the premise is a fiction that has nothing to do with reality.

In expressive beauty, consequently, the indi[p. 449]vidual must relive within himself the expressive psychic phenomenon in order to enjoy it aesthetically; but it is not necessary that he relive it as a real phenomenon, which is impossible in the greater part of cases; it is enough that he do so as a phenomenon of fantasy and that he contemplate it, obtaining thus an intuitive representation of that same phenomenon, without any other corresponding to it. Witasek concludes this analysis by affirming «that it is the end of the aesthetic object to stimulate and promote the reproduction of the psychic phenomenon, whether that object be a work of art or a natural object».

Witasek departs from the psychological aesthetics of Einfühlung, because the latter does not characterize aesthetic expression as a phenomenon of fantasy. The fusion, accord, or harmony between the contemplating subject and the contemplated object—that is, Einfühlung—has great importance in aesthetics. Witasek acknowledges this; but «that fusion consists in the subject's reliving, as a phenomenon of fantasy, the psychic phenomena expressed by the object and representing them to himself intuitively. The object of this intuitive representation is afterward associated, by means of a fiction or a judgment, with the perception of the expressive object, so that there results a complex object, intuitively represented, endowed with physical qualities and, at the same time, with psychic qualities».

«The accord, the sentimental transposition, the enesthesis of the psychic phenomena thus relived, consists in the fact that the subject represents them, in a single complex, together with the perceived physical object; in which case the psychic and physical phenomena are associated in the single complex, in the mode in which alone such complexes are formed. And what in the accord or fusion has been called Einfühlung must be understood in the sense that the subject may regard, as his own, the psychic phenomena that he projects into the object».

[p. 450]Now then, for Witasek it is the feelings of fantasy, like the other phenomena of fantasy, that constitute the nucleus of Einfühlung. But besides the feelings localized by the subject in the expressive object, the aesthetic object often arouses in the subject fantastic feelings of another kind, which Witasek calls «aesthetic feelings of co-participation, which are distinguished from the foregoing in that they do not reproduce, according to the subject's conception, the psychic life of the object, and are not localized in the object, but rather represent the sentimental reaction of the subject himself before the object. Through them is manifested the sentimental participation of the subject in the represented aesthetic object. But just as the feelings of accord, so too the feelings of co-participation or of sympathy cannot form, by themselves and directly, the psychic premise of aesthetic pleasure, except when they are consciously relived, seen, intuited, with the inner eye».

From this it follows that sympathy cannot be regarded as the fundamental phenomenon of the aesthetic attitude, nor be completely identified with it, as the aesthetics of Lipps does, however great the importance of that feeling may be in aesthetic contemplation and enjoyment. That importance, according to Witasek, lies in the fact that sympathy forms the basis of all the feelings of co-participation and, consequently, of a whole class of factors of aesthetic pleasure. If sympathy disappears, all the other feelings disappear as well. The aesthetic object therefore loses much; a loss that is not confined to the feelings of co-participation, since, if sympathy is lacking, the will too lacks the strongest stimulus toward accord, toward Einfühlung, and there disappears besides the tension, an element of aesthetic pleasure of great importance especially in literary works.

[p. 451]Notwithstanding the great importance that Witasek attributes to the phenomena of fantasy, he does not deny that real scenes may also be objects of aesthetic contemplation and enjoyment, even though this happens with more difficulty, on account of the superior influence of the real feelings in the soul of the subject. As a general thesis, says Witasek, the aesthetic contemplation of real feelings is possible and can also be demonstrated empirically, provided that the aesthetic capacity of the subject allows him to master them and make them the pure object of that contemplation. But in every case, whether it be a question of the aesthetic state determined by simple objects or of objects of the beauty of value or of inner beauty, the common note observed in the aesthetic attitude of the subject consists, in substance, of a feeling of pleasure or displeasure joined to an intuitive representation, so that the representation forms the psychic premise of the feeling. Aesthetic feelings are therefore, above all, feelings of representation, it being indifferent whether the representation be derived from the activity of the senses or from central excitation—that is, whether it be a perceptive representation or a representation of fantasy or of memory—although the most frequent case is that in which both forms act together, the cooperation of associated representations having great importance in the aesthetic enjoyment they produce.

The form of an aesthetic object is what perception offers, or would offer if—though it were not real—it were present only in memory or in fantasy; all the rest, that is, everything that the subject, excited by the form, adds of his own by means of fantasy, of reproduction, or of inner perception in order to be able to enjoy an object aesthetically, is its content.

Since representations are complexes of sensations, the character that Witasek attributes to the aesthetic attitude would comprise the whole of psychic activity, [p. 452]and there would be no difference at all between any sensory feeling whatever and an aesthetic one—which is contrary to the experience that radically distinguishes them. Witasek accepts that distinction, but makes it consist in two different aspects of sensation, which he calls the act and the content. For aesthetic feelings, decisive is the content of the representations with which those feelings are associated; for feelings of sensation, on the contrary, decisive is the act of sensation. Hence the aesthetic feelings of pleasure or displeasure are agreeable or disagreeable feelings for which the psychic premise consists in intuitive representations, in the sense that it is especially their content that, in that case, acts as the determining cause of such feelings. The aesthetic attitude is, in substance, this feeling together with its premise.

Witasek marks this difference between the feeling of act and the feeling of content, showing that the former—which comprises the lower sensory feeling and the purely logical one—is not accessible to fantasy; not so the latter, which falls into the category of the fantastic feelings and which is offered also in the sensations of the higher senses. The lower sensory feeling in act is not aesthetic, even though its contemplation as an object of art may arouse an aesthetic pleasure; for here it is no longer a question of the lower sensory pleasure in itself, but of causing to relive a psychic state whose intuitive representation arouses aesthetic pleasure—that is, of a feeling of content represented by fantasy. The real sensory feelings do not permit aesthetic contemplation, and for that reason there is no aesthetic fusion of feelings of sensation, which not only are not aesthetic pleasures but even cease to be objects of aesthetic enjoyment.

The incompatibility existing between the feeling [p. 453]of act and the aesthetic feeling thus results from the ineptitude of the former to be represented by fantasy, which means that it is fantasy that gives to aesthetic representation its essential character. This is clearly deduced from the whole preceding analysis and is confirmed by the significance that Witasek attributes to the dominant position of aesthetic enjoyment.

«If by this,» he says, «one means to speak of the freedom that is exalted as a special value of aesthetic enjoyment, one affirms a fact that is easily explained by our formula. The freedom that is here meant is certainly none other than a relative independence of the one who enjoys and of the one who creates the objects of enjoyment, with respect to things that are, for the most part, withdrawn from his dominion—an independence that derives from the fact that his activity unfolds in a field in which his will is dominant, almost absolute. And this is precisely the case when man does not judge but represents; for by judgment he is bound to reality and must adapt himself to it, whereas by representation, on the contrary, he holds it in his power through fantasy, even though reality does not offer itself to him in the form desired by his will. Moreover, he has within himself an infinitely fecund source of pleasure, since it is known that the realm of the representable is infinite. And, finally, to enjoy this source implies only relatively small difficulties, being for that reason possible for many and in great measure».

This fantastic representation, which is thus associated with freedom, is the creative work of the imagination, which explains the radical difference that Witasek establishes between science and art and the analogy between artistic activity and that of play as products of fantasy. It is what engenders the feelings that Witasek terms fantastic, and in which he makes the essential character of the pure aesthetic attitude consist—an attitude to which there are [p. 454]always associated extra-aesthetic factors of pseudo-aesthetic enjoyment, corresponding to diverse values, logical, moral, or religious, which explain the importance of imitation and of the characteristic in art, as well as the nature of the so-called aesthetic categories in traditional aesthetics.

Nevertheless, Witasek does not claim to give a complete and certain explanation, but only, as he himself says, an explanation of the second degree, a semi-explanation. What he sets out to do is to determine the causes of the aesthetic attitude; and since, in his conception, the nucleus of the latter is found in aesthetic feeling, he investigates its causes, ordering them, in order to ascertain afterward whether they can be subordinated to a more satisfactory causal law of psychic phenomena. His method is purely psychological, and for that reason he rejects the explanation of Lipps, who finds the root of aesthetic pleasure in an enrichment of psychic life, superior to its limited individual measure—that is, in the extension of that life to another self; in an expansion of one's own personality, or else in the feeling of sympathy, which Witasek regards as a feeling of value essentially different from the pleasure of the aesthetic attitude and which would explain only the beauty of value.

For that same reason he rejects the criterion of harmony, or conformity of the psychic with the physical, as well as that of unity and variety and that of illusion established by Lange, so as to hold exclusively to the empirical method advocated by the inductive sciences—without realizing that this method presupposes a directing idea, and that this idea is to be found in the faculty of producing representations, whose special aesthetic importance he declares, and which is none other than the free and creative imagination that characterizes the «fantastic feelings», aesthetic par excellence, and which, acquiring by intuition the representations of the aesthetic object, [p. 455]has, as Witasek says, «the mission of setting in motion the true and purely aesthetic disposition that makes aesthetic feeling possible».

There is, then, an aesthetic activity in the attitude of aesthetic contemplation and enjoyment, which must be studied as an imaginative function—that is, as a free and creative activity that may have aesthetic enjoyment either as its cause or as its effect; and this enjoyment, in its complete evolution, forms a circle that is born in that enjoyment and returns to it after having engendered the work of art, or that begins in the work of art to end in a new artistic production—without its being possible to find a more satisfactory explanation of that process than the free and creative expansion of the spirit, which delights in its own activity, whether in itself or in the objects that serve it as expressive symbols.

The norm of aesthetic value—or, better said, the criterion of aesthetic valuation—cannot therefore be the traditional criterion of classical harmony, which makes of a logical relation between the many and the one, proper to all knowledge, the determining cause of that value, deriving from it an enjoyment that is nevertheless not logical, and that has its cause in a passive feeling of freedom, in the feeling of non-coercion, expressed by the equilibrium of the human energies—the ideal of Hellenic life, in which the rational factor has so much importance.

Nor can the feeling of aesthetic enjoyment be a criterion of value, since its specific quality depends not simply upon its being an enjoyment, but upon the special nature of the fantastic representation that produces it. Aesthetic valuation itself produces an enjoyment of this kind, which cannot in its turn become the valuator. Moreover, by reason of the complexity of this subjective phenomenon and its infinite variability, it cannot give rise to a nor[p. 456]m, even when one descends to the elementary aesthetic feelings, which are those of the widest extension. The criterion would always be individual and arbitrary. The universality of taste, as a feeling, cannot be founded upon the homogeneity of human nature, as Kant believed and Witasek repeats; for that homogeneity is purely ideal and is founded upon cognitive activity, which is not the most radical in consciousness. That homogeneity does not exist, not even in the diverse moments of a single consciousness, which in its development renews itself without cease, as Bergson affirms. To claim to find in that infinite variety of sentimental moments a norm is the same as to claim the psychic measure of the heterogeneous.

The criterion of aesthetic valuation can be founded only upon the nature of the creative imagination, which is creative because it is free, because it expresses the free expansion of the spirit. Aesthetic activity, as an integral activity comprising the intelligence, the feeling, and the will, always creates, even in the state of pure admiration; for it is not pure reality, stripped of all fantastic vesture, that is admired in the very things that art has not engendered—it is not, not even when that reality is beautiful with a static beauty; for even in this case the imagination identifies its ideal with reality, and it is that ideal that it admires, thus fused into reality. Reality then enfolds in its harmony the static expression of freedom, which the spirit finds even in repose and which it loves in any of its expressions, without need of defining it, merely feeling it throb beneath some one of its infinite symbols.

If in aesthetics there must exist some norm of valuation, it must be founded upon the free activity that creates both aesthetic emotion and the work of art.

[p. 457]Wherever that activity engenders an ideal, there exists an aesthetic phenomenon, a work of the imagination. The error of the intellectualists, as of the sentimentalists, lies in always seeing, at the bottom or on the surface of the aesthetic phenomenon, order, harmony—whether of ideas or of feelings—and in regarding as the typical state of aesthetic activity that of pure contemplation, by reason of its disinterested character, of the absence of all practical finality, which imprints upon it an aspect in which the will loses the ostensible dynamism of the transcendent human actions and presents as dominant the phenomenon of emotion, determined by the representation of the aesthetic object.

It has been believed that in that state one finds the simplest form of the phenomenon and, consequently, its essential element, without reflecting that this is also its most attenuated form, in which the energy of the will, which brings about the psychic synthesis of the imagination, does not exercise its creative action in its plenitude and is reduced to a purely ideal activity and to an energy of tension that sustains such activity. That restriction of aesthetic experience has not allowed one to comprehend that the true typical state of aesthetic activity is that of artistic creation, in which the free will realizes its whole efficacy and offers the aesthetic phenomenon in its integrity, comprising within its intense, vast, and profound complexity all the aesthetic and extra-aesthetic factors that are fused in the artistic work by the free and powerful effort of the creative genius, which is the supreme exponent of freedom.
