In the intellectual character, aesthetic expression loses its value as representation, but it may have value, and very great value, as an artistic symbol of a great inner freedom associated with a great fecundity; and in that case, its inner beauty may even surpass the external beauty of the impulsive and combative character.

For Nietzsche, the superman, who is the aesthetically perfect man, expresses an omnipotent and destructive will that aspires to perfect humanity by destroying whatever there is in it of submissive humiliation, of religious resignation. For the religious ideal, on the other hand, the aesthetically perfect man is he who destroys human egoism, breaks his bonds with the world that surrounds him, and puts into this work of salvation all the effort of will that the superman employs. In the one ideal and the other, the aesthetically perfect is the free will, or the will that tends to emancipate itself from what it considers a slavery.

The diverse forms of the aesthetic character correspond, then, to the same criterion, which explains other variants of human beauty. Its distinction by reason of sex is simply a distinction by reason of the degree of freedom. All the attributes that serve man for the exercise of his activity betoken a higher degree of free life. Between the beauty of man and that of woman there exists the same relation as between dynamic beauty, which puts aesthetic harmony in second place and gives preference to the expansive force of the spirit, and that which sacrifices this expansion to the harmony of move[p. 502]ments.

For this reason one speaks of grace when it is a question of feminine beauty, and Souben is right to compare it with vegetable beauty. «Woman», says Souben, «has more of the plant, and man more of the animal, in her forms. In the latter, all the forms indicate advance, impetus, attack, dominion; in the former they indicate rather nutrition and rootedness in a place, as in vegetative life. Compared with woman, man tends more toward the sublime and the powerful; compared with man, woman appears more charming and amiable, more lovely».

It is when man and woman are united in marriage that they show the true human harmony. Marriage, it has been said, is a free harmony that perfects human beauty through fecund love. The child, by fortifying the woman's expression, serves to complete that harmony of power between her and the man, as art demonstrates in the Holy Family, considering only the equilibrium of the forms.

The aesthetic distinction by reason of age answers to the same criterion. The beauty of the child, like that of the woman and like that of feeling, is spontaneity, is grace, a form that reveals a free life, without the energy of a vigorous will, without any content of a value different from aesthetic value, with no content but the psychic energy fused into vital activity; a purely plastic beauty that lacks true psychic expression. Age enhances these qualities in the woman, associates psychic beauty with them, but preserves in her too the same characters of grace. In man, in the fullness of his development, beauty acquires all the elements expressive of the energetic will that predominates in his action. It is, above all, a beauty of free will, represented by forms in action or disposed for it. To the weak or disordered dynamism of the child succeeds the vigorous and harmonious dynamism of the mature man, who is conscious of his freedom, who feels the longing [p. 503] to externalize it, and who sets it in action, overcoming the obstacles that present themselves to him.

In the old man intellectual beauty shines. If the mature man aesthetically represents a conqueror of freedom, the old man symbolizes the inner freedom already conquered by experience and meditation. Old age that is pure inertia is not beautiful; its beauty springs from the inner freedom of his spirit, purified by time and by profound knowledge of reality. «If the old man», says Souben, «preserves the purity of his feelings, if egoism does not destroy his flight, and if intellectual development maintains the inner life with the freshness of new ideas, the old man, venerable for his gray hairs, may still have a moral beauty that makes his physical deformities forgotten».

The physical and the social environment introduce new causes of variety to those already noted, causes explained as diverse expressions of freedom exercised under the dominion of those very conditions. Lemcke points out the aesthetic superiority of the inhabitants of the mountains—agile, accustomed to varied movements—over those who live on the plains, who are heavy by reason of their activity subjected to the same movement. The hunter does not develop aesthetically as the shepherd does, because his hazardous activity does not permit him to introduce into his life the conditions that would give his freedom the harmony with which the shepherd models his own. For this reason the shepherd's aesthetic sense is superior. So too is that of the fisherman, who enjoys greater stability than the hunter and finds in it the aptitude for developing his artistic capacity. The farmer and the sailor present more developed characters than the shepherd and the fisherman, and their activity, under opposite conditions of stability and movement, presents a notable contrast. The incessant struggle with the elements of nature develops in the sailor [p. 504] the feeling of freedom; on the contrary, the sedentary life adapted to the physical environment produces an opposite effect in the tiller of the soil. But, on the other hand, these conditions favor the harmonious development of the external forms; so that, while in the former these forms are expressive principally of a moral beauty, in the sedentary tiller they are expressive principally of a biological beauty.

If country life becomes as eventful as that of the sailor, then the contrary may occur. «The constant struggle of the sailor with nature», says Lemcke, «shapes his character, valiant and provident, frank and rough, disciplined and sociable, and at the same time a lover of freedom»; but «as regards his bodily development, the sailor is not so normal as the tiller of the soil, by reason of the nature of his functions». Adaptation to the environment, more or less perfect, favors or thwarts the development of aesthetic vital forms; for at times they preserve the seal of that constraint, and at others, on the contrary, they exhibit their free expansion, ordered by life itself.

This is observed in the artisan who works in the open air, exercising functions that impose no excessive and mortifying exertions, and in the one who labors under opposite conditions. The biological forms acquire the aesthetic value of the beautiful in the first case, and in the second they are indifferent and may become ugly.

«The warrior ought properly to be the representation of the typical man, as regards bodily conformation», says Lemcke; but it does not so happen when military training turns him into a mere instrument of destruction. «By his valor in defying death, the warrior comes to touch the sublime», adds Lemcke; «but, because of the strict discipline to which the soldier is subject and because of his obedience to his superi[p. 505]ors», his mission is denatured. A defender of freedom, he becomes its enemy; a free force in action, he comes at last to be a force blindly submitted to the despotic will of discipline.

Ruskin, in his lecture on war, pronounces in favor of the warrior who dies defending the freedom of his fatherland and against the warrior who kills in order to destroy that freedom by conquest. Ruskin, in this preference, is consistent with the moralist tendency of his whole aesthetics; but the aesthetic value possessed by the power of the will, even against moral value, is undeniable—though in this case the contrast makes either the moral or the biological beauty predominate, according to the psychological state of the one who appreciates the one or the other. Moral beauty can make physical deformities forgotten, just as the beauty of the will can make forgotten the egoistic finality it pursues, before the grandiose spectacle of its destructive force, touching, in this case, the limits of the dynamically sublime, as in the spectacle of the destructive forces of nature. And this happens because aesthetic freedom surpasses and comprehends moral freedom.

If the warrior expresses the freedom of willing, the scholar, the man of letters, expresses the freedom of knowing. Hence the aesthetic difference between the two types, which correspond, respectively, to dynamic and to static beauty. Both types are fused in the aesthetic type of the integral man, who has developed all his energies harmoniously, at the impulse of that feeling of freedom which constitutes the essential motive of human activity.

Lemcke finds this type in the gentleman, the hidalgo, the knight, who «is the man developed, beautifully and solidly, in body as much as in spirit». This man, in effect, not only acts with the totality of his psychic energies in the determination of his acts, thus realizing the Bergsonian conception of freedom, [p. 506] but integrates that psychic activity with the totality of his physical and biological energies, putting himself, entire, into each one of his actions.

The aesthetic man thus realizes the whole human ideal, causing to disappear all the oppositions created by fragmentary activity, which gives predominance to one particular interest over the others and sacrifices true freedom, claiming to attain it in a single one of its manifestations.

The beauty of the free man is reflected also in the institutions of which he forms a part. Beautiful are all those that pursue an ideal end foreign to the egoistic motives of economic life: the teaching institutions, the artistic ones, and those of charity; beautiful too are the political institutions that arouse free activity, that develop it and defend it with energy. The State is beautiful, for this very reason, if it is inspired by that ideal of freedom, as Voituron demonstrates. Tyranny is opposed to this beauty, as the despotic will is opposed to moral beauty—which does not prevent the fantastic representation of the tyrant from acquiring an aesthetic character for the spirits that contemplate in him only a powerful force in tragic struggle with moral value. In that case, beauty acquires a biological character or is translated into an artistic form.

All the beings of nature associate and interpenetrate, producing a beautiful whole, which is called the landscape and which is the combination of the inorganic, vegetable, and animal beautiful, in which the intervention of man gives it a complete signification, impressing upon it a new life that it lacks as a mere harmony of colors, forms, and movements. That harmony is the work of the imagination, which makes of the landscape the expression of states of soul, a true manifestation of lyricism, in which the landscape acquires the character of a symbol of the free[p. 507]dom of the soul.

For this reason the feeling of the landscape presupposes a superior aesthetic culture in the one who contemplates it, a culture that excludes all scientific and economic finality. For him who observes nature with interested ends, its beauty does not shine forth; it hides behind the real representations produced by the industrial imagination or by scientific observation. This explains the keen repugnance with which Ruskin regarded the industrial development of England, which in its expansion treated with disdain the beautiful forms of nature. For the landscape has not only a physical and biological beauty, but also an idyllic beauty, as a reaction against the slavery imposed by social conventions in very complex and utilitarian civilizations.

Dauzat makes a classification of landscapes according to whether the sea, the mountain, or the forest predominates in them, and he regards as the type opposed to these the landscape without water, without relief, and without trees, whose synthesis is realized in the bare plain, the steppe or heath, or the desert, if all vegetation disappears. In the first three types the imagination is capable of creating representations that satisfy the aesthetic feeling aroused by their contemplation; but the contrary type engenders the feeling of the sublime through the introduction of the idea of the infinite, which escapes the comprehension of the senses. Art can, nevertheless, create symbols that answer to that feeling and perpetuate it. But in all these types it is the longing for freedom that constitutes their aesthetic content.

### VII. LO BELLO EN EL ARTE — VII. THE BEAUTIFUL IN ART

Nature cannot satisfy the longings of the spirit, however great its beauty may be. The rigidity of geometrical forms in inert matter, the fragility of living forms, the fleetingness of movements and of actions, the variety of objects—which is always framed within the more or less elastic limits of the genera—the impurity of reality, which the imagination is always capable of perfecting, are so many obstacles to the realization of that satisfaction. And even if they did not exist, there would never disappear the longing to create, to objectify the freedom of the spirit in signs that express, no longer the appearances of freedom that nature offers, but the true freedom of the spirit, which imagines superior realities and imprints upon them a spiritual life, by means of art, which may be regarded as a second creation of nature—not direct, but indirect, through human consciousness, in which the creative life is converted into creative spirit. The work of art, it may thus be said, is the continuation of the work of nature, which is the final work to which life aspires in its creative flight. Both answer to the universal evolution of which Bergson speaks. «Art», says Séailles, «is not the spirit that detaches itself from nature, but the spirit that penetrates it more and more, that sees and manifests itself in it; the beautiful lies in the reconciliation of the spirit with nature». But rather than a reconciliation it is a continuation of the creative activity of life, which is not in [p. 509]opposition to the creative activity of the spirit, even though, by its limitation, it offers resistance to it. Only the inert is in opposition to the spirit, which is not reconciled with it, and life is the destruction of inertia. Art and nature are always in accord. Art, as Bergson observes, «is surely nothing but a more direct vision of reality, a pure vision, which implies a rupture with useful convention, an innate and specially localized disinterestedness of sense or of consciousness, and, finally, a certain immateriality of life».

This explains the integral character of the artistic work, the sign of an activity that excludes no reality, but tends to comprehend them all, in order to satisfy, in the field of the imagination, the end of universality that philosophy pursues in the domain of the abstract idea, and in which science realizes particular ends, the theoretical and practical ends of thought. It also explains why art cannot resolve its problems in an aesthetic purely subjective, of emotion, nor in one purely objective, of the idea, which eliminate the true source of artistic creation or attribute it to emotion or to the idea—both derived from that same source, the will to create, without which the objectification of the spirit cannot be conceived, even though the representation of reality may arouse emotion and the first moment of aesthetic activity be realized. Emotion may end in a feeling that closes its cycle, as Wundt says, without being translated into an artistic action, into an act of the will whose result is the work of art. Aesthetic activity may be purely contemplative, even when it is associated with mimetic expressions; it need not be objectified in a work of art. This happens only when the soul feels the need to objectify an ideal of freedom, perpetuating [p. 510]it in an indelible sign, and when life identifies itself with that feeling and offers it, with greater or lesser spontaneity, the means of making it practical. Then the artist arises, and with him the integral activity that creates art.

«The work of art», as Gaultier affirms, «is the ineffable synthesis of subject and object, of the person of the artist with the living beings and with the things that move him». The activity that produces it does not, in fact, limit itself to fusing in an ideal all the energies of the artist, to expressing that fusion in a symbol, but goes so far as to fuse in a single rhythm of sympathy all the souls that receive its suggestive influence, thereby realizing what psychological aesthetics calls the Einfühlung of emotion; only that the suggestive force, which the activity of the artist transmits to the spectator and which tends to identify both spirits, does not derive, nor can it derive, from the idea, nor from the emotion associated with it, even though the mimetic manifestations of the latter be contagious; for aesthetic solidarity is not that of sensory pleasure, nor that of ideal pleasure, merely because it is ideal; it is not to be confused with the solidarity of logical, moral, or religious pleasure, although these values may serve as content for the higher aesthetic phenomenon. Aesthetic solidarity is born of the sympathy produced by free activity, because it is free alone and for no other reason than that it is free. Interior freedom, incarnated in an artistic symbol, has the power to unite souls with greater cohesion in pleasure, because it can unite them even in the midst of pain. The intensity with which it reveals itself in that sign, the rhythmic vibration with which the latter expresses the communicative soul of the artist, is not explained by aesthetic emotion, which is tranquil, which reaches its summit in aesthetic ecstasy, akin to the religious, and which, however disinterested it may seem, by reason of its lack of exterior finality, is egoistic in [p. 511]the sense of the absorption of the self in that ineffable enjoyment. What is called aestheticism has that character; it is not opposed to solidarity in enjoyment, but its supreme aspiration is to submerge itself entirely in aesthetic admiration, like the mystic in the bosom of God.

The intense suggestion of the work of art proceeds from the will of the artist, from his power to create, from the creation of a symbol of freedom. It does not derive, as Gaultier thinks, from aesthetic activity, in that this is ordered and harmonious; for in the works that reach the summit of sublimity, in which that harmony of the classical ideal disappears, replaced by the power of the will, the suggestion attains its maximum of intensity.

The work of art, like the beautiful work of nature, has its sole explanation in the principle of freedom. In Architecture, which is the artistic expression of the inorganic, of the inert, freedom reveals its beauty. Sully Prudhomme, following Schopenhauer, demonstrates this. «Architectural beauty expresses the joys of the intelligence and of voluntary activity in their triumph over the force of gravitation, which is the great orderer of the material world. These two powers remain, with respect to each other, in a state of persistent hostility; hence every sensible perception that attenuates or suppresses in thought the constant preoccupation with heaviness is agreeable for that reason alone. A form is condemned by saying that it is heavy, and it is praised by saying that it is light and graceful. The straight line, which is indifferent to us in objects that are mobile and light by their destination, pleases us to the sight when it is vertical or horizontal, in objects that must triumph over heaviness in order to conform to their end or to our utility. The vertical then gives us a feeling of security, and the horizontal likewise, because they awaken the idea of equilibrium, of a normal position. Thus we spontaneously [p. 512]rejoice whenever we see the action of heaviness annulled. With far greater reason do we sympathize with every image of a free flight toward the sky. The ascensional movement offers to the gaze a trajectory that expresses the triumph of the human will over its chain». Souriau, Guyau, and Deussen abound in these same ideas, which erect the principle of freedom as the aesthetic criterion of architectural beauty.

It has been sought to demonstrate that between architecture and music, which is the free art par excellence, there exists an analogy, to the point that the former has been called a frozen music. That analogy is found not only in the harmonic composition of its elements, but also in rhythm. «Architectural beauty», says Udine, «does not proceed from its forms, but from its material equilibrium, from its static rhythm, from the more or less perfect imitation of the heaviness that it suggests to us». According to Udine, the architectural emotion belongs to touch, but once in operation it moves the plastic and musical sensibilities, associating them—that is, communicating to them that quality which its free rhythm has of producing an aesthetic effect.

Architecture, that most mechanical of arts, derives its aesthetic value from the freedom that it suggests, whether by its ascensional type or by the static rhythm that results from its equilibrium, which is likewise an expression of freedom. That principle is found realized in the several architectural types.

Oriental architecture, which by its dimensions, forms, and materials translates the Egyptian ideal of repose, is not considered a work of art, but a revelation of the religious feeling, which has invented colossal signs, rivaling nature, in order to give symbolic form to its myths. Architecture is subordinated to religion in its meaning, and to the sci[p. 513]ence of construction in its structure. The emotion produced by those great masses, which serve as temples or as tombs, is that of the grandiose, which does not always become the sublime, as Witasek observes. They may lead to the meditation upon the energies consumed in those works, which presuppose immense durations and embrace considerable spaces; but the astonishment that may result from that meditation does not constitute an aesthetic feeling so long as the imagination does not incarnate, in a free and powerful spirit, the motor center of that unmeasured materiality; in which case the aesthetic value would lie in that imaginary creation, not in the elements that had suggested it, all of them expressive of inertia.

The same may be said of Indian architecture. Not so of Assyrian architecture, and especially of the Persian, in which art, without losing its utilitarian and finalistic character, tends to realize its aesthetic character.

Architecture realizes it definitively in its two fundamental types: the classical of the Hellenic temple and the romantic of the Gothic temple, of which the rest are derivations or intermediate forms. In the Greek temple, equilibrium—what Udine calls the static rhythm—imprints upon it, by means of its imperceptibly curved lines, the organic life of eurhythmy, producing the emotion of a mass that is capable of emancipating itself from the enslaving force of gravity. In the Gothic cathedral, its ascensional form, terminating in sharp angles, renders that emotion of freedom more vivid. The balanced soul of the Greek genius, incarnated in its gods, is reflected in its temple; the ardent soul that aspires to fly to heaven, in Christian mysticism, has its perfect expression in the Gothic cathedral.

Roman architecture, gigantic and terminating [p. 514]in curved lines, is the transition from the one type to the other, and expresses political power, which in the Roman empire, as in the Assyrian and Persian, aspires to universal domination. All the other forms involve the same content of freedom. Even the strange forms of Chinese and Japanese architecture produce the feeling of the graceful by the disposition of their ascending lines.

Sculpture has been able to accomplish the miracle of reconciling repose with free movement, imprinting upon matter the appearance of life. It has been able to fuse soul and life in a static expression that suggests the emotion of the dynamic, and in that fusion it has realized the classical ideal of beauty. But, as Sully Prudhomme observes, sculpture must not stop there; rather, its ideal of the future is to associate, in a just proportion, physical life and moral life, aspiring to express a psychic freedom that Hellenic art had not conceived. Sculpture may thus penetrate into the domain of the pictorial ideal and clothe itself in forms in which the dynamism of the romantic soul is revealed. Classical or romantic, sculpture always expresses the freedom of the spirit, whether in the attitude of equilibrium, of static harmony, or in that of a spirit which tends to break the mold of the plastic imagination and to raise itself freely to a superior harmony.

It lacks the means to realize the pictorial expression completely; it prefers, therefore, to present the human spirit in a tranquil attitude, or when movement and grouping indicate only the beginning or the end of the action, avoiding the exhibition of the soul engaged in all the collisions, internal or external struggles, or developing in a multiplicity of actions, as Hegel says; but it leaves to the imagination the labor of refining the rigidity of the forms and of penetrating through them in or[p. 515]der to discover the depth of the free soul, untranslatable by the mere perception of matter in its three dimensions.

Thus contemporary sculpture has been able, with Rodin, to attain even the domain of music, which is the free art of the free soul par excellence. Blanc believes that it is capable even of rising to the sublime, when it awakens the idea of an eternal duration and the feeling of the infinite by means of colossal figures conformable to the genius of architecture. Sully Prudhomme finds that sublime expression in statuary, which offers the triumph of the will in heroism; but within the very limits of its psychological expression it may reveal the profound intuition of the whole of life and be the sublime symbol of humanity, like the statue of meditation sculpted by Rodin.

This great sculptor used to say: «I reproduce, not only the exterior, but also the spirit, which likewise constitutes a part of nature… I accentuate the lines that best express the spiritual state I interpret». Rodin saw forms not in their extension but in their depth; he seized upon the interior feelings with intuition and expressed them through the apparent mobility of the muscles and the transition in the attitudes. He believed that he thus saw «the whole truth», and what he saw was the free force of the spirit creating its forms and translating them to the exterior. «The statuary of Michelangelo», he said, «expresses the painful concentration of the being upon itself, the restless energy, the will to act without hope of success; in short, the martyrdom of the creature tormented by unrealizable aspirations». But that artistic expression was also that of the soul of Michelangelo, endowed with a powerful and inextinguishable free force.

By this principle of freedom is explained the evolution [p. 516]of sculpture, from the anti-aesthetic forms of Assyrian statuary, which replaces the naturalism of Babylonian sculpture with the architectural rigidity of the human figures; from the colossal, rigid forms—likewise architectural or hieratic—of Egyptian art, to the archaic expressions of Aeginetan sculpture, which is transformed into the statuary of free life with the great Athenian sculptors. So long as freedom did not triumph over rigidity or over inexpressiveness, sculpture was not an aesthetic art. The expression of static freedom engendered it in Athens. Romanticism imparts a great flight to interior freedom, sacrificing the visible harmony of the forms, and the Renaissance reconciles those two ideals of freedom and imparts new life to statuary, creating models that contemporary art has exceeded in expression, finding forms that enclose the new aspirations of the soul.

Painting, converting the material reality of form into a mere artistic appearance, as Hegel says, extends its domain to all physical and psychic reality, comprehending the architectural and sculptural forms, but making of them the reflection of spiritual activity, in whose world it chooses especially its own proper forms. Painting thus expresses «spiritual subjectivity in what is most intimate in it and in its slightest accidents», being able, like music, to lay hold even of pure feeling as the subject of its representations. Its ideal is the dynamic ideal, which finds felicity in the conquest of freedom after the struggle; not only in the serenity of the struggle and of the interior lacerations that characterize the romantic ideal, according to Hegel, but in every satisfaction obtained by the triumph of freedom over the obstacles opposed to its expansion. That ideal is revealed as much in religious and symbolic painting as in [p. 517]historical and genre painting, and even in the reproduction of all those insignificant realities to which the painter has given individuality, rendering them independent of the ensemble that surrounds the pictorial personage and to which we always refer them, associating them with his felicity, as if they were his expressive symbols.

If the sculptural ideal, in its classical realization, is constituted by a freedom engendered by effortless harmony; if it eliminates every idea of struggle and of victory that would break the equilibrium of its elements, the pictorial ideal is the freedom born of movement, which aspires to create a superior order, raising itself above the finite of the sensible world. For this reason, in the classical sculptural ideal eurhythmy predominates; it is what determines freedom; but in the romantic pictorial ideal, which lives upon the most profound emotions of the spirit, that predominance does not exist, even though artistic freedom has for its limits those imposed upon it by the nature of its means of expression, drawing and coloring.

In that flight toward the infinite, which painting undertakes in order to satisfy the longing of the spirit, it may attain the representation of the sublime in heroism and sanctity, in the symbolic expression of the divine—an expression always animated by the breath of the interior life of the artist, who makes of that symbol the exclusive product of his imagination. It is that subjectivity which always explains pictorial beauty, even in its forms objectively devoid of any moral value. The painting of still life communicates to us the soul of the painter; its suggestive force is derived from there, as Hannequin demonstrates; the landscape is a state of the artist's soul; the diversity of its colors constitutes a symphony like that of sounds, in which the living spiritual rhythm moves in unison the soul of the artist with that of the spectator; genre painting fixes moments of felicity which [p. 518]are such because they are moments of freedom, and what seems most objective, the portrait, reproduces the emotion of the artist as he penetrates to the very depth of the spirit of his model. Thus Leonardo portrayed Mona Lisa. For this reason it is said, with reason, that «pictorial personages are characters rather than symbols; men rather than gods».

By that greater freedom in expression and in the employment of its means, painting exceeds sculpture, even though drawing unites the two. That greater freedom introduces the ugly into painting; disorder is not foreign to it as it is in sculpture; what matters to it is free movement, the individuality that translates it, and the coloring that fixes that individuality. Hence painting, as an art, has emancipated itself from the other plastic arts when the soul, breaking the mold of Hellenic equilibrium expressed by static forms, made of feeling the focus of the interior life and aspired to emancipate itself from the finite in order to scale the infinite. Painting, as an art, is born, in reality, with the Christian soul; it gave it its essential content, its own proper forms, which the resurrection of classicism modified, embellishing them, but without distorting that content. Nature and society, with their representations, have drunk at that source of subjectivity, departing from the religious symbols, but leaving intact the signification of art, which is the product of the free activity of the soul.

In painting, the idea of heaviness disappears; reality becomes a colored surface, which vividly suggests physical and especially psychic dynamism; but with music the appearance of free movement is replaced by the reality of that movement, inertia ceases to exist, and matter is in a certain manner spiritualized. «The particular character of music», says Hegel, «is to express the soul in itself, both by the form and [p. 519]by the content, since this art expresses the interior feeling and offers still, in its sensible form, something intimate and individual, that is, sound, which may be regarded as the destruction of the visible form». Combarieu calls it «interpreter and creator of profound psychic states, fine emanation of the spirit, subtle dynamism of the moral life, feeling and thought at once». A beautiful example of the spontaneity of reason, which rises higher than theology and philosophy, as Beethoven said; its knowledge is the work of direct intuition, as Schopenhauer affirmed.

For Combarieu, who has analyzed all the aesthetic theories of music, music expresses a «musical thought», by which is understood not an act of pure intelligence, but also a work of feeling. «Directly, music cannot translate any determinate feeling, but it translates from psychic life the intensity, the interior and general dynamism with all its degrees, and this means of expression, joined to the images that complete it, is one of the secrets of its power. Music abandons the representations and concepts that accompany the affective state; it retains only its energy; it is, so to speak, the dynamometer of the sentimental life». But Combarieu, who attributes to music the power of penetrating the personality in its essence in order to create feelings, forgets that creative power so as to fix his attention solely upon its effects. According to him, the musical composer creates not with feeling alone, but «with the whole soul»; but in that totality he comprehends nothing more than feeling with its energy and intelligence with the image, interpenetrating each other, without reflecting that in this interpenetration, in which the creative work consists, the will performs the synthesizing function of art. For Combarieu, music is the art of thinking with sounds.

[p. 520]Torrefranca excludes every intellectual and logical element from music in order to construct a theory that is, at bottom, related to contemporary philosophical intuitionism. He does not admit, however, the Schopenhauerian voluntarism that leads to the unconscious, considered as an «extinct form», as the memory of a mystical and heroic life of the spirit. «An aesthetics», he says, «ought never to ignore that there exist images which are not images, in the vulgar acceptation nor in the psychological acceptation of the word, but pure dynamic, abstractive, most general, unconcrete intuitions, which constitute the musical motifs, truly motifs of the spirit, concentrated movements of inspiration». «Musical intuition is a germinal and global intuition, the first form of the knowledge of the spirit in itself and for itself, and which comprehends also science, history, and philosophy, because all theoretical activity necessarily proceeds from this original knowledge of musical intuition, which is the form of knowledge most proper to the spirit, the truest, and the one that offers certitudes which do not change, which do not perish, which do not waver; in a word, the one that the human spirit offers directly».

Torrefranca thus reduces the two activities, theoretical and practical, which his compatriot Croce admits, to a single integral activity, of which those two activities are symbols. «Of that double form, the one is predominantly musical; that is, essentially dynamic, abstractive, inherent in the first apprehensions of the spirit, anterior to all external experience, and it expresses an activity of pure qualitative relations, having for their content aspirations toward the intimate life of the being; whereas, in the second degree, it is predominantly figurative, that is, essentially penetrated by concrete images, bound to the external world of sen[p. 521]sations; made, so to speak, of aspirations toward things and toward the relations between things and the spirit». «Music is the purest product of that first form of activity». «Musical intuition is an intuition ex novo, gathered at the moment when it arises in the spirit out of the vast sea of the fluid, undifferentiated intuitions that constitute the ground of consciousness. It is not an image absolutely, but a "moment" of a spiritual tendency, gathered germinally as a global consolidation, as affective intensity, and as a coenesthetic tendency of ascent and of pressure. Hence the character of profound intimacy of music, the ever-renewed desire and attention that inform it, and its fervent religiosity».

According to this new doctrine, musical intuition is the ground and the essence of the aesthetic phenomenon. Music is the art of pure intuition, which comprehends all the original psychic activity. Musical activity is the basis of all psychic activity, inasmuch as musical knowledge is the first form of knowledge. It serves not only to gather the various activities together, but to render them concrete, to sustain them, to coordinate them, and to direct them. «This fundamental intuition of the spirit, it may be said, is the first apperception of the total life of the spirit, the movement of the spirit and of all things at the same time. And the consciousness of a total life that transcends our life is, at the same time, the first foundation of religious knowledge».

Nevertheless, Torrefranca does not believe, as Croce does, that intuition and expression are identical; for although they form a single thing, expression is a quid that is isolated or isolable, wherein intuition obtains its just expressive value from the whole impulse of the spirit and of the form. He insists here on affirming the character of totality of [p. 522]musical intuition. The aesthetic phenomenon is for him the global, the freedom, and the indefiniteness of the spiritual affinities that expression contains within itself. For this reason he goes so far as to deny that spiritual musicality is identical with the will of the modern philosophy of the spirit—the will being considered as a specialized abstraction of the psyche; because musicality is the most generic aspect of the very unity of the spirit and does not represent, consequently, the will insofar as it manifests itself in the states of mind, which are not primary, as are the chords and the fundamental tendencies of the spirit. Music is, consequently, the first form of knowledge, as the first value of the spirit and the very condition of abstract thought.

In the midst of the obscurity with which Torrefranca expresses his ideas, he reveals a mystical tendency, openly opposed to the scientific one, and related to the intuitionism of Croce and of Bergson. Like both of them, and like Schopenhauer, the art of music penetrates into the depth of consciousness, by means of intuition, in order to find there the root of the personality, that original activity in which its elements are not yet differentiated, and in order to express it by means of the sounds, which are its necessary symbols. Like Bergson, he calls that integral or global activity freedom; like him, he affirms that this free activity can be known only directly, not through the figurative images. His conception of music conforms to the Bergsonian theory, which makes of freedom the essence of art. «Nothing in the world can make the soul so elemental, nor can reveal the interior harmony and freedom, as music, save religion», says this writer; only that, he adds, «while the latter tends toward systematization, which is dogma and limitation, the former tends toward increase, which is freedom». «For this reason all the epochs of spir[p. 523]itual freedom and of the reform of thought have been nourished and marked by fervent musical geniuses».

This amounts to declaring that what constitutes the ground of the art of music, like that of the other arts, is freedom; music being the art that, par excellence, expresses that feeling of autonomy, the fundamental tendency, the essence of the spirit. Torrefranca, fleeing from sentimentalism in art, has fallen into mysticism, forgetting that it is by freedom that feeling and thought are explained and that one arrives at that global and germinal conception in which he founds the aesthetic phenomenon. In the necessity of giving to that totality a content other than the image or the musical thought, he fills it with love. «At the bottom of all our actions or of our spiritual deeds», he says, «we find this capacity for love, in which, above all, art consists»; but he does not demonstrate in what this capacity consists—which is also an essential religious factor—nor how it is related to the growth of spiritual energy, to the freedom with which he had earlier been concerned.

Torrefranca makes the fundamental character of music consist in the activity of integration of the spirit; but that power, at once synthetic and creative, can be no other than the free will, which tends to expand and which finds in sound, in sonorous constructions, a direct means of exteriorizing itself. Thus music is essentially qualitative and not quantitative; the most qualitative of expressions; a true spiritual value expressed immediately, as Torrefranca would have it be. The aesthetic will may be composed «of atoms that are pure impulses; that are secret interjections of the spirit excited and exasperated in the closed mystery of its own passions, which it strives to know and of which it can only note the breathing of life and feel the gesture, as of an [p. 524]invisible divinity that stirs the air around it», as Torrefranca metaphorically describes it; but, in any case, it is a free and creative will, seized at that moment in which the representations, isolated from the ensemble, constitute motifs and determine that activity. He himself gives this to be understood when he speaks of music as the unconscious notation of consciousness, as ordered freedom, conditioned by an instinct of life that makes it tend toward the fullest efficiency of itself.

If in music the form is spiritualized, in a certain manner, by means of sound, adapting itself to the innumerable modes of the creative activity of the soul, in poetry the form is the image, a spiritual form that surpasses sound in its expressive capacity. Art attains, with poetry, the highest degree of freedom.

Hegel, notwithstanding his panlogism, makes of freedom the essential character of poetry. In contrast to the prosaic idea, in which logical concatenation dominates, poetry reveals that «free unity which, notwithstanding the multiplicity of the parts and of their developments, forms an organic, free whole, in which the parts are nothing but the development and the manifestation of the principle that animates them». That freedom is not that of speculative thought, which resolves itself into pure ideas, but that of ideal life, which is translated into images. The poetic work is for Hegel «a living organism, perfect in itself, free, rich in its content, and this developed under a form of its own, full of unity, yet without being governed by a logical law that subjects the particular to the general». «The poetic work offers, in its parts, that living independence which forms a harmonious whole, without revealing its finality. Full and penetrated by reality, and without depending absolutely upon it, nor upon any other foreign end that be[p. 525]longs to another domain of thought, the poetic work is the product of a free activity, which proposes to harmonize exterior nature and the interior world in an ideal order of freedom».

This exigency of freedom Hegel accentuates in treating of the lyric poem. The plot and the basis here is the intimate idea of the poet himself; but «it is necessary», he adds, «that this basis be really poetic; that the poet be endowed with a rich imagination, full of sensibility; that he be great, profound in his ideas, and, above all, free and independent. His soul must appear as a complete interior world, foreign to the necessities and to the servility of prose».

The ideal of freedom in art has not been understood and expressed in the same manner throughout history, and hence the great difference that separates classical from romantic poetry. The Greek ideal was sculptural; all art reflected it with the diversity of the external forms proper to each work, from architecture to poetry; freedom, as harmony, as equilibrium, constituted the ground of that ideal. For this reason, the epic element dominates in all Hellenic poetry, which is objective even in its lyric form. The Homeric epic has been compared to a bas-relief, in which the personages have the same expression as the statues; they are complete like these; they present man in the harmonious totality of his energies, without sacrificing them to the predominance of a single quality, notwithstanding the passions that diversify them; they are different, like the incarnations of the Olympian gods; but that difference does not spring from the depth of the self; the Greek soul is the same; it is a harmony that is identified with the Hellenic spirit. For this reason the most notable personages of the Iliad, as Croiset observes, are at once very living and of a very simple nature; and [p. 526]as to their gods, these are as living and as interesting as the heroes.

That harmony, which is translated into an independence within solidarity, is reflected in the cooperation of the heroes in the Iliad; their submission to a chief does not deprive them of their freedom to act in the common enterprise: they are thus beautiful, like the statue that concurs by its independent value in the beauty of an architectural ensemble; in their military actions they possess likewise a powerful individuality; they fight as if they were gods; and the poetic character of that struggle lies precisely in the grandeur of that free attitude, and its epic value depends, as Hegel says, upon the civilization whose freedom the heroes of the Iliad defend. That same grandeur makes Ulysses the hero of the Odyssey. Ulysses defends his freedom and his patriotic love against nature and the gods themselves. As Croiset says, Ulysses is the type of the man who wills because he loves and who realizes his will because he wills. The external forms with which these two poems express that content of freedom are simple beautiful signs of a superior moral beauty.

Lyric poetry among the Greeks was impregnated with that epic factor. In contrast to modern lyric poetry, which is, according to Croiset, «a poetry of a bolder inspiration, of a freer turn, of a more varied rhythm, and destined to translate the strongest emotions», Greek lyric poetry «was essentially destined for song, to which dance was joined; the beauty of the human form, animated by a cadenced movement, completed the beauty of the ideas and of the melody». It was dance, the dynamic development of sculpture, that imprinted rhythm upon poetry and music. Greek lyricism was thus inseparable from that same sculptural ideal, vividly expressed in epic poetry, which in its origin was likewise sung. Not all [p. 527]the lyric poems were danced, certainly, but the most beautiful were, such as the Pindaric odes, and the rhythm was always derived from dance. Greek lyricism did not depend, then, as the modern does, upon the musicality of the spirit, expressed by the most profound feelings, but upon the accompaniment of music, of song, and of dance. It was not feeling that was the essential and dominant factor, but the idea contained in the verse—the rational, objective element, which had to maintain its clarity of expression in the midst of that consortium.

Lyricism lay in the accessory form; at bottom the harmonic ideal of sculpture was maintained. The feelings it expressed were, sometimes, strictly personal, as Croiset observes; the poet then sang his own impressions in compositions generally lively and short; but the great and true lyric poetry of Greece was choral poetry, that is, sung by a chorus and danced, which could not limit itself, like the former, to the feelings produced by love or hatred, having, as it did for its object, to celebrate the great ceremonies of worship, the public or private festivals. The poet was thus constrained to submit his inspiration to a certain number of sources.

Of all those sources the principal one was myth. According to Croiset, «it may be said that there was in Greece no true poetry that was not mythical; because poetry in Greece was idealist and the Greek ideal was essentially mythical. For the poet and for the artist myth was always the ideal mirror of human life». But myth, or the idealization of Hellenic life, was a sculptural expression that contained what there is of generality in the spirit of the race. Hence the triumphal ode, like all Greek poetry, offered the double character of rising above the individual and above reality.

[p. 528]The freedom of the poet was, then, concentrated in style and in language. The lyric style had to rejuvenate the narrow circle of the ideas and feelings contained in the lyric poem. All audacities were permitted to it there. «The poet had full freedom to deploy all the luxury of words and of images, all the resources of a consummate art, sustained by a powerful inspiration and by an inexhaustible invention», as Croiset affirms. The lyric spirit, in the midst of this formal freedom, consisted in «a certain assemblage of tendencies that imposed themselves, in a certain manner, upon the lyric poet in the way of judging things and persons and in the expression of ideas and feelings, and thus the freedom of his thought and of his language entered within limits that he was not permitted to overstep». The Greek lyric poet did not let himself be governed solely by his emotions, like the modern lyric poet. «Pindar does not deliver to us the depth of his soul, he reveals to us hardly anything but what each one may let the indifferent see; he makes us no confidences. He is the impersonal voice of the Muse, and of this he is conscious. The duty of the poet, in the eyes of Musset, consists in listening in his heart to the echo of his genius. Pindar understands it otherwise; his role seems to be that of concentrating in his imagination all the beauty of visible nature and of abstract thought and condensing it into traits of fire, which he then hurls forth, with a sure hand, with a tranquil vigor and a reflective exactitude». «His spirit investigates the true and the durable; he likes to rest in the idea of the composite, in the idea of the nature of music, and thence his transition to epideictic eloquence».

Greek tragedy chose its subjects, taking them likewise from the heroic and mythical narrations. Those narrations, which referred to Mythology, expressed [p. 529]the history of the efforts made by society in order to organize, in a fictitious time in which «life was tempestuous, duty difficult and obscure, in which the individual superiorities shone vividly, in which loves, hatreds, sacrifices, shames, furies, and vengeances were prodigiously exalted». But the heroes of those legends were not fictitious, and «their life», as Croiset himself says, «was conceived only in what it has of the most elevated and essential».

The tragic personages were thus transferred from epic poetry and presented with the same sculptural character, even though in tragedy they are preoccupied with a single end, which leads them to the disastrous denouement. The tragic will is subjected to an ordering principle which, under the name of Destiny, governs even the will of the gods themselves. The tragic heroes struggle with their own passions and also with the gods, in order that that ordering and mysterious will may render its commands effective. Tragic beauty lies in that struggle, in which the hero sacrifices himself for a principle that at bottom is liberating. Prometheus is the symbol of the emancipation of the spirit, which combats the tyranny of the gods, the enemies of men. Oedipus symbolizes the purifying struggle of man with his passions, resigning himself to his fate with the intuition of the grandeur of his sacrifice. For this reason, as Hegel says, «perversity gives no occasion to tragic collisions in Greek tragedy; the tragic heroes are guilty and innocent at the same time; they act in virtue of their firm and true character and, by the exclusiveness of their will, provoke conflicts that annihilate that very will».

Harmony is reestablished by that fatal annihilation; but the grandeur of the struggle, in which free individuality submits itself to the moral order, is what properly constitutes the aesthetic character of tragedy. The [p. 530]purifying harmony of the denouement, the Greek catharsis, produced a feeling of moral value and even of logical value, as a rational consequence of the factors in opposition; but those extra-aesthetic feelings were in themselves associated with the aesthetic feeling of the liberating struggle, which produced a disaster. For the Hellenic spirit, enamored of the objective, those extra-aesthetic factors, symbols of a realized harmony, had the highest importance. Thus is explained the pedagogical character of the aesthetics of Plato and Aristotle.

The lyric element of the choruses in tragedy answered to the same pedagogical end; but by its adhesion to or its opposition to the tragic hero, it contributed, in truth, to enhancing the grandeur of his action, which, even though it obeyed the irresistible force of destiny, did not thereby cease to be a voluntary action and, at times, one of an almost divine rebelliousness, as in Prometheus. Precisely the legendary epoch, by which tragedy was inspired, is characterized by that struggle between the indomitable valor of the heroes and the ordering action of that immanent principle of morality which the Hellenes placed in Destiny and above the gods themselves, personifications of those capricious wills of the heroes.

Croiset describes a hero of tragedy, according to the ideas of the Greeks, as «a man capable of all the passions and of all the sufferings of which ordinary men are capable; differing from the epic hero in that he was not, like the latter, in possession of a supernatural force and, consequently, did not accomplish marvelous feats, his preeminence being purely moral, reduced to a certain majesty of language and of exterior that answered almost to the idea the Greek people formed of a king». Although this description does not coincide with all the tragic personages, in whom a divine principle was discovered, as in Prometheus, it does not exclu[p. 531]de the superior grandeur of the struggle, into which the tragic will of the hero entered, nor the aesthetic value that it offers, independently of the principle of harmony. The dramatic conflict is explained only by the concurrence of free wills; and just as in Greek tragedy pure perversity did not produce a conflict of a tragic nature, the pure automatism of a will absolutely subjected to destiny could not produce it either.

Only the struggle of great wills constituted the tragic interest. The aesthetic content is, consequently, there; and if so much importance has been given to the denouement, even to the point of making of it a basis of dramatic classification, this has depended upon the importance attributed to the moral factor, upon the ideal of harmony pursued by ancient art, and, on the other hand, upon the quality of the moral powers incarnated in the wills of the men or of the gods engaged in the dramatic conflict. The essential of tragedy lies, then, in the conflict innocently provoked by the human will that becomes tragic. Hence ancient tragedy has been characterized as a continuous lament, because that lament derived from contemplating the blindness of man, believing that he sees evil there where the good is, and preparing his own ruin by the very means that seem to assure his success. «That is what made tragic the powerful will of the hero, and that», according to Croiset, «is what may be called the essence of tragedy and what the strange religion of Dionysus contains, so full of turbulence and so powerful». «The bravery and the freedom of feeling, before a powerful enemy, before a sublime adversity, before a problem that awakens terror—that victorious state is the one that the tragic artist chooses and the one that he glorifies», says Nietzsche.

In comedy one must recognize likewise as essen[p. 532]tial an act of liberation. The purely comic involves that act, as has been said. The comic of intention, associated with irony and censure, arouses that same feeling of joy which derives from the destruction of the false considered as a menace. «The serenity of classical comedy», says Hegel, «is attained because the conflict disappears through the destruction of the insignificant, of the indifferent, placing the personality in safety». «What Aristophanes puts upon the stage», Hegel adds, «is the absolute contradiction between the true nature of the gods, the true principles of political and moral life, and the ideas, the passions, and the absurdities of those men incapable of realizing those principles, but who clothe themselves in the appearance of the eternal moral powers». The destruction of those apparent and false powers is what saves the personality; that is, the freedom menaced by them, without giving occasion to a tragic conflict and provoking the joyous feeling of the comic.

In the romantic drama it is the freedom of the personage, dominated by an overwhelming passion, that provokes the conflict and the tragic struggle and engenders the disastrous denouement. Whereas in classical drama freedom itself pursues a harmony or resigns itself to it by sacrificing itself, in the romantic that harmony disappears as the ideal of the personage and freedom acquires a completely dynamic character, the impulsive one imparted to it by unbridled passion, which leads it to disaster. In this conflict created by passion, perversity may enter as a determining cause. The moral interest varies in aspect; but the aesthetic phenomenon always has the same content: the free will which offers, in the struggle against other wills, the sublime spectacle of a power that aspires to the infinite and that succumbs under the action of superior moral forces. The denouement is [p. 533]always a harmony; but its moral value does not constitute the aesthetic content of the drama. Only the conflict is dramatic. When it disappears, the aesthetic emotion is absorbed by the moral emotion.

What predominates here is, consequently, the value of the self, the value of the free will in action. The tragic personage is eminently lyric; his passion engenders the tragedy entirely. That lyricism characterizes all romantic poetry. The Dantean epic is lyric; in its development it traverses the pictorial world of hell in order to become musical in purgatory and especially in heaven, which it floods with musical harmonies and melodies. The soul of Dante is of a profound lyricism. His character is determined by the free will, to which he sacrifices every other good. Lyricism, in short, is musical even in its descriptions and narrations; objectivity is found subjected to the subject, serving as a symbol of his longings, attaining in humor its annihilating form. Poetic beauty answers exclusively to that state of absolute freedom to which the romantic soul aspires, which maintains its artistic ideal even in the midst of the overwhelming adverse action of contemporary positivism.

The criterion of freedom is, then, the aesthetic criterion; because beauty, in its widest acceptation, is essentially freedom. «True art is the highest freedom and cannot proclaim anything but the highest freedom», says Wagner. And since freedom cannot develop except within a solidarity that is love, freedom and love must build art. «Only strong men know love; only love comprehends beauty; only beauty forms art», adds Wagner, that artistic genius who was the incarnation of freedom and of love.

### VIII. LA ESENCIA Y LA FORMA EN LO BELLO — VIII. ESSENCE AND FORM IN THE BEAUTIFUL

The aesthetic problem is not definitively resolved by the study of the phenomenon of the beautiful as conscious activity. Psychological analysis cannot lead to absolute conclusions, but only to inductions always susceptible of modification through the relativity of the elements that serve it as a basis. After the most complete examination, there will always remain pending a question concerning the investigations of the future. An absolute criterion can be founded only upon a Metaphysics.

So believes a disciple of Schopenhauer, the philosopher P. Deussen. Setting out from the disinterested and contemplative character of the beautiful, Deussen affirms that, since aesthetic pleasure cannot reside in the Will while the latter is individualized in space, time, and causality, while it is enveloped in the web of relations, it is necessary that the Will rise above the individuality that is its manifestation: whence it is seen that the disinterested pleasure of aesthetic contemplation is a phenomenon which leads beyond the physical order and whose explanation must be given by Metaphysics.

That explanation, in the end, Kant himself sought to give, notwithstanding the psychological character of his subjectivist theory of morality.

Metaphysics being combated by the positive or scientific conception of reality, both physical and psychic, the at[p. 535]tempt was made to explain the whole aesthetic phenomenon by the analysis of consciousness in its evolutionary process; but that effort, which has notably enriched aesthetic experience, has not left human thought satisfied, and still less feeling, which claims to find in the creation of an ideal order the cause of that specific pleasure which analysis has distinguished from other kinds of ideal feelings.

For this reason, in Aesthetics, as in Morals and as in the whole domain of human values, there has arisen anew, with vigor, the need to surpass the positive explanation by means of a philosophical one, which takes into account the experience acquired and integrates it with the results obtained through its own methods. To this end tend the contemporary philosophical theories concerning the existence and nature of freedom, whose modalities explain life and consciousness, their phenomena in the various orders classified by thought, as well as the values attributed by feeling, in the manner of characteristic qualities of those diverse categories.

To attempt this metaphysical explanation of the beautiful would be a premature and very lofty undertaking; but, at the least, it is fitting to leave set down some ideas in this regard, which may permit a better understanding of those set forth by the contemporary philosophers who react victoriously against scientific positivism.

The properties of Being having been classified by Philosophy into essential and formal properties, it has been debated whether beauty is an essential property, or whether it is pure form, or whether rather it consists in the relation between essence and form.

The ideas of essence and of form lack precision in philosophy and still more in aesthetics. By essence are understood the primary determinations that our under[p. 536]standing conceives in every being, the properties that constitute it such as it is and not otherwise: there corresponding to form the accidental or secondary attributes, the aspects of its reality. Consequently, by form has been understood the ensemble of exterior qualities with which physical and psychic phenomena manifest and represent themselves, in relation to the nature, the genius, and the characters of the order to which they belong.

Essence, says the «Technical and Critical Vocabulary of Philosophy», is that which makes a being be what it is. Metaphysically, it is that which forms the ground of being, as opposed to the modifications that touch it only superficially or temporarily. This essence is placed by some in the general and by others in the particular. Logically, it has two senses: 1º In the conceptualist sense, it is the ensemble of determinations that define an object of thought. Essence is then opposed to existence, as the rational to the data of experience or as the possible to the actual; 2º In the nominalist sense, there is no essence, but what the realists and the conceptualists have called by this name is nothing but the ensemble of characters connoted by a word.

The term form is almost always opposed to that of matter, in the Aristotelian sense. That term signifies A) A geometric figure constituted by the contours of an object. It is opposed to the matter of which this object is made. B) As a metaphor and by tradition of a very broad sense, given in the School to the opposition of form and matter, these words are applied to all analogous oppositions and particularly to certain oppositions of a logical, moral, or juridical character.

[p. 537]Form is made to depend on two relations: one internal and the other external: the first is that which it maintains with the essence, with the content of the object informed and its individual conditions; the second corresponds to the objects that surround it and with which it is compared, these contributing to heighten or to lower it.

In physical bodies, form obeys the conditions of geometric extension and of mechanical succession; in psychic phenomena, it obeys the qualitative principles that constitute them; but both offer representations which, making use of figures, of movements, of sounds and words, externalize either masses, bodies, or physical forces, or impressions, feelings, ideas, actions, and psychic forces.

Philosophical intellectualism introduced these ideas into the aesthetic order, opposing the idea of essence, as the content or ground of the beautiful, to the idea of form, as imaginative expression, whence came the division of aestheticians into aestheticians of content and of form.

The opposition between the ideas of Hegel and of Herbart, says Croce, created a struggle between the aesthetics of content and the aesthetics of form, whose protagonists were, in Germany, Zimmermann, Vischer, and Lotze. Form and content, he adds, are words to which a diverse meaning is given in the philosophical terminology of this epoch and, in particular, in aesthetics. Sometimes, what one calls form is called, by another, content. There is sometimes cited by the Herbartians, in their support, the saying of Schiller: that the secret of art consists in effacing the content by means of the form. But Croce observes that there is nothing in common between the «form» of Schiller, in which the aesthetic power is compared to moral and intellectual energy, and the form of Herbart, which does not penetrate and dominate, but clothes and adorns a con[p. 538]tent.

Hegel, on the other hand, often calls «form» what Schiller would have called matter, that is, the sensible material that spiritual energy must obtain. The «content» of Hegel is the Idea, metaphysical truth, the constitutive element of beauty; the «content» of Herbart is the element, both passional and intellectual, extrinsic to the beautiful. The aesthetics of «form» in Italy is the aesthetics of expressive activity: form is neither vesture, nor metaphysical idea, nor sensible material, but a representative or fantastic power, the shaper of impressions; and yet, one believes, says Croce, that one refutes this Italian aesthetic formalism with the arguments by which German aesthetic formalism is combated, a thing altogether different.

Considered as the ensemble of external qualities, form is for some insignificant, while others attribute to it an exclusive value in the constitution of the beautiful. For the idealists, the sensible conditions of form have value only as a means of expression, whereas for the sensualists or sentimentalists the essential or intelligible conditions of being play a secondary role; the beautiful belongs to the order of forms alone. Those who reconcile both theories do not admit the profound difference between essence and form, between the intelligible and sensible properties of beings, between the primary and secondary determinations; and attributing to them only a logical value, they give to those two factors the important role that belongs to them as inseparable and necessary elements of the beautiful.

But if form is considered, in its internal aspect, as the determination of the idea in the logical or in the imaginative order, that dependence is such that essence and form cannot be conceived as separable, except by classifying the qualities into primary and secon[p. 539]dary, a vague classification, which does not prevent disputing over their category. Thus, while some philosophers of the Scottish school maintained that regularity, order, and proportion were formal qualities of the beautiful, others of the same school considered them as essential.

The beautiful having been defined as a harmony between Nature and ideal freedom, that necessary reconciliation entails that of ideas and their forms, inasmuch as the individual ideal informed in the imagination by the idea is not beauty unless it is realized or incarnated in the sensible forms of Nature or of Art. Formal reality and essential ideality are, consequently, constitutive of the beautiful, and cannot exist separately in the aesthetic order, which is real par excellence, except in the logical analysis of the understanding, which cannot embrace at once the sensible and intelligible conditions of beings. The spirit can, logically, separate the idea from the form and from the expression, studying them in isolation; but aesthetic emotion cannot exist without there being a content expressed by a harmonious form, that is to say, without these three elements interpenetrating in such a way that they constitute a harmony: for, otherwise, pleasure would disappear, giving place to that state of indifference in which abstract ideas are thought or empty and insignificant forms are felt; a state to which one may arrive by a successive elimination, produced by habit and exclusive attention, which lead to the simplicity of the abstract.

In Taine's view, the artist, in producing the work of art, modifies the relations existing between the parts of an object, doing so in the same sense, deliberately, with the object of rendering sensible a certain essential character of the object and, consequently, the principal idea [p. 540]that is formed of it. This character, he says, is what the philosophers call the essence of things, and hence they define art as having for its end to manifest the essence of things. Taine substitutes for the word essence that of character, defines the essential character as a quality from which all the others, or at least many others, derive, according to fixed relations, and affirms that art has for its end to manifest the particular character, some salient and notable quality, an important point of view, a principal manner of being of the object, in a manner clearer and more complete than real objects do. Taine thus confounds the beautiful with the characteristic, or envelops the beautiful in the characteristic, which is the ideal, the perfect, force already ordered in its essence as in its direction; but not force ordered and free, free force principally, which engenders the beautiful in its graceful expression.

The characteristic, the typical, the purely ideal does not constitute the beautiful, as Taine believes, in his intellectualist conception of art, just as neither does mere form or expression constitute it. The characteristic, that clear and brief manifestation of the essence, is certainly agreeable. The characteristic interests, fosters the very comprehension of the form, is significant with respect to the essence of the object and even with respect to the essence of the genus to which it belongs; it is, moreover, as Lemcke says, of the highest general aesthetic significance, because the aesthetic depends much upon a sure perception and representation; it may, in many cases, be confounded with the beautiful, which encloses an idea of perfection that also produces an intellectual pleasure; but, in others, it may be confounded with the ugly or the aesthetically indifferent, as happens when one contemplates the types of ugly species, which are characteristic, or of species that have no aesthetic value through their lack of perceptible and sensible freedom.

[p. 541]The ape, for example, may offer a characteristic type of the species, which enthuses the naturalist, but which repels others; and, in Nature as in Art, there may present themselves objects, individuals, that realize all the external conditions of their genus without being either beautiful or ugly. If these ugly and indifferent objects in Nature produce an aesthetic feeling when transported into art, it is because the freedom of the artist imprints upon them its value. Artistic beauty has, through the force of expression of the artist's soul, that power of revealing itself in the production of objects that in Nature are ugly or indifferent.

The characteristic is, consequently, a mode more general than that of the beautiful, and one that may coincide with it. But if by character is understood, no longer the type, the ideal of an object, but freedom considered as essential, then the characteristic and the beautiful are confounded, whenever that character is translated into a graceful form that expresses the said freedom.

In this sense must be understood the classification that Deussen makes of character into generic and individual, in connection with human beauty. According to this philosopher, man is, above all, the representative of his species, of the Idea, of the human type. Resemblance, more or less perfect, to that type constitutes human beauty. Moreover, every man possesses an individual character proper to him. It is this that gives the characteristic to the actions and to the outward aspect of man. These two types must stand out in the work of art. The beautiful without the characteristic is insignificant; the characteristic without the beautiful becomes caricature. According to this, the characteristic is not a new principle alongside the beautiful; the one and the other serve to reveal the type, the one that of the species and the other that of the individual, which confirms the definition of the beautiful [p. 542]by order, which is the generic character, and by freedom, which is the individual characteristic.

Soriano Sánchez makes, in this regard, a distinction that may be referred to the foregoing. He distinguishes character from expression, in examining the natural forms manifestative of objects. In those forms, he says, we find something permanent, which corresponds to the essence or nature of beings, and something variable, transient, which corresponds to their state or the changes of their inner life; the first he calls character and the second expression. According to this, the character of an object is the aspect or proper seal of the genus to which it belongs, by means of which we discover its nature or essence, insofar as this is manifested outwardly, and expression is the excellence offered by the external form of the object, as manifestative of its inner state or changes. This distinction does not seem well founded; for without expression character is not known, and the most characteristic is precisely the most expressive.

According to this author, there is no beauty without character, because each genus has its particular beauties; nor is there character without beauty; but this does not mean that to equality of character there corresponds equality of beauty, because, within one and the same genus, as the character is made more specific the beauty does not increase, nor to a greater character does there always correspond a greater beauty. Nor does it seem certain that there is no character without beauty, if character is taken in a generic sense and not exclusively moral, in which case the affirmation is exact. Nor, moreover, can it be accepted that character and expression are not positive elements of beauty, as Soriano Sánchez maintains; because order and freedom, which constitute in the aesthetic phenomenon what is truly characteristic, and the grace that expresses them, are positive elements that integrate the beautiful.

[p. 543]It is inferred from what has been set forth that, if by characteristic or essential is understood only force ordered according to a type, it may or may not be identified with the beautiful; but if freedom ordered by feeling is comprehended, then the characteristic is identified with the beautiful. In the first case one will have the general characteristic; in the second, the individual characteristic or, in other terms, the ideal characteristic and the real or natural characteristic.

Croce, who reduces the aesthetic phenomenon to expression, debates this problem relative to matter and form or, as is habitually said, to content and form. Does the aesthetic phenomenon consist in the content alone, or in the form alone, or in both, in content and form? he asks. According to Croce, this question has had several meanings; but when the words have been taken in their true sense, when by matter has been understood emotionality, not aesthetically elaborated, or the impressions, and by form the elaboration, the spiritual activity, or the expression, one must reject both the thesis that affirms that the aesthetic phenomenon consists in the content alone, that is, in the simple impressions, and the other, which affirms that it consists in the addition of form to content, that is, in the impressions plus the expressions. In the aesthetic phenomenon, expressive activity is not associated with the phenomenon of impressions, but these are elaborated and formed by it. The impressions reappear in the expression, like water placed in a filter, which reappears the same and at the same time diverse, on the other side of the filter. The aesthetic phenomenon is, for this reason, form and nothing but form. Whence Croce deduces that the content is not something superfluous, but the necessary point of departure of the expressive phenomenon; but that, from the quality of the content to the quality of the form there is no tran[p. 544]sition.

It has sometimes been thought, he says, that the content, in order to be aesthetic content, that is, transformable into form, ought to have some determining or determinable quality: but that, if this were true, form would be one and the same fact with content, expression with impression. The content is, certainly, that which is transformable into form; but so long as it has not been transformed, it has no determinable quality; we know nothing of it.
