The content becomes aesthetic, not before, but only when it has effectively been transformed. Aesthetic content has even been defined, he adds, as the interesting, which is not false, but empty.

This theory differs from the foregoing in that the content is no longer an ideal, the result of a cognitive function, but an ensemble of impressions, of emotions, with an indeterminate subjective value, which is converted into aesthetic content by means of the informing or expressive activity of art. The distinction is established not between essence and form, but between matter and form, taking the word matter as synonymous with content. The conclusion at which Croce arrives, affirming that the aesthetic phenomenon is pure form, proceeds from the way in which he conceives aesthetic activity. For him, the aesthetic phenomenon belongs to cognitive activity, which is exercised as intuition and which is confounded with expression; it is theoretical and not practical activity, formal and not real; it serves as the foundation of logical cognitive activity as well as of practical activity, whether economic or moral; but it is not confounded with them, but is clearly distinguished from them.

Aesthetic activity is productive of images, logical activity of concepts, and practical activity of useful or good actions. Thus is explained the aesthetic formalism of Croce; but then the question is converted into this other one, that of knowing whether the aesthetic phenomenon ought to be included in theoretical or in practical activity; a question debated since Plato and Aristotle, and which contemporary voluntarist doctrines [p. 545]tend to resolve by explaining the aesthetic phenomenon as a spontaneous production of the spirit, in which the elements of consciousness have not yet been dissociated and constituted into isolated functions, like reflection, which engenders the concept or formulates laws, independent of the reality that is their content.

In the aesthetic phenomenon the free psychic activity and its direction are inseparable; because it is freedom that creates the content and the form at the same time. It cannot be said, therefore, that this phenomenon is only content or only form; because, precisely, it is its nature to destroy that separation, which is impossible to realize in the domain of the spirit, in which the imaginative form and the emotional content are the same thing. The separation can be found only when it is a question of the external forms, which are not always capable of translating the content into the internal forms established by the entire soul, as happens in the romantic forms of art. It is necessary to fail to recognize the synthetic activity of consciousness in the generation of the beautiful, in order to establish these logical distinctions of essence and form in the productions of the free activity of the spirit, which creates a concrete ideal and aspires, not merely to contemplate it, but to realize it as an object of happiness. To reduce the importance of the aesthetic phenomenon to pure content is to confound it with the moral phenomenon, which may restrict its action to the domain of pure feeling: to reduce it to form, with indifference to content, is to accept the formula of art for art's sake, an independence that is contradicted by the psychological analysis of aesthetic feeling, which recognizes the close solidarity of all the modalities of consciousness and the necessary concurrence of the social element in aesthetic genesis. Only the exigencies of method can, for that reason, permit the distinguishing of aesthetic forms, setting aside the [p. 546]content that animates them all.

This question of content and form has engendered the much-debated one between idealism and realism in art. Idealism, positing as the content of the artistic work the Idea, makes of it the essence of art, reducing form to the condition of an expressive means, more or less adequate to the Idea. Realism, giving to perception a value superior to that of the general Idea, places in the form, considered as image or percept, the whole explanation of art. Idealists and realists thus transfer to the aesthetic domain the opposition established, as fundamental, between the value of reason, which engenders the Idea, and that of representation, derived from the senses.

The logical problem of the origin of ideas has thus served to disfigure the aesthetic problem, attributing to those two sources of knowledge an importance that they lack in the genesis of the artistic work, the fruit of the imagination, which comprehends and surpasses the cognitive faculties, synthesizing the entire activity of consciousness.

Without the imagination, the Idea cannot explain the aesthetic phenomenon, either as emotion or as work of art; because the tendency of the Idea is to detach itself from the sensible form and adopt the logical form of the concept, which annihilates aesthetic emotion. Without the imagination, form, such as Herbartian realism understands it, also tends to convert itself into a logical expression of relations, when it claims to raise itself to an aesthetic system. Without the imagination, idealism and formalism lack life, lack affective significance, and, entering by different paths into logical determinism, deprive art of the freedom that is its essential character.

If Hellenic idealism created classical sculptural art, it was not because it expressed ideas alone, but because the Greek imagination expressed, through that artistic medium, the harmony [p. 547]of the Greek soul, which realized a static freedom. If romanticism destroyed that ideal, introducing into art the expression of the real, it did not wish to make of the expressed reality the end of art, but aspired to engender a superior synthesis of life, which should comprehend all reality and respond better to that dynamic freedom yearning for the infinite and the universal. In idealism, as in realism or formalism, art does not find its explanation, because it is placed outside the center in which it ought to be situated. And that center is the imagination, which embraces and surpasses both the Idea and the Form.<sup>1</sup>

<sup>1</sup> For greater clarity, some ideas expressed earlier have been repeated in this chapter.

### IX. LA PERFECCIÓN Y LA BELLEZA — IX. PERFECTION AND BEAUTY

Intellectualist philosophy always confuses these two ideas, thus serving as the basis of an aesthetic criterion that, in turn, confuses art with science or with morality. This twofold confusion arises from the vague, unlimited, and consequently imprecise sense of the idea of perfection, and from the predominance attributed to the intellectual factor in the constitution and appreciation of human values.

In ancient philosophy «the idea of perfection», as Boirac says, «figures, so to speak, only incidentally. Nevertheless, Plato places that idea at the origin of things under the name of the One-Good; in it he makes the essence of the true and of the beautiful consist, and he conceives it as being, at the same time, the purity, the plenitude, and the harmony of being. In Plato's eyes, that is perfect which contains no contradiction, no admixture; that which is absolutely one; yet not an empty and poor unity, but rather one that, on the contrary, encompasses a rich plurality of attributes and of powers, on the sole condition of bringing them into agreement and making them interpenetrate within the bosom of a comprehensive unity.»

«For Aristotle, perfection lies in the form that moves and organizes matter. The final cause owes its efficacy to its perfection alone, and the divine thought is the mover of the Universe solely by being that which is most perfect.»

[p. 549]«In Christianity, the idea of perfection, which among the Greeks had remained almost entirely intellectual or metaphysical, tends to take on a moral character», as Boirac observes. Upon the logical perfection of the idea there follows the moral perfection of virtue.

But if the idea of perfection is manifested in the ancient age and in the middle age, the same was not the case with that of perfectibility, which, like that of evolution and progress, arises in modern thought. Ranzoli affirms that in those ages it was a general concept that the nature of things was immutable, and that if anything changed, this change was always a degeneration that worsened it.

It is with Descartes that the idea of perfection acquires a primary and central value. He is the first, according to Boirac, to have defined God not by his relations with the world—as primary cause, as universal mover, or as the true intelligence of things—but by his essence, and this essence is, for him, perfection. «God is, by definition, the perfect being, just as the soul is the thinking thing and matter the extended thing. To prove the existence of God is to prove that there exists an absolutely perfect being; and the decisive proof of this existence can be deduced from the very idea of perfection. The perfect being is that to which nothing is lacking and to which existence necessarily belongs.»

Leibniz sought to define perfection by the quantity of essence or of reality contained in a being. This almost mathematical concept of perfection is confused, in the mind of the greater part of philosophers, with a wholly different and properly moral conception. Leibniz himself, as Masci says, calls the clarity of thought perfection—a logical concept that harmonizes with the quantitative one indicated above.

«Perfection, says Leibniz, is plenitude, force, and [p. 550]also order, fitness, goodness. Perfection is a kind of elevation, of loftiness of being; in other terms, it is an eminent degree of being or of force; perfection and excellence are the same. And the more elevated the activity or the greater the force, the more elevated and the more free is the being. But since force is the greater in proportion as a greater plurality issues from unity or is referred to it—being governed by it or finding in it its inmost principle—and since this unity in plurality is harmony, it follows that perfection is harmony and harmony produces beauty, which engenders love. Thus felicity, pleasure, love, perfection, being, force, freedom, harmony, order, and beauty—all this is one and the same thing.»

Ollé-Laprune, to whom the foregoing citation belongs, expresses himself concerning the perfect being in these terms: «To be perfect is to be such as one ought to be, to have in act all that to which one is destined by one's own nature: the perfection of a being is the development of the being in conformity with the true nature of the being, with its essence, with its reason or notion, with its ideal. And since the intelligent being is capable of recognizing this ideal within itself—which it bears precisely within itself by the very fact of existence—and since, moreover, it is capable of conforming to it through the free choice of its will, and it is itself the one that realizes it, perfection consists in living according to reason, according to right reason, and such a life is beautiful; and to act in view of the beautiful is also to act in view of the true and supreme end of man, which is happiness.»

In view of this discordance of opinions on the meaning of perfection, Boirac confesses «that the analysis and criticism of this idea remain still to be done; for even though Kant attempted that labor in certain passages of his transcendental dialectic, these are the most obscure of his work». It seems to Boirac, [p. 551]nevertheless, that «one may distinguish two senses in the word perfection, a relative sense and an absolute sense. In the first sense, a thing is perfect when it corresponds exactly to the end for which it exists, or again when it realizes exactly the type of the species to which it belongs. Perfection, so understood, might be defined, according to Plato, as the conformity of a being with its idea. In this sense, perfection is only a relation; it necessarily supposes a relation of comparison or of subordination between one term and another, and it varies necessarily with the nature of those terms. But the question of perfection may also be raised with respect to ends and types. It will be said, for example, that such an end, such a type, are more perfect than certain others, and this in an absolute manner. Perfection understood in that way has, so to speak, a content of its own; it exists intrinsically: it concerns the internal nature, the essence of the being, and not merely its relations of dependence or of resemblance to some other extraneous term. From this point of view, a thing, as Leibniz says, is the more perfect the greater its content of essence or of reality, the richer it is in attributes, the more fecund in effects; so that the absolutely perfect being is the one that contains the maximum of possible reality, the Omnitudo realitatis, as Kant says, the infinite of quality and of power.»

The idea of perfection consequently excludes all deficiency and even all limitation when it is considered as absolute; it denies the limit, which entails an imperfection; but it is incapable of fixing its maximum, because it entails the infinity of the qualities. In this sense God alone is perfect; but in the order of finite realities there is room for degrees of perfection, not only in the relative sense, but also in that of the comparison of

[p. 552]ends or types to which Boirac refers. The types perfect in their kind form, nevertheless, a scale of ideal values, according to the importance that thought attributes to them.

«A being, says Goblot, may have some perfection, a limited perfection; perfection does not mean supreme perfection.» Perfection is thus, as its etymological meaning indicates, that which completes a being and inwardly realizes its nature; whence perfection, as Bertrand observes, «is often synonymous with the absolute and with the infinite». «In this sense there are as many possible types of perfection as there are possible types of being», as Cresson affirms.

The relativity of perfection must therefore be understood in two senses as well: a thing may be more or less perfect according as it realizes more or less the genus, type, or ideal to which it refers; but these same genera, types, or ideals form a scale of perfection according to the qualities they contain and the ends they realize.

Kant attributes to this idea of finality an important role in perfection. The concept of perfection, says Kant, may be taken in a theoretical sense, and then it signifies only the completion and integrity of each thing in its kind, or of a thing simply as a thing in general; but in the practical sense, the concept of perfection indicates the state of a thing that is suitable or sufficient for every kind of end. Kant here surely refers to the particular end that is suitable to each thing. In the first sense, perfection is a schematic concept, a schema toward which are directed all the images that must render it concrete or individual, as is inferred from Bergson's theory of intellectual effort; but in the second, the internal or external finality attributed to the object is not the exclusive crea[p. 553]tion of thought, for there may also intervene in its formation the desire that is related to the practical end, by means of which the perfection of a thing is appraised.

It is upon this finality that Kant relies in order to distinguish the beautiful from the perfect, which in this case he confuses with the good. The finality of the perfect is objective, real, and internal, and can be recognized only by a concept; it is not external like that of the useful, nor subjective and formal like that of the beautiful. To appraise the internal objective finality we have need of the concept of an internal end, which constitutes the principle of the interior possibility of the object; consequently, in order to represent the objective finality of a thing, it is necessary to have beforehand the concept of the thing itself, or of what it ought to be, as well as the concept of the diversity of the elements of this thing in relation to that concept; which constitutes the qualitative perfection of the thing, and must not be confused with the quantitative perfection of each thing in its kind, which is a mere concept of totality, in which, what the thing ought to be having been determined beforehand, one seeks only whether all that pertains to it is found in it.

With this sense of qualitative perfection, founded on finality, another important interpretation is associated. If the end determines a direction of the criterion, it necessarily comprises the law, concept, or norm that the activity must follow in order to fulfill this end; in which case perfection may consist in the exact observance of the law, and the activity will be the more perfect the better it realizes the norm that leads to the previously conceived end.

All these conceptions of the perfect fall within the general idea of order. The Platonic idea, like the Aristotelian form, are expressions of order. The per[p. 554]fect, for Ancient Philosophy, was the ordered. This signification does not vary in the Middle Ages and is expressed by the absolute perfection of Descartes, which is, at bottom, the quantitative perfection of Leibniz, even though there enters into it the infinite character of divine perfection.

The idea of finality substitutes the dynamic order for the static; but in the former the end performs the same role as the type or ideal of static perfection; it is ordering, like the latter, as is likewise ordering the norm whose practice determines degrees of perfection.

Traditional intellectualism created that idea of the perfect, as the fruit of the effort of thought, in order to impress a fixed direction upon logical activity, as upon practical activity, the latter being considered a derivation of the former.

Since that idea of order enters into the concept of beauty, as into that of truth and of the good, one understands why perfection should have been confused with these universal values. Perfection thus turns out to be a generic idea applied to the other ideas regarded as specific. Even from the point of view of finality, although Kant established a radical difference between the objective and real finality of the perfect and the subjective and formal finality of the purely beautiful, of the beautiful in Nature, he recognizes a finality in Art and contemplates the order imposed by its norms as an order of the perfect in which that radical difference disappears.

For all those who judge aesthetic value by that aspect of order alone, the distinction is not essential. In art, as an activity creative of the beautiful, the perfect consists, as in every other activity, in the exact execution of the norms or laws. The beautiful is the perfect, and aesthetic emotion is a mere form of the logical satisfaction produced by the exact practice of the law. It is thus that the artist and the critic of [p. 555]art appraise the value of works of art, to which natural beauties are assimilated as an imitation.

The same does not happen if the beautiful is appraised as an expression of freedom. By that criterion, the perfect may awaken feelings different from the aesthetic one, and may even leave the spirit indifferent, if the perfection is indifferent, and may even arouse the feeling of the ugly. In the teleological order, perfection is judged by the conditions of the fitness of a being to its end and its milieu; but this relation of fitness or of harmony may be conceived through being felt, or else be felt with repugnance, as happens, for example, with the monkey; because in this relation freedom may be compromised, whether through excess or through deficiency of energy. Whence aesthetic perfection sometimes proceeds at variance with teleological perfection, and even in the opposite sense, as is observed in comparing the monkey with the butterfly.

Moreover, perfection, in order to exist, has no need of feeling; it suffices for it to be conceived and demonstrated; but the beautiful is a perfection perceived intuitively and not demonstrated by reflection, and above all it is a perfection felt with joy, with the joy of aesthetic emotion. In the merely perfect there is not realized that reconciliation between the ideal and the real which produces aesthetic satisfaction. In aesthetic perfection it does not suffice that the being realize its own internal end; it is necessary, besides, that there be expression, as Levêque says—that there be expressed the ordered freedom with which the being lives and develops; one must perceive and feel the free force of existence, within the ordered combination of forms, whether or not it tends toward the realization of an end.

There is not, then, a radical separation between the perfect and the beautiful, such that they cannot be reconciled as Kant believes, because in the beautiful there may al[p. 556]so be the idea of the end, and it does in fact enter as inherent in the character of freedom, which is essential to it.

The pleasure of the beautiful is the feeling of a perfection, as Fouillée says, and not the abstract judgment of this perfection, as Kant understood it.

What has been said serves to demonstrate that, when the characteristic is confused with the beautiful, one incurs the error of confusing the perfect with the beautiful, because the characteristic is, in short, a form of the perfect. What Deussen calls character is nothing other than the perfection of the being, whether it serve to reveal the type of the species or of the individual. Character is taken, in the same sense of perfection, by Taine as by Sánchez Soriano. The characteristic, if it be no more than the typical—leaving aside the element of freedom—is the generic perfect that comprises the beautiful, but does not specify it. The characteristic, like the perfect, refer essentially to the ideal factor of order, to the rational or cognitive factor, which does not explain the beautiful as a species of the perfect, because it leaves aside the affective and volitional elements that determine its nature.

A contemporary aesthetician, Paul Souriau, in his «Rational Aesthetics», defines beauty as evident perfection. Souriau defines perfection by the finality of a being. «Objectively, he says, a thing may be called perfect when it is what it wants to be or what it ought to be; in a word, when it is in conformity with its end.» This end, in so far as it is conceived by us, is what he calls an ideal. To find that ideal, or the end of each thing—such is the essential labor of aesthetics.

This philosopher acknowledges that, in reducing beauty to a relation of means to end, he has eliminated from his aesthetics almost entirely a very important element that other theorists have, on the contrary, devoted themselves to bringing into concord: the very idea of freedom; but he affirms that, if [p. 557]there are free beauties, as Kant establishes, common sense, reason, and taste itself agree in recognizing in the beauty of finality the maximum of aesthetic value.

Summarizing his observations on the hierarchy of ends, he arrives at the following consequences: Beauty is found in evident perfection. Every thing is perfect in its kind when it is in conformity with its end. The degrees of perfection are measured by the relative value of the ends. The highest end we can conceive consists in the full expansion of conscious life.

Souriau does not say, however, how this expansion of life is appraised—which might have as its criterion the degree of organization or order of the being, in accordance with its type, or the degree of freedom acquired by means of that organization. According to him, intelligence is finality itself; it is the faculty of ordering actions in view of an end or according to a directing idea; but intelligence, by itself alone, may qualify as perfect certain beings that are repugnant to feeling, ugly beings, which would be beautiful for being perfect.

The beauty of the perfect, by reason of finality, is thus confused with the beauty of the typical or of the characteristic, even when the factor of evolutionary expansion is included, as Souriau does. To define the beautiful by the perfect is to define it by order, confusing it with other ideas in which this element enters as essential; and to define it by order is to suppose that beauty is subject to a categorical imperative, which is contrary to its nature.

Souriau falls into this error. Between the good and the beautiful he sees only a difference of degree: the beautiful is the good raised to such a degree that it deserves to excite admiration.

Another contemporary aesthetician, Lalo, makes the idea [p. 558]of perfection more precise by reducing it to a relation of beauty with artistic technique and by suppressing, for that purpose, the spontaneous beauty of nature. The technical criterion, by means of which the value of art is appraised, in reality introduces the idea of the perfect as essential in the beautiful; but that idea excludes the absolute freedom of genius and is contrary to artistic creation. Creation and freedom are identical. The one cannot be conceived without the other.

Absolute submission to technique is opposed to those ideas essential in art and disregards the very origin of the rules imposed by tradition. If one does not admit an aesthetic noumenon as legislator, it must be admitted that the aesthetic canons were born of the freedom of the artist, together with the works of art. On the other hand, if beauty consisted in that perfection, it would increase in proportion as submission to technique became greater, reaching its maximum with the complete servility of the artist—which it is absurd to suppose and is contrary to the facts.

The perfect, even in this sense of obedience to technique, does not explain the beautiful, nor is it confused with it. The feeling of the perfect is not necessarily aesthetic. It may be associated with the latter or not: it is a logical feeling that is related to the aesthetic one and may produce an enjoyment resembling the pleasure of the beautiful, or substituting for it, as happens when only the technical conditions of the artist are appraised in a work. The criterion is then reflective and not intuitive. It is more logical than aesthetic. The spectator, without technical culture but with a spontaneous aesthetic culture, makes no use of that criterion: he intuits beauty in intuiting the free life that it expresses, and pronounces upon its value freely, not by virtue of submission to a norm.

### X. LA BELLEZA Y LA VERDAD — X. BEAUTY AND TRUTH

It seems, at first glance, that it would be easy to establish, among these general ideas, their relations of resemblance or difference, taking their content and extension as already known. And yet, nothing is more difficult than to define those concepts, and, consequently, nothing more difficult than to determine that content and extension. General ideas, which in their concrete realization produce clear representations, in their abstract form lose that precision and are susceptible of diverse interpretations and meanings.

The ideas of beauty and of truth are subject to that indeterminacy, and hence the necessity of adopting one of their meanings in order then to fix their reciprocal relations of resemblance or difference. The idea of beauty presents as its essential marks those of order and freedom, being defined by the one or by the other according to whether one adopts, as its type, classical beauty, in which order predominates, or romantic beauty, in which freedom surpasses and subordinates order.

The ideas of beauty and of truth resemble one another, because in both there exists order, the product of intellectual activity, and they differ in the manner in which the dynamic principle of freedom enters into them. For this reason, in order to mark the difference between the aesthetic concept and the logical one, it is necessary to adopt the definition of the beautiful by freedom and not by the order that confounds them.

On another occasion we have justified that necessity, [p. 560]demonstrating that, from the subjective point of view as well as the objective, freedom is the essential mark of beauty in its diverse expressions. As regards truth, the analysis that has been made of its varied forms reveals that, in all of them, what is generic is a relation, a logical form of thought.

G. Ramousse, in his «Essay on a Scientific Theory of the Concept of Truth», reduces to four the acceptations that this concept receives in the collective consciousness, as the result of an oscillation between two fundamental conceptions of truth, grounded upon the autonomy of the subject and of the object.

The first is the idealist conception, which consists in suppressing the opposition of those two terms by the absorption of the one into the other, or in declaring the object unknowable; whence result subjective idealism, objective idealism, and absolute idealism, or logical or syllogistic formalism. In all these cases, the element common to those forms of idealism is the absolute freedom of the spirit, whence proceeds this definition of truth: the agreement of thought with itself. The realist conception, on the contrary, keeps the two terms, subject and object, separate, whether the object be radically different from the spirit or partially identical with it; whence results this other definition of truth: the agreement of thought with the object.

The element common to these two antithetical definitions is that truth consists in a relation between two terms. But, for the idealist conception, truth is absolute, infinite, impersonal, necessary, and resides wholly in the unconditioned unity of the Idea, from which it is deduced according to the principle of identity; whereas, for the realist conception, truth possesses the opposite characters.

For Ramousse truth is, in every case, a relation; though it must not be understood as a rela[p. 561]tion of static elements, but rather in its mobile reality, as a relation between dynamic elements, as the relation of that indefinite possibility of representation which constitutes the object, in each of the moments of its realization, within the consciousness of the thinking subject.

Prattle attributes three senses to truth: truth as identical with reality or with being, or, as Bradley defines it, as the whole Universe realizing itself of itself under one of its aspects: the metaphysical sense; truth as belief, as verified and accepted opinion: the sense attributed to it by logic and positive psychology; and truth as property or relation, by virtue of which an idea is true or exact.

Paulhan increases still further the diverse significations of this concept and admits what he calls the mirror-truth, the symbol-truth, the harmony-truth, the free-belief-truth, the opinion-truth, the illusion-truth, and the utility-truth, or pragmatic conception of the true. These are so many relations, from among which Paulhan chooses, as the definition of true-truth, of truth in the full and entire sense of the word, the mirror-truth: not as it is commonly understood, as the agreement of reality and of thought, but as the abstract identity of the represented object and of the idea that represents it, a resemblance of relations and of tendencies, which reflects of objects only their essential relations. Truth is thus a kind of organization, of systematization of resemblance.

But «the mirror-truth, even with the complications it demands, does not lead us very far», says Paulhan. «Real existences remain to us, if not absolutely unknown, at least very strange, unknowable or unknown under many aspects. Between them and us there are often few true communications. [p. 562]They lack the details that would make them precise, that would fix them in the spirit, that would associate them with known tendencies, with concrete images. These are invented, if they do not possess them, or else they must be invented. The symbol-truth and the harmony-truth serve as useful means or necessary procedures of the mirror-truth, supplying it when we cannot attain it, or allowing us to reach it in the measure of the possible». But it is in this domain that there swarm what Paulhan calls truths-errors.

Not only are varied acceptations given to truth, but there is even a conspiracy against its worth, tending to destroy it. «Under the action of the double analysis that Nietzsche makes, from the metaphysical point of view as well as from the phenomenal point of view», says Gaultier, «truth loses its interest, its prestige, and its divinity. From the first point of view, it implies contradiction; from the second, it governs only a category of realities indifferent to humanity. Whereas the world of Knowledge springs expressly from the concept of truth, the world of Being never undergoes the application of that concept.» «It is in order to mark this difference strongly», adds Gaultier, «that Nietzsche has given non-truth as the condition of Being; non-truth being thus understood as the entire content of Knowledge, in opposition to its form. Non-truth is that which supports no integral explanation, that which withdraws itself from everything; for it is also everything that is real; it is sensation in its intangible essence, it is the object, taste, vision, desire, all that involves struggle, conflict, appreciation, and the fixing of values.»

Through these varied conceptions of truth, we may find, as a common ground, the idea of a system of relations between the subject and the representation of the object, first, and afterwards between the subject and the concept of the object, which is a transformation and a [p. 563]progress of the earlier form. A system of relations and not a simple relation, because the two terms they unite are complexes of phenomena, of data, or of logical marks. Hence the two coordinate forms of truth: real truth and logical truth, which tend to identify the subject with the object. The idea of truth, circumscribed in that manner, may be replaced by the idea of order, which expresses a system of relations.

This idea of order excludes every form or content that would deprive it of its abstract, strictly logical character, as a relation between logical marks, concepts, or judgments; in which case it has no connection whatever with beauty, which is a reality, in some manner free, and which falls under the dominion of imagination; but which may be converted into organic harmony, in which freedom is represented by equilibrium, by non-coercion, the static form of freedom. Such is the classical concept of the beautiful.

It is in this sense that Hellenic idealism, like Hegelian idealism and Herbartian realism, appraises the beautiful, setting out now from the Idea, now from the representation, so as to make the true the basis of the aesthetic conception. Hellenic idealism finds in Plotinus a definition of the beautiful as «the splendor of truth»; Aristotelian realism does not depart from this confusion between the true and the beautiful.

But it is Hegel who has made this relation precise. «We call beauty», says this philosopher, «the idea of the beautiful. The beautiful must therefore be conceived as idea and, at the same time, as the idea under a particular form, as the ideal. The beautiful is not, consequently, the abstract or unrealized idea, but the concrete or realized idea, inseparable from the form, as this is inseparable from the principle that appears in it. Nor is one to see in the idea a mere generality or a grouping of quali[p. 564]ties, deduced from real objects. The idea of the beautiful is the ground, the very essence of all existence, the type, the real and living unity of which visible objects are but the exterior realization. Thus the true idea, the concrete idea, is that which gathers the totality of its elements developed and manifested by the assemblage of beings. The idea, in a word, is a whole, the harmonious unity of that universal assemblage, which develops itself exteriorly in nature and in the moral world, or the world of spirit». «Only thus», adds Hegel, «is it that the idea is truth and all truth. All that exists has therefore of truth only that which of the idea has passed into the state of existence, because the idea is the true and absolute reality. All that appears as real to the senses and to consciousness is not true by this concept, but because it corresponds to the idea, because it realizes it. Otherwise the real is a mere appearance».

Hegel deduces from this definition of the idea or of the ideal that, if it is said that beauty is the idea, it is because beauty and truth, from one point of view, are identical. Nevertheless, he establishes a difference between the true and the beautiful. Truth is the idea considered in itself, in its general principle and in itself, and thought as such; for it exists for reason not in its external and sensible form, but in its general, universal character. When truth presents itself immediately to the spirit in external reality, and the idea remains merged and identified with its exterior appearance, then the idea is not only true but beautiful. The beautiful is defined, then, as the sensible manifestation of the idea.

This definition reproduces the Hellenic concept, in which the harmony between the ground and the form, that is, between the idea and the sensible expression, constituted the beautiful. Such [p. 565]an idea was the Platonic archetype, the model of real things, or the Aristotelian form, the essence of beings, an idea likewise, truth as was the former, which in its determination constituted beauty, creating that harmony. For Plato, as for Aristotle, harmony or order defined truth as well as beauty, confounding them.

If Hegel reproduces classical idealism, reconciling Plato and Aristotle, as Plotinus did, Herbart, with his realism, follows Aristotle in giving to the real representation a value superior to the idea understood as universal; but Herbart defines beauty as a relation between representations and forms, and thus he too confounds beauty with truth, the aesthetic judgment with the logical judgment, orienting toward positive science the conception of the beautiful, as Hegel had done, in the contrary sense, toward Ontology.

This confusion of the true with the beautiful has been maintained, notwithstanding the efforts made to distinguish these concepts; for, both having been grounded upon the idea of order, the difference marked by Hegel between the abstract order and the concrete, between the pure idea and the realized one, has not been sufficient to explain a more profound difference, which is born of the content of the beautiful, into which enter all the factors of consciousness, subordinated to that of freedom, and not only the intellectual elements that engender the idea, whether the abstract universal or the concrete particular, whether the pure concept or the representation that serves as its origin.

This confusion is not avoided by considering truth as a force, as Gestinel does, or by attributing to the concept of truth the dynamic and moral character with which Eucken defines it. «The content of a new conception of truth», says Eucken, «is determined by the nature and the direction of activity. [p. 566]Truth does not signify only concordance with an object situated exteriorly, but an ascent toward an order superior to all human arbitrariness, and which, by a creative activity, embraces the opposition of subject and object. This tendency toward truth has nothing in common with an immobile being that would exist independently of all life; truth is found, on the contrary, within life, and can be attained only through life, which must not be considered as something relative to man pure and simple, but as an absolute value. Truth is thus not a mere means of elevating this life, but forms part of its essence, and its conquest is not the work of an instant, but of a spiritual progress, sustained throughout history; for there is no intellectual truth without a truth of the whole spirit, which signifies the transformation of the world into personal life».

This conception of truth, which may be considered as derived from Fichtean subjectivism, is one of the four acceptations that Ramousse considers. The truth of the whole spirit is that of the I, in which the not-I is, in the end, absorbed; but the evolution it undergoes does not suppress its character as a relation between the subject and the object, established by thought, even when that relation is lost at the moment of absorption, in which truth becomes existence. Eucken himself admits that the life of the spirit constitutes the ultimate ground of reality, and that the syntheses of that life presuppose a struggle in which knowledge has a directing role, so as to give to that life its cosmic character. Truth forms, certainly, part of the essence of spiritual life; but it constitutes it, in this case, by establishing a relation, not by creating the reality of that life, through which the intellectual tendency attains its object.

[p. 567]With a criterion opposed to that of the intellectualists, who have made of beauty an expression of truth, the finalist aestheticians, grounding themselves likewise upon the view that the beautiful is harmony only, have subordinated truth to beauty, incurring the same error of confounding different categories of thought. Fouillée, referring to the philosophical movement inspired by Ravaisson, observes that this philosopher and his disciples «are not content to admit that mechanism does not explain everything in nature, but hold that even mechanism is explained by considerations of order and of harmony, and that its laws find in aesthetics their ultimate and radical reason. Induction, upon which all knowledge of Nature reposes, is, in their eyes, a kind of poetry that seeks to penetrate the sense of the Universe.»

Thus for Ravaisson «beauty is not only the sign of morality, but also that of truth itself, and above all of philosophical truth; aesthetics, at bottom, conceals science; beauty, and chiefly the most divine and the most perfect, contains the secret of the world; the ultimate and radical reason of all mathematics, which is merged with creative activity, is, without doubt, symmetry and beauty; this explains crystallization and organization in the forms of Nature, which seems to seek the beautiful for the beautiful's sake, to make art for art's sake. The whole world, for Ravaisson, is the work of an absolute beauty, which is the cause of things through the love it places in them.» Lachelier, a disciple of Ravaisson, does not fear to say that a truth which was not beautiful would be only a logical game of our spirit, and that, harmony being a degree of beauty, however feeble it may be, the only solid truth worthy of this name is beauty.»

Lachelier, like his master, thus recasts all philosophy, and even all science, into aesthetics. For Boutroux, who upholds the same doctrine, «the superior principles of things are moral and aesthetic laws, expres[p. 568]sions more or less immediate of the perfection of God, pre-existing to phenomena and presupposing agents endowed with spontaneity.» Janet, «without going so far as the preceding philosophers, admits, nevertheless, a universal finality and a universal art, which presupposes an eternal artist». For Thouverez, aesthetics is the ultimate criterion of things; works are appraised and classified by rational relations, by the distinction established between incoherence and harmony. Substance, causality, finality, duty, all signify order and activity. The principle of harmony is the soul of science, of morals, and of aesthetics.

This subordination of truth to beauty is found even among contemporary men of science. Léon Brunschvicg, in his work «Nature and Freedom», affirms that «for Poincaré beauty is the end of science», as the neo-Aristotelianism of Ravaisson's school has maintained—a school which, like the determinists of efficient causes, confounds, in the idea of order or harmony, beauty and truth, both constituted by a system of relations.

Truth and beauty do not stand in that relation of reciprocal subordination which some have wished to establish by attributing to both that essential character of harmony or order proper to the first; but their difference, however radical it may be, does not make of them an insoluble antithesis, as though they were opposed realities, incapable of coordination. Leopardi, as a poet, affirmed that the true was the ugly, «because it destroyed cheerful dreams and stripped away the freshness of things, although it might, at times, offer some delight». On the other hand, Benda, in his «Essay on the Aesthetic of Present-Day French Society», maintains that «aesthetic mysticism, an exaggeration of philosophical subjectivism, carries its odium for thought and for truth so far as to eliminate completely, [p. 569]from aesthetic emotion, that factor, and to reduce it to a pure affective state», as though truth were the enemy of beauty; a conception that reduces consciousness to an inexplicable passivity, and that can be sustained only by the artist in the paroxysm of a maddening emotion.

Aesthetic emotion has not that efficacy; on the contrary, it is liberating, and in its genesis it neither rejects the idea, which is image, nor tends toward disorder in the spirit. Far from it, it is the most perfect synthesis of conscious activity, which seeks, in the integrity of the real, a symbol of its perfection. Truth and beauty are not opposed, for this reason; but neither are they confounded, as those think who attribute to the one and the other properties they do not possess.

Truth is nothing more than a system of relations, even in its dynamic or pragmatic conception, without there being attributable to it, as its own property, the power to systematize, to unify, which, in a voluntarist psychology, belongs to the total energy of consciousness. Truth, in the last result, is either an order established definitively as absolute, or an order that integrates itself successively with the progress of life; but it is nothing more than order, a product of thought, which offers empirical data or rational marks that are identified, or tend to be identified, with thought in the exercise of its function of knowing. In the very pragmatic concept of truth, in which James refers to the practical character of all experience, capable of provoking a mental satisfaction, an impression of repose and of peace, a feeling of coherence and of rationality, Moulin, his commentator, observes «that thus the investigation of truth is merged, in a certain measure, with the investigation of order; for it consists in seeing clearly into phenomena, in bringing into accord with one another the diverse elements of an experience.»

[p. 570]This idea of order is merged with the idea of truth, because order is an intelligible relation, as Parodi says, a relation of succession or of coherence, as Lachelier thinks, always founded upon an Idea and always forming a kind of whole of the ordered things; that is, a system, which, at bottom, is truth itself, provided one refrains from considering the latter as a substance, as a creative force, identifying it with the entire activity of the spirit. Truth, like order, is an intelligible relation between the subject that affirms it and the representation or concept of the object, whether this duality subsists together with the relation or disappears through the fusion of the two terms.

Beauty, on the other hand, is essentially freedom. «The center whence all Aesthetics radiates is the idea of autonomy», says Christiansen Broder, in his Philosophy of the Beautiful. «Aesthetic values are essentially autonomous», he adds. «It is not in the works of the masters that they are to be sought, but in ourselves; for the law of the beautiful is our own law; in us resides the criterion of its worth». But that freedom—which is not free will in the traditional sense, which is the very sign of the energy with which the activity of life unfolds, which is not, like truth, a means of making life more intense, as Gaultier defines it in interpreting Nietzsche—is a power of expansion that struggles with the forces opposed to it and that tends to overcome them, developing its virtual energy.

This energy, creative by nature, which constitutes universal life, produces beauty everywhere. Thought serves it as a means of action, and contributes to that work in human creations; but its own, specific activity, which differs radically from intuition, left to itself, creates nothing, be[p. 571]cause its function is limited to offering materials to the free imagination, which bears within itself the power to select and to unite what, without that power, would be a dispersion and a chaos. For this reason, for beauty the appearance of that freedom in a spectacle suffices; and, for this reason too, Nietzsche makes of art the representation of the essentially metaphysical activity of man and the supreme explanation of life. There where the idea of the good, there where the idea of truth have run aground and have had to confess their inanity, the concept of beauty succeeds in solving the enigma.

The anti-intellectualism of Bergson coincides, though not totally, with that of Nietzsche. For Bergson the creative spirit is freedom; creative life is likewise freedom; the one engenders artistic beauty; the other, natural beauty in its infinite variety of forms.

Beauty and truth being considered, the first as symbol of freedom and the second as expression of order, the one as the integral product of life and the other as the fragmentary effect of that activity, the difference between the two is fundamental. It is for not having established it in those terms that the aesthetic problem has been treated as a logical or gnoseological problem; that truth has been distinguished from beauty by superficial considerations; and that questions bearing no relation to the beautiful, or affecting its nature only collaterally, have been discussed as aesthetic ones.

The distinctions that have been made by reason of content, of fecundity, of the psychic function to which the true and the beautiful are respectively directed, by reason of the form they affect, of the nature of the pleasure they produce, and of the method employed in the acquisition of each of these values, do not touch their very essence, or do not define it with precision, or are derived from the one we have indicated. In all these differ[p. 572]ences the beautiful is always treated as a phenomenon of knowledge, as an idea, different from the idea of truth.

As a consequence of this confusion, art has been denatured, being likewise considered as a logical product, and there have been carried into its domain the problems raised by gnoseology or by technique. Thus the question concerning the nature of art has been discussed, in order to ascertain whether it is a mere imitation of empirical reality or a creation of thought, repeating here the problem of the origin of knowledge and of truth—whether it be a concrete truth, derived from sensible experience, or an ideal truth, the exclusive fruit of reason. In this way, realists or naturalists and pure idealists have projected onto aesthetics, transformed into gnoseology, the capital problem that belongs to them.

Art being judged as the expression of real truth, and this being confounded with phenomenal existence, there arose naturally the definition of art as imitation of the real; that is, realism, naturalism, or verism in art. Judged as the expression of ideal truth, taken in the Platonic sense, there arose the opposite definition, as imitation of the ideal; in the one case as in the other, art was reduced to a means of expressing truth. The idea of imaginative creation entered there as an alien imposition, born of artistic experience or of its antithesis with science.

It was not understood, within traditional intellectualism, that the beautiful could not be defined as a concept, that it was indefinable, like the freedom that is its essence, and that, instead of finding in technique the explanation of art, it was necessary to seek in ourselves the criterion of aesthetic value, as Broder says.

Investigating there, one would have found that the [p. 573]work of art results from the struggle between the expansive and free force of consciousness, which creates new forms of activity, and the forms of existing and perceived reality, which raise obstacles more or less powerful to that expansion. These two factors, the spiritual force and the sensible form, end by merging, through the submission of the second to the first, leaving impressed upon their harmony their opposed activities. Freedom, in its flight, may content itself with the veil of sensible reality in order to externalize itself; but nature, with its seduction, may detain the spirit within the limits of sensible representation, without truth's discharging, in the one case or the other, its own function. Idealists, then, are those who sacrifice real life to the infinite ambitions of creative freedom. Realists, naturalists, or verists are those who prefer to find in nature those supple meshes of forms, colors, and sounds, which lovingly retain the force of that élan of life, which would perhaps be extinguished if those nets did not enclose it in harmonious syntheses.

Lachelier has therefore been right to state that idealism, in the aesthetic sense, refers only very remotely to the metaphysical sense of the word idealism. «Aesthetic, moral, etc., idealism is the pursuit of an ideal, and the question of the existence of this ideal and of the possibility of realizing it has nothing to do with the doctrine that composes the world, whether of my ideas or of the Ideas», says Lachelier.

The difficulty of explaining that movement of purification through freedom, without leaving the gnoseological criterion, has introduced into art the question of the verisimilar, an elastic concept with which some have sought to reconcile historical truth or present reality with the absolute freedom of the artist. A similar difficulty shows through in the profound appraisal that the philosopher G. Sim[p. 574]mel makes of naturalism, when he attributes to reality, as such, a metaphysical value, «it not being the senses that give it to us, but, on the contrary, something we give to the senses, a relation of the spirit with the great secret of being. Reality loses its sensible signification in order to save the independence of art; it ceases to be a visible and particular property of things; it has only a signification that extends over the whole of its qualities; it thus becomes a reality alien to art, which merely combines its qualities.» By means of this dissipation of the sensible and its conversion into the abstract, Simmel finds artistic truth to be a concordance of the work of art with its own idea.

For him, every work of art that is inwardly true, however fantastic and subjective it may be, expresses some manner or other according to which life is possible; a manner that at bottom involves the concordance he calls truth. Simmel has found it necessary to render the concrete reality abstract in order to reconcile these two ideas: the independence of art and the value of the great works of naturalist art, which are reconciled without identifying the emotion that perceived reality and that represented by art produce in us, notwithstanding the radical difference with which he presents them.

The confusion of the beautiful and the true has prevented, finally, the fixing of the limits that separate art and science, and the determination of the relations that exist between art and philosophy. Delbos, like Simmel, considers nature in relation to art as a mere object of contemplation, as an abstraction, in order to differentiate it from science, which conceives nature in its indifferent objectivity. «Art, aesthetic activity, draws its reasons for being from nature, in so far as nature is bound to our faculties. That it be touched by science matters little; for-[p. 575]it is from the spirit itself, it is from the free play of its faculties, that art draws its reason».

«The matter offered to art, even in realist art», adds Delbos, «is a matter always human, in a certain degree, through its adhesion to the faculties, through its relation to the human manner of representing things to oneself». Delbos, who defines the beautiful as Kant does, realizes, nevertheless, the superficiality of this difference, which is reduced to that between naturalist art and the natural sciences, which cannot be considered as absolutely objective. For this reason he declares «that art and science are not opposed in themselves, and that their apparent opposition depends on a degenerate dogmatism; for behind science, which offers itself as a kind of truth on the march, mechanically, is found what is, in reality, the principle of science, the creative and organizing spirit; that behind art, even when it seeks to adapt itself as exactly as possible to the exigencies of our civilization and to the need for precise realities, is found the primitive and primordial principle; and that behind art and behind science one arrives at the living spirit, whence they derive and in which the opposition falls of itself».

An absolute separation between art and science does not hold, without doubt, because it would presuppose the disaggregation of consciousness, which is not formed exclusively by the intellectual function, nor does it exclude this; but there is one relatively to the expression of spiritual life, which corresponds to the modes of its activity. In that sense, there is art when consciousness entire, when the creative imagination that comprehends it, discovers, by intuition, a new reality in the depths of beings, and externalizes it freely by its natural means of objectification; there is art thus in all the domains of human activity; there is art in the sciences, empiri[p. 576]cal as well as rational; but that radical imaginative function, which offers elements to science, is not science in the logical sense of the word; for science excludes feeling and freedom, and submits all phenomena to the rigorous determinism of law. There is science also in art, but it is restricted to technique, which does not constitute the essence of art and which is not art in the conception of philosophers such as Croce. Technique may be very poor, almost null, and the art be profound, as happens with the first manifestations of Christian art.

Science and art are distinguished, consequently, as order and freedom are distinguished, as science and philosophy are distinguished today.

If art, in the Aristotelian sense, differs from science, this separation is more profound still between beautiful art and science, because the essential character of the former is free creation, whereas science is subjected to the most rigorous determinism. Artistic knowledge is intuitive and scientific knowledge is logical, even when reflection intervenes in artistic production to develop the imaginative intuition, and even when intuition is not alien to the primitive process of science, at the moment in which it constitutes experience as the basis of its judgments; which shows that the intuitive judgment and the logical judgment complete one another. It is, moreover, a character of the artistic judgment that it is a judgment of appreciation in which feeling intervenes, that is, a judgment of valuation or of value, whereas the scientific judgment is assertoric, affirming mere existence, independently of all function of feeling.

Science is a conciliation of thought with reality, the latter considered as a complex or as a succession of phenomena, whose relations one seeks to fix in laws, establishing a logical order, purely ideal, composed of representa[p. 577]tive elements, and in which mechanical causality predominates, to the exclusion of the effects of freedom and feeling. Science thus establishes a relation between phenomenon and phenomenon, aspiring to found universal and necessary laws, induced from the whole of reality and applicable to the whole of reality; it seeks to create an ideal order of abstractions, a pure order, in which thought and reality are absolutely harmonized, as happens in Mathematics and Logic. In this form of conciliation, which science realizes between the subjective and the objective, order excludes freedom.

Aesthetic art, on the contrary, is a conciliation between individual freedom and all reality opposed to it, between a freedom conceived without limits and the objects to which the tendency toward that freedom refers. Art establishes a relation between the phenomenon and freedom, by means of feeling, creating a relative order in the world of imagination and an individual law, which escapes mechanical necessity through the predominance of freedom. Freedom thus creates its own order, without ever being able to realize it in the sphere of actions, but only in the world of feeling and of imagination, and in that of artistic representations.

The aesthetic law, founded upon subjective finality, likewise escapes the predictions of science; it has a psychological foundation, comprehends all the elements of the spirit, and extends both to man and to physical nature, in so far as the latter reflects an appearance of freedom and produces aesthetic enjoyment. In the aesthetic order it is a matter of conquering the world for freedom, making the subjective predominate; in the moral order it is a matter of reconciling freedom with a superior principle, giving predominance to the objective; in the scientific order it is a matter of conquering reality for the law, which is objective. For this reason, morals stand closer to science than does art.

[p. 578]Notwithstanding the profound distinction between art and science, since art, in order to express its ideal of freedom, needs to penetrate into the world of physical reality, from which it chooses its forms, and since that world is subjected to the empire of science, art associates itself with science so closely that from this there arise the formalist theories, which aspire to reduce art to the canons of science, leaving aside its content.

If art moves away from science through its content and approaches it through its form, the contrary happens between art and philosophy, which are wont to be confounded through their ground, especially in the romantic philosophies. Already Schopenhauer maintained that art is fit to solve, in union with philosophy, the problem of life. Both are capable of giving an answer to that problem; but with this difference, «that while reflection gives, in an abstract manner, an answer fit to persuade seriously, art, in its turn, answers by means of the naïve and childlike language of intuition; and for this reason the answer is always constituted by a fleeting image and does not give a general and lasting idea, always procuring a provisional and definitive satisfaction. Philosophy alone can give an entire, lasting, and satisfactory answer, by means of the universality of the concept». Thus «philosophy and art meet at their roots, although in their ramifications they diversify, in their direction and in their secondary elements». Art and metaphysics being destined, according to Schopenhauer, to express the thing-in-itself, the noumenon, this relation was logical within his system.

Before Schopenhauer, Schelling, in his absolute idealism, had reduced all philosophy to art, and that same tendency is found, as has been seen, in his disciple Ravaisson and in the finalist aestheticians.

Other contemporary philosophers, who depart from them, ma[p. 579]ke of the philosophy of the beautiful the whole of philosophy, or associate art and philosophy at their base or their summit: the philosophy of Wundt resolves itself into an aesthetics, and that of Croce sets out from an aesthetics of intuition and aspires to be merged with it. For Bergson, «intuition is that kind of intellectual sympathy by means of which one penetrates into the interior of an object, so as to coincide with what it has of the unique, and consequently of the inexpressible. True metaphysics is a kind of intellectual auscultation in which one feels the soul throb». This intuition is aesthetic and may serve as the basis of a new philosophy, according to Bergson, for whom art and philosophy, beauty and metaphysical truth, are merged in their germ.

In an analogous sense Eucken understands philosophy, which, in his conception, «is charged with the interior illumination of the spirit and with the comprehension of reality». «Every great philosophical work involves a flight of the whole life of the spirit. It is not the product of an intellectual skill, but the work and the confirmation of our entire spiritual nature, which embraces the world. The principal function of philosophy is not to form well-ordered doctrines, but to elevate inwardly the process of life, to augment what there is in us of the autonomous, of the original, to render us capable of seeing things more as a whole, with more interiority, with more essentiality». This conception of the philosophy of life reflects the superior, sovereign manner of artistic creation.

Baldwin seeks today, with his Pancalism, to realize the purpose of Schelling and Ravaisson, and aesthetic questions invade ever more the domain of philosophy, as Le Roy, Parodi, and Chiapelle show. Artist-philosophers, such as Torrefranca, accentuate the aesthetic value of philosophy. According to this philosopher-musician, «[p. 580]music must be considered as art par excellence, of pure intuitive relations, upon which all metaphysics of the absolute must be constructed. A metaphysics of the absolute, after the manner of Bergson, which installs itself in movement and adopts the very life of things, ought to set out explicitly from music, to be grounded upon it, as upon the first and fundamental spiritual experience with which everything must be brought into accord. Cosmic idealism itself, which some advocate, if it wishes to live little or much in the history of human thought, will have to lean explicitly upon music, by reason of that germinal character which identifies it with the first apperceptions of things».

The center of life being thus transported from the intelligence to the free will; the latter being considered, as Eucken says, as the only thing that can give it warmth, force, and solidity; the free and omnipotent will being conceived as the essential of reality, the philosophy of the spirit had to postulate creative freedom and necessarily to find art in that freedom, which is its essence.

This philosophical orientation is opposed to the scientific one advocated by intellectualism; and hence the opposition between art and science is reproduced in that between philosophy and science. Philosophy sets for itself, it is true, the investigation of truth, but it does not do so as science does; the philosophical intuition that serves as the basis of the former is not the logical process that serves as the instrument of the latter and defines its nature: «the truth that philosophy seeks is a superior and comprehensive truth, in which the reason of all particular truths must be found», as Delbos writes;

«and since it is a truth that transcends the limited horizons of our usual life, the effort to represent it is analogous, at the least, to the effort of the artist who pur[p. 581]sues a beauty more harmonious and more pure than the material beauty of things». Delbos finds thus a profound analogy between the artistic instinct and the mission of philosophy; between poetry, at the highest point of its flight, and the metaphysics of feeling and of life; between the great philosophical systems and artistic activity; between philosophical production and artistic production; only that the great philosopher does not construct his system because he finds it beautiful, but because he deems it true; art adheres to the organization of thought in that work.

Delbos, in studying the relation between art and philosophy and determining their resemblances, has not, however, left the concept of superior harmony that the one and the other realize; in that sense, all philosophy offers the analogies established by that philosopher; but the concept of harmony is insufficient to determine the relations between art and philosophy, as expressions of interior freedom, and it is these relations that it is fitting to establish, if the aim is to mark the exclusive domain of the beautiful in respect to that of the true.

### XI. LA BELLEZA Y EL BIEN — XI. BEAUTY AND THE GOOD

Like the ideas of perfection and of truth, the idea of the good has no precise meaning either.

«The word good and its derivatives, says the Philosophical Vocabulary of the French Society of Philosophy, present five principal meanings, of which the first is a genus, to which the other four are related, as its species. It signifies that which is worthy of approval, in general; that which realizes exactly the ideal type, which we consider as that of its species; that which usefully serves an end; that which is worthy of ethical approval and the character of the benevolent being. In Greek philosophy, it adds, the good par excellence is that which is good only in itself and in relation to which all the others are but means. In the second place, and especially in Aristotle, it is the end of all activity in the world. The sovereign good, says Aristotle, would be the object that satisfied the entire faculty of desire of finite rational beings. In modern philosophy and in particular in Kant, it is a good such that it satisfies the whole man, both with respect to reason and to sensibility and to activity».

Lachalier, making the critique of these definitions, finds that in all the employments of the word good and its derivatives there is a fundamental duality of meaning: the good is perfection, in itself, or happiness for him who possesses them. «Historically, he says, this last meaning is the first; the good is that of which we have [p. 583]need, that which satisfies us. The good, in the sense of perfection, is, probably, that which causes us an objective satisfaction, that which satisfies us as rational beings.»

In this diversity of meanings, the Vocabulary advises employing by preference the word perfect, whenever there may be confusion with the sense of the moral good, as that which is worthy of ethical approval, and reserving the expression The Good in the ethical sense.

Following Lachalier, there is a double acceptation of the idea of the good: one objective, which confounds it with that of perfection or of utility; and another subjective, in which the feelings of approval, of benevolence or of happiness constitute the content of that concept. The good, as divine will or as good will or noumenal will in Kant, may be included in this expression. «For Aristotle, says Goblot, the good of a being is its end or its act, and when the good is distinguished from pleasure, one comes to identify it with being.» This finality serves Kant, in his critique of judgment, to distinguish the beautiful from the useful as from the good, which he confounds with the perfect, in the common signification of objective or teleological finality.

Once the subjective forms of the good are set apart, there remains as the essential objective expression that which defines it as that which realizes exactly the ideal type, which we consider as that of its species. Under this definition may be comprised both the physical good and the moral good, because both enter into the concept of perfection or of order, which implies the idea of type and which is equivalent to the Platonic Idea or Ideal. The ideal type, indeed, is but an idea of order, whose content is composed of all the generic notes that correspond to a group of phenomena alike in their nature and finali[p. 584]ty. Objectively, the moral good is also an order, as the moral evil is a disorder. So Goblot establishes it, for whom the moral good is, moreover, the progress in perfection or in dignity that results from the good action, as the moral evil is the decadence that results from the fault.

The good is, consequently, the perfect, the ideal order, but it is not simply perfection or order, but a particular species of both, differing from the rest by its content. In this it is distinguished from truth, which is pure order, and resembles beauty, which is an order that has for its content freedom and feeling.

The good having been defined in the sense of perfection, as Leibniz also did, the difference with the beautiful is resolved; but defined in the sense of love or of freedom, the question is reduced to knowing the role that these elements play in the aesthetic phenomenon and in the moral one.

Kant, for whom the beautiful and the good differ radically, founds that difference on the diverse manner in which the logical categories, according to which he sought to define the aesthetic judgment of taste, are applied to the one and to the other. «The beautiful pleases immediately, but only in reflective intuition; not, like morality, in the concept: the beautiful pleases independently of all interest, and the moral good is, in truth, bound to an interest necessarily, but not to an interest that precedes the judgment of satisfaction, because this very judgment is what produces it; the freedom of the imagination and, consequently, of our sensibility, is represented in the judgment of the beautiful as conforming to the legality of the understanding; in the moral judgment, the freedom of the will is conceived as the accord of this faculty with itself, according to the universal laws of reason; [p. 585]lastly, the subjective principle of the judgment of the beautiful is represented as universal, that is to say as acceptable for all, although it cannot be determined by any universal concept; whereas the objective principle of morality is, also, represented as universal, that is to say, as admissible for all subjects, as well as for all the actions of each subject; but also as being determinable by a universal concept.»

The Kantian distinction refers to the forms that aesthetic and teleological knowledge assume, but not to the objects themselves, which have no phenomenal reality in his subjective philosophy. For this reason, in considering freedom, he refers it to the mode in which it is represented in the judgment of the beautiful, conforming to the laws of the understanding, consistent with his definition of aesthetic pleasure as the free play of the cognitive faculties.

Kant had also distinguished the beautiful from the good by reason of finality. The finality of the beautiful was apparent and subjective, it was a finality without an end; the finality of the good was real and objective; this radical separation serving as the foundation for the difference between the aesthetic judgment and the teleological judgment, which rest, respectively, on immediate pleasure or on the concept.

Schelling departs from this Kantian formula, explaining, by the principle of absolute love, the nature of the beautiful as of the good, and thus confounding Aesthetics with Morality. Fouillée, who criticizes this thesis, finds a secret opposition between the ideas of goodness and of beauty properly so called; because, in his conception, «beauty supposes an adequation of the object to our means of knowing and feeling, which permits, at [p. 586]once its vigorous and easy, and consequently agreeable, exercise; conditions that are not applicable to the idea of the absolute, since this idea is above and perhaps below every sensible or intelligible form and escapes knowledge as it does the imagination and the sensibility; whence it results that the pure absolute cannot be beautiful, strictly speaking; there is no true beauty save where life is found, or at least the appearance of life.» «The aesthetic emotion once analyzed, adds Fouillée, it demonstrates that all true beauty is, by itself or by what we put into it, the symbol of universal love, as a cause of joy, and comes to be the symbol of universal pity when it causes sadness; it is an infinity felt or foreseen; it is the symbol of the good; but that does not mean that the beautiful and the good are confounded in a supernatural being, identical with the absolute. The absolute plays in aesthetics, as in morality, only a negative role, a role limited according to Kant's own expression.»

Thus eliminating the absolute character, there subsists only the feeling of love for the ideal, which informs both the beautiful and the good; but this joyous feeling which, in the moral order, is born of the submission of the will to the norm or to the imposed ideal, recognizes as its cause, in the aesthetic order, the free creation of the ideal. In the aesthetic order, freedom lacks constraint, it unfolds, without limits, in the world of the imagination, and only thus is it reconciled with nature; but, in the moral order, it is limited by duty. «Whoever says beautiful, says a conception that is free and that no law governs and represses; such is not the notion of the good,» writes Chaignet.

»Whoever says beautiful, adds this philosopher, says an indefinite ideal, to which, according to its creative power, the imagination adds, elevates and corrects; but the notion of the good is not thus indeterminate. Whoever says beautiful, says a feeling whose essence is to be agreeable; but the essence of the sacri[p. 587]fice for the good seems to be a pain, because it is a combat, and the victory itself is acquired at the price of suffering. The beautiful is a creative art, which rests only on the contemplation of the exterior object it has produced, in which it has deposited the ideal and whose vision enchants it; the beautiful tends always to an expression, not so the good.» Chaignet acknowledges «that man, in moral action, in practice, imposes upon himself the good, which is his end as something distinct from him; but that is an abstract form, exclusively general, which has nothing imaginable, nor particular, nor individual; it is an idea of reason, which man conceives and which he wishes to realize in himself; and this abstract form, devoid of being, when it has been realized, produces no new being, nor any substantial change in being. Man, through virtue, perfects his essence; but he does not change it, nor create anything as in the beautiful.»

Such is the role that feeling plays in the beautiful and in the good. Both feelings may be contemporaneous and bound together; but, as Kant says, «the moral feeling is united to aesthetic pleasure, in the sense that one can represent, as aesthetic, the beauty of an action. But this force of aesthetic representation does not belong to the morality itself of the action, but to the imagination, and may go so far as to dissipate, without destroying, the purely moral character».

Considered objectively, the beautiful and the good both admit the ideas of order and of freedom, though under different conditions, being confounded in the geometric form of beauty and separating as soon as life suggests the idea of freedom, as non-constraint or as free expansion. In Nature, the beautiful is measured by the perfect, in the sphere of the inorganic, in which beauty is appreciated simply by order, converted into harmony, by a kind of transference of the subjective [p. 588]harmony to the contemplated object.
