In the sphere of the organized and living, that parallelism disappears, and the aesthetic criterion resides in the freedom of movement and of expression. In the sphere of actions, that separation is accentuated. To the order imposed by the moral norm is opposed the free order created by the imagination; to the freedom subordinated to duty or to pleasure is opposed the infinite freedom of aesthetic creation.

Freedom dominates in beauty; what dominates in the good is order, the law, the norm, duty, as the impassable limit of moral freedom. Freedom in the beautiful receives rules only from itself or from the imagination; order obeys, in the good, the law that reason imposes upon it. We love in the beautiful the free force, so that pleasure subsists even when that force, in the excess of its freedom, reaches disorder and disregards the law of reason. Thus we find beauty even in the somber regions of evil.

Since freedom and order enter into both the beautiful and the good, it is understood that, when the good is translated into forms that reveal a freedom in harmony with an ideal order engendered by feeling, it is confounded with the beautiful. There is no moral beauty whose content is not an action considered as good. When that does not happen, then beauty ceases to be moral and becomes pure artistic beauty. This explains why virtue has been sought to be confounded with art, as Herbart and Novalis do; it explains, moreover, why the aesthetic and moral values struggle for supremacy, each adjudging to itself, respectively, the title of the value of values.

An intellectualist aesthetics, which attributes to order or harmony the essential value of the beautiful, subordinates it to the moral order imposed by the divine will or by noumenal reason; but a voluntarist aesthetics, which makes creative [p. 589]freedom the essence of the spirit, subordinating to it all order, all ideal, will attribute to itself, necessarily, the power to create the moral ideal, like any other ideal, imposing it by the force of collective satisfaction and converting it into a dogma of practical reason.

From this confusion between the good and the beautiful there has derived, in artistic theory, the debate over the didactic finality of art; because art is not only the expression of an ideal freedom, but also a process of liberation or of emancipation, meeting in this sense, and associating itself, with morality and religion.

«From very ancient times a pedagogical end was attributed to art, as Croce observes. Upon the hedonistic basis, which considered art as a thing of sensual pleasure only, there was constructed among the Greeks the moralistic and pedagogical theory of art. This educative end is found already in Plato and Aristotle, whether in the Politics, where it determines the educative uses of music; or perhaps even in the Poetics, where there is obscure mention of a tragic catharsis or purification by means of tragedy. The modern idea of the liberating virtue of art seems to have been also glimpsed by Aristotle. But it was the Stoic school that proclaimed the moralizing end of art».

This end has always been preserved; not only by those who have seen in art an ordering power over the psychic energies, like the Socratic philosophers, for whom the beautiful is the moral rule, but even by those who have made of freedom the essential aesthetic character. The aesthetic theory of Schiller, which makes the instinct of free play the generating principle of art, avails itself of this theory for a pedagogical end. The aesthetic theory of Schopenhauer, which dominates his whole philosophy, makes of liberation the end of art. Art is, therefore, beati[p. 590]fic.

The artistic contemplator is no longer an individual, but a conscious, pure, free subject, who has been able to emancipate himself from the tyranny of the blind will and, by the same token, from pain and from time. Aesthetic contemplation is liberating, because we know the object not as individual, but as a Platonic idea; that is to say, as the permanent form of the whole species of objects, and because the intimate consciousness of the knowing subject is no longer an individual consciousness, but the consciousness of the purely conscious subject, independent of the will. The contemplator needs to emancipate himself from the principle of causality, which serves the will, in order to rise to that pure knowledge of the idea, in which state cease the whirlwind of the passions or of desire and the torments of the individual will, and the quietude that is happiness is attained.

Only through art, which realizes that contemplation, can such happiness be obtained, which predisposes to piety and serves as the foundation of morality. Aesthetic contemplation, annihilating the will, annihilates egoism, which is its essence. Emancipated from the I and converted into pure subjects of knowledge, we identify ourselves with the contemplated objects. The world as representation is all that remains; the world as blind and egoistic will disappears completely, converted into a contemplated idea; because every idea, for Schopenhauer, is nothing more than the immediate and consequently adequate objectivation of the thing in itself, of the will, which has not yet objectified itself, nor converted itself into representation.

Notwithstanding the obscurity of this aesthetic theory, its moralizing end is understood. Man being condemned to pain, by force of a will bent on living in an adverse and insufficient world, cannot emancipate himself [p. 591]from that pain and conquer happiness save by emancipating himself from that will: consequently, from action, and taking refuge in the contemplative life, which is satisfied with the ideals that, in their turn, objectify, but in an immediate and adequate manner, that will, that tendency to live, before it presents itself in struggle with reality, before the free and omnipotent will is reduced to the slavery of the representations of the opposed reality and produces necessarily and exclusively pain.

This pessimistic conclusion, born of an incomplete study of the functions of the will in the individual consciousness, has led Schopenhauer to the disregard of the active function of liberation and purification that art entails, by effect of that same tendency to live which explains the progressive evolution of the ideal and presupposes the aspiration of a free, omnipotent and creative will.

By this factor of freedom, united to feeling, art and morality are closely associated. Morality is an attempt at conciliation between individual freedom and the social order, founded on the conception of an absolute order, admitted by society.

Morality establishes a relation between the subjective phenomenon and an absolute, objective rational law, superior to man, a universal teleological law, which escapes the previsions of science, which has a metaphysical foundation and creates an opposition between freedom and order; an opposition or antinomy which man aspires to destroy by means of an absolute and definitive conciliation, wrought by the complete realization of the moral order in practical life, without ever achieving it. Into this attempt at conciliation there enter all the psychological elements: representation, feeling and will; the idea of ob[p. 592]jective finality predominates; the ideal order is imposed; the object is not the real in its totality, but the spiritual real only, nor does it apply to all the real, but to practical life endowed with freedom.

Freedom and feeling enter into the genesis of art as into that of the moral act; but in a diverse manner. In art, freedom creates its own order; representation is subordinated to feeling; the law does not govern the activity of the artist in what constitutes the essential imaginative function: creative inspiration; freedom is absolute in the world of the imagination; in the moral act the contrary happens. The moral genius may radically reform the moral law, by force of a superior ideal; but in this case, the genius proceeds as an artist, who creates that ideal, rising by the imagination above experience, and may then be condemned as immoral by the society in which he acts.

With the artistic genius the same does not happen; his freedom can be condemned only when morality and religion create a hieratic art, destined to serve as the symbol of the dogmas of the one or the other; that is to say, when art disappears, replaced by morality or religion.

But, outside of this case, in which a moral reform is in question, actions are good or bad, not so much by the freedom that enters into them, as by their conformity or disconformity with the unalterable moral norm. Freedom enters into their appreciation only when responsibility is in question. A good or bad action does not become indifferent or change its nature according to whether the freedom with which it is practiced exists or not; its value is measured by its relation to the order it affirms or overturns, even when one does not wish to give that order the name of morality. In contrast, the aesthetic phenomenon disappears, [p. 593]disappearing with the real or apparent freedom, even when the order subsists as a physical, logical or social form.

In moral beauty itself, in which the two diverse expressions of ideal freedom are fused, the established difference can be found. The good action is besides beautiful, when he who executes it reveals a great effort to fulfill the moral law, as happens in the cases in which it recommends sacrifice and this is accepted, not passively, by force of resignation, but actively, freely, for the sole attraction of the ideality enclosed in the sacrifice. In contrast, good actions habitually practiced are not beautiful; they are like the works produced by machines, taking as their model the creations of genius.

Finality, finally, understood not in the Kantian sense, but in a superior sense, demonstrates the relation in which the beautiful and the good stand. The beautiful lacks, properly, finality; the beautiful work expresses an aspiration of freedom, which is realized in an appearance forged by the imagination, without ulterior end to determine it; the good work, on the contrary, tends to an end, to its conformity with a moral norm, absolute, which expresses a definitive ideal crystallized in a dogma. For this reason it is said that the beautiful has its end in itself, independently of its effects, be these pleasure or education.<sup>1</sup>

<sup>1</sup> See page 382.

«Art, as Durkheim says, is absolutely refractory to everything that resembles an obligation, because it is the domain of freedom. Art answers to the need of expanding our activity without end, for the pleasure of expanding it, whereas morality constrains us to follow a determined way toward a de[p. 594]fined object; whoever says obligation says, at the same time, constraint. Thus, even when it may be animated by moral ideas or found mixed with the evolution of the moral phenomena, properly so called, art is not moral by itself».

Lalo, in his recent work on art and morality, poses this problem of their relation, after having analyzed the theories that subordinate the first to the second, the opposite ones that give preeminence to art, and those that maintain a Thomistic communion between the beautiful and the good. For Lalo, these theories are equally false, because those values, like the logical value, are independent, but not irreconcilable. Lalo calls value the synthesis of impulses of every kind that make us act, think or feel, and calls imperative that value when it is conscious.

In the measure in which a state of mind is not imposed upon us passively from without, but is an active product of our nature, we must suppose a value in it, almost as when we are led to suppose a force at the origin of every movement or an energy at the source of every labor. Value thus turns out to be the psychological form of universal energy. Value in its diverse degrees presents the forms of negative or abnormal, positive or normal, and hypothetical or ideal values, forms that have as their common norm the laws of individual or collective evolution. For Lalo, the syntheses that create each value are formed of elements that, by themselves, lack value, or, at least, have no value of the same order. Moral values synthesize amoral data; scientific or logical values are combinations of alogical or prescientific factors, and aesthetic values are born of anaesthetic elements. Whatever their superior unity may be, these are the three principal [p. 595]shades of human values, according as this or that element dominates in their syntheses and impresses upon it one of the three characteristic forms of duty, of knowing, or of play.

Considered thus as heterogeneous syntheses, values are independent and differ by their nature, their constitution and their norms, giving rise to morality, in the narrow sense, to science, and to art; but in the progression of syntheses, whence all imperatives are born, there is no reason to stop at the three great classic values of the true, the beautiful and the good, as if they ought to remain definitively isolated and themselves withdrawn from all superior synthesis. Carrying, on the contrary, the progression to a more elevated power, one conceives a synthesis of all those syntheses, which, without having an absolute character, constitutes a fourth species of superior value, which completes what may be called, by analogy with the «cardinal virtues» of the ancients, the series of «cardinal values» of human life.

«Just as with anaesthetic, alogical and amoral data the human consciousness constructs, respectively, the logical, aesthetic and moral values, so likewise with truth, beauty and goodness it gives birth to a new value, which is more and better than the other three, without reducing itself to any of them, and which comprises them as elements with which it makes the mental synthesis, just as each of them makes the synthesis of simpler elements, the same ones that have been, doubtless, synthetic, and so on to infinity; because there is absolutely no intelligible limit, neither upward nor downward, in this progression by synthesis or in this regression by analysis».

«This supreme value would embrace, at last, all the powers of life at once, without excluding any, and would give to each its harmonious place in the whole. For lack of [p. 596]a more fitting term, we would call it a superior morality, although it is not, rather, morality than beauty or than truth; because it is all this at once. It is a pantheistic conception of life and of the world, and, for that reason, it has something metaphysical or religious about it. It is like the metaphysical moment of all values or like the religious aspect of life, which makes it sacred, and which erects each of its functions into one of the indispensable formulas of a cult: the cult of Man for Humanity; because with it comes, at last, the reign of Man over the earth and in Heaven.»

There is, then, for Lalo «a narrow sense and a broad sense of those terms Morality or the Moral. In the narrow sense morality is very different from art and from science, which it considers, with just title, as competitors, and it tolerates their invasions only thanks to a very unstable modus vivendi. Always threatened or threatening, it is almost always, with respect to its rivals, in the attitude of attack or of defense; rarely and with difficulty, in that of accord and of organic solidarity.»

«From this narrow point of view, morality is serious and interested action, art is the delirium of play, science is disinterested thought. All the place that one of its functions occupies in life it takes forcibly from one of the other two; it is struggle and anarchy, until a strange force comes to reduce those pretensions to the common discipline of a superior synthesis. A morality thus narrow is a struggle against nature, that is to say, against all the other values.»

«Understood in the broad sense, on the contrary, far from excluding the other values and from struggling [p. 597]against them for life, the superior morality presupposes them. It does not subordinate them, save to organize them; it is the expansion of the human personality and not the restriction of its functions.»

Lalo, however, does not explain how those syntheses are formed; what is the principle around which the less complex elements are ordered, first, and then the syntheses of values. To judge by his words relative to the expansion of the human personality, as the end of the superior organization, it would seem that that principle were that of the free expansion of the spirit; but that interpretation does not accord with the intellectualism of Lalo, who reduces the diverse values to mental or logical syntheses. Lalo, moreover, does not resolve the fundamental problem of the criterion of value, which is posed in the domain of the valuing consciousness; he considers value as objective, dispensing with the idea of finality, which is essential in the theory of value. His inclination to reduce all values to that of a superior morality, with no other factor than that of an indefinite progression in synthesis, answers to his sociological aesthetic theory, in which he admits an aesthetic imperative, an aesthetic obligation, imposed by a normative technique, after the manner of a moral imperative. Once aesthetic freedom is admitted, superior to all social norm, that analogy disappears and there arises, naturally, the autonomy of art, which, in engendering ideals, extends that power to human actions and establishes the bases of morality.

In the same sense in which art meets morality it meets also religion. The artistic consciousness and the religious consciousness are confounded in the domain of pure ideality.

«The mystical theory, which considers art as a [p. 598]special mode of beatification, of entering into relation with the absolute, with the highest good, with the ultimate root of things, appears only at the close of Antiquity, almost at the beginning of the Middle Ages. Plotinus, founder of the neoplatonic school, is the representative of this direction. With Plotinus, the beautiful and art, which had been separated, are both resolved into a mystical passion and elevation of the spirit. The beautiful is that which we welcome as a thing of our own nature; the ugly, that which repels as contradictory. The affinity of beautiful things with our soul, which perceives them, has its origin in the idea, which produces the one and the other. A beautiful body is such by its communion with the divine. Beauty is the splendor of the divine, of the idea. Matter is beautiful, not now by itself, but only insofar as it is illumined by the idea. Light and fire, as nearest to the latter, as the most spiritual among bodies, spread the beautiful over visible things. But, in order to perceive it, the soul must purify itself and render efficacious that force of the idea which is inborn in it. Moderation, fortitude, prudence and every other virtue are nothing but purifications. Thus there is opened to the soul another eye beyond that of sensible beauty, which permits it to contemplate the divine beauty, which coincides with the good, the supreme condition of beatitude. Into this contemplation art enters. Beauty in things made by man proceeds from the mind, from the interior. The beauty of natural things is the archetype existing in the soul, which is the source of all natural beauty. This is, adds Croce, the first affirmation of mystical aesthetics, destined to so much fortune in modern times, especially in the first half of the nineteenth century.»

If art draws away from science to the point where both constitute the two poles of psychic activity, whose essential elements are freedom and order, the non-coor[p. 599]dinable and the coordinable, as Gourd says, art and religion resemble each other to the point of constituting states of consciousness that are defined by that resemblance. The soul of the mystic is a lyre, James has said; and, in effect, it is in music, principally, that mysticism and artistic genesis can be confounded. Religious inspiration, in the other arts, can also produce those states of religious unction, in which the soul, in order to raise itself to the most elevated ideality, breaks all the bonds that tie it to sensual desire and enters into the world of beatific purification.

Freedom, the more it is idealized, the more it draws near to religiosity. The domain of pure freedom would be that of the suprasensible, the domain of mystery and of pure religiosity, in which the whole of life would be reduced to a pure love for the absolute; but to arrive there, man would have to renounce all representation, all imaginative form, an unrealizable term, because it is contrary to his nature. Hence religiosity cannot dispense with some form, art being the obligatory vehicle of the religious ideal. Whatever our conception may be, reality imposes itself upon our intelligence.

Notwithstanding this coordination between art and religiosity, their domains are different. Art is not only inspired by the divine; nature and man are also sources of ideals that it realizes. Art is not pure feeling, however intense it may be; it is feeling united to a representation and to a work. To dispense with the latter is to mutilate art, to confound it with science.

Religion consists in a special disposition of the feelings and supposes two habitual dispositions of the soul: humility and confidence, the fear of God and faith in Him. This implies a feeling of dependence [p. 600]in the process of liberation, which differs radically from the artistic process, because it recognizes different origins and ends. The religious feeling, informed by the feelings of longing, joy, admiration, aspires to emancipate itself from the world, disillusioned and weary of life, in order to be absorbed in God and thus conquer absolute freedom; the spirit, as absolute value, aspires to two forms of liberation from the servitudes that enchain it: the servitude of nature and the servitude of the body; but the artistic spirit seeks only the emancipation of all that opposes its growth as a free power; the life of relation imposes upon it limits that it seeks to discover or to widen, creating ideals that escape that relativity and discover what there is of the universal and absolute in the interior of things. The aesthetic feeling is not, consequently, a feeling of dependence upon the absolute, but the feeling of the absolute, which aspires to realize itself in the world of phenomena, by successive and progressive artistic creations. In the religious consciousness there exists a categorical imperative, which favors absolute liberation; but the aesthetic consciousness lacks a heteronomous imperative; it is the autonomous activity par excellence, even when it is necessarily limited by objective reality, which is an element of its creative function.

This difference does not prevent, however, the community that binds the forms of religion and of art, which is realized, as Simmel says, «when the believer feels his unity with God, when he who contemplates a work of art feels it as an inner necessity; because then it is no longer individual and particular elements that come into play, but profound strata in which the soul feels the totality of its being stir, [p. 601]conceiving this being as referred to an order and to a meaning of existence that surpasses its personality and the determined forms of its life.»

NOTE.—If freedom were considered as the supreme good, if the sovereign good did not consist in the fusion of virtue and of happiness, as Kant believed; if it consisted in the fusion of freedom and happiness; if duty were to be replaced by freedom, as Wentscher establishes, in his voluntarist morality, and as Croce would have admitted; if the free action were a true work of art, as Bergson thinks; if freedom were the value of values, because it explains all values according to the measure in which it enters into each of them, then the good and the beautiful would not differ substantially; because the beautiful would explain the good and would be confounded with it, and morality would be a derivation of aesthetics. But would this thesis be true? It is properly in the domain of morality that this grave question must be discussed and resolved

### XII. LA BELLEZA Y LA UTILIDAD — XII. BEAUTY AND UTILITY

[p. 602] Just as the question of idealism and realism in art bears on the nature of the beautiful and of its expression, so the question of didactic art bears on its finality. For those who believe that art has for its primary end to serve as a vehicle for science, for morality, and for religion, the pedagogical finality is essential. On the other hand, those who proclaim the freedom of the beautiful and of its artistic expression condemn that objective finality and affirm that the beautiful has its finality in itself, in the aesthetic emotion it produces—beauty being formal and indifferent as regards its content. This theory of art for art's sake, which fails to recognize the social finality of the beautiful—reducing the limits of aesthetic action to the narrow circle of the psychological finality and constituting a kind of contradictory egoism—is associated with the theory of play, begun by Kant, followed by Schiller, and maintained by Spencer and all the positivists, his disciples.

Kant had established, as the qualitative attribute of the judgment of taste, its disinterestedness, which was closely bound to its subjective, formal, and apparent finality—which he called finality without an end; and although afterward, through a profound veneration for morality, he made the beautiful a symbol of morality, he maintained the absolute freedom of the beautiful, whose subjective definition he made consist in the free play of the cognitive faculties. Schiller, his disciple, notwithstanding his cultural theory—in which [p. 603] he sought to demonstrate that the aesthetic state was necessary in order to conquer the moral state—maintained the principle of play as the instinct that generates art, and likewise condemned didactic art in the name of the freedom essential to the artistic ideal.

In maintaining, as Kant and Schiller did, that aesthetic activity was one of pure play and consequently disinterested, they established a radical difference between the beautiful and the useful, which the former made consist in the difference that exists between subjective and formal finality and objective, real, and external finality. Beauty was formal for Schiller too. Spencer, adopting these ideas, confirmed the uselessness of art and gave rise to the controversy over the relation that exists between the ideas of the beautiful and of the useful.

According to Spencer, the idea of the beautiful excludes, first, what is necessary to life; second, what is useful to life; and, third, it excludes also, in general, every real object of desire and of possession, in order to reduce itself to the simple free exercise, to the mere play of our activity. Spencer regards necessity, and the desire that is born of it, as excluding all aesthetic emotion. «To seek an end, as serving life—that is, as good and useful—is necessarily to lose sight of its aesthetic character,» says Spencer.

Grant Allen, his disciple, refuses all aesthetic character to the arrangement of parts in view of an end. Like Kant, he establishes, at the same time, an opposition between the vital functions and aesthetic emotion, although he recognizes necessity and desire as factors in the evolution of aesthetic feeling. «The beautiful,» he says, «seems, in great part, derived from the profitable and the desirable; to give the genesis of aesthetic feeling, one must give the history of human needs and desires.»

Guyau, combating these ideas, establishes «that the beautiful, reduced to the full consciousness of life itself, cannot exclude what is necessary to life, because the first manifestation of aesthetic feeling is need satisfied, is life recovering its equilibrium, the rebirth of interior harmony—and that is what constitutes the elemental beauty of sensations. In the same way,» Guyau adds, «the beautiful, far from excluding what is useful, presupposes the idea of a will spontaneously accommodating the means to the ends, that of an activity that seeks to spend the minimum of force to attain an end. Hence results the beauty of movements. Lastly, the beautiful, far from excluding the idea of the desirable, is identified, at bottom, with this idea. The beautiful and the useful are thus one and the same thing, and this unity, visible in our feelings, lets itself be divined in movements or in sensations. Human life, for Guyau, is dominated by four great needs or desires, corresponding to essential functions of the being: to breathe, to move, to nourish oneself, to reproduce. We believe,» he says, «that these various functions can take on an aesthetic character.»

Replying to Grant Allen, Guyau maintains, like Dumont, that «all organization of parts in relation to an end constitutes an order, a harmony, and, consequently, that there is a beauty of utility». Thus, in external objects, utility seems to him to be a first degree of beauty. Passing from the objects to the sentient subject, to utility there corresponds a need; this need, made conscious, gives rise to a desire, which is the source of aesthetic emotions. To desire, to love is, in a certain way, to admire, provided that the desire be not too violent. Need and desire—that is, the agreeable, what serves life—there is the primitive and crude criterion of aesthetics. Guyau regards them not only as essential fac[p. 605]tors in the evolution of aesthetic feeling, but as elements of aesthetic emotion, and he does not accept the irremediable egoism of desire and of the pleasures bound to it.

«Precisely because we identify the beautiful with the intellectually agreeable,» Guyau says afterward, «we cannot think of identifying it with the useful, which differs so often from the agreeable itself. The useful is a set of means that have in view a future enjoyment; it is not, then, the agreeable, but the pursuit—often painful—of the agreeable. Now, the beautiful must please immediately. Utility may often constitute, in objects, a first, very inferior degree of beauty; but utility is beautiful only insofar as it is not opposed to the agreeable; the useful must make us enjoy in anticipation an effect, must move us aesthetically—which does not mean that the beautiful and the useful are inseparable, because the agreeable and the beautiful can subsist independently of the useful, nor that, in order to admire the beauty of an object, it is necessary to demonstrate its practical utility, however much the useful—that is, what is adapted to a certain end, what is ordered by this end—may of itself bring to the intelligence a satisfaction and thereby acquire a certain degree of beauty.»

The useful is beautiful, according to Guyau, «by the intellectual element of finality perceived and by the sensible element of satisfaction experienced in advance; there is an anticipation of the agreeable through the perception of a set of means well ordered toward this end; it thus satisfies the intelligence and the will, and can also, in the present, satisfy the sensibility. When that triple result is produced, when the useful transports us in advance to the term and to the object, Guyau believes that finality comes to be beauty.»

For those who regard the aesthetic phenomenon as the product of theoretical cognitive activity, the difference from the useful, which belongs to the domain of the practical, is radical. So it is in the aesthetics of Croce. For this philosopher, the aesthetic phenomenon is completely exhausted in the expressive elaboration of impressions. «When we have won the inner word, conceived clearly and vividly a figure or a statue, or found a musical motif, the expression is clear and is complete. It has no need of more. The actions we perform afterward, in order to give sensible forms to that interior expression, are of another nature; they belong to the economic or technical order. Art, thus reduced to an interior function, is independent both of science and of the useful and the moral. To will economically is to will an end; to will morally is to will a rational end; but art has nothing to do with the will: it is mere intuitive knowledge, or knowledge through fantasy.» The function of willing being thus absolutely eliminated, and with it the whole external expression of the beautiful, it was easy to conclude the separation of the aesthetic and the economic; but Croce, in the first place, does not explain clearly in what that intuition consists, which, for other philosophers, is an act, a power of the will; and, in the second place, one does not understand how the formation of the ideal is possible by means of fantastic or imaginative activity, whose essential character is freedom—unless the beautiful be reduced to pure expression, as Croce does, in which case it is impossible to explain the rich variety of forms and of feelings that aesthetic activity engenders. Theoretical activity and practical activity are inseparable, as Croce himself recognizes; consequently, it is not possible to give the value of absolute realities to what are merely logical separations, fruits of abstraction.

We believe, therefore, with Guyau, that the beautiful and the [p. 607] useful are bound together by the principle of harmony, which is realized not only between the parts and the whole, but also between the means and the end—which is what Kant calls external objective finality; but the useful, in order to realize that harmony, need not demonstrate the element of freedom, even though it may express it in a certain degree, because all harmony virtually involves that principle. For this reason the useful and the beautiful can be separated and associated in reality. The useful can be beautiful, as it can be indifferent or ugly; to be beautiful it needs that the soul receive from the useful harmonies expressing an idea of freedom, the idea of a force developing after the manner of free life. Only thus is produced that intellectual enjoyment characteristic of aesthetic emotion, and only thus can the disinterested and free character of this emotion be reconciled with the relation of objective finality that seems to oppose it.

The beautiful, in effect, is the disinterested, but it is not the useless, nor the absolutely disinterested; the beautiful is not subject to a calculation, as the useful is, certainly; aesthetic feeling is spontaneous and generous; but the beautiful, contributing to the education of our being and, for that very reason, to our happiness, is of great utility, and hence results its interested and interesting character, in a sense superior to the economic sense of the useful. The beautiful, Fouillée adds, can be absolutely disinterested only in the case of a Platonic love, and that is not the character of aesthetic feeling in the fullness of its evolution. «If by the useful,» says Voituron, «one understands only what pertains to the satisfaction or interest of the senses, the beautiful will not be useful, at least in general; but if one takes into account the interest of the soul, beauty will have a true utility—although it cannot be said that all that is useful to the soul is beautiful.»

Consequently, when it is said that all that is beauti[p. 608]ful is not useful, or that all that is useful is not beautiful, one announces a proposition which, in its generality, is not absolutely objectionable and has no need of demonstration; but when one wishes to conclude that the beautiful is in no way useful to us, one falls into an error, as when one absolutely denies to the useful the aesthetic character it may have. The beautiful, the good, the useful, the agreeable are, then, no more than apparent differences, as Piazzi says.

According to Soret, the most interesting form of modern art is the one that brings beauty completely down to utility. It is not difficult to observe—says this writer—that there is a very marked tendency to grasp the utility of according an aesthetic value to our great means of production; work is better done when everything surrounding the worker is treated with art.

Souriau, in his treatise on rational beauty, abounds in the same ideas of conciliation. Combating the thesis of absolute disinterestedness, on which Kant founds himself in order to separate the beautiful radically from the useful, he does not believe that the ideal is to disinterest oneself in everything. Aesthetics must be disinterested in the sense that it proposes to us ends higher than our pleasure and even than our personal interest; but it does not prevent us from seeking it. Souriau finds, in the aid that the useful offers us for the realization of those ends, a motive of admiration in which there is a certain disinterestedness and an aesthetic value—an admiration that responds not only to the perfection of the useful in its relation to one's own self, but also to that perfection of utility for others. This shows that there is no reason to refuse the useful all aesthetic value. Souriau believes, moreover, that in pursuing the useful one can attain, at the same time, sovereign beauty, and that there is, at least, one case in which utility coincides [p. 609] absolutely with beauty: when the object is made especially with an end of utility. In effect, in this case, what we must ask, above all, is that it conform to its destination; and in that lies its perfection and, consequently, its beauty.

Souriau confounds the perfect with the beautiful, and hence his foregoing conclusion, which errs by its generality. Nevertheless, his thesis is not false for the rest. Nor is it false when he maintains that the utility of an object enhances its beauty and predisposes sympathy in its favor, attenuating ugliness when this exists in the object. Things very useful but very ugly are almost always things useful in one sense but harmful in another, in which they affect us disagreeably. Souriau observes, finally, that, though it is true that beauty begins when life presents itself in its plenitude and ample expansion, as a superfluous superabundance, one cannot conclude from this that the necessary can never be endowed with aesthetic value; because the possession of the necessary gives us the physical well-being and the moral security indispensable for the expansion of all aesthetic feelings. It is said sometimes that we have a tendency to prefer the superfluous to the necessary; but what we prefer is to possess both. We disdain the necessary only when we have it; from the moment it is lacking, we feel its value. For Souriau, what is truly useful to us must always have some beauty, and the conflict does not exist between the useful and the beautiful, but between diverse ends in opposition.

These diverse opinions reflect the importance acquired by economic value in these times of dominant scientism and individualism, in which the useful rivals and even tends to surpass the beautiful. In the evolution of human feelings, in which the interested and the disinterested combine incessantly, [p. 610] one of those factors prevails without coming to acquire an absolute dominion, as happens with the egoistic and altruistic forms of the moral conscience. In that combination, the useful and the beautiful interpenetrate, aiding one another reciprocally. In art there are impure forms that realize that combination. Architecture and oratory express those forms; the beautiful and the useful are presented in the one and the other so closely interlinked that the beautiful gives relief to the useful, and the latter, in the most perfect realization of its end, imprints on the work that non-coercion of harmony which is static freedom in architecture and the dynamism of the idea in eloquence.

The transition from the useful to the beautiful is so imperceptible, and the change of the one into the other is effected in such a way, that architecture—an art principally useful—comes to be transformed into an aesthetic art, which answers to a moral or religious end that has with utility only a very remote relation; and eloquence abandons the practical end of convincing and stirring and limits itself to producing aesthetic emotions, like pure art.

And this happens because the aesthetic content and form do not absolutely exclude the categories of the true, the good, and the useful. The work of art, in the universality of its expression, is related to the whole of reality; but it requires of the diversity of its content not only the order in which the data of truth and the moral and economic phenomena are gathered, but chiefly freedom, which vivifies that content and makes it susceptible of receiving the artistic form—which fuses with the content to form the organism that is called a work of art.

The relation between the beautiful and the useful has been treated by Lalo, in his work on art and social life, in studying the relation existing between art and craft. Lalo maintains that these ought not to be separated. In his vi[p. 611]ew, «art, in separating itself from the craft, loses some of its best aesthetic qualities; it becomes a craft apart, self-sufficient and by which one can make a living; it becomes industrialized; its values are estimated more and more, and legitimately, in money; the craft kills technique by substituting itself for it, instead of being its support». «Art ought to be the luxury of a craft and not a craft of luxury.»

Lalo does not believe, however, that art ought to be confounded with the craft, because that has impeded the advent of new forms of the division of labor, which have cooperated in the greatest aesthetic reforms, as happened in the Middle Ages; so that the complete separation of art from the craft—produced by the inevitable fact of the division of artistic labor—is equally injurious to art as is the confusion of both disciplines of aesthetic activity.

It results from this that economic development is often contrary to aesthetic development. The concordance is not constant between those two groups of social phenomena. «When it occurs,» says Lalo, «it is only an interference of anaesthetic phenomena with purely aesthetic phenomena or laws.» «The great developments of art,» he adds, «follow upon the great economic activities, instead of accompanying them—being in no way a direct and necessary product of them.»

This relation between the disinterested aesthetic activity of art and the economic function of the craft—which is opposed to the antinomy established by Kantianism, and which affirms the solidarity between technique and the aesthetic content of the work of art, and even between the diverse forms of human activity that bear on art—confirms the theory of Guyau and the appraisal that Fouillée makes of the positivist movement in contempo[p. 612]rary art, whose tendency toward organic unity contrasts with the analytic spirit of the earlier idealist aesthetics.

This unity must not, however, be understood in the sense that it prevails with the same intensity in all works of art; because the alliance of the beautiful and the useful is not the same in all. Economic influence makes itself felt more in the forms that depart from pure art, such as architecture and eloquence; and if it can present itself in music and poetry, its appearance in these has the character of an aspiration foreign to art, or takes on forms of adaptation to equally foreign interests, which do not destroy the freedom of the artist within the very limits of the preconceived application. Pure art may subordinate itself to a decorative end or to an imposed theme, answering to utilitarian exigencies; but it can, likewise, within that limit, display a great freedom—all that it needs in order not to be confounded with a craft.

The beautiful and the useful are associated, then, very closely, but they are never confounded. The aesthetic criterion is always capable of distinguishing them, even when in the beautiful there predominates order, the essential character of the useful, and even when in the mechanism of the useful craft a certain sum of freedom is displayed. Art descends toward the craft by becoming mechanized, and the craft rises to art by gaining in interior freedom and technical freedom.

The aesthetic phenomenon, like all social phenomena, has a double aspect: it is psychic-social, and, in expressing itself in objective forms, it cannot escape the finality of action, which enters the domain of the useful, the practical, the verifiable. To emancipate it from that tendency, it is necessary to restrict that phenomenon to the sphere of knowledge, to the theoretical function, as [p. 613] Croce does—including then, in order to make it logical, within the economic order the expressive forms of the aesthetic arts, as happens in the strange thesis of that philosopher. For this reason James does not hesitate to attribute to the useful the criterion for appreciating the true; because the logical phenomenon, in all its amplitude, partakes also of a social element, tends toward a practical end, and is not purely theoretical, as traditional intellectualism has maintained.

The useful gives authority to the true when the latter comes out of its virtual condition of absolute truth—without that authorizing us to confound the true with the useful, to the point of making utility the essence of truth; the logical phase always surpasses the economic in the region of thought; but in social action finality imposes itself as a determining condition. The same happens with the aesthetic phenomenon, though in this the said finality must subordinate itself to the free and creative activity, which still has room within the circuit marked out by the destination of the work of art. This confirms the opinion that the finality of art is double—psychological and sociological—and that the theories of art for art's sake and of didactic art are false when considered in isolation. Art draws its inspiration from reality, present or historical, and returns upon it with the fruit of its inspiration.

### XIII. LA ESTÉTICA DE LA LIBERTAD — XIII. THE AESTHETICS OF FREEDOM

[p. 614] The principle of freedom, as essential to the aesthetic concept, is postulated for the first time in Kantian aesthetics, «which brings to a close the period of fruitless attempts, begun by Baumgarten, to create a system of ideas that would give form to this science». Notwithstanding the intellectualism of Kant's philosophy, aesthetic representation acquires a new value in his «Critique of Judgment». For this philosopher, «a representation is aesthetic when it is not bound up with a determinate concept of the object, but there dominates in it the pleasure that springs from the free play of our cognitive faculties, without any special purpose; in which case the finality, or harmony, that we suppose in nature lacks any positive end: it is a finality without an end».

It has been observed that the whole of the Critique of Judgment has for its object the resolving of the harmony between the concept of nature and the concept of freedom—engendered, respectively, by theoretical and by practical philosophy—thus making finality, or harmony, a fundamental idea in that Critique. But, even while granting this finalist character to Kant's aesthetic theory, and the deficiencies and contradictions Basch discovers in it, one must agree that in it is to be found the fertile germ of a new aesthetic orientation, which transfers the philosophical criterion from the idea of order, on which ancient aesthetics was founded, to the idea of freedom, radically separating art from science.

[p. 615] For Kant, «it is the proper character of art to be the work of free will. It is distinguished from science as the practical faculty from the theoretical, and it is distinguished from the trade as free art from the mercenary. Art is a play and the trade a labor; which does not mean that art has no hard and laborious technical apprenticeship». «The final artistic form must appear as free of all coercion by arbitrary rules as if it were the effect of nature alone. Art can be called beautiful only when we are conscious that it is art, though it seem to us nature; when it retains no apparent vestige of scholastic form; when we cannot even suspect that the rules have fettered the artist's fancy. In a word, the artistic form must be final without seeming so».

Exalting the value of poetry, Kant says of it «that it dilates the soul, that it gives freedom to the imagination and temper and strength to the will, reminding us of the existence of a faculty free, spontaneous, and independent of all natural determination».

But Kant did not derive these ideas from a psychological analysis; rather he referred them to a metaphysical postulate, to a noumenon, to a supersensible substratum of the phenomena. «There is no determinate objective principle of taste,» says Kant; «but there is an objective principle, that is, the determinate idea of the supersensible that exists within us». The aesthetic idea is, according to Kant, an inexplicable idea, because its foundation or substratum exceeds every intellectual concept.

Disdaining psychology, Kant did not deepen the study of the creative imagination so as to find there the source of artistic production and of aesthetic emotion. More inclined to the moralist tendency, Kant ended his critique of aesthetic judgment by studying beauty as a symbol of morality, [p. 616] «as an intuition which, not by its content but by the mode of reflection, by the procedure and rule of judgment, has some analogy with the concept of the good, to which no sensory vision can correspond».

Kant, it is true, attributes to the imagination, as Ambrosi affirms, the very lofty function of forming the ideal of the beautiful, to which he gives the name of the ideal of the imagination, and he makes of the imagination the creative power of genius; but genius, for him, is, in substance, a powerful imagination which, guided by the understanding, comes to give sensible and expressive form to the thoughts—in themselves vague and indeterminate—that the feeling of the beautiful arouses in us.

The imagination would enter, moreover, according to Kant, into the production of the feeling of the sublime and into the formation of the elements of spirit and of taste which, together with genius, form the productive faculty of art. But, as Ambrosi remarks, «given the noumenal aspect of psychic reality itself, the manner in which the imagination elaborates its conceptions and realizes them, it becomes almost impossible to divine that imaginative function; one being able to say only that this faculty is reduced to uniting and combining, by a wholly artificial process, sensible forms abstracted from all reality with intellectual ideas likewise abstracted from all reality. [p. 617] Artistic creation thus comes to be an evocation of shades and phantoms, stripped of all other subsistence than that which comes to them from the spirit that contemplates them».

Kant, for the rest, could not make of the imagination a faculty of free creation, having established that it was obliged to submit to the understanding or to reason in order to produce its aesthetic works. The essence of that creation was opposed to his critical intellectualism.

Kant's aesthetics, thus, did no more than contemplate, under the subjective aspect, the same problem that had been examined before under the objective aspect—transferring to the domain of feeling the aesthetic order placed in the objects themselves, but without altering the nature of the pleasure, which in ancient aesthetics was derived from interior harmony. That pleasure, of a logical character, subsists in Kantian aesthetics, which analyzes not taste in itself, as feeling, but the judgment of taste as an aesthetic faculty of knowing.

The idea of order prevails, consequently, in Kantian aesthetics, notwithstanding its efforts to introduce into it the factor of freedom, in the form of the free play of the cognitive faculties. That idea, as Bosanquet observes, is the objective of his whole philosophy. «It may be affirmed,» says this historian of aesthetics, «that Kant pursued three cardinal points, imposed upon him by the converging movements of thought, at whose focus he placed himself. First, he wished to justify the conception of a natural order in his Critique of theoretical Reason; second, the conception of a moral order in the Critique of practical Reason; and [p. 618] third, the conception of the compatibility between the two orders in the Critique of Judgment. The order of nature and the moral order were to have a common path, one that is strongly revealed in the spontaneous harmony between natural necessity and the ideal end, exhibited by the perceptive and creative sense of beauty».

Kant could not abandon that static concept of the beautiful, formulated ever since Plato, because he did not penetrate into the nature of the creative activity of fine art, which contains the principle of freedom essential to beauty. For this reason Croce criticizes Kantian aesthetics as deficient and explains why Kant does not connect his theory of the beautiful with that of art and falls, in the end, into the moralism of the neo-Platonic school.

Schiller develops that germ of free play, making the postulate of freedom the basis of his aesthetics. But, as Basch remarks, «Schiller does not trust to experience for determining the pure rational concept of beauty; rather he affirms that this concept can be investigated only by abstraction and must be deduced from the possibility of the sensible and rational nature of man. Beauty must thus be regarded as a necessary condition of humanity. It is a matter, consequently, of ascending to the pure concept of humanity and of deducing from that concept of humanity, as a genus, the idea of the beautiful. And this is what Schiller does, analyzing man as a genus».

In that analysis, Schiller distinguishes in man two fundamental elements: his permanent self and his transitory, differing states, which, considered in themselves, would make of man only a pure form or a chaotic content, and would engender two opposed instincts—yet correlative and necessary for human perfection: the formal instinct and the sensuous instinct, the first destined to unify, by means of reason, the manifold, contingent, and chaotic reality derived from the second.

Schiller finds in the mutual action and reaction of these two essential instincts of nature the ideal, the very idea of humanity; for, if there were a case in which man had consciousness, at once, of his person and of his states, of his unlimited freedom and of his limited existence—feeling himself as matter and knowing himself as form—he would then possess the complete intuition of his humanity, and the object of that intuition would be, for him, a symbol of the total realization of his destiny, and would therefore serve him to repre[p. 619]sent the infinite. Schiller believes that there would then awaken in man a new impulse, which would reconcile both instincts and would suppress, at once, the tyranny of the external world, which is imposed of necessity upon our senses, and the tyranny of reason, which of necessity imposes its laws upon the world of the senses. This new instinct, which Schiller calls the play instinct, would give man absolute freedom and would have for its object the fusing of sensuous life and rational form into a living form, which would serve to designate all the aesthetic qualities of phenomena.

Beauty is not, then, for Schiller, a phenomenon of experience; it is only a postulate of reason, the ideal end toward which humanity tends and which results from the ordinary play of the two fundamental forces of man. Only when man contemplates beauty is he truly free and capable of play, and only when he plays is he capable of aesthetic contemplation. Man ought to play only with beauty; for man plays only when he is truly man, and he is not truly man save when he plays—when all his faculties are in perfect equilibrium.

For Schiller, in the aesthetic state man learns to desire nobly, to fulfill freely the law of reason; but in that state the absence of necessity does not imply the lack of laws. Aesthetic freedom is distinguished from the logical necessity of thought and from the moral necessity of the will only in that the laws by virtue of which the soul proceeds in this sphere do not present themselves in the form of laws, nor meet with any resistance. Pure indetermination is, for Schiller, an empty infinitude; aesthetic freedom, or freedom of determination, is a full infinitude.

This aesthetic freedom, which resides in form—this [p. 620] perfect equanimity of the soul, joined to strength and vigor—is the disposition in which a true work of art should leave us, and the surest touchstone for judging of its value.

Schiller develops this idea of the play instinct, applying it to the various orders of beauty, from physical play to aesthetic play properly so called. The principle of freedom that he postulates serves him also to explain the sublime as well as the graceful, and to determine the value of art, emancipating aesthetic activity from every moral imperative. «In aesthetic judgments,» says Schiller, «what excites our interest is not morality in itself, but only freedom; and moral purity cannot please our imagination except insofar as it throws into relief the force of the will».

Notwithstanding this affirmation of the ideal of freedom as an aesthetic criterion, Schiller, a rationalist like his master Kant, attributes to thought a superior importance. It is true that he distinguishes the imagination from the understanding, on the ground that the former reveals a free activity that does not exist in the latter; but he calls that freedom capricious and apparent and subordinates it, in a certain way, to the logical concatenation of discourse. The imagination cleaving to the very nature of the object, and the understanding to a higher idea, the former finds movement and variety in the very place where the latter ascertains the most perfect continuity. Concepts develop according to the law of necessity, but they pass before the imagination according to the law of freedom.

Schiller applies this distinction to poetry, which he defines as the art of affecting our sensibility in a determinate manner, by means of the free effect of our productive imagination. This end imposed upon [p. 621] poetry necessarily implies two imperatives: on the one hand, it must let our imagination judge freely and act in an autonomous manner; and on the other hand, it must, on the contrary, direct this imagination so as to produce in us determinate sensations and feelings. Hence an antinomy for the imagination, autonomous and obedient at once, which Schiller resolves by making it obey nature and transform external necessity into interior necessity. The poet must preserve in his imagination all its freedom and all its spontaneity, reducing the whole free play of the association of perceptions and organic laws to necessary syntheses.

For Schiller, the pleasure that art causes is a free pleasure, whose finality is perceived by the intellectual faculties with which we represent it, and whose agreeable impression does no more than accompany this representation—being distinguished thereby from sensuous pleasure, which is only the wholly physical consciousness of an organic need that does not reach our consciousness. For this reason all ideas—such as those of the good, the true, and the perfect, which occupy our understanding; that of the beautiful, which occupies the understanding together with the imagination; and those of the moving and the sublime, which occupy our reason together with the imagination—are sources of free pleasure and can be put at the service of art, as ideas with respect to which we represent finality to ourselves. Schiller, in these conceptions, reproduces the Kantian ideas under a different form.

It is in the case of tragedy that Schiller expresses most clearly that subordination of artistic activity to a higher principle of harmony which reason alone can furnish. The proper object of tragedy, for Schiller, is to embrace all the cases in which a natural finality is sacrificed to a higher moral [p. 622] finality, as in the moving and the sublime. In order that we may enjoy the higher harmony that reigns in the empire of freedom, it is indispensable that all the contradictions that rend the world of nature be disclosed to us. In a later evolution, Schiller substitutes for the moral character the purely aesthetic one of free play; but, as Basch says, he moves more and more toward idealism, so as to arrive, at least theoretically, at the extreme form of idealism, at the symbolism of the musical drama. The mission of art, of the sublime play of the poets, is to free man from the chains of the sensible world, transforming the latter into a free creation of our spirit, one in harmony with nature conceived as an ideal that does not fall under the dominion of the senses.

Such is, in sum, the aesthetics of Schiller, in which freedom—as the ideal of perfect humanity and as the end and essence of the beautiful—has a capital importance. It presents, however, a contradictory duality between Schiller the philosopher, disciple of Kant, and Schiller the autonomous poet, who acts in a milieu dominated by philosophical intellectualism and classical idealism. As a poet, Schiller feels the autonomy of aesthetic activity, which refuses all rule and carries its creations as far as the musical form, the freest of poetry; but as a philosopher he does not admit an artistic imagination that withdraws itself from the precepts of logic. As a romantic poet, he rises to the greatest heights of the sentimental poem; but, under the influence of Goethe, he reacts in the direction of Hellenic art and makes harmony the end of the beautiful. His aesthetic state and his play instinct, which define the beautiful, modify the Kantian thought of the «free play of the cognitive faculties» into a free play of two instincts, the sensuous and [p. 623] the formal, which correspond to the cognitive faculties of imagination and understanding in Kant—expressions, in their turn, of the manifold and the one of ancient aesthetics, as Basch observes—and which reduce that definition of the beautiful to the old concept of order as the aesthetic criterion.

Schiller, a genius of transition, moving between Kant and Goethe, could not translate his aesthetic feelings into ideas that departed radically from Kantian intellectualism and from Goethe's realist classicism. Philosophical thought, joined to a psychological content that had not been purified of metaphysical influence, had not yet come to glimpse a true and profound concept of freedom—which engenders harmony, but is not engendered by it. This explains the oscillations, obscurities, deficiencies, and contradictions of this theory, which had so great an influence on the aesthetic culture of its age and which may be regarded as the source of modern philosophical aesthetics.

Schiller did not understand freedom as the creative function of the beautiful, but as an end, as an ideal to be pursued. His point of departure was not psychological, but metaphysical. For Schiller, the beautiful is that which gives birth to freedom; and so he could not derive from freedom the art that is a means of realizing it. Hence the necessity of deriving art from a natural instinct, the play instinct.

According to Basch, the aesthetics of romanticism, set forth by Friedrich Schlegel, did no more than exaggerate the conceptions of Schiller. For Schlegel, Greek art is regarded as absolute art, emanating from the harmony of all the faculties of man; and modern art as emanating from the scission of the human faculties and characterized by the lacerations and the intense melancholy produced by the insatiable thirst for the [p. 624] ideal—that is, for lost harmony. What enchants our heart and satisfies our spirit, said Schlegel, is not particular beauties, but harmony, perfection, calm, and satisfaction; it is beauty complete, total, and permanent. There is in modern poetry an intense aspiration toward the eternal and toward harmony; but this aspiration is not realized, because the supreme principle of this poetry is not the beautiful.

Romanticism, proclaiming the empire of subjectivity in art, introduces, it is true, the principle of infinite freedom—to which romantic irony reduces itself—carrying its creative activity to times and events in which that free subjectivity reigns; but, instead of transferring to the domain of the will the center of aesthetic activity, it makes feeling the essential character of that activity, substituting for the classical harmony of the finite and plastic the romantic harmony of the infinite and musical. Romanticism did not express, as classicism did, harmony realized, but harmony sought—after the scission, or the rupture of equilibrium, produced in the spirit, had destroyed the unity of the human soul.

Freedom, that aspiration toward the infinite proper to romanticism, produced the scission that art was to destroy by means of a new interior harmony.

Friedrich Schlegel, the theorist of romanticism, in his book on the «Limits of Beauty,» seeks, as Knight says, to make the highest beauty reside in these three elements: nature, love, and art; he regards perpetual vitality as the most characteristic factor of nature, and as the fundamental factors of art, unity, harmony, and symmetry, which he associates as the formal conditions of complete beauty. As na[p. 625]ture, it is inexhaustible; as art, it is without limits. Schlegel thus confirms his aesthetic criterion, determined by the idea of harmony.

A romantic, the humorist Jean Paul Friedrich Richter, said in this period, referring to the aesthetic theories: «True aesthetics can be written, some day, only by a man who is, at once, philosopher and poet. The transcendental aesthetics of the pure philosophers is only a doctrine of mathematical harmony, which decomposes into numerical proportions the sounds of the poetic lyre. The empirical aesthetics of the artists and critics, who follow the path opened by Aristotle, is a theory of harmony, which teaches only the negative correctness of composition». Making the essence of poetry consist in a beautiful and immaterial imitation, he combats the poetic nihilists, as he does poetic materialism, but he does not define beauty. For him, the artistic faculty par excellence is the productive or fantastic imagination, which is the elemental spirit of all our faculties—which builds worlds with each fragment of the world, which universalizes everything with the infinite universe, and which reveals intuitively the absolute and the infinite of reason.

Jean Paul thus withdraws from the arbitrary freedom of the nihilist romantics, introducing reflection and instinct into the creative activity of genius. The flight of the poet is the free flight of the flame, not the explosion of a mine that is set off. The true genius finds calm within himself. Enthusiasm must animate the whole; but the parts of the work of art are wrought with coolness and repose. For this reason the reflection of the poet has a hidden kinship with that of the philosopher.

This conciliatory tendency of Richter's, between reflective classical art and romantic art—which consists, [p. 626] for him, in indeterminate beauty, or in the infinitely beautiful—gives his aesthetics an eclectic character in which the two opposed (though not contradictory) ideas of order and freedom find application. Nevertheless, in treating of humor, or of the romantic comic, as he calls it, Richter seems to incline toward the principle of the freedom that annihilates every ideal, toward the poetic nihilism he had condemned. But even in this form he declares that humor is a very serious thing, as one that involves the annihilating and infinite idea—that is, the philosophical and reflective ground of art—in this expressive form of the greatest freedom, in which everything is annihilated save the reality of the self, which analyzes the contrasts of life and laughs gently at human vanity in order to resolve them. True humor demands a poetic spirit, capable of rising to freedom and to philosophy, and endowed not with an empty taste, but with a loftier manner of considering the universe.

Fichte, notwithstanding the subjectivism of his philosophy of freedom, did not treat of aesthetic ideas, being occupied almost exclusively with the moral problem. But there is attributed to his influence the aesthetic doctrine of irony, as the foundation of art, which Friedrich Schlegel and Ludwig Tieck developed and which Richter applied to his aesthetics of humor.

It was Schelling who posed the aesthetic problem, raising it to the rank of a metaphysical problem and founding what Baldwin has aptly called pancalism. Schelling regards art as the realization of the absolute, in which the conscious and the unconscious are harmonized and identified. This immutable identity is, for artistic production, what destiny is for action: a dark and unknown power that adds to the imperfect work of freedom objective perfec[p. 627]tion, without the consent of freedom and, in a certain degree, against freedom itself, as Menéndez Pelayo says. This unknown potency we designate by the obscure notion of genius. The artistic product is, then, the work of genius, in which the unconscious element predominates. By force of its nature, genius resolves the romantic scission by transforming it into an infinite harmony. For this reason Schelling establishes that the fundamental character of the work of art is an unconscious infinite, which the artist puts there by instinctive impulse, beyond his purpose and sometimes against it. For this reason, too, he brands as usurpers of the title of works of art those that are the faithful expression of the artist's conscious activity, which speak only to reflection and never to intuition—that intuition which loves to lose itself in the depths of its object and can find repose only in the infinite.

But Schelling, like the romantics, derives all aesthetic production from an infinite scission in itself of the two activities that are separated in every free production, and he regards aesthetic feeling as a feeling of harmony and of infinite satisfaction, whose outward expression is one of calm and tranquil grandeur, even when it is necessary to express the most intense degree of pain or of joy. His ideal is classical; in reality it is an ideal of order, of harmony, not of freedom—even while he makes intuition the aesthetic criterion and proclaims the absolute independence of art. Thus is explained why Schelling identifies the work of art with an organism; why he gives exclusive importance to the works of ancient art, especially to sculpture; and why he creates a universe of art, seizing upon the metaphor «the poetic universe,» used by the romantics and made by them the postulate of their criticism, which consists in discovering, in works of art, the development of this single organism, as Bréhier observes.

[p. 628] When Schelling, in his last metaphysical speculations, which he calls positive philosophy, pronounces in favor of the predominance of freedom—departing from his primitive idealism, influenced by Winckelmann and Spinoza—when he makes of becoming an expression of free life and makes of the creative function the character of freedom, he no longer formulates any application to aesthetic theory, but plunges into a religious mysticism, in which the absolute is God, personal and free, prior to becoming, though manifesting himself only in it. Nevertheless, this divine freedom is not yet unconditioned, because it presupposes the elements at the disposal of God's creative function. Schelling introduces contingency and freedom into becoming as well; but Bréhier judges that his contingentism does not go so far as to make human consciousness come out of itself in order to abandon itself freely to the flux of becoming. For Schelling, man is a microcosm, in which not only are the elements that enter into human nature the same as those that enter into the world, but the becoming, or the construction, of humanity is effected in an order and according to a law rigorously identical with that of all cosmic processes.

The philosophical point of view having been transferred by Schelling from the subject to the object, and true art having been regarded as the representation of infinite life, as transcendental intuition made objective, freedom lost the capital importance it had enjoyed in the subjective philosophy of Fichte, and necessity was to take its place as the product of the unconscious activity dominant in the genius who produces the work of art. Thus is explained, too, how beauty comes here to comprehend truth and goodness, necessity and freedom, and how this system ends in a pancalism—an expression of the absolute—in which the Platonic ideas re-[p. 629]emerge under the title of gods. The particular forms of art, being at once representatives of the infinite and of the universe, are called «ideas.» For Schelling, to art alone is granted absolute objectivity and, with it, universal validity. Hence its superiority over philosophy, which, though it attains the supreme truth, carries up to the exalted sign of art only a fragment of man; art, on the contrary, carries the whole man, and therein lies its eternal miracle. Art turns out to be, as Menéndez Pelayo observes, the highest thing that exists for the philosopher, because it is the sole and true organ of philosophy and, at the same time, the document that ceaselessly confirms what philosophy cannot express outwardly—that is, what is unconscious in activity and in production, and its primitive identity with all that has consciousness.

For Schelling, the freedom of the artist, resembling divine freedom, is, at the same time, the purest and highest necessity; genius is the highest conformity with law, deriving from its unconscious activity. Where the unconscious power we call genius manifests itself, art communicates to its works an inexhaustible reality, which makes them resemble the works of nature and rival that spirit which throbs within the interior of beings and which manifests itself by their external forms, as by so many symbols.

The theory of the imagination is intimately bound up with that of genius. Both derive from that activity, unconscious and conscious at the same time, whose products are characterized simultaneously by the necessity of nature and the freedom of the spirit. The imagination is identified, as Ambrosi says, with the mysterious force that unites body to soul, matter to life, nature to spirit. Fantasy in this [p. 630] system is transformed into a true creative potency, which reconstructs, consciously and freely, what the eternal and divine activity produces unconsciously and with necessary spontaneity. In the dark labyrinths of the absolute unconsciousness proper to natural forces, there has its root the genius that marks the summit of the imaginative function.

If the Schellingian philosophy is pancalist, that of Hegel is panlogist; if Schelling places art at the summit of the representations of the absolute, Hegel places it at the base, surpassed by religion and philosophy—ideas that proclaim the absolute freedom of the absolute reason. Nevertheless, freedom has in the Hegelian system a superior importance. For Hegel, the highest faculty that man can enclose within himself is freedom, which contains the highest destiny of the spirit. Freedom consists in the subject's finding nothing foreign, nothing that limits it. Through freedom, the subject puts itself in harmony with the world and is satisfied in it; by means of it, all opposition, all contradiction disappears, and, consequently, necessity and misfortune are eliminated. But this freedom is inseparable from reason in general, from morality in action, and from truth in thought, and can be attained only in the region of absolute truth, in which all contraries are absorbed and reconciled by means of philosophy, or free reason. Thus freedom becomes a freedom of reason, a formal freedom, a freedom of the idea, the activity that generates reality itself.

This interpretation is modified, however, in Hegelian aesthetics, in which experience exercised an effective influence and in which the theory of the beautiful is restricted to the limits of a philosophy of art. Hegel, in opposition to Schelling, maintains that the science of art imposes itself [p. 631] despotically upon the artist himself in modern times. Art is a science, because it is rigorously determined by ideas that interest our intelligence and by the laws of its development, whatever be the inexhaustible variety of its forms. Art creates images, appearances destined to represent the ideas, to show the truth under sensible forms, whose contemplation is wholly disinterested; but it is independent of science as of morality. Art represents to us, in a visible image, the realized harmony of the two terms of existence—of the law of beings and of their manifestation, of essence and of form. The beautiful is essence realized, activity conformed to its end and identified with it—happy, serene, free in its harmonious development, even in the midst of pain. To represent harmony, to manifest the beautiful, is the end of art. The idea of the beautiful consists in the union and harmony of two terms that present themselves to thought as separate and opposed: the ideal and the real, the idea and the form, whose opposition is, at bottom, the capital problem of philosophy.

The beautiful, though it be idea, is not, however, confounded with truth. The beautiful always adds a note to the true; and, its two terms, essence and form, being inseparable, it has a character of infinitude and of freedom and is inaccessible to logical reason and to abstraction. The contemplation of the beautiful is a liberal contemplation, which leaves the object in its independent existence and excludes from the subject every desire to possess it and to convert it into an instrument for its own ends.

The idea of freedom, though without the importance it has in Schiller's aesthetics, enters here too as an aesthetic factor. In the aesthetic conception of the physical world the idea of ordered force prevails; but in that of the biological world harmony is associated with freedom: its [p. 632] beauty is force manifested by an ensemble of forms, of independent and free movements. Nevertheless, neither animal life nor human life can enjoy the absolute freedom that art realizes—as the expression of the life of the spirit, as the expression of the ideal in its infinite freedom, in its beatific serenity, as the symbol of the triumph of freedom concentrated within itself.

Hegel introduces the principle of evolution into the development of the aesthetic ideal, accepting the static and dynamic forms and their symbolic, classical, and romantic manifestations—characterizing the last as the expression of a free and dynamic life, and the classical as the expression of a harmony or equilibrium that Christian civilization breaks, creating that scission between content and form which aspires to a harmony in the infinite. Architecture is symbolic; sculpture represents classical art; and the other arts the romantic element, especially music.
