Hegel did not give great importance to psychological aesthetics. His deficient analysis is analogous to that of his contemporaries and predecessors. He distinguishes the artist's imagination from the purely passive capacity to perceive and recall images. Artistic imagination, or fantasy, is for him essentially active and creative; but the exercise of its power presupposes, in the first place, the natural datum of a singular aptitude for perceiving the real in all the vividness of its forms; in the second place, a lively attention which, kept continually awake to all that impresses the ear and the eye, imprints upon the spirit the diverse images of things; and, finally, a happy memory that conserves this whole world of sensible representations. The first bases of a general artistic imagination consist in this natural datum of taking [p. 633] an interest in everything, of perceiving the individual and characteristic side of things and their real forms, as also in the faculty of retaining all that has been seen and observed. Hegel concerns himself with the intimate knowledge of external things, as of internal ones, in analyzing the imagination; but he does not see in that creative function the aspect of freedom which is essential to it. For him, reflection and meditation have more importance. By means of them the artist is to discover the rational element, the idea, the intimate essence of things, even when he does not proceed by a philosophical method; for the true end of the artistic imagination is to reveal the reason and the essence of things in a concrete form, in an individual reality. The work of the imagination consists, consequently, for Hegel, as for Schelling, in fusing into a harmonious whole the rational element and the sensible form of things.

The Hegelian panlogism, which makes of the idea the principle of all reality, producing it in its evolution, places this aesthetic system, more than any other, within the domain of the idea of order—notwithstanding the use it makes of freedom as an aspiration, in the same sense as Schiller. The Hegelian idea does not imply consciousness, though it is dynamic, though life and consciousness are comprised in the forms of its manifestation. The idea, says Bosanquet, is regarded by Hegel as a systematic unity, as is the concrete process of the world. The idea, even while it distinguishes the beautiful from the true, is truth, and this is the beautiful in its sensible manifestation. Hegelian intellectualism was not favorable, for that reason, to the concept of beauty as the expression of the free activity of the spirit.

The principle of aesthetic freedom acquires notable importance in the theory of the Hegelian Rosenkranz re[p. 634]lating to the nature of the ugly, a theory destined to supply the deficiency of Hegelian aesthetics on this matter. The ugly is, for Rosenkranz, the absence or the negation of freedom in beings. In the physical order, it comes from the obstacles offered to the free development of energy; in the moral order, the consciousness of free and harmonious development beautifies: non-freedom—that is, the impossibility of determining oneself in an infinite manner—renders ugly; an ugliness that passes over into the body. Ugliness is thus the absence of freedom, a servitude of the spirit, which manifests itself even in the movements and attitudes of the body. If the ugly enters into art, it is not by way of contrast, as is believed, but because art has the need to manifest sensibly the totality of the Idea in all its free development.

It would seem, then, that Rosenkranz had tried to demonstrate that a physical, biological, or psychic force acting without freedom engenders the ugly, and, consequently, that those same forces, acting freely, would engender the beautiful. But, at bottom, freedom does not have that exclusive value. Rosenkranz, as a faithful disciple of Hegel, does not abandon the Idea as the creator of both aesthetic categories; and the idea is order, and nothing but order. Harmony, for that reason, has in this aesthetics such significance that it is introduced even into the ugly, which is disharmony. Rosenkranz would have even the ugly idealized, would have a certain manner of harmony established within it; so that, if non-freedom constitutes the ugly, it is because order—essential to the idea—is thereby destroyed, a disturbance is produced, and the ugly is introduced, along with the accidental, thus integrating the reality of the idea, which is not pure abstraction.

With Herbart, founder of realism, opposed to Hegelian idealism within the intellectualism common to [p. 635] both, aesthetics tends to acquire a scientific and positive orientation, eliminating the concept of freedom as an aesthetic factor.

The German aestheticians of this period receive the influence of both systems and tend to reconcile them, but sacrificing the principle of freedom and giving exclusive importance—notwithstanding the vindication of the individual element in art—to the ideal of harmony. This happens with Vischer, with Carriere, with Lotze, with Max Schasler, and even with Schleiermacher himself, who sympathized with Schiller and compared the free creation of art with the production of free thoughts in dreams, making their difference consist in the power that consciousness has, in artistic production, to order its images.

The philosophy of Schopenhauer, radically opposed to Hegelian intellectualism, might have reacted vigorously in the direction of a voluntarist aesthetics, since the center of his system was the will and not the idea. But it was not so.

According to Schopenhauer, art, the work of genius, is the mode of knowledge that investigates the will—that essence proper to the world, which is independent and outside all relation, which is the true substance of phenomena, which is not subject to change and whose knowledge always remains the same; in a word, it is the mode of knowledge that investigates the ideas which are the immediate objectivation of the thing in itself, that is, of the will.

Art conceives and reproduces, by means of pure contemplation, the eternal Ideas, that which is essential in all the phenomena of this world. Its sole origin is the knowledge of the ideas, and its sole end, to communicate this knowledge. One can, then, define art, says Schopenhauer, as the contemplation of [p. 636] things independently of the principle of reason, in opposition to that other contemplation which is subject to that principle and which is the contemplation of experience and of the sciences. Artistic contemplation keeps to the region of pure intuition, absorbing itself entirely in it and severing knowledge from the will, to whose service it stands from its origin.

The intuition of the general in the particular, attained by means of the total emancipation of the spirit, is, then, the key to this whole aesthetic theory, in which genius presents itself as a faculty against nature, since it consists in the intelligence—whose proper destiny is to serve the will—emancipating itself from that subjection in order to function on its own account. Genius thus turns out to be an intelligence that declares itself unfaithful to its practical mission, by effect of a truly abnormal superabundance that borders on madness. By its very excess, the intelligence of genius acquires that predominant activity; it succeeds in detaching itself from the will and, forgetful of its origin, in setting itself in activity freely, by its own force and by virtue of its own elasticity, and in creating the great works of art, which realize no useful end, as the works of the practical man do.

The end of art lies thus in facilitating the understanding of the ideas of the universe, the ideas being taken in the Platonic acceptation of the word. Art is constituted by the ascent toward the permanent, eternal, and immutable ideas; it is not the product of the free activity of the spirit, which Schopenhauer does not directly recognize as its proper and essential character.

Aesthetic activity being reduced to the pure contemplation of the idea acquired by intuition, Schopenhauer declares that, when we say a thing is beautiful, we ex[p. 637]press by this that it is an object of our contemplation; that every object is beautiful, inasmuch as every existing object can be considered objectively and outside all relation, and the will manifests itself in every object in some degree of objectivity expressive of an idea, the degree of beauty depending on the elevation of the idea it enshrines.

The metaphysical aesthetics of Schopenhauer, as his critic Fauconnet recognizes, is a theory of the knowledge of the will, as Kant's was of the noumenon: a contemplative knowledge, which produces a liberation, an emancipation of the spirit, which thus escapes the tyranny of the practical will and which, for that very reason, does not derive from a principle of freedom essential to the spirit—that individual freedom which Schopenhauer excludes from his system.

This notwithstanding, Schopenhauer, in the study of the particular arts, and even in that of beautiful nature, is wont to explain the aesthetic phenomenon by the energy of the will, which tends to overcome the tyranny of the obstacles opposed to its objectifying itself.

Art has in Schopenhauer's philosophy a close relation with morality. Man, in order to withdraw himself momentarily from the pain imposed by the tendency of the will, has art at his disposal, which emancipates him from the reality that enslaves him. The first and only possible means of enjoying a pleasure is conditioned by the same circumstances that can lead to the knowledge of the ideas, from which art springs—originating in the rapture of intuition, in the fusion of subject with object, in the forgetting of individuality, in the suppression of the knowledge that obeys the principle of reason and knows only relations. Aesthetic pleasure thus has, as its subjective condition, the emancipation of know[p. 638]ledge with respect to the will. On the other hand, fantasy is a valuable aid in arousing and maintaining aesthetic pleasure, emancipating us from the tyranny of desire and of pain and making us know what is highest in art. The emancipation of the individual will and the free action of fantasy are, then, the fundamental elements on which rests all aesthetic pleasure produced by the beautiful.

The aesthetics of Schopenhauer has, as is seen, a close affinity with that of Schelling and even with that of Kant. Its importance lies, not so much in the liberating power it attributes to art, as in the role played by intuition, which is, for him, the first source of all evidence and of all wisdom, the sole means of knowing and revealing the idea, the expression of the will. The imagination plays a secondary function: that of furnishing the expressive forms of intuition, the images expressive of life, in order to order them, color them, fix them, and reproduce them at will, as the object of a penetrating and profound study requires, and as the significant work of art, destined to communicate it, requires. Intuition thus furnishes the ground of the work of art, and imagination its expressive forms. The former is the work of reason, the latter of perception.

The voluntarism of Schopenhauer is not, consequently, non-rational; far from it, it ends, in the end, by placing reason, like Kant, above all activity and by making the classical ideal of order the aesthetic ideal. The idea triumphs over action, and therefore not-willing-to-live is worth more than willing-to-live in his philosophical system, and pessimism springs up naturally. The contemplation of the idea is, as in Aristotle, the sole ideal of happiness; only that here the artist takes the place of the sage, the mystic that of the practical man.

[p. 639] After Schopenhauer it is not possible to find another system of an aesthetics of freedom save in Jakob Frohschammer, who converted the theory of the imagination into a pancalist theory, to judge by Ambrosi's analysis. Not only the field of science, but even sensory life and the field of art, like volitional life and the field of morality, are alike dominated by the imagination. Now, this faculty—so independent, having a very wide share in the whole of our psychic life and in its various manifestations, and capable of giving a certain reality even to the impossible—is not a faculty derived from the elements and forces of the inorganic world, subject to the necessary and invariable laws of nature; nor can it result from the other faculties of the spirit, because all these have need of its stimulus in order to pass from potency to act and to accomplish their work. That faculty is primitive.

According to Frohschammer, there exists in nature a power that presents the greatest analogy with the human imagination, and it is, precisely, the force which, elaborating the inorganic elements, brings individuals out of their combinations and thus develops the infinite wealth of living beings. One single fundamental difference exists between the human imagination and this force, which may be called the imagination of nature, and it is that, while the former is completely free in itself, the latter submits to the laws of the physico-chemical forces; which does not prevent, however, so close a relation existing between the two that the subjective imagination of man is regarded as the highest form of the objective imagination of nature. Identical in their essence, they differ only in the degree of their development and in their manner of functioning. While the psychological imagination is a faculty [p. 640] primitive with respect to the others of our spirit, it can be called derived only insofar as it has its roots in the cosmic imagination.

This universal imagination, having reached in its development its highest creative power, emancipates itself from mechanical necessity and, become human, pursues its end and continues, under a new form, the work it began in nature, creating works still more beautiful. Thus, in the human will, the imagination reveals itself as a creative virtue, which first conceives and then enacts what it has conceived; which first proposes an end to itself and then seeks to attain it—being, at the same time, thought and action, dream and reality.

In this metaphysics, the imagination plays the same role as the Hegelian Idea and the Schopenhauerian Will; it is a power that creates all living reality as well as all fictitious reality; it is a free power that engenders art.

Aesthetic philosophy offers no other attempt to construct a voluntarist theory until Spencer, who revives Schiller's theory of play and imparts to it a high scientific prestige that still holds, notwithstanding the objections formulated by the adversaries of positivism and even by some of those who follow the scientific direction.

According to Spencer, play is a biological phenomenon that derives from an excess of energy, spent in movements and actions that lack practical finality and are, for that very reason, disinterested. Artistic activity would thus be an activity of play, a free activity, and consequently an activity of pure luxury, as has been said since. By this principle of freedom [p. 641] in movements Spencer explains grace, which is economy of force, or a force easy and sympathetic.

This biological principle of play was welcomed by all the positivists as the basis of an aesthetic science in which it was possible to discover laws similar to those that govern physical phenomena. The evolutionists explained its origin and development; and even though someone, like Grosse, discovered at the bottom of that phenomenon, as its root, freedom, this was not understood as a creative power of art. The determinist exigencies of the scientific spirit at last eliminated that factor.

Aestheticians like Guyau and Nietzsche, who believe they find in the expansion of life the explanation of art, ignore the end of freedom. For Guyau, the beautiful lies chiefly in sympathy, in solidarity. For Nietzsche—who makes of the instinct of power the generating cause of every strong, dominating, and for that reason free, action; for whom life is that instinct, is that which eternally wills to surpass itself—the beautiful is also a phenomenon of knowledge. Nietzsche's non-rationalism did not carry him so far as to discover in the expansive force of the will what he believed existed only in the biological stimuli. The influence of Schopenhauer and of the positive philosophy of his age did not permit him to reach the logical term of his great aversion to intellectualism. Hence he adopted the principle of play as well, and regarded life as a game, as art had taught the Greeks. Thus the work of art is the supreme explanation of life, resolving the enigma that neither the idea of the good nor that of the true had been able to decipher. The artist is, for Nietzsche, the philosopher, as he had been for Schelling.

Nietzsche declares that pleasure and displeasure are mere consequences, mere secondary phenomena. [p. 642] What man wills, what the smallest particle of a living organism wills, he says, is an increase of power. In the aspirations toward an end there is pleasure as much as displeasure; in each of his volitions man seeks resistance, has need of something to oppose him. But Nietzsche does not observe that, if the love of free life did not exist as the stimulus of that power, the obstacle would not be the stimulant of the will to power, and power itself would not exist. This desire for freedom is not, as Nietzsche believes, a disguised form of the will to power, any more than is the desire for equilibrium, for peace, and for coordination, which, once realized, prepares for a greater aspiration toward freedom. Both desires constitute the rhythm of life and are the explanation of all energy, which tends to expand and to organize itself at the same time.

In France, the eclectic and positivist schools have maintained aesthetic intellectualism. In the Aristotelian neo-spiritualism begun by Ravaisson and continued by Lachelier, even though the principle of harmony has been pronounced, it has given rise to a current that has ended in a contingentist movement, which has favored the non-rational voluntarism of recent times.

Ravaisson, drawing inspiration from Schelling's pancalism, has arrived at this conclusion, as Fouillée maintains: that beauty, and chiefly the most divine and the most perfect beauty, contains the secret of the world. The whole world, for Ravaisson, in agreement with Plato and Aristotle, is the work of an absolute beauty, which is the cause of things by the love it puts in them and which, consequently, is efficient only because it is final.

The ideas of order, of love, and of grace enter a[p. 643]s factors of the beautiful into the aesthetics of Ravaisson. It is in the order and concert of the elements that the character of life resides; the spontaneous and automatic determination of vital phenomena presupposes the action of an organic idea in nature, a principle analogous to the one that exists in us. Since order and fitness direct the productive activity, there is no necessity but a moral one. But this form of necessity implies freedom, spontaneity, individuality. The world is an act of love and of generous condescension, the manifestation of absolute beauty and goodness, which in a certain manner unfolds and degrades itself into a series of forms. Individuals remain independent and free, not because beauty has created them, «but by the love it puts in them»; yet all are the reflection and the imitation of the divine. For Ravaisson, beauty appears when we contemplate each being in its individuality and in its easy movement full of grace, which expresses the expansion and, as it were, the abandon of creative activity. Fugitive beauty evokes love, because it is the image of the good that remains. The artist imitates nature, but the higher nature. He communicates to things a stamp of individuality and the «grace that makes them lovable, making them seem to love».

These ideas, which Lenoir attributes to Ravaisson, do not permit us to affirm that this philosopher made freedom the essential character of the beautiful, notwithstanding the importance he recognizes in the principle of individuality. Freedom is understood here too in the sense of non-constraint, as in classical beauty; creation tends toward harmonic unity. Man, according to this philosophy, is placed in the middle region, in which the being feels the intimate contradictions of his nature and desires to give to his very life the harmonic uni[p. 644]ty of a creation. The art of living permits him this. But, if positive freedom is not offered as the generator of the beautiful, the idea of «grace,» developed later by disciples of Ravaisson, contains it and exhibits it as the symbol of beauty.

Lachelier, like his master Ravaisson, recasts all philosophy and even all science into aesthetics, affirming finality and harmony as supreme principles. The same doctrine is maintained by Boutroux, although he goes so far as to replace all the seemingly necessary laws by contingency, this itself having its reason in finality. Boutroux thus serves as a transition to the theory of the creative freedom of the spirit, which radically combats intellectualism and which has created a new philosophy with Bergson.

Fouillée, who combated the harmonism of Ravaisson and his disciples and who, afterward, set himself up as the champion of intellectualism, oscillating between freedom and determinism, underwent also the influence of Ravaisson's aestheticism, of his principle of love and of grace, formulating an aesthetic theory in which freedom plays an essential role.

Fouillée, opposing the transcendental idea of beauty, affirms that this idea implies a contradiction. Beauty is, for him, a formal finality, and the idea of the absolute must stand above all sensible or intelligible form. It cannot be said, with philosophical rigor, that the absolute is beautiful. Fouillée concedes, however, that the feeling of the beautiful, like that of the good, engenders in the spirit a more or less obscure feeling of illimitation and becomes, for us, a symbol of the infinite. But he does not wish that any trans[p. 645]cendental and objective value be given to this purely psychological fact, by admitting a real consciousness of the absolute. And as for the fact itself, he seeks to explain it, like the English psychologists, by means of the laws of association, which govern ideas as well as images and feelings.

Fouillée seeks to explain the character of infinitude of aesthetic emotion, and in this explanation he seems to coincide with Ravaisson, regarding, like him, the beautiful object as a symbol of universal love and identifying aesthetic grace with moral grace.

According to Fouillée, grace, from the mechanical point of view, presupposes movement easily accomplished and easily perceived, presupposes the greatest employment of force with the least possible loss and expenditure. From the psychological point of view, it excludes everything that feels effort, the labor of reflection, the subjection of the will; it demands natural well-being, the greatest effect with the least means; in a word, inspiration, in its spontaneous appearance, which finds without seeking. Grace is the superabundance of an activity that has more than it needs to accomplish a movement or to attain an end and that seems to wish to extend beyond its limits. There is, for this reason, in grace, an image of the infinite and of the absolute, and that is what makes it be called divine. From the moral point of view, freedom being the principle of liberality, grace is a gift, and a disinterested gift; the graceful is gratuitous. Lastly, the gratuitous being the superabundance and creative fecundity proper to love, grace loves, or seems to love, according to Schelling's thought, and that is what makes it lovable. Kant said that beauty is the symbolic representation of morality; one can say, more particularly of grace, according to Fouillée, that it is, from the moral point of view, the symbol of loving goodness. [p. 646] Grace, which the ancients did not separate from love, Fouillée continues, is that which, in the very bosom of a truly necessary mechanism and of an organism in which the parts truly depend on the whole, escapes and lets us glimpse, like a dream, a principle free of all material or formal necessity; grace is the aesthetic expression of freedom.

For this reason Fouillée, in agreement with the Platonic school, finds the good in the beautiful. The good gives to loved things grace, and to him who loves them, loves. It is not by itself alone that the beautiful form has the power to excite love; for, while the gaze of the intelligence embraces this form, the will passes beyond its limits and places within the form, as the ground from which it derives, a living will, which aspires to act, to expand, and to love.

Beauty, and chiefly grace, invites us, then, already, says Fouillée, to conceive a principle of action and of spontaneous determination, superior to the mechanical faculties; it is the intermediary between the natural world and the moral world. It seems to figure forth the ideal freedom of the will at the moment when the latter would take delight in itself, before imposing upon itself a law and a necessary rule, a limit and a sacrifice; for that very reason, beauty is an expression of the happy life, of happiness. When later, by a final effort, freedom seems to rise above all limit and all sacrifice, in the fullness and infinitude of the love of another, it unites in itself moral sublimity and moral grace. If there is grace and beauty in the spontaneous expression of innocence, there is grace and sublimity in the effortless disinterestedness of charity.

For Fouillée, scientific and mechanical determinism, destroying the illusion of freedom, tends to des[p. 647]troy the moral charm of the beautiful and takes from beauty its merit. Nevertheless, once completed by the idea of freedom and by the desire it excites, moral determinism can be maintained within the domain of aesthetics. If art, which is chiefly of a contemplative nature, makes us divine a distant freedom, of which grace is as it were a ray, it could not show it in its very focus, nor offer a sufficient reason for making us affirm its existence.

According to this analysis, grace is the aesthetic expression of ideal freedom, though it is not freedom itself, nor does it prove, by itself alone, the existence of freedom. Nevertheless, Fouillée, synthesizing later the result of the scientific investigations of biological aesthetics, defines the beautiful as that which gives us the immediate consciousness of a maximum of effort, at once, in our sensibility, in our intelligence, and in our will, as the consequence of an excess of vitality and enjoyment—a definition that springs from the positivist concept of the beautiful.

Fouillée seeks to reconcile this biological concept of the beautiful with his voluntarist doctrine. The power of life, arranged and regularized by order, translates itself under the form of desire fulfilled and of will satisfied. This satisfaction of the will can also be called freedom, says Fouillée. Hence the most profound element that has been discovered in the pleasure of the beautiful—the voluntary element, which completes the sensible and the intellectual element, serving them as base or as center. Freedom is thus, under its various forms—whether in the physical order or in the intellectual and moral—that which gives grace to beauty.

Fouillée's attitude toward the aesthetic problem is not decisive, however; because the concept of free[p. 648]dom in his philosophy does not differ radically from the one maintained by traditional intellectualism; but his theory of grace orients the aesthetic problem in a direction different from that adopted by the partisans of the principle of order.

Fonsegrive is also an aesthetician of grace. Grace, he says, is not an element of beauty, but is beauty itself—what is most intimate and most enchanting in it. And since grace can receive its full and entire meaning only from moral considerations, and since it implies freedom, one can say that beauty is the reflection or the symbol of freedom—not, doubtless, of all freedom, but of that freedom which reason recognizes, whose laws it freely accepts and easily realizes. Things, Fonsegrive adds, are beautiful in proportion as they manifest more the harmony of freedom and reason. This conception restricts the value of grace considerably.

Freedom being understood thus, in subjection to reason, one returns to the old intellectualism, which does not resolve the aesthetic problem by regarding the beautiful as a value. It was necessary to take up the question of the irrationality or non-rationality of the beautiful in order to make it an expression of true freedom, as Bergson has done.

Roussel-Despierres, in his theory of the aesthetic Ideal, seems to approach that solution, establishing that the creative will has no need of the support of a belief, since it is itself an affirmation, a faith, because it carries within itself that certitude, precisely by being a fact, a reality. The creative will ignores or dominates the dogmas that would oppress it. The ideal is imposed on the will by the triumphant evidence of desire alone. Born of desire and of love, [p. 649] the voluntary ideal will have the smiling seduction of beauty. Roussel-Despierres maintains that, by all roads, by all methods through which the ideal is sought, we arrive at one and the same twofold conclusion: at the complete emancipation of the individual and at the indefinite ascent of beings toward beauty—a twofold conclusion that may be summed up in this formula: the aesthetic ideal realized in freedom.

«I love my independence, I love my freedom, as I love to live—this philosopher adds—. Freedom is the pleasure of existing, of exercising one's forces, one's faculties; it is the joy of thinking, of willing; it is, if one likes, the simple mechanical play of natural activity, unfolding without resistance. Whatever its form, every attack upon my freedom is a pain; I hate coercion; there is no being in the world that ought not to hate coercion and adore freedom, since there does not exist a single one that does not love life. Life and freedom can scarcely be conceived apart from one another; individualism is synonymous with freedom and, in a certain measure too, with existence.»

But, for this philosopher, freedom is not an ideal, not an end, not an activity; it is only a form, a condition of activity, a means to an end, the guarantee of the Ideal. The ideal of the free individual is the moral ideal, which is a universal ideal. Beauty is subordinated to it. Beauty truly dies to the world through desire. In order that the moral ideal may acquire all its power, it must adorn itself with all the seductions of the aesthetic ideal and be absorbed in it, because there is no beauty higher than the moral act, and the perfection of the aesthetic life implies absolute morality—although it does not suppress the beauty of nature nor that of works of art.

[p. 650] Roussel-Despierres ends, at last, by giving to the idea a dominant value in that moralist tendency of his doctrine. For him, there is an individuality higher, more worthy of respect, than that of the human being: the individuality of the idea. What makes man worthy of respect to man is the will of the Ideal. The idea is of universal order; respect for the idea is the essential interest of all, because it can become the common good of all; individual life acquires value only in the service of the idea; the health of the idea is incomparably more precious than the preservation of some few living units. But higher than the idea, and more worthy of respect than it, when it is distinguished, is the moral will, the radiant flowering of the Ideal.

Notwithstanding these affirmations, Roussel-Despierres believes that, if all philosophy requires a criterion of certitude, psychology will discover it in the feeling of the beautiful, establishing that, under its highest and purest form, the feeling of pleasure or pain is completely aesthetic, and that this is how beauty comes to be the supreme and definitive certitude of the spirit.

In his view, aesthetic intuition will always be truer than scientific knowledge, because it is founded on the qualities of things, in which the spirit perceives, precisely, their general relations and their cohesion, whereas scientific analysis, incapable of obtaining the complete elements of things, remains a fragmentary, illogical, and deceptive knowledge. Psychology shows us in beauty the highest degree of pleasure and of desire. Beauty is the ground of the human soul; it appears when one attempts to conceive the significance of the infinite desires that move the world, as the supreme aspiration of universal existence.

[p. 651] Roussel-Despierres infers from this that the aesthetic ideal symbolizes the term toward which the universe mysteriously tends and which, at least, resolves the enigma of human destiny; but that ideal is an ideal of order, of harmony, and one that resolves itself, in the end, into the moral ideal conceived as a supreme harmony. The aesthetic ideal contains all morality; the latter has no other criterion than beauty, which is a universal criterion; but that criterion is not, for Roussel-Despierres, the criterion of freedom, reduced as it is to the condition of a means. «Perhaps,» he says, «every beautiful thing has a moral value, simply by being educative, and because, adding something to the culture of the spirit, it exerts a similar influence in the aesthetic preparation for the moral life». Beauty would thus be the ground of morality; but the moral ideal would be, in the end, the aesthetic ideal.

This philosopher does not admit, certainly, a definitive harmony, which would be contradictory to the idea of the infinite; but he admits a constant evolution of harmonies ever more perfect—that is, of aesthetic states that prepare the realization of the moral ideal. Morality and the Ideal are the highest terms of the evolution of nature. The aesthetic ideal—an ideal of pure morality, the most optimistic of all moral conceptions, the most moral of all optimistic systems—prepares, in joy, in beauty, and in love, the reign of the absolute good.

The aesthetic ideal being understood thus, as a harmony, one understands why Roussel-Despierres declares that this ideal is truly universal—that it dominates morality, education, practical life, and politics itself, whose first law is to put no obstacle in the way of the reign of the ideal: all of them forms of an aesthetic morality that [p. 652] this philosopher has sought to offer in his dissertation on the aesthetic ideal, discoursing on freedom, understood as a condition of morality.

The concept of beauty as free expansion enters into this system. Beauty is the expansion of life in the species and in the individual—an expansion of physical powers, of feelings, of ideas, of wills, of all those moral forces that are the final effort of the evolution of nature and whose final aspiration is aesthetic sovereignty; but that creative expansion has morality for its end, because beauty is morality, is an ideal of harmony. Beauty has freedom for its condition, but harmony for its end.

In a later work, entitled Freedom and Beauty, Roussel-Despierres aspires to found upon the aesthetic ideal an aesthetic morality that may satisfy contemporary skepticism, which refuses to accept religious dogmatism, as well as the scientific and metaphysical, and recognizes value only in the autonomous individual. That ideal—which is, at once, a universal metaphysics and a principle of action—resolves, in his view, the antinomy of the social problems and of the moral problems and fixes the orientation of the individual conscience and of the society of consciences. The ideal of the skeptic is the aesthetic ideal, because beauty is for him the meaning of things and the supreme reason for living. To live with autonomy, or rather to live in freedom, he has need of only two things: the consciousness of his autonomy and the will to realize it; and to love beauty, to seek it in the universe, to fill the eyes and the thought with splendid visions, to cultivate the soul, to rise toward an ideal, it suffices to possess that innate aesthetic sense which every beauty sets vibrating and which tends toward the beauty of a longed-for infinite.

[p. 653] Desire, under its primary form, encloses the principle of an irreducible certitude, which develops in the order of feeling. Under its cultivated form it becomes the will, which is the individual power, which the principle of autonomy substitutes for truth; because the sentimental order is the order of the individual, as the intellectual order is that of the universal. The ideal that the will tends to realize—that is complete certitude. It is not a metaphysical entity, but a principle of life, an animate reality. In an élan of desire, by an act of will, the skeptic reconquers certitude and the ideal. To the absolute dogmas, to the universal laws, he opposes the sovereignty of the self. In the ideal, the will embraces the future being of a world to be realized. The self is a power of nature, which nature wills to be free; it is an end that nature intends to realize. To live is to affirm a self; living reality is summed up in the self. The ideal is imposed upon the will by a kind of interior illumination; the will formulates it and wills it.

The ideal contains the moral will, and it is here that we perceive the ultimate reason of autonomy. From this derive all freedoms, all rights—or rather, integral freedom and absolute right. If the ideal constitutes the autonomous conscience, what constitutes the individual is the feeling and the exercise of his freedom. He who is not free does not exist. To be [p. 654] oneself, different from the others, to affirm one's individuality: therein lies the whole joy of life.

Roussel-Despierres believes, like Renouvier, that the reality of freedom is not necessary for morality, as it is not for autonomy. The illusion of free-dom suffices to create moral obligation, as the illusion of individuality suffices to liberate the individual will and to found the right of the Ideal.

The Ideal, the Idea—these supreme expressions of desire and of the will—are thus what is most intimate in man and most individual in this world. Their essence is integral freedom; for this is nothing but the freedom of the ideal, in which is summed up the autonomy of the conscience, and which comprises the freedom of thought and of belief, the autonomy of feeling and of moral activity, the independence of personal ends, and the free pursuit of social ends: forms that need to be objectified, because man is not truly free save when he makes use of his freedom, which is the great educator of man and the creator of his morality.

For Roussel-Despierres, beauty—the supreme desire of man—comes to be the Ideal itself, and moral certitude itself is a will to beauty, which offers us the purest, most profound, and inexhaustible pleasure and which awakens in us a very powerful desire, so as to set itself up as an ideal.

Freedom plays in this aesthetic-moral theory a great role. It is not only the essence of the Ideal, created by desire and by the will, but also the instrument of that same aesthetic Ideal. It is impossible for the individual, according to this moralist, to conceive individuality under any other aspect than that of an aesthetic type, or the realization of individuality under any other conditions than an aesthetic realization. Beauty constitutes the reason, the definition of individuality and, besides, its guarantee. Free is the pleasure of the beautiful; free, creation. Freedom makes men; it is the mother of the arts. In these the expansion of social life is completed—social life of which right was the first manifesta[p. 655]tion. And if beauty has need of freedom, it is in its turn a liberator. Artistic culture, better than any other, frees thought and develops the personality of the conscience.

Beauty, he adds, would not exist without freedom, and still less without the notion of individuality. The tangible manifestation of individuality is desire. Desire creates beauty in the conscience; but, in return, the beauty of things awakens desire; almost by a double process, subjective and objective, desire and beauty successively reach and animate the ideal—which means that the individual tends toward beauty, and beauty reveals to him his very self, the individual, who is the aesthetic unity.

Freedom, in itself, is beautiful; individuality is the highest expression of human beauty; all the feelings are aesthetic, because they contribute to forming individuality. The ideal is the object of freedom, as it is its work; the ideal of a free individual is an aesthetic ideal, founded on individual autonomy, an absolute ideal. Moreover, the soul unfolds only in freedom; only the pleasure of acting is fruitful; freedom is the richest source of production, the tutelary principle of social peace.

But, in this exaltation of the aesthetic ideal engendered by freedom, Roussel-Despierres is not precise as to the meaning of this word, to which he attributes various modalities without clearly establishing that it is a creative activity of the aesthetic Ideal. For him, freedom is no more than the right to choose among many possible ends; it is only an empty form, the condition of all philosophy, but one that does not constitute a philosophy; integral freedom means as much as absolute right, or autonomy of right; it is the mistress of the milieu that acts upon the individual; its func[p. 656]tion is objective and is equivalent to emancipation. Freedom becomes, from an instrument, a method of realizing the aesthetic life, and it signifies, on the other hand, diversity or differentiation of individuals. Still more, freedom is subordinated to autonomy and to the notion of the individual. Autonomy is the principle of right, whose exercise constitutes freedom, individualism having for its object the realization of the rights of man.

The aesthetics of the eminent Italian philosopher Croce contains, at bottom, a principle of free activity as the explanation of the aesthetic phenomenon; but that principle is not expressed directly and clearly, because in his philosophy of spirit Croce distinguishes theoretical from practical activity, includes in the first, as fundamental forms, aesthetic activity, as the primary one, and logical activity, as the secondary, which are followed by the practical activities, economic and moral, and studies these forms chiefly from the point of view of knowledge.

[p. 657] The aesthetic phenomenon being thus considered, Croce reduces it to intuition, expressed by an interior image. The first and global activity of consciousness, which is aesthetic activity, is known by means of that intuition, which constitutes a single act with expression, because the one does not exist without the other. Hence these two definitions of the aesthetic phenomenon: the beautiful is expressed intuition; the ugly is failed intuition. We can define beauty, he says, as successful expression (riuscita) or, better still, as expression simply. The ugly, with its correlative displeasure, is the aesthetic activity that has not managed to overcome the obstacle; the beautiful is the expressive activity «that unfolds triumphant». We recognize as beautiful, he adds, every act of expressive activity that is really such, and as ugly every fact in which activity and passivity enter into an insoluble and disordered struggle. This definition implies the idea of a power, which is none other than that of the will in its work of systematizing and expressing the whole content of theoretical activity, which «consists entirely of impressions, spiritual products, memories or reproductions of these products, and productions of new spiritual facts».

Croce calls this aesthetic activity fantasy—this first form of human knowledge, an intuitive knowledge of the individual, which differs from intellectual or logical knowledge, which is of the universal, of things or else of their relations, the former the product of images and the latter of concepts. But in his treatise on Economics and Ethics, Croce affirms that «to be purely theoretical it is necessary to be, at the same time, in a certain way practical; the energy of pure fantasy and of pure thought is born from the trunk of volition, and hence the importance of the will for the aesthetic and the intellectual life; the will is not theory, but it promotes and restrains the force of fantasy and of thought, making them operate in the best way—that is, making them be truly what they ought to be: fantasy and thought, in their purest manifestation. From this aspect, it is rather practical activity that prevails».

After these affirmations, one might believe that Croce attributed to the will and to freedom a great role in aesthetic activity. It is not so, however. When Croce speaks of the will as a form or practical activity, he does not take that word in the metaphysical sense of some philosophical system, in which the will is the foundation of the universe, the principle of things, or creative reality; nor yet in the broad sen[p. 658]se of other philosophers, who understand the will as the energy of the spirit, the spirit or activity in general, making of every act of man's spirit an act of will (voluntarism). The will is for Croce, as in the common acceptation, the part of the spirit distinct from the mere theoretical contemplation of things, productive not of knowledge but of actions. Action is truly such insofar as it is voluntary; otherwise it is mere movement and physical phenomenon.

«Man forms the volitional act, not because he has that prodigious faculty of extending willing beyond the limits of the intellect, but, on the contrary, because he has that of circumscribing himself, in each case, within the limits of his intellect, and that of willing upon that basis and within those limits». «The volitional act is necessary and free at the same time: it is necessary because it is always conditioned by an intuition, by a situation, by the one out of which it arises; but it is free, because it is not adherent to the situation of fact nor repeats it, constituting a duplicate—a superfluous thing and, consequently, impossible in the elective development of the real, which involves no superfluity. Volition produces something different, that is, something new; something that did not exist before and that comes into existence; it is initiative, creation, and, consequently, an act of freedom. If it were not so, volition would not be volition and reality would not change, would not come to be, would not develop. And since without necessity there is no freedom—because without a situation of fact there is no volition—without freedom there is no necessity, that is, the situations of fact would not be formed, ever new and necessary with respect to the new volitions». The volitional act is the unity of both moments of the process of willing.

[p. 659] What happens in every sphere of spiritual activity happens in aesthetic activity, which receives the influence of the milieu and produces freely with the elements the latter offers it. Freedom and necessity are inseparable. «The spirit,» says Croce, «is freedom, and, being such, not abstractly but concretely, it must be, at the same time, necessity, not abstractly».

This theory of freedom has no application in Croce's aesthetics, because this philosopher identifies the freedom to create with the freedom to choose and rejects the idea that in aesthetic activity there is freedom of choice—an error that comes from excluding, from the creative function, spontaneous activity, which is free par excellence. Choice is a creative act, certainly, as Bergson affirms; but spontaneous activity is not elective, because it is not reflective; creation comprises choice, but this is only a form or species of creation in the moral order, and if it is freedom it is because in it spontaneity surpasses the motives.

Croce, on the other hand, does not depart from the cognitive point of view, even when he treats of the liberating effect of aesthetic activity and of the independence of art, as traditional aesthetics does, and he develops his theory of freedom in his treatise on morality, in which he finds, nonetheless, some occasions to return to his aesthetic ideas. What interests this philosopher in aesthetics is to mark well the intuitive and theoretical character of aesthetic knowledge. «From not having rightly recognized the cognitive character of simple intuition, distinct from intellectual knowledge and even from the perception of the real; from believing that only the intellectual, or at most the perception of the real, is knowledge, there has arisen the affirmation, so often repeated, that art is not knowledge, that it offers no truths, that it belongs not to the theoretical world but to the [p. 660] sentimental one», and others like it. Art, Croce adds, is knowledge, is form; it does not belong to feeling and to psychic matter.

Hence the primacy of theoretical activity. «By the theoretical form man comprehends things; by the practical form he goes on changing them; by the first he appropriates the universe, by the other he creates it; but the first constitutes the base of the second. A knowing independent of willing is thinkable; a will independent of knowing is unthinkable. The blind will is not will; the true will is full of eyes».

This oscillation between the value of the two activities, theoretical and practical, makes it impossible to affirm whether, in Croce's view, aesthetic activity, or that of fantasy, is at bottom an activity born from the trunk of volition, regarded by him as the fundamental energy of theoretical activity. This obscures the aesthetic problem, as it also obscures the concept of feeling as an organic and preliminary function of the «cognitive and volitional» activities, and that of fantastic activity, which is for Croce the activity of desire, different from the combinations of the imagination, which he calls secondary. Fantastic activity would be that which engenders the ideal, different from the perception of the real, which enters as an element of the imagination; but such an activity, though it would be eminently free, would be at odds with the theory of freedom inseparable from necessity, and it would not explain, on the other hand, the formation of the expressive image, which cannot be foreign to reality. Croce obscures this theory still more by attributing to fantasy an absolute character in its activity. The intuitive activity of fantasy, which he calls concrete and individual, is so absolute in its affirma[p. 661]tion that, were that character denied it, the absoluteness of intellectual or conceptual truth—and, implicitly, of moral truth—would disappear. For this to be exact it would be necessary to recognize that aesthetic intuition, the fruit of free activity, fuses into a single whole the individual and the universal, expresses the whole activity of consciousness, which is freedom and freedom alone.

What Croce has said about the theoretical, intuitive activity of the aesthetic phenomenon does not prevent him from affirming, in his Ethics, that «pure intuition, naïve representation of reality, representation of feeling, musicality, and personal intonation are all equivalent formulas and all definitions of aesthetic activity and of art».

Croce decides, at last, in his article on «Pure Intuition and the Lyrical Character of Art,» for this subjective ground of aesthetic activity. Expounding the current tendencies of aesthetics, he pronounces for the one that returns to romantic aesthetics, which is, undoubtedly, the orientation that has sought to find in the principle of freedom the explanation of the nature of the aesthetic phenomenon. Croce affirms that this higher degree is reached with the aesthetics of pure intuition, or of expression, which eliminates the mystical factor and is not opposed to scientific investigation. Pure intuition is essentially lyrical, says Croce, and such must be the character of Aesthetics, which thus enters the domain of the free activity of the spirit, because lyricism and freedom are identical.

In his «Breviary of Aesthetics,» Croce renounces his disdain for the autonomy of feeling and, understanding that intuition and expression, by themselves alone, do not explain the reality of the aesthetic phenomenon but only its form as a notion, makes feeling the content [p. 662] of that phenomenon—forgetting that he had maintained that Spirit and Freedom were identical in his moral philosophy, and that for that very reason he had no need to have recourse to feeling in order to give reality to the aesthetic life. «What gives coherence and unity to intuition,» says Croce, «is feeling: intuition is truly such because it represents a feeling, and only from it and upon it can it arise; not the idea, but feeling, is what confers on art the aerial lightness of the symbol»; and he then adds: «Art is a true aesthetic synthesis a priori of feeling and image in intuition». Only that Croce understands by feeling, or state of mind, here, not a particular content, but the whole universe sub specie intuitionis.

Baldwin, in his Genetic of Reality, has likewise asserted the rights of the aesthetic norm to constitute a philosophy, which he has aptly called a pancalist explanation, destined to destroy the antinomies created by thought.

In artistic beauty—which is for Baldwin beauty properly speaking—the contradiction between subject and object disappears. Through the play of what has been called Einfühlung, the artist could not see a material object, a movement, a line itself, without «sympathizing with them as with souls». The theory of play acquires here a great importance. Art is so closely related to play that they have been able to be confounded, because it gives complete satisfaction to the need for free activity and for stimulus—although it exceeds play in what art has of the serious, in what it takes as true and good from reality. Hence the perfect work of art is, at the same time, absolute [p. 663] knowledge of objectivity and a supreme, immediate personal value. The work of art thus realizes the miracle of bringing the logic of ideas into accord with the logic of feelings, because it is, at once, objective and singular—neither of those logics being, for that reason, adequate to it taken separately. To dispense with the second would destroy the springs of valuation and the creative and revelatory functions of art; to dispense with the first is inadmissible, since the very framework of all valuation and of all artistic production is formed of cognitive and rational processes.

This synthetic and autonomous character of art explains its supremacy over logic and morality, which respectively presuppose the error and the evil against which they struggle. Art has for its matter a world that contains evil and error, which it can and must represent. But, far from accepting and recognizing, as the other normative functions do, the existence of what contradicts its norm, it eliminates and sets it aside. The ugly, the repugnant remain outside art, which ignores or annuls them, excluding them with the serenity and disinterestedness of the aesthetic function—unlike morality and religion, which struggle with their contraries.

The real which aesthetics creates is not composed only of logical ideas or of moral agents and values; it is not simply nature or freedom, but the one and the other. The freedom of play, the caprice of a fancy without rule, is not true freedom; the latter consists in developing a self, in producing a work in a resistant matter and under conditions defined beforehand. Moreover, this matter arouses the judgment and the decision of freedom, since it becomes a work of art only inasmuch as it is chosen.

Aesthetic intuition thus unites the actual and the ideal; it presents the double character of a synthesis by con[p. 664]ciliation and by perfecting. Aesthetic reason is the synthesis of theoretical reason and practical reason, of science and morality, of truth and the good. The work of art embodies a personality that concentrates in itself the whole prior human evolution and, consequently, contains, at once, the individual and the social. Man finds himself, at last, in it. The real, in the last analysis, is the ensemble of the contents of consciousness insofar as they are organized or are susceptible of organization under the aesthetic form. Individual consciousness is the organ of reality, and the whole of reality would be the integral experience, capable of perceiving that content and of contemplating it as one contemplates a work of art in its perfect unity.

According to Lalande, this pancalism presents itself as the only doctrine capable of reconciling intellectualism, pragmatism, and intuitionism, and of giving satisfaction to all our tendencies and answering, as far as possible, our need for the absolute—an aspiration that Lalande finds seductive but unrealizable. Once the work of art is produced, it must be able to recover its place in the world, as if it had never ceased to form part of it. In that microcosm we should thus have realized, in an artificial manner, the identity of nature and spirit; we should have reconciled there presupposition and postulate, freedom and necessity, unity and universal value; we should be in the presence of a kind of absolute—the unique privilege of the beautiful—which results from eliminating entirely all that is external to it, which does not even maintain its contrary in order to deny or reject it, as logic and morality do, but forgets, purely and simply, that there is anything beyond. If the whole world were organized upon that type, it would be, at once, «absolute» in the order of intelligibility and in the mo[p. 665]ral order, so that we should have nothing more to ask.

But if art achieves this success, Lalande adds, it is precisely on condition of being fictitious and limited; and when we say that the work of art, once produced, must find its place again in the world, we must understand that it is thanks to our ignorance and to the measure in which the world is not yet intelligible, nor even perfectly known.

Baldwin's pancalism, as is seen, is, at bottom, an attempt at conciliation similar to that of Schelling, in which genius represents the synthesis of spontaneity and reflection, and art expresses that of subject and object in the indifference of the absolute. Baldwin aspires to fuse the scientific order, or that of nature, with the moral order, or that of freedom, in order to create the aesthetic order, in which the principle of harmony is predominant. His concept of freedom is the same as that of the intellectualist philosophers—a concept restricted to the domain of morality, which postulates a rational imperative; it is not the concept of aesthetic freedom, which creates its own law in the domain of the imagination. Baldwin does not admit this form of freedom, which he rejects as the freedom of play or the caprice of a fancy without rule. His rationalism therefore places him too among the aestheticians who make the principle of order the aesthetic criterion, like the old Greek philosophers.

The cause of the failure of all these attempts comes from considering freedom exclusively as a character of moral activity, and not as the expression of all creative activity and, chiefly, of artistic activity, as Bergson establishes.

G. A. Cesareo, in his «Essay on Creative Art,» affirms that art is creation and the consciousness of that creation, the fruit of a fantastic activity different from the [p. 666] cognitive and the volitional or practical activities. Art is thus freedom. The activity of fantasy is, it is true, accompanied by the will; but it is a will to create a new reality and not to change, by physical means, the known reality.

The first and most evident character of the work of art is freedom. There is no true work of art if it does not withdraw itself from all laws, both of knowledge and of the practical will. Hence the absolute freedom of art, which can create moral values of its own, giving to the moral problem a particular solution of its own.

Cesareo refuses to give exclusive value to the passional element, which is only an element of creation—like sensation, perception, the idea—and which, even if it is creation, remains annulled in the total creation, which is pure form and absorbs the content. Creation is the synthesis, or inspiration made conscious in its determinations, and the value of the work of art lies not in this or that determination, in this or that group of determinations, but in the synthesis in itself, in the perfect coherence of all the determinations, which aspire to it but acquire it only, precisely, in their unity, which is the synthesis; hence Cesareo calls art the self-consciousness of creation—original and total, a full, perennial, infinite reality, which the spirit longs for because it is free and eternal, and which it does not find realized in phenomenal reality.

Cesareo makes the essence of art consist in that unconscious and total synthesis of the whole world of the spirit, effected by fantasy and identified by him with inspiration. Whatever be the passionality of the poet, whatever be the force of the feeling, if the [p. 667] synthesis is lacking, the work of art does not exist. Beauty thus consists in the synthesis in itself, that is, in the total form that absorbs and annuls each particular determination: intuition, thought, passionality. The true essence of art is pure form—that is, ideal coherence, the harmony of the parts, the synthesis in itself, and this alone.

This appraisal of art as unity, coherence, or harmony is opposed to the preceding one, which regards art as freedom, the product of fantastic creation, and thus leaves aesthetic valuation with a double and opposed criterion. If art is pure form, pure coherence or synthesis, freedom remains on the margin of aesthetic creation, whether as the end of art or as the cause of the artistic activity that is carried out as a means. But a creative activity that is not freedom cannot be conceived; so that Cesareo, apparently voluntarist and romantic, reproduces the classical criterion of art, regarded as harmony. The freedom of which he speaks is independence only—that is, a negative factor.

The great merit of Bergson's philosophy has been, for this reason, to identify creation with freedom and thus to establish the double postulate of aesthetics and of morality.
